papers.aim: To measure the uncertainty and confidence of black-box LLM answers, where only the generated text is available (no token probabilities or embeddings). The measures are used for selective generation, where unreliable answers are rejected or sent for further checking.
papers.method: For each question, m answers are sampled from the LLM and pairwise similarity is computed with Jaccard similarity or an NLI model (DeBERTa-large-MNLI). A similarity graph is built and simple dispersion measures are computed: number of semantic sets, sum of graph Laplacian eigenvalues (EigV), degree (Deg) and eccentricity (Ecc). They are tested on how well they rank answers by correctness (AUROC and AUARC) on three QA datasets with four LLMs.
papers.result: Entailment-based measures beat the black-box baselines and often beat the white-box semantic entropy. Example (TriviaQA, LLaMA-13B): confidence AUARC Deg(E) = 88.86 versus semantic entropy 79.15, P(true) 67.27, random 61.18 and oracle 91.24. Selecting the top 50% of answers by Deg(E) raised accuracy from 62% to about 90%. Even m = 3 samples gave good results. After histogram-binning calibration, adaptive calibration error was about 0.02-0.04 (e.g. Ecc(E) on TriviaQA-LLaMA gap 0.026).
papers.tools: LLMs: OPT-13B, LLaMA-13B, LLaMA2 (model size not stated in the main text), gpt-3.5-turbo (0301, via OpenAI API). Similarity: Jaccard; DeBERTa-large-MNLI (microsoft/deberta-large-mnli). Spectral graph methods (graph Laplacian, eigenvectors); UMAP for visualisation; histogram binning for calibration. gpt-3.5-turbo as correctness judge. Hardware: 2x AMD EPYC Milan 7513 CPU, 512 GB RAM, 8x NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. Code: github.com/zlin7/UQ-NLG.
papers.gap: Only short-answer question answering was tested. Correctness labels come mostly from GPT, not humans. Uncertainty and confidence are evaluated separately, not combined. No medical or multi-step agent setting, and no formal guarantee on error rates when answers are rejected.
papers.relation: For O1, the orchestrator may use API-based LLM agents (for example, a report-drafting or guideline agent) that give no token probabilities. These black-box measures need only several sampled outputs and a small NLI model, so the orchestrator can score each agent output and defer to clinicians when confidence is low. The per-response confidence (Deg, Ecc) can also pick the best of several agent drafts, and the paper shows that these scores can be calibrated with histogram binning on a 1,000-item calibration set, which supports calibrated deferral thresholds in the PhD framework.
papers.limitations: Evaluation is restricted to QA because reliability labels are hard to get for open conversation. GPT judging improves on Rouge-L but is not perfect (90.9% to 98.0% agreement with humans) and may use its own knowledge. With temperature 0 (greedy decoding) all sampling-based measures fail; at lower temperature (0.5) white-box semantic entropy often does better. The measures reflect the LLM's own posterior, so they cannot catch factual errors learned from training data or overconfidence. Confidence scores are not directly interpretable without calibration. Future work: combine uncertainty and confidence, use human labels, and extend beyond QA.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors want uncertainty scores that work when an LLM is only reachable through an API. They separate uncertainty U(x), which describes how spread out the possible answers to an input are, from confidence C(x, s), which describes one specific answer. They use three public QA datasets: CoQA development (7,983 questions), TriviaQA rc.nocontext validation (9,960) and Natural Questions validation (3,610). Four LLMs are tested: OPT-13B, LLaMA-13B, LLaMA2 and gpt-3.5-turbo, with default sampling settings (temperature 1, or 0.6 with top_p 0.9 for LLaMA2). For each question they sample 20 answers. Every pair of answers is scored for similarity with Jaccard overlap or with DeBERTa-large-MNLI, giving either the entailment probability or one minus the contradiction probability. These scores form a weighted graph with one node per answer. From the graph they compute: the number of semantic sets; EigV, the sum of max(0, 1 - eigenvalue) of the normalised Laplacian, which estimates the number of meanings; Deg, based on how connected each answer is; and Ecc, the distance of each answer from the centre in a spectral embedding. Deg and Ecc also give a confidence per answer. Correctness is judged by gpt-3.5-turbo on a 0-100 scale against the reference (above 70 = correct), with human checks showing 90.9-98.0% agreement. Each experiment is repeated 10 times: 1,000 random questions tune the NLI temperature and eigenvalue cut-off, and the rest are used for testing. They report AUROC and AUARC (mean +/- SD) and adaptive calibration error after 15-bin histogram binning. Entailment-based Deg and Ecc gave the best results, for example AUARC 88.86 versus 79.15 for white-box semantic entropy on TriviaQA-LLaMA, and keeping the top 50% raised accuracy from 62% to about 90%. To adapt this, an orchestrator can sample each agent several times, score agreement with a clinical NLI model, calibrate the confidence on a local labelled set, and defer low-confidence cases to clinicians.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological machine-learning study with retrospective experiments on public QA benchmarks. University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (including Carle Illinois College of Medicine) and MIT CSAIL, United States. No patients involved.
papers.datasets: 1) CoQA (open-book conversational QA): development split, 7,983 questions. 2) TriviaQA (closed-book QA): validation split of the rc.nocontext subset, 9,960 de-duplicated questions. 3) Natural Questions (nq, harder closed-book QA): validation split, 3,610 questions. Modality: English text. No classes; each question has a reference answer. Human verification set: 33 samples per dataset and model (OPT, LLaMA, GPT), e.g. 99 pairs for TriviaQA. No other inclusion or exclusion criteria reported.
papers.preprocessing: Split: each experiment repeated 10 times; each time a random subset of 1,000 questions is the calibration set (for choosing hyper-parameters of the uncertainty and confidence measures) and the rest is the test set. Prompts: TriviaQA uses the LLaMA paper prompt ('Answer these questions: Q: In Scotland a bothy/bothie is a? A: House Q: [question] A:'); Natural Questions uses a 5-shot version with 5 random training questions; CoQA uses the context paragraph, earlier Q/A turns and the question (code from Kuhn et al. 2023). NLI input format: '[question] [answer_1] [SEP] [question] [answer_2]'. Default generation configs: temperature 1 and top_p 1 for all models except LLaMA2 (temperature 0.6, top_p 0.9); an ablation uses temperature 0.5. No augmentation.
papers.modelDetails: Step 1: For input x, sample m responses (default m = 20; ablation m = 1, 3, 5, 10, 20). Step 2: Compute pairwise similarity a(sj1, sj2): Jaccard (word-set intersection over union); NLI-entail = softmax probability of entailment; NLI-contra = 1 - probability of contradiction (from DeBERTa-large-MNLI, with an NLI temperature chosen from 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 3, 5, 7). Step 3: Build a symmetric weighted adjacency matrix W with w = (a12 + a21)/2, degree matrix D, and normalised graph Laplacian L = I - D^-1/2 W D^-1/2. Measures: (a) NumSet: number of semantic sets from bidirectional entailment (merge two answers if p_entail > p_contra in both directions); (b) EigV: U = sum over eigenvalues of max(0, 1 - lambda_k), a continuous number of meanings; (c) Deg: U = trace(mI - D)/m^2 (average pairwise distance) and confidence C(x, sj) = D_jj/m; (d) Ecc: embed each response with the k smallest eigenvectors of L, centre them, U = norm of all centred embeddings, C(x, sj) = minus the distance of response j from the centre; eigenvalue cut-off chosen from 0.4 to 0.9. Uncertainty U(x) depends only on the input; confidence C(x, s) is per response. Selective generation: reject inputs or responses with high U or low C. Optional calibration: histogram binning with 15 bins fitted on the first generation of the 1,000 calibration questions.
papers.training: No LLM training. Only hyper-parameters (NLI temperature, eigenvalue threshold) are chosen on the 1,000-question calibration set in each of 10 random runs. Hardware: 2x AMD EPYC Milan 7513 CPU, 512 GB RAM, 8x A6000 GPUs. Generating 20 responses with OPT/LLaMA took 2.5 to 15 hours per dataset (2 to 11 seconds per question; CoQA slowest). Running the NLI model for 20 responses (380 comparisons, worst case) took about 0.8 seconds.
papers.evaluation: Correctness: gpt-3.5-turbo rates each response against the reference from 0 to 100 using a few-shot prompt; scores above 0.7 (70) count as correct; 99.34% of ratings could be parsed. Human check of GPT judgement: accuracy 90.9% (CoQA), 98.0% (TriviaQA, 97 of 99), 95.9% (NQ). Settings: U + expected accuracy (U+EA, expected accuracy = mean correctness of the m responses), C + individual accuracy (C+IA), and U + individual accuracy. Metrics: AUROC for predicting correctness and AUARC (area under the accuracy-rejection curve; random = base accuracy, oracle = upper bound). Calibration: adaptive calibration error (ACE) after histogram binning. All metrics reported as mean +/- standard deviation over 10 random calibration/test splits.
papers.baselines: Black-box: NumSet (number of semantic sets, Kuhn et al. 2023); LexiSim (average Rouge-L between responses). White-box (not for GPT): semantic entropy (SE, Kuhn et al. 2023) and P(true) (Kadavath et al. 2022). Reference lines: Random (base accuracy) and Oracle.
papers.results: Table 1, AUARC for U(x) predicting expected accuracy (mean +/- SD, in %). TriviaQA: LLaMA random 61.18, oracle 87.03, NumSet 78.78, LexiSim 80.32, EigV(E) 85.01, Ecc(E) 84.66, Deg(E) 85.27, SE 79.15, P(true) 64.98; LLaMA2 random 76.24, EigV(E) 93.07, SE 93.99; OPT random 25.75, Deg(E) 52.06, SE 51.11; GPT random 87.42, Ecc(E) 95.21, LexiSim 94.69. CoQA: LLaMA random 62.46, Deg(E) 81.50, SE 78.83; LLaMA2 EigV(E) 90.21, SE 89.29; OPT Deg(E) 73.91, SE 70.75; GPT EigV(E) 88.80, LexiSim 86.60. NQ: LLaMA random 23.63, Deg(E) 41.07, SE 36.03; LLaMA2 EigV(E) 63.58, SE 62.40; OPT Ecc(E) 18.82, SE 18.40; GPT Ecc(E) 75.40, LexiSim 73.40. Table 2, AUARC for C(x, s) predicting individual accuracy: TriviaQA-LLaMA Deg(E) 88.86 +/- 0.05 (oracle 91.24), Ecc(E) 88.17, SE 79.15, P(true) 67.27; TriviaQA-OPT Deg(E) 56.11; CoQA-LLaMA Ecc(E) 84.62, Deg(E) 84.60; CoQA-OPT Ecc(E) 78.14; NQ-LLaMA Deg(E) 46.54; NQ-OPT Deg(E) 21.30; NQ-GPT Ecc(E) 75.43. Rejecting the 50% least confident (Deg(E), LLaMA, TriviaQA) raised accuracy from 62% to about 90%. ACE after calibration (x 10^-2), TriviaQA-LLaMA: Deg(E) 2.37, Ecc(E) 2.60, SE 4.56, P(true) 4.30. NLI-entail similarity was the best choice in general.
papers.statistics: Mean and standard deviation over 10 random calibration/test splits are reported for all metrics. No formal hypothesis tests or p-values. Human-GPT agreement on correctness: 90.9%, 98.0%, 95.9%.
papers.availability: Code: https://github.com/zlin7/UQ-NLG. Datasets: public CoQA, TriviaQA and Natural Questions. NLI model: microsoft/deberta-large-mnli on HuggingFace.

papers.title: Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees
papers.authors: Christopher Mohri, Tatsunori Hashimoto
papers.aim: To give high-probability correctness (factuality) guarantees for any black-box language model output by linking factuality to conformal prediction.
papers.method: The LM output is split into sub-claims by GPT-4, each sub-claim gets a confidence score, and claims below a threshold are removed and the rest merged back into one answer. The threshold is chosen by split conformal prediction on a small human-annotated calibration set so that the final output is fully correct with probability at least 1-alpha. Lower-confidence claims are removed first, so the answer becomes less specific but more reliable (a 'back-off' algorithm).
papers.result: Correctness rose from about 30% to 80% on FActScore, 78% to 93% on Natural Questions, and 75% to 95% on MATH while keeping most sub-claims. With frequency scoring, FActScore factuality went from about 25% to about 80% while keeping about half of the sub-claims; NQ gained about 15% by removing about a quarter of claims; MATH gained about 15% by removing about 10% of claims. Empirical factuality closely tracked the target 1-alpha over 1000 random splits.
papers.tools: GPT-4 as base LM, sub-claim separator, merger, confidence scorer and frequency counter; Python code released (github.com/tatsu-lab/conformal-factual-lm); Google search for manual fact checking.
papers.gap: Guarantee is marginal (on average over inputs and calibration draws), not per-input; it assumes exchangeable data and fails under distribution shift; validated only on 50 examples per dataset and only with GPT-4; utility depends heavily on the quality of the claim scoring function.
papers.relation: Gives distribution-free correctness guarantees on LLM outputs, a basis for calibrated thresholds in the orchestrator's deferral decisions.
papers.limitations: Authors state: coverage is not conditional (one domain or user may differ from the target); it is marginal over the calibration draw, so a small fixed calibration set may deviate (empirical standard deviation about 0.09 with high-probability guarantees over the calibration set); under distribution shift the threshold may lose coverage; guarantees restricted to a prescribed distribution P. Partial-factuality variant gave small gains. Future work: apply conformal methods robust to distribution shift and conditional coverage.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors want an LM answer that is fully correct with probability at least 1-alpha. They take 50 inputs each from FActScore (biographies), Natural Questions (long-form answers) and MATH (step-by-step solutions). GPT-4 writes an answer for each input. A second GPT-4 prompt splits the answer into atomic sub-claims; for MATH each reasoning step is a sub-claim. The authors themselves label every sub-claim as Factual, Subjective, Unverifiable or False after checking with Google; Factual and Subjective count as true. Each sub-claim then gets a confidence score. The best practical scorer is frequency scoring: GPT-4 generates 5 more answers at temperature 1.0 and counts how many of them support the sub-claim, with ties broken by GPT-4's own stated confidence and tiny N(0, 0.001) noise. For a threshold t, the output keeps only sub-claims with score at least t and GPT-4 merges them into fluent text; a very high t gives an empty (abstaining) answer. For each calibration example the score r is the smallest threshold above which every kept claim is true; this needs only claim-level labels. The final threshold is the ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))/n quantile of these r values. At test time, claims below the threshold are dropped. To check the guarantee, each dataset was split in half 1000 times: the threshold was fitted on one half and factuality measured on the other. They also plot factuality against the percent of claims removed, using leave-one-out, to show utility. For a clinical multi-agent system, the same pipeline can filter an LLM-generated radiology or planning summary: split into findings, score them by agreement across samples or agents, calibrate on clinician-checked reports, and send the case to a clinician when too many claims must be removed.
papers.studyDesign: Methods paper with empirical evaluation (Stanford University, USA). Retrospective evaluation on public benchmark questions with author-made factuality annotations.
papers.datasets: Three datasets, first 50 inputs from each: (1) FActScore biography generation (people entities), sub-claims regenerated with the separator S; (2) Natural Questions (simplified training set, real Google queries) answered as long-form text; (3) MATH word problems, where each reasoning step is a sub-claim. GPT-4 outputs were annotated manually by the authors with a 4-way label (Factual, Subjective, Unverifiable, False) verified with Google; Factual and Subjective counted as entailed. Annotation done before experiments.
papers.preprocessing: GPT-4 generates the answer; GPT-4 with a prompt separates it into sub-claims; each sub-claim is scored; ties broken with N(0, 0.001) noise kept consistent across scoring functions. Calibration/test: each dataset randomly split in half 1000 times (threshold fitted on first half, factuality measured on second half); utility curves use leave-one-out evaluation.
papers.modelDetails: Entailment set E(y) = {y' : y' implies y}; output is correct iff reference y* is in E(y). Back-off function F_t(x) = M({c in S(L(x)) : s(c) >= t}), merging all sub-claims with score at least t; F_sup T returns abstention (empty output), so F_t is 'sound'. Score r(x, y*) = inf{t : for all j >= t, y* entails F_j(x)}, which under Assumption 5.1 needs only sub-claim-level entailment labels. Threshold q-hat_alpha = ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))/n quantile of the calibration scores; output F_q-hat(x). Theorem 4.1: P(correct) >= 1-alpha for alpha in [1/(n+1), 1], and <= 1-alpha+1/(n+1) when nested. Partial factuality (Corollary 5.3): guarantee that at least a fraction a of kept claims are true (tested with a = 0.7 FActScore, 0.9 NQ, 0.8 MATH). Scoring functions: random N(0,1); ordinal (n - j); GPT-4 verbal confidence; frequency scoring (5 alternate samples at temperature 1.0, GPT-4 counts how often each claim appears; ties broken by GPT-4 confidence); oracle (true entailment). Ranking-based variants in Appendix C.
papers.training: No training. GPT-4 used through prompts only. Frequency scoring samples 5 extra outputs at temperature 1.0. Calibration uses half of 50 annotated examples per split. Hardware and time: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Empirical factuality versus target 1-alpha over 1000 random half/half splits (frequency scoring; other scorers in Appendix E). Utility = percent of sub-claims removed versus factuality, leave-one-out, across alpha values; standard errors shown. Qualitative examples at alpha = 0.2 (FActScore) and alpha = 0.1 (NQ, MATH).
papers.baselines: Base GPT-4 output without filtering; random scoring; ordinal scoring; GPT-4 confidence scoring; oracle scoring as upper bound.
papers.results: Base GPT-4 factuality: about 25-30% on FActScore, about 75-78% on NQ and MATH. With conformal factuality: 30% to 80% (FActScore), 78% to 93% (NQ), 75% to 95% (MATH) while retaining most claims. Frequency scoring: FActScore about 25% to about 80% keeping about half the claims; NQ +about 15% removing about one quarter; MATH +about 15% removing about 10%; 20-50% gains in correctness overall. At alpha = 0.2 on FActScore most examples had about 50% of claims removed (not just whole-answer abstention). Empirical factuality tracked target closely; extra variation with standard deviation about 0.09 across calibration draws.
papers.statistics: Distribution-free conformal bounds (Theorem 4.1). Standard errors over 1000 random splits. No hypothesis tests reported.
papers.availability: Code: https://github.com/tatsu-lab/conformal-factual-lm. Datasets are public (FActScore, Natural Questions, MATH); annotations released with the code (as stated by repository release).

papers.title: The challenge of uncertainty quantification of large language models in medicine
papers.authors: Atf Z, Safavi-Naini SAA, Lewis PR, Mahjoubfar A, Naderi N, Savage TR, Soroush A
papers.aim: To review how uncertainty in large language models (LLMs) used in medicine can be measured, explained and managed. The paper also proposes a conceptual framework that separates epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty and links them to clinical decisions.
papers.method: A narrative (non-systematic) literature review combined with a philosophical discussion of uncertainty. The authors group the sources of uncertainty into data, model, user and context, summarise methods in two thematic tables, and then propose an eight-component conceptual framework. No new model is built and no experiment is run.
papers.result: No quantitative results. The main output is a conceptual framework with eight parts: probabilistic modelling and Bayesian inference; hybrid uncertainty reduction (deep ensembles, Monte Carlo dropout); linguistic confidence estimation (predictive and semantic entropy, sample consistency); surrogate models (for example Llama-2) for closed APIs such as GPT-4; multi-source data integration; dynamic calibration with continual and meta-learning and human-in-the-loop feedback; explainability tools (uncertainty maps, trust scores, composite confidence metrics); and clinical integration that routes high-uncertainty cases to human experts.
papers.tools: No tools were used in experiments. Methods discussed: Bayesian neural networks, MAP estimation, MCMC, Gaussian process emulators, deep ensembles, Monte Carlo dropout, deep evidential regression, predictive and semantic entropy, sample consistency, token-level probabilities, surrogate LLMs (Llama-2) for GPT-4, Grad-CAM, LIME, LRP, Lasso and SVM text classifiers, Dirichlet-multinomial models, GRADE framework, PEAS agent framework, federated learning (mentioned).
papers.gap: No empirical test of the proposed framework. No benchmark, dataset or metric values are given. It is not shown how the uncertainty scores should be turned into concrete deferral thresholds, and computational cost of sampling-based methods in real time is left open.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration), the paper gives the conceptual basis for an uncertainty-aware orchestrator: separate epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty, compute semantic entropy or sample consistency for LLM agents, use a surrogate model when internal probabilities are hidden, and route high-uncertainty brain-tumour cases to clinicians. It also frames the clinical setting as multi-agent, partially observable and dynamic (PEAS), which matches our orchestrator design. It does not give numbers, so our project must supply the empirical calibration and deferral evaluation.
papers.limitations: Conceptual paper only; no data, experiments or validation. The review is not systematic (no search strategy, inclusion criteria or PRISMA). The framework is described at a high level without algorithms or thresholds. Future work suggested: build and test uncertainty-aware LLM systems, align uncertainty metrics with clinical risk factors, and develop reflective and responsible AI that can judge its own limits.
papers.methodologyDetail: This paper is a review and position paper, so there is no data pipeline to copy. The authors first define uncertainty from philosophical, statistical and AI viewpoints. They separate epistemic uncertainty (lack of knowledge of the model) from aleatoric uncertainty (random noise in the data), and also discuss ontological uncertainty in medicine, using examples such as chronic illness, psychosocial factors and emergent effects like antibiotic resistance. Next they group the drivers of uncertainty in an LLM answer into four parts: data (input and output quality, multimodal fusion), model (architecture, Bayesian layers, dropout, evidential learning), user (expertise, bias, explanation needs) and context (local disease patterns, guidelines, patient background). They describe the medical task with the PEAS agent framework and note that the medical setting is partially observable, multi-agent, non-deterministic, sequential and dynamic. They then summarise the literature in two tables. Table 1 links themes such as Monte Carlo dropout, deep ensembles, uncertainty maps, OOD detection and lexicon-based classifiers to measurement challenges and to trust. Table 2 lists methods (Bayesian neural networks, MC dropout, deep ensembles, Lasso and SVM uncertainty text detection, Delphi-based clinical uncertainty vocabulary, Dirichlet-multinomial time-series models, referral of high-uncertainty cases to experts, Grad-CAM, LIME, LRP, permutation testing, GRADE) with their reported uses. From this they build an eight-part framework: Bayesian modelling at the top; ensembles and MC dropout plus surrogate models such as Llama-2 for closed models like GPT-4; semantic entropy and sample consistency for text; multi-source data fusion; continual and meta-learning with human-in-the-loop recalibration; uncertainty maps and composite confidence scores; and finally clinical integration that refers uncertain cases to clinicians. A PhD student can adapt this as a design checklist for an uncertainty-aware orchestrator, but must add their own metrics, thresholds and validation, because the paper gives no numbers.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative literature review and position paper with a proposed conceptual framework. Authors from Ontario Tech University (Canada), Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai and Stanford University (USA), and Iran University of Medical Sciences (Iran). Not prospective or retrospective; no patients involved.
papers.datasets: Not applicable. No dataset was used. The paper discusses general data types (EHR, clinical notes, imaging reports, genetic data, wearable data) as sources of uncertainty.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable. No data processing was done. Data preprocessing and augmentation are only mentioned as general ways to reduce input-related uncertainty.
papers.modelDetails: No model was built. The proposed framework (Figure 7) has a top node, probabilistic modelling and Bayesian inference (MAP, MCMC), which feeds two branches: (a) hybrid uncertainty reduction (deep ensembles and MC dropout produce multiple outputs, from which entropy-based metrics are computed), leading to surrogate modelling for proprietary systems (for example Llama-2 used to obtain internal probabilities for GPT-4 answers, combined with token-level probabilities); and (b) linguistic confidence estimation (predictive and semantic entropy from generated text, sample consistency over repeated generations), leading to multi-source data integration (structured EHR and imaging reports plus unstructured notes and articles). These feed dynamic calibration and adaptive learning (human-in-the-loop feedback, continual learning, meta-learning) and explainability tools (uncertainty maps, trust scores, composite confidence metrics). All converge on clinical integration and decision support, which aligns uncertainty with clinical risk factors and refers high-uncertainty cases to human experts. No thresholds or numeric values are given.
papers.training: Not applicable. No training was done.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable. No evaluation protocol or metrics were applied. The paper mentions AUROC and calibration as measures used in the reviewed surrogate-model work, but reports no values.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Not reported. The paper has no quantitative results. Its outputs are two summary tables (Table 1: themes and challenges in measuring uncertainty; Table 2: methods and applications for LLM uncertainty quantification) and the eight-component conceptual framework.
papers.statistics: Not reported.
papers.availability: Not available (no code or data; paper is open on arXiv).

papers.title: Enhancing the reliability and accuracy of AI-enabled diagnosis via complementarity-driven deferral to clinicians
papers.authors: Dvijotham K, Winkens J, Barsbey M, Ghaisas S, Stanforth R, Pawlowski N, Strachan P, Ahmed Z, Azizi S, Bachrach Y, Culp L, Daswani M, Freyberg J, Kelly C, Kiraly A, Kohlberger T, McKinney S, Mustafa B, Natarajan V, Geras K, Witowski J, Qin ZZ, Creswell J, Shetty S, Sieniek M, Spitz T, Corrado G, Kohli P, Cemgil T, Karthikesalingam A
papers.aim: To build a system (CoDoC) that learns, for each case, whether to trust a locked diagnostic AI model or to defer to the clinician workflow. The goal is higher accuracy than AI alone or clinicians alone, with less clinician workload.
papers.method: CoDoC is a small 'deferral AI' wrapped around a black-box diagnostic AI. It takes only the AI confidence score, and uses kernel density estimates of four conditional distributions (from a tuning set of AI score, clinician opinion and ground truth) to build a smoothed advantage function whose zero crossings define the score regions where the case is deferred to clinicians. It was tested retrospectively on UK and US mammography and on TB chest X-ray triage in Bangladesh with 5 commercial AI systems.
papers.result: UK mammography, deferral to double reading: sensitivity +3.4% (95% CI 1.3-5.4%, P<0.001) or specificity +0.8% (95% CI 0.6-1.0%, P<0.001) vs double reading, with 1.4 fewer human reads per case (published abstract: 25% fewer false positives at the same false-negative rate and 66% less clinician workload). US Dataset 2: specificity +6.5% (95% CI 5.9-7.0%) vs single reader with 53% fewer reads, and +20.9% (95% CI 19.8-22.0%) vs standalone AI. TB: specificity +2.7%, +1.7% and +5.0% vs AI from manufacturers 1-3 (all P<0.001); no gain for manufacturers 4 and 5 (published abstract: 5-15% fewer false positives for 3 of 5 systems).
papers.tools: Locked diagnostic AI models: Mammography Diagnostic AI 1 (Google, updated McKinney et al. 2020 model with supervised transfer learning and self-supervised pretraining improvements), Mammography Diagnostic AI 2 (NYU model), 5 commercial CXR TB AI products (anonymised as manufacturers 1-5). Deferral AI: kernel density estimation, dynamic programming for multiple deferral regions, McNemar and Wald tests. Code in Python 3 with numpy and scipy (github.com/google-research/codoc).
papers.gap: Deferral uses only the scalar AI confidence score; it does not co-train the diagnostic model and deferral model, does not use image features or case metadata, and was only tested retrospectively with independent (not AI-assisted) clinician reads. No prospective reader study or health economic study yet.
papers.relation: Directly relevant to O1 (multi-agent orchestration with calibrated selective autonomy): CoDoC is a model-agnostic wrapper that decides when the AI agent acts autonomously and when to defer to the clinician. The same tuning-set recipe (AI score, clinician opinion, ground truth) and KDE-smoothed advantage function can be used by our orchestrator to set deferral regions for brain-tumour MRI agents, and it works with small tuning sets (as few as 26-40 positive or local cases), which suits limited Sri Lankan data. The 'limits of confidence-based deferral' analysis is a useful test of whether deferral can help at all for a given agent.
papers.limitations: Retrospective simulation only; assumes clinicians and AI read independently (not AI-assisted reading). US Mammography Dataset 2 was enriched for cancer. TB reference standard was Xpert, not full sputum culture; non-TB findings were not modelled. Gains are not uniform across the whole ROC curve. Subgroup fairness effects need more validation. Future work: prospective reader studies, health economics, tunable deferral-rate penalties, co-training diagnostic and deferral AI, more distribution shifts (equipment, acquisition).
papers.methodologyDetail: CoDoC treats the diagnostic AI as a frozen black box and learns only when to defer. For each case in a tuning set the authors stored three numbers: the AI confidence score (mean softmax from an ensemble), the binary clinician decision, and the ground truth (biopsy for breast cancer, Xpert MTB/RIF for TB). The AI operating point theta was set halfway between the thresholds that match the clinician on sensitivity and on specificity. They then estimated, with kernel density estimation, the distribution of AI scores in four groups (disease present or absent, crossed with clinician correct or wrong). From these they computed an advantage function over the score axis, weighted by lambda to trade sensitivity against specificity. Score intervals where the advantage is positive become deferral regions: cases there go to the clinician workflow, all others are decided by thresholding the AI score. Smoothing (KDE bandwidth) removes the underspecification of raw threshold search; the bandwidth and model choice were picked on a separate validation split, and the test set was used once. Data: UK mammography tuning 60,755 cases (1,198 cancers) with 12,169 used for fitting and the rest for validation; UK test 25,856 women (414 cancers, 39-month follow-up); US NYU set 7,074 train / 7,074 test (only 26 tuning cancers); a new US population with 4,392 / 4,391 / 8,981 cases; TB 23,954 Bangladeshi adults split 50/50 with 3 radiologists and 5 commercial AIs. Evaluation compared CoDoC to AI-only and clinician-only with McNemar (superiority, alpha 0.05) and Wald (non-inferiority, margin 0.05) tests, reported 95% CIs, reads per case, recall rates and Xpert tests saved. Stress tests covered new population, unseen readers, subgroups, and an oracle upper bound (up to 10 regions, fit on test data) showing when confidence-only deferral cannot help. To adapt: collect a local tuning set of agent scores, clinician reads and confirmed diagnoses for brain-tumour MRI, fit deferral regions per agent, and validate on a held-out Sri Lankan set.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective, multi-dataset simulation study of human-AI deferral. Settings: UK breast screening (two screening centres in England, double reading with arbitration), US breast screening (NYU Langone Health; a US community screening centre), and TB triage at 3 screening centres in Dhaka, Bangladesh (Stop TB Partnership / icddr,b). Industry-led (Google, DeepMind) with NYU and Stop TB collaborators.
papers.datasets: (1) UK Mammography: CoDoC tuning data = 60,755 cases (1,198 biopsy-confirmed cancers) from the diagnostic AI's hyperparameter-tuning subset, split into a deferral training subset of 12,169 cases (243 cancers) and a validation subset (remaining cases). UK held-out test set: screening mammograms from 25,856 women, 2012-2015, two English screening centres (10% random sample), ground truth by biopsy-confirmed follow-up over 39 months, 414 cancers; historical First reader and Double read (with arbitration) decisions. (2) US Mammography Dataset 2 (NYU): CoDoC trained on 7,074 exams and tested on 7,074 exams of women aged 27-92 (May-August 2017); cancer = positive biopsy within 120 days; combined, 307 benign-only, 40 malignant-only, 21 benign and malignant, 13,780 not biopsied; lesions split evenly across sets. Only 26 positive cancers available for tuning. (3) New-population study (Mammography AI 1 on a new US community centre with yearly screening and DBT-assisted single reader): tuning 8,783 cases (139 cancers) from 2,926 women, split 4,392 training / 4,391 model selection; test 8,981 cases (174 cancers). (4) TB: individuals aged 15+ at 3 TB centres in Dhaka, May 2014-Oct 2016, digital PA chest X-ray plus Xpert MTB/RIF; 23,954 included after excluding under-15s and missing valid CXR or Xpert; split evenly into CoDoC training and test sets. Read by 3 registered radiologists (dichotomised possible TB vs not TB) and 5 commercial AI systems with no site training. Reference standard: Xpert.
papers.preprocessing: No image preprocessing by CoDoC: each case is reduced to a 3-tuple (average softmax score from an ensemble of diagnostic AI models, clinician/reader binary opinion, ground truth label) stored as 'DeferralData'. Radiologist TB reads were dichotomised (highly suggestive/possibly TB = positive; abnormal not TB/normal = negative). Splits: all data split into training and a held-out test set touched once; training further split into a tuning set (fits deferral AI) and a validation set (chooses smoothing hyperparameters / model). UK: 12,169 training vs remaining ~48,586 validation; US Dataset 2: 7,074 train / 7,074 test; new US population: 4,392 / 4,391 / 8,981 test; TB: 50/50 train/test. AI operating point set as the mean of the thresholds matching the clinical workflow on sensitivity and on specificity.
papers.modelDetails: Step 1: the locked diagnostic AI outputs a confidence score z per case. Step 2: an operating point theta turns z into an AI opinion (positive if z above theta). Step 3: from the tuning set, estimate four conditional densities of z given ground truth (positive/negative) and clinician correct/incorrect using kernel density estimation. Step 4: with a trade-off weight lambda in [0,1] between sensitivity and specificity, compute an advantage function A(z) = expected gain in the weighted objective from deferring at score z versus using the AI. Step 5: defer to the clinician workflow wherever the smoothed A(z) > 0; the zero crossings of the smoothed function give unique deferral intervals (unlike plain threshold search, which is underspecified). This is proved optimal for a given theta (Appendix A.1.1.1). Step 6: KDE smoothing hyperparameters are chosen on the validation set. Deployment: if z is inside a deferral region, the clinical workflow decides; otherwise threshold z (green region = no disease, red = disease). Clinical workflows deferred to: single first reader, double reading with arbitration, single US reader, TB radiologist. Upper-bound analysis: up to 10 deferral regions found by dynamic programming and trained on the test set to estimate the best possible confidence-based deferral. Optimised either for higher sensitivity at non-inferior specificity or vice versa (operating points OP1-OP4).
papers.training: Non-iterative fitting (density estimation plus search over thresholds and smoothing parameters); no optimizer, learning rate, epochs or batch size are reported. Hardware and training time: Not reported. The diagnostic AI models were pretrained and frozen; they are not retrained.
papers.evaluation: Held-out test sets used once. Comparison of CoDoC vs standalone AI and vs clinician workflow on sensitivity and specificity at matched operating points. Superiority tested with McNemar test (alpha 0.05) and non-inferiority with Wald test (margin 0.05). Workload measured as human reads per case. Clinical translation measured as recall-to-assessment rate per 1000 cases and proportion of Xpert tests avoided. Generalisation stress tests: new population (US community centre), unseen readers (per-reader analysis on UK test set), different AI manufacturers, different workflows; subgroup analysis by age and breast density; comparison with threshold search; theoretical upper bound of confidence-based deferral; summary ROC curves for Pareto front.
papers.baselines: Standalone diagnostic AI (Mammography AI 1, Mammography AI 2, TB AI manufacturers 1-5); clinician-only workflows (UK first reader, UK double reading with arbitration, US single reader, Bangladesh radiologists); threshold-search deferral (Leibig et al. 2022).
papers.results: Table 1 (sensitivity/specificity %, CoDoC vs clinician vs AI). UK, defer to first reader OP1: CoDoC 72.6/91.8, reader 62.7/92.8, AI 64.9/93.9; OP2: 64.4/96.5. UK, defer to double read OP3: CoDoC 71.0/95.1, double read 67.6/96.1; OP4: 68.3/96.9. US Dataset 1 (AI 1), defer to single reader OP1: 56.9/87.5 vs reader 50.0/88.0 vs AI 48.3/86.3; OP2: 50.0/91.2. US Dataset 2 (AI 2): CoDoC 96.7/90.9, reader 96.7/84.5, AI 86.7/70.0. TB CoDoC vs AI (reader 89.4/62.4): M1 90.5/68.3 vs 90.9/65.6; M2 89.3/64.2 vs 89.5/62.5; M3 89.2/67.7 vs 89.7/62.7; M4 90.6/70.8 vs 91.9/67.9; M5 91.8/71.7 vs 92.8/69.1. UK single reader: specificity +2.6% (95% CI 2.3-2.9, P=0.005) or sensitivity +7.7% (95% CI 4.5-10.7, P<0.001) vs AI at 0.15 and 0.34 extra reads/case; recall rate 70 to 44 per 1000 using 15% of one reader's workload. UK double reading: recall 48 to 41 per 1000, reads 2.1 to 0.7 per case. US Dataset 2: recall 159 to 88 per 1000; one read every 2.1 cases. TB: Xpert tests avoided +5.2%, +3.3%, +9.5% (M1-M3), one human read per 2.9, 3.7, 3.8 cases. New US population: sensitivity +6.9% (95% CI 0.4-13.2, P=0.033) or specificity +3.2% (95% CI 2.6-3.7, P=0.037) vs reader with 55% fewer reads; vs AI specificity +4.9% (95% CI 4.1-5.6) or sensitivity +8.6% (95% CI 1.9-15.2, P=0.011); recall 127 to 96 per 1000. Unseen readers: mean +5.4% sensitivity (2.5-8.2) and +0.9% specificity (0.6-1.1). CoDoC beat threshold search when tuning sets were small (<1000 samples); nearly identical on large sets. Worked with only 40 local tuning cases.
papers.statistics: McNemar test for superiority (significance 0.05) and Wald test for non-inferiority (margin 0.05); 95% confidence intervals for absolute sensitivity/specificity differences; P values reported (e.g. P=0.005, P<0.001, P=0.019, P=0.033, P=0.037, P=0.011). Inter-rater agreement: Not reported.
papers.availability: Code, trained deferral models and the tuning/test data needed to reproduce results (AI scores, clinician opinions, labels) at https://github.com/google-research/codoc. Raw images not public (OPTIMAM access by application; NYU, Northwestern, St Clair, Stop TB/icddr,b under licence).

papers.title: Who Should Predict? Exact Algorithms For Learning to Defer to Humans
papers.authors: Mozannar H, Lang H, Wei D, Sattigeri P, Das S, Sontag D
papers.venue: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS 2023), PMLR 206; arXiv:2301.06197
papers.aim: To learn a classifier and a rejector together, so that the rejector decides for each case whether the AI or the human should predict. The authors want methods that find a good human-AI pair where earlier surrogate losses fail.
papers.method: They prove that learning a linear classifier and linear rejector with deferral is NP-hard, even when a zero-error pair exists. They give an exact mixed-integer linear program (MILP) for the linear case and a new differentiable loss, RealizableSurrogate, that is realizable-consistent. Both are tested on synthetic data and on six real or semi-real datasets (CIFAR-K, CIFAR-10H, ImageNet-16H, HateSpeech, COMPASS, NIH chest X-ray) against six baselines.
papers.result: On realizable synthetic data, MILP and RealizableSurrogate reached near-zero error while all other methods failed (operating-point accuracy RealizableSurrogate 0.979 vs best non-MoE baseline 0.918). On non-realizable synthetic data (optimal error 7.5 +/- 1.0%), MILP error 11.2%, RealizableSurrogate 17.8 +/- 1.0%, best baseline 21.4 +/- 1.1%. On CIFAR-K it beat the second-best method by 0.8% on average (up to 2.8%). On real data it was competitive or best, e.g. NIH airspace opacity 0.913 vs 0.894-0.908 for baselines; pneumothorax 0.976 vs best 0.978.
papers.tools: Gurobi Optimizer (MILP, Python); PyTorch-style training with Adam and AdamW; pretrained WideResNet (CIFAR-10H), DenseNet121 (ImageNet-16H, NIH chest X-ray), three-layer CNN (CIFAR-K), feedforward network on SBERT embeddings (HateSpeech), linear models (COMPASS, synthetic). Code: https://github.com/clinicalml/human_ai_deferral. Hardware: Not reported.
papers.gap: MILP only scales to moderate data sizes (runtime grows with n; up to about 6,000 s at n = 5,000, d = 30). It is not known if RealizableSurrogate is classification-consistent. A surrogate that is both consistent and realizable-consistent is still open. Non-realizable theory, provable optimisation of non-convex surrogates and online deferral are left for future work. Only single-expert deferral; no calibration of uncertainty or clinical user study.
papers.relation: For O1, this paper gives the core maths for the orchestrator's AI-or-clinician routing: a joint classifier-rejector loss, coverage constraints that cap how many cases are sent to the clinician (useful when Sri Lankan neuroradiologist time is scarce), and fairness constraints across patient groups. The MILP suits our small, clinician-labelled MRI sets with linear heads on pretrained features, and the accuracy-coverage curves are a direct template for evaluating selective autonomy.
papers.limitations: MILP is costly for large n and needs careful l1 regularisation to avoid overfitting; it is formulated for binary labels in the main text (multiclass in the appendix). RealizableSurrogate is non-convex, and with the alpha term it is no longer realizable-consistent, so a threshold tau must be tuned on validation data. Differentiable Triage was tested outside its intended setting. On NIH fracture and nodule/mass tasks no method beat the human alone. Future work: consistency in the non-realizable setting, efficient minimisation of non-convex surrogates, online learning to defer.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors frame deferral as learning two functions: a classifier m(x) and a rejector r(x) that sends a case to the human when r(x) = 1. The training data are triples (x_i, human prediction h_i, label y_i), where the label (for example a radiologist consensus) differs from the single human's prediction. The goal is to minimise the team's 0-1 error, optionally with a coverage limit on how often the system defers and a fairness rule that equalises error across groups. First they prove that even for linear models this problem is NP-hard to approximate. Second they write it exactly as a MILP: binary defer and error variables per case, big-M margin constraints for linear M and R, and an objective counting classifier errors on kept cases plus human errors on deferred cases; coverage and fairness are one extra linear constraint each, and Gurobi solves it. Third, for larger or non-linear models, they add a 'defer' score to the classifier outputs and train with RealizableSurrogate, -2 log of (exp score of the true class plus exp defer score if the human is right) over the softmax sum; mixed with cross-entropy by a weight alpha, and the defer threshold tau is tuned on validation. They test on synthetic data (d = 30, 5,000 test points), CIFAR-K with a 3-layer CNN, CIFAR-10H with WideResNet, ImageNet-16H with a DenseNet121 last-layer fine-tune, HateSpeech with SBERT plus feedforward net, COMPASS with a linear model, and four NIH chest X-ray tasks with a DenseNet121, each split 70-10-20 and repeated 5 times. Training uses Adam or AdamW (for NIH: AdamW, 3 epochs, lr 0.001). They report team accuracy at the operating point and accuracy-coverage curves, e.g. NIH airspace opacity 0.913 vs 0.894-0.908 for six baselines. A PhD student can reuse the loss and coverage curves for an MRI deferral head.
papers.studyDesign: Theoretical and methodological machine-learning study with retrospective benchmark experiments on public datasets. MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab, Massachusetts Institute of Technology and IBM Research, USA. No prospective clinical study.
papers.datasets: SyntheticData: arbitrary n, binary, linear realizable or non-realizable; inputs from uniform or mixture-of-Gaussians; test set 5,000 points. CIFAR-K: 60k images, 10 classes, synthetic expert perfect on the first K classes and random on others (K = 1 to 9; 10 tasks). CIFAR-10H: 10k images, 10 classes, separate human annotation. ImageNet-16H: 1.2k images, 16 classes, 4 noise versions (80, 95, 110, 125), separate human annotation. HateSpeech (Davidson et al.): 25k tweets, 3 classes, human = random annotator, target = consensus. COMPASS (Dressel and Farid): 1k cases, 2 classes, separate human annotation. NIH Chest X-ray (Wang et al. 2017; Majkowska et al. 2020): about 4k images, 2 classes per task, 4 tasks (airspace opacity, pneumothorax, fracture, nodule or mass), human = random single radiologist, target = consensus of radiologists. Class counts per dataset and inclusion criteria: Not reported.
papers.preprocessing: Each dataset randomly split 70-10-20 into training, validation and test. Each run repeated for 5 trials with different splits (synthetic: 10 trials). For the MILP, features are assumed bounded and normalised (for example unit norm). HateSpeech uses SBERT sentence embeddings. Image resolution, normalisation and augmentation: Not reported.
papers.modelDetails: Setup: target Y in {1..C}; classifier m(x); rejector r(x) in {0,1}; human h(z) with possibly extra information z. System 0-1 loss = 1/n sum [I(m(x_i) != y_i) I(r(x_i)=0) + I(h_i != y_i) I(r(x_i)=1)]. Optional coverage constraint P(r(X)=1) <= beta and fairness constraint (equal system error across demographic groups). Theory: learning halfspace classifier and rejector (LWD-H) is hard to approximate to error 1/2 - epsilon unless NP = RP, even when realizable (proof by reduction from learning intersections of two halfspaces). MILP: binary variables r_i (defer) and t_i (classifier error) and continuous phi_i >= t_i - r_i, phi_i >= 0; minimise sum phi_i + r_i I(h_i != y_i); big-M constraints K_m t_i >= gamma_m - y_i M^T x_i and R^T x_i <= K_r r_i + gamma_r (r_i - 1), R^T x_i >= K_r (r_i - 1) + gamma_r r_i, with margin gamma and bounds K; 2n binary variables, n + 2d continuous variables, 4n constraints; optional l1 regularisation; coverage constraint sum r_i / n <= beta and fairness constraint added linearly. Generalisation bound given in Proposition 1. RealizableSurrogate: scores g_1..g_C and g_defer; m(x) = argmax_y g_y(x); defer if g_defer(x) >= max_y g_y(x); loss L_RS = -2 log[(exp(g_y) + I(h = y) exp(g_defer)) / sum over all C+1 scores exp]. When the human is correct, the model may either fit the label or defer at no extra cost, so it learns to complement the human. Proven realizable-consistent for model classes closed under scaling and an upper bound of the 0-1 deferral loss. Practical variant L_RS^alpha = alpha * L_RS + (1 - alpha) * cross-entropy on classifier scores, alpha in [0,1] tuned on validation; rejector r(x) = I(g_defer - max_y g_y >= tau) with tau set by line search to maximise validation system accuracy.
papers.training: Optimisers, epochs, learning rates (Table 3, appendix): SyntheticData Adam, 300 epochs, lr 0.1; CIFAR-K Adam, 100 epochs, lr 0.001; CIFAR-10H AdamW, 20 epochs, lr 0.001; ImageNet-16H Adam, 20 epochs, lr 0.001; HateSpeech Adam, 50 epochs, lr 0.001; COMPASS Adam, 300 epochs, lr 0.1; NIH chest X-ray AdamW, 3 epochs, lr 0.001. All baselines use the same learning rate and epochs. Best model chosen by validation system accuracy at each epoch. CrossEntropySurrogate alpha tuned over [0, 0.1, 0.5, 1]. MILP solved with Gurobi; runtime up to about 3,000 s as d grows (n = 1,000) and about 6,000 s at n = 5,000 (d = 30). ImageNet-16H model fine-tunes only the last layer of a pretrained DenseNet121. Batch size and hardware: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Main metric: system test accuracy of the human-AI team at the learned operating point. Accuracy-coverage curves: coverage = fraction of test points the classifier predicts; curves made by sorting rejection scores and varying the threshold c (operating point c = 0). Sample-complexity curves on synthetic data with increasing training size (10 trials, standard errors). CIFAR-K accuracy vs expert strength K. Sensitivity analysis of alpha (overall accuracy, classifier accuracy on non-deferred, human accuracy on deferred, coverage). 5 trials with different random 70-10-20 splits for real datasets. No external validation or reader study.
papers.baselines: CompareConfidence (Raghu et al. 2019), CrossEntropySurrogate L_CE^alpha (Mozannar and Sontag 2020), OvASurrogate (Verma and Nalisnick 2022), DifferentiableTriage (Okati et al. 2021), MixOfExps mixture of experts (Madras et al. 2018), SelectivePrediction (threshold on classifier confidence), plus HumanAlone, ClassifierAlone and Random Deferral reference points.
papers.results: Operating-point test accuracy (L_RS^alpha / L_CE / OvA / SP / CC / DIFT / MoE): Synthetic realizable 0.979 / 0.891 / 0.918 / 0.882 / 0.918 / 0.870 / 0.992; Synthetic non-realizable 0.879 / 0.828 / 0.839 / 0.797 / 0.836 / 0.770 / 0.774; CIFAR-K (K=5) 0.795 / 0.785 / 0.786 / 0.747 / 0.621 / 0.749 / 0.550; COMPASS 0.670 / 0.668 / 0.682 / 0.678 / 0.677 / 0.662 / 0.663; CIFAR-10H 0.969 / 0.960 / 0.963 / 0.966 / 0.968 / 0.949 / 0.953; HateSpeech 0.924 / 0.913 / 0.919 / 0.926 / 0.921 / 0.906 / 0.907; ImageNet-16H noise 80 0.912 / 0.908 / 0.909 / 0.910 / 0.908 / 0.898 / 0.904; noise 95 0.865 / 0.872 / 0.872 / 0.875 / 0.868 / 0.856 / 0.861; noise 110 0.802 / 0.791 / 0.791 / 0.809 / 0.792 / 0.756 / 0.761; noise 125 0.755 / 0.707 / 0.732 / 0.756 / 0.743 / 0.655 / 0.604; NIH pneumothorax 0.976 / 0.963 / 0.978 / 0.972 / 0.978 / 0.978 / 0.978; NIH airspace opacity 0.913 / 0.908 / 0.906 / 0.899 / 0.905 / 0.894 / 0.894. Synthetic sample complexity (mixture of Gaussians, d = 30, pm = 0, ph0 = 0.3, ph1 = 0): MILP and RealizableSurrogate near zero error; others fail. Non-realizable (pm = 0.1, ph0 = 0.4, ph1 = 0.1, n = 1,000): optimal error 7.5 +/- 1.0%, MILP 11.2%, RealizableSurrogate 17.8 +/- 1.0%, CrossEntropySurrogate 21.4 +/- 1.1%. CIFAR-K: +0.8% on average, up to +2.8%, over the second-best method. NIH fracture and nodule/mass: no method beat the human alone; RealizableSurrogate deferred to the human.
papers.statistics: Standard errors over 10 random trials (synthetic) and repeated runs over 5 random splits (real data); errors reported as mean +/- standard error for synthetic results. Formal theorems: NP-hardness (Theorem 1, Corollaries 1-2), generalisation bound (Proposition 1, holds with probability at least 1 - delta), realizable consistency (Theorem 2). No hypothesis tests or p-values.
papers.availability: Code and datasets: https://github.com/clinicalml/human_ai_deferral. Datasets are public (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-10H, ImageNet-16H, HateSpeech, COMPASS, NIH ChestX-ray with Majkowska labels).

papers.title: Learning to Defer with Limited Expert Predictions
papers.authors: Hemmer P, Thede L, Vossing M, Jakubik J, Kuhl N
papers.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, 37(5) (AAAI 2023); arXiv:2304.07306
papers.aim: To reduce the number of human expert predictions needed to train learning-to-defer (L2D) algorithms. The authors learn an expert's strengths from a few labelled cases and generate artificial expert predictions for the rest.
papers.method: A three-step approach: (1) train an embedding model on ground-truth labels; (2) train an expertise predictor on the embeddings to predict whether the expert is correct (binary), using semi-supervised learning (FixMatch or CoMatch) over expert-labelled and unlabelled cases; (3) generate artificial expert predictions for unlabelled cases and use them to train three existing L2D algorithms. Tested on CIFAR-100 with synthetic experts and NIH chest X-rays with a real radiologist.
papers.result: With six expert predictions per class, all tested L2D algorithms beat both the AI alone and the radiologist alone, reaching on average 98.96% of the accuracy obtained with a full set of expert predictions. On NIH, Embedding-FixMatch reached F0.5 = 90.74 with only 4 expert predictions (vs FixMatch 56.97, CoMatch 70.88). On NIH, the Mozannar and Sontag L2D reached 99.12% and Raghu et al. and Okati et al. 98.83% of full-label accuracy with six predictions per class. On CIFAR-100, Embedding-SSL beat SSL baselines by 8.13% (H60) and 3.80% (H90) for l < 1000.
papers.tools: EfficientNet-B1 (ImageNet-pretrained) embedding model for CIFAR-100; WideResNet backbone for the L2D algorithms on CIFAR-100; ResNet18 pretrained on CheXpert for NIH; single fully connected layer with softmax as expertise predictor; FixMatch and CoMatch semi-supervised learning; SGD with Nesterov momentum; support vector classifier and single-layer neural network as baselines. Code: https://github.com/ptrckhmmr/learning-to-defer-with-limited-expert-predictions. Hardware: Not reported.
papers.gap: Instances that the expert labels are chosen at random; better selection (active or representative sampling) is not studied. Only one real radiologist and one finding (airspace opacity) are used in the main paper. Expert errors are reduced to correct or incorrect, so systematic class confusions are not modelled. No clinical deployment or prospective test.
papers.relation: For O1, this paper directly supports training the orchestrator's AI-or-clinician deferral rule when Sri Lankan neuroradiologists and neurosurgeons can label only a few cases. We can embed MRI cases with a model trained on ground truth (for example BraTS labels), learn each clinician's correctness from a few labelled cases with FixMatch, and generate artificial clinician predictions to train an L2D router. It also shows a fairness check (gender and age bias) that we should repeat for our patient groups.
papers.limitations: Labelled expert cases are drawn at random. The expertise predictor works on a binary correct/incorrect target, so wrong labels are filled in at random among other classes. Synthetic experts on CIFAR-100 are simplified. The NIH study uses one radiologist (a second in the appendix) and one finding with 2,350 images. Artificial predictions may change subgroup bias: for age, bias rose by 2.63 pp (Mozannar and Sontag), 1.74 pp (Raghu) and 0.8 pp (Okati). Future work: smarter selection of instances for expert labelling to make onboarding of new experts easier.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors want to train a learning-to-defer router when a human expert has labelled only a few cases. Step 1: they train an embedding network on all training images using ground-truth labels and cross-entropy. For CIFAR-100 (40,000 train, 10,000 validation, 10,000 test; 20 superclasses) this is EfficientNet-B1 trained for 200 epochs with SGD, Nesterov momentum and learning rate 0.1. For the NIH chest X-ray airspace-opacity task (2,350 images, 20% of patients held out for test) it is a CheXpert-pretrained ResNet18 trained for 200 epochs at learning rate 0.001. Step 2: they take a small set of l cases labelled by the expert, with l = m x classes and m from 2 to 250 (CIFAR-100: 40 to 5000; NIH: 4 to 500), drawn at random with balanced classes. Each expert label becomes a binary target: 1 if the expert was right, 0 if wrong. A one-layer softmax 'expertise predictor' on top of the frozen-feature embeddings learns this target with FixMatch or CoMatch, using all other training cases as unlabelled data with weak and strong augmentation and a confidence threshold for pseudo-labels. It is trained for 50 epochs (CIFAR-100) or 25 epochs (NIH) with SGD at learning rate 0.03. Step 3: for every unlabelled case the predictor says if the expert would be correct; if yes the artificial label is the ground truth, if no a random wrong class. These artificial labels plus the real ones then train three L2D methods (Mozannar and Sontag; Raghu et al.; Okati et al.) using a WideResNet (CIFAR-100) or ResNet18 (NIH). The synthetic experts are H90 and H60; the real expert is radiologist 4295342357. Evaluation uses F0.5 for artificial predictions and system test accuracy as a percentage of training with complete expert labels, over five seeds. With six labels per class, systems reached about 99% of full-label accuracy and beat both human and AI alone. A PhD student can reuse this pipeline with MRI embeddings and a few clinician reads to train a deferral policy.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological machine-learning study with retrospective experiments on two public datasets. Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Germany. No prospective clinical study.
papers.datasets: (1) CIFAR-100: 60,000 natural images, 100 subclasses grouped into 20 equal superclasses. The 20 superclasses are the task; the 100 subclasses are used to build synthetic experts. Two synthetic experts: H90 (strong, 90 of 100 subclasses are strengths) and H60 (weaker, 60 of 100). Strength subclasses are drawn around a random 'strength base' weighted by similarity (average cosine distance of EfficientNet-B1 ImageNet features); on weakness subclasses the expert predicts randomly weighted by similarity to the true subclass. (2) NIH chest X-ray (ChestX-ray8 with Majkowska et al. 2020 labels): radiologists' predictions for four findings on 4,374 chest X-rays. Each image has an adjudicated 'gold standard' label from a panel of three radiologists plus the three individual radiologists' predictions. The study uses the radiologist with most predictions (labeler-id 4295342357) and the finding airspace opacity (chosen for balanced prevalence), giving 2,350 available images. Both datasets are described as class-balanced.
papers.preprocessing: CIFAR-100 split: 40,000 training, 10,000 validation, 10,000 test images. NIH split: 2,350 images split into training and test by randomly selecting 20% of patients as test patients (patient-level split). Number of expert-labelled instances l = m x k with m in {2, 4, 6, 10, 20, 50, 250}: for CIFAR-100 (k = 20) l in {40, 80, 120, 200, 400, 1000, 5000}; for NIH (k = 2) l in {4, 8, 12, 20, 40, 100, 500}. Labelled instances drawn randomly with balanced class proportions. Weak and strong augmentations are used inside FixMatch/CoMatch (details in the appendix). Image resolution and normalisation: Not reported in the main paper.
papers.modelDetails: Step 1, embedding model: a feature extractor Phi_emb: X -> R^d trained together with a classifier Omega on all instances D using cross-entropy with ground-truth labels (Eq. 1). Step 2, expertise predictor: each multi-class expert prediction h_i is turned into a binary target h_bin = 1 if h_i = y_i else 0 (Eq. 2). The expertise predictor Phi_ex: R^d -> {0,1} (one fully connected layer + softmax) is trained on the embeddings with a semi-supervised loss (Eq. 3): supervised cross-entropy on weakly augmented labelled cases L_s; plus lambda_u times an unsupervised term L_u, where a pseudo-label from a weakly augmented unlabelled image is kept only if max(q_j) >= threshold tau and is compared with the prediction on a strongly augmented version (FixMatch uses hard pseudo-labels; CoMatch uses memory-smoothed pseudo-labels); CoMatch adds lambda_c times a contrastive graph loss L_c between a pseudo-label graph and an embedding graph produced by a two-layer projection head. Values of lambda_u, lambda_c and tau: Not reported in the main paper (appendix). Step 3, generation: for each unlabelled case, h_bin_hat = argmax Phi_ex(Phi_emb(x_j)); if 1 the artificial expert prediction is the true label y_j, otherwise a class drawn uniformly from the other k-1 classes (Eq. 4). Human plus artificial predictions then train three L2D algorithms: Mozannar and Sontag (2020) consistent surrogate loss with an extra defer class; Raghu et al. (2019) separate classifier and human-error model, defer by comparing confidences; Okati et al. (2021) triage with per-instance negative log-likelihood for classifier and expert. The deferral system A(x) = 1 means defer to the human.
papers.training: CIFAR-100: embedding model (EfficientNet-B1) trained 200 epochs, SGD with Nesterov momentum, learning rate 0.1; each Embedding-SSL expertise predictor trained 50 epochs, SGD, learning rate 0.03. NIH: embedding model (ResNet18 pretrained on CheXpert) trained 200 epochs, SGD with Nesterov momentum, learning rate 0.001; expertise predictor trained 25 epochs, SGD, learning rate 0.03. Each experiment repeated with five random seeds. Batch size, scheduler, hardware and training time: Not reported in the main paper.
papers.evaluation: Two-stage evaluation. (1) Quality of artificial binary expert predictions against the true binary expert predictions, using the F0.5-score (chosen because correct vs incorrect is imbalanced). (2) System test accuracy of each L2D algorithm trained on human + artificial predictions, reported as a percentage of the accuracy of the same algorithm trained with complete expert predictions (upper bound). Lower bounds are Human Expert Alone and Classifier Alone. Mean and standard deviation over five seeds. Bias analysis on NIH: gender bias = absolute accuracy difference between male and female patients; age bias = mean absolute deviation of accuracy in five age bins from overall accuracy; compared with the complete-prediction upper bound.
papers.baselines: SSL baselines without an embedding model: FixMatch and CoMatch. Embedding supervised baselines: Embedding-NN (single-layer neural network) and Embedding-SVM (support vector classifier). Bounds: Complete Expert Predictions (upper), Human Expert Alone and Classifier Alone (lower). L2D algorithms used: Mozannar and Sontag (2020), Raghu et al. (2019), Okati, De and Rodriguez (2021).
papers.results: CIFAR-100 F0.5 (l = 40 / 120 / 5000). H60: FixMatch 68.81 / 74.93 / 82.67; CoMatch 75.00 / 79.17 / 87.62; Embedding-NN 75.74 / 79.32 / 83.77; Embedding-SVM 74.49 / 81.61 / 89.16; Embedding-FixMatch 79.69 / 84.06 / 86.95; Embedding-CoMatch 79.65 / 84.01 / 86.87. H90: FixMatch 89.51 / 91.44 / 95.84; CoMatch 87.24 / 91.72 / 96.62; Embedding-NN 92.10 / 92.70 / 93.68; Embedding-SVM 92.08 / 93.46 / 96.38; Embedding-FixMatch 92.44 / 95.34 / 96.25; Embedding-CoMatch 94.75 / 95.46 / 96.14. For l < 1000 Embedding-SSL beat SSL by 8.13% (H60) and 3.80% (H90), and Embedding-SL by 4.09% and 1.97%. L2D on CIFAR-100: Mozannar and Sontag reached 99.02% (H60) and 98.81% (H90) of the upper bound with six predictions per class; for l < 400, Embedding-SSL beat SSL by 3.27%/2.47% and Embedding-SL by 1.99%/1.25%; Raghu: +1.78%/1.68% over SSL, +0.53%/1.22% over Embedding-SL; Okati: +1.96%/3.92% over SSL, +0.40%/0.06% over Embedding-SL. NIH F0.5 (l = 4 / 12 / 500): FixMatch 56.97 / 72.63 / 87.25; CoMatch 70.88 / 76.76 / 89.77; Embedding-NN 85.87 / 89.03 / 92.29; Embedding-SVM 59.86 (+/-33.44) / 86.89 / 92.74; Embedding-FixMatch 90.74 / 92.56 / 91.96; Embedding-CoMatch 88.56 / 92.63 / 91.07. For l < 100 Embedding-SSL beat SSL by 38.83% and Embedding-SL by 7.04%. L2D on NIH for l < 100: Mozannar and Sontag +1.97% over SSL, +2.10% over Embedding-SL; Raghu +1.67% and +1.06%; Okati +2.42% and +0.69%. With six predictions per class: 99.12% (Mozannar and Sontag) and 98.83% (Raghu, Okati) of full-label accuracy. All L2D systems exceeded human alone and classifier alone for all l.
papers.statistics: Mean and standard deviation over five random seeds. No significance tests, p-values or confidence intervals reported. Bias reported as percentage-point differences: gender bias change -0.72 pp (Mozannar and Sontag), -1.53 pp (Raghu), +0.29 pp (Okati); age bias change +2.63 pp, +1.74 pp, +0.8 pp.
papers.availability: Code and appendix: https://github.com/ptrckhmmr/learning-to-defer-with-limited-expert-predictions. Data: public CIFAR-100 and NIH ChestX-ray8 with Majkowska et al. radiologist labels.

papers.title: A benchmarking framework and dataset for learning to defer in human-AI decision-making
papers.authors: Alves JV, Leitao D, Jesus S, Sampaio MOP, Liebana J, Saleiro P, Figueiredo MAT, Bizarro P
papers.aim: To provide a framework (OpenL2D) that creates realistic synthetic human experts with work-capacity limits, and a ready dataset (FiFAR) for benchmarking learning-to-defer (L2D) methods. The authors also show that L2D rankings change with the expert team.
papers.method: OpenL2D simulates each expert's false-positive and false-negative error probabilities as sigmoid functions of pre-processed features and the model score (instance-dependent label noise). It was applied to the public Bank Account Fraud (BAF) dataset to create 50 synthetic fraud analysts for about 30K alerted cases, with 25 training scenarios (one expert prediction per case under capacity limits) and 25 testing scenarios. Two capacity-aware L2D methods (OvA and DeCCaF) were benchmarked against non-L2D baselines using misclassification cost.
papers.result: Synthetic experts showed inter-rater Cohen's kappa from 0.06 to 0.79 (mean 0.49) and pairwise agreement 0.32 to 0.95 (mean 0.75), close to values reported for real cardiologists. Classifier h: ROC AUC 0.71, ECE 4.9%. Expert-correctness models: OvA AUC 0.58-0.61, ECE 5.4-6.0%; DeCCaF AUC 0.60-0.64, ECE 3.8-5.2%. Misclassification cost on test: Full Rejection 213.5, Only Classifier 204, Random 151.2-169.6, OvA 131.3-151.7, DeCCaF 126.2-145.3. OvA and DeCCaF cut cost by 11% and 15% on average vs random assignment, but their ranking changed across teams.
papers.tools: LightGBM (Alert Model, classifier h, OvA classifiers, DeCCaF team model, expert-behaviour models); Optuna Tree-structured Parzen Estimator for hyperparameter search; constraint programming for DeCCaF assignment; bisection method to solve error-rate parameters; Cohen's kappa; expected calibration error; Intel Xeon Gold 5120 CPU @ 2.20 GHz (10-30 cores). Code: https://github.com/feedzai/openl2d. Data: figshare.
papers.gap: Only binary classification and tabular data are supported. Experts are synthetic and cannot replace real human data. Expert-correctness models reach AUC of at most about 0.65, so modelling human behaviour under realistic data limits is still hard. No medical imaging use case. Parameter tuning to get realistic behaviour is slow and needs domain literature.
papers.relation: For O1, this paper gives a way to evaluate how the orchestrator allocates brain-tumour cases between the AI and a small team of clinicians under real workload limits, which matters in Sri Lanka where neuroradiologists are few. Its ideas of capacity constraints per batch, one clinician read per case, team-dependent rankings and cost-based evaluation can be copied into our deferral benchmark. Its limits (tabular, binary only) mean we would need to adapt the expert simulation to MRI-derived features or use real clinician reads.
papers.limitations: Framework limited to binary classification and tabular data; the authors advise against applying it to image or text embeddings. Needs ground-truth labels. Creating realistic experts requires knowledge of human decision-making literature and time-consuming parameter tuning. Synthetic experts are for benchmarking only and are not a substitute for real experts. Real fraud analysts were less predictable (lower AUC) than synthetic ones. Uncritical use of a single team can give misleading L2D rankings. Future work: add new L2D methods to the benchmark repository; extend to other datasets.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors start from the public BAF tabular fraud dataset (1 million account applications, 8 months, 1.1% fraud). They train a LightGBM 'Alert Model' on months 1-3 and tune it on month 4 with Optuna (100 rounds) to maximise recall at 5% FPR, giving threshold 0.050969 and recall 57.9%. Cases above this threshold in months 4-8 (about 30K alerts) are the cases that humans review. From the threshold they derive the cost ratio lambda = 0.057 for false positives versus false negatives. Next they simulate 50 fraud analysts. Features are turned into quantiles (numeric) or target-encoded values (categorical). For each analyst, the chance of a false positive or false negative is a sigmoid of a weighted sum of features and the model score, scaled by a consistency parameter alpha ~ N(15, 3.5). Weights for the 15 features most correlated with fraud are drawn around their correlation (sd 0.1), others from N(0, 0.05), the model-score weight from N(0.7, 0.3) and the age weight from N(0.07, 0.02) to create age bias. Target cost is drawn from N(0.035, 0.005) within [0.02, 0.046], and the bias terms are solved by bisection. Labels are flipped with these probabilities to give each analyst's decision on every alert. They then build 25 training sets for months 4-7 by randomly assigning each alert to one of 10 available analysts (5 teams x 5 batch seeds), so each case has one human decision. Testing uses month 8 (4,457 alerts) as one batch with one homogeneous and four variable capacity settings, and a deferral rate of 10/11. They validate realism with Cohen's kappa (inter-rater mean 0.49), FPR/FNR plots, predictive equality and feature-importance comparison with 20 real analysts. Finally they train OvA and DeCCaF (LightGBM, weighted log-loss, 120 Optuna rounds) and compare total misclassification cost with baselines. A PhD student can copy this design to simulate clinician capacity and benchmark case allocation.
papers.studyDesign: Data descriptor with a simulation framework and a benchmark experiment. Feedzai (Portugal), Instituto Superior Tecnico, ULisboa and Instituto de Telecomunicacoes (Lisbon). Retrospective use of a public GAN-generated fraud dataset; validation against published human-agreement studies and a private dataset of 20 real transaction-fraud analysts.
papers.datasets: (1) Bank Account Fraud (BAF) dataset, base variant version 1 (Kaggle, Jesus et al.): 1,000,000 bank account opening applications over 8 months, generated by GANs from anonymised real data; 30 features (numeric, categorical, binary, e.g. income, customer_age, credit_risk_score, velocity_6h, device_os); binary label fraud_bool; fraud prevalence 1.1%; concept drift over months. (2) FiFAR (Financial Fraud Alert Review): alerted cases from months 4-8 (about 30K instances) with predictions from all 50 synthetic experts for every case; test month 8 has 4,457 alerts. Fraud prevalence within alerts: about 13% for older customers (>= 50 years) and about 11% for younger customers. (3) Private dataset of real transaction-fraud analyst decisions: 20 analysts, about 10K decisions each, 116 features, one analyst per case, no ground-truth labels; used only to validate feature dependence. External reference values from literature (cardiologists, ophthalmologists, software estimators) used for agreement and performance comparison.
papers.preprocessing: Data split by month: Alert Model trained on months 1-3, validated on month 4; expert predictions generated for months 4-8; L2D systems trained on months 4-6, validated on month 7 and tested on month 8. For expert simulation, numeric features were transformed to quantiles and shifted by -0.5 (range [-0.5, 0.5]); categorical features were target-encoded by ascending fraud prevalence, divided by the number of categories and shifted to zero mean. Training scenarios: deferral rate 1, homogeneous capacity, random assignment, 5 teams of 10 experts (5 availability seeds) x 5 batch-shuffle seeds = 25 scenarios. Testing: the whole month-8 alert set as one batch of 4,457 cases; per team one homogeneous and four variable capacity settings (sigma_d = 0.2); deferral rate 10/11 so each of the 10 experts and the classifier handle about 1/11 of cases. Expert-behaviour models (validation): 60-20-20 split for real experts; for synthetic experts 10K predictions with training from months 4-6, validation month 7, test month 8.
papers.modelDetails: Expert simulation (Eq. 1): for expert j and case i, P(FP) = sigmoid(beta_0 - alpha * (w . x_i + w_M * M(x_i)) / ||w||) when y = 0, and P(FN) = sigmoid(beta_1 + alpha * (w . x_i + w_M * M(x_i)) / ||w||) when y = 1 (shared weights with opposite signs so more FPs in a region imply fewer FNs). The label is flipped with these probabilities. w = feature weights (normal per feature or spike-and-slab prior), w_M = weight on the Alert Model score, w_p = weight on protected attribute (age), alpha = consistency (alpha = 0 gives class-dependent noise; large alpha gives deterministic decisions). beta_0 and beta_1 are found by bisection to hit target FPR and FNR sampled so that expected misclassification cost C = lambda*FPR*N0/N + FNR*N1/N matches a target. Cost ratio lambda = c_FP/c_FN = t/(1-t) = 0.057 derived from the Alert Model threshold. FiFAR parameters: alpha ~ N(15, 3.5); target cost ~ N(0.035, 0.005) with bounds [0.02, 0.046] (better than rejecting all alerts, cost 0.0496); FPR and FNR in [0.01, 1]; 15 features most correlated with the label (Pearson or Cramer's V) get weight mean = correlation, sd 0.1 (e.g. proposed_credit_limit 0.735, credit_risk_score 0.626, velocity_4w -0.447); other features N(0, 0.05); customer_age N(0.07, 0.02); model_score N(0.7, 0.3). Capacity constraints: batch size, deferral rate, homogeneous or variable capacity ~ N(Deferral_Rate x Batch_Size / n_experts, sigma_d x mu_d), number of available experts. Alert Model: LightGBM, threshold t = 0.050969 for 5% FPR. L2D methods: OvA trains one LightGBM per expert to predict that expert's correctness; defers greedily to the most-likely-correct decision maker until capacity is used up. DeCCaF trains one team LightGBM taking expert_id as input; assigns by constraint programming to maximise global probability of correctness under capacity. Both share classifier h (LightGBM trained with weighted log-loss, weight 1 for positives and lambda for negatives; init_score from {0.782, 0.982, ..., 2.582}, selected 1.982).
papers.training: Alert Model (LightGBM, binary cross-entropy): Optuna TPE, 100 rounds, early stop after 10 rounds, objective recall at 5% FPR on month 4; selected boosting goss, n_estimators 94, max_depth 2, num_leaves 145, min_child_samples 59, learning_rate 0.3031421, reg_alpha 0.0012637, reg_lambda 0.0017007; 13 minutes on 25 cores of Intel Xeon Gold 5120 @ 2.20 GHz; validation recall 57.9%. Classifier h: weighted log-loss, months 4-6; TPE 300 rounds with 200 startup per init_score value (20 minutes, 10 cores), then 1,700 trials with 1,500 startup with max_depth fixed at 2 (90 minutes); selected dart, n_estimators 160, max_depth 2, num_leaves 708, min_child_samples 89, learning_rate 0.779, reg_alpha 1.673, reg_lambda 1.932, init_score 1.982. OvA and DeCCaF: LightGBM dart, weighted log-loss, TPE 120 rounds with 100 startup, search n_estimators [50,250], max_depth [2,20], num_leaves [100,1000], min_child_samples [5,100], learning_rate [0.005,0.5]; trained in all 25 scenarios; 4 h 12 min (OvA) and 1 h 23 min (DeCCaF) on 10 cores. Expert-behaviour models for validation: TPE 50 rounds, early stop 10, objective ROC AUC; 4 minutes on 30 cores (real) and 8 minutes on 10 cores (synthetic).
papers.evaluation: Realism checks: intra-rater agreement by sampling 10 decision sets per expert and averaging pairwise Cohen's kappa; inter-rater agreement by pairwise Cohen's kappa and proportion of agreement over months 4-8; expert performance as FPR vs FNR and expected misclassification cost against the Full Rejection line; fairness by predictive equality (ratio of FPRs between older and younger customers, fair = 1); feature dependence by fitting LightGBM to each expert's decisions and comparing information-gain feature importance and ROC AUC between 20 real and synthetic experts. L2D benchmark: classifier h judged by ROC AUC and expected calibration error (ECE); OvA and DeCCaF expert-correctness models by AUC and ECE with 95% CI; deferral quality by total misclassification cost on the month-8 test set (cost = lambda per FP, 1 per FN), averaged over 5 training scenarios x 5 capacity settings per team, with 95% CI.
papers.baselines: Full Rejection (reject all alerts), Only Classifier h, Random Assignment (random deferral until capacities are met), OvA (one-vs-all multi-expert L2D), and DeCCaF (deferral under cost and capacity constraints).
papers.results: Alert Model: recall 57.9% at 5% FPR in validation. Classifier h: ROC AUC 0.71, ECE 4.9%. OvA / DeCCaF AUC and ECE (%), mean +/- 95% CI: team_1 0.61+/-0.01, 6.0+/-0.5 / 0.64+/-0.01, 4.6+/-0.5; team_2 0.58, 6.0 / 0.60, 4.8; team_3 0.60, 5.5 / 0.62, 5.2; team_4 0.59, 5.4 / 0.60, 3.8; team_5 0.59, 5.5 / 0.61, 4.9. DeCCaF gave on average 4% higher AUC and 17% better calibration. Misclassification cost (Full Rejection / Only Classifier / Random / OvA / DeCCaF): team_1 213.5 / 204 / 169.6+/-2.53 / 151.7+/-1.99 / 138.1+/-5.14; team_2 213.5 / 204 / 157.8+/-1.39 / 142.0+/-1.61 / 145.3+/-4.28; team_3 213.5 / 204 / 151.2+/-1.84 / 131.3+/-2.19 / 126.2+/-4.52; team_4 213.5 / 204 / 163.1+/-1.61 / 145.8+/-3.51 / 141.6+/-5.32; team_5 213.5 / 204 / 163.3+/-1.58 / 141.2+/-2.57 / 132.0+/-1.93. OvA and DeCCaF lowered cost by 11% and 15% on average vs Random; DeCCaF was clearly better only for team_1 and team_5. Expert realism: inter-rater kappa 0.06-0.79 (mean 0.49), agreement 0.32-0.95 (mean 0.75); experts #3 and #4 had mean kappa 0.33 and 0.28 with others but 0.71 with each other; some experts were almost 50% more likely to wrongly reject older customers. Real analysts' behaviour models had lower AUC than all synthetic ones.
