Specialty: 'matched' score = number of correct predicted specialties divided by the length of the shorter list (truth or prediction), averaged over patients; and 'at least one' match. Diagnosis: Claude 3.5 Sonnet judge returns True if a predicted diagnosis matches or falls in a broader category of a true primary diagnosis; same two scores. Inter-model agreement for triage and specialty. Reader study: 4 clinicians, 400 of 2000 cases, each clinician 200 cases; clinicians 1 and 2 share one subset, 3 and 4 another. Specialty labels rated Correct / Partially Correct / Reasonable but Suboptimal / Incorrect. Diagnoses (clinical-user outputs of Claude 3.5 Sonnet and RAG LLM) rated Exact Match / Clinically Equivalent / Clinically Related / Incorrect; LLM True mapped to the first two. Agreement reported per clinician and as union (at least one of the pair agrees) and intersection (both agree). No external validation set.
papers.baselines: Claude 3 Haiku, Claude 3 Sonnet and Claude 3.5 Sonnet compared with each other and with the RAG-assisted Claude 3.5 Sonnet; general-user vs clinical-user inputs. No human clinician baseline on the prediction tasks.
papers.results: General user (triage exact / range; specialty matched / at least one; diagnosis matched / at least one; average): RAG 64.10/78.20; 77.12/86.35; 69.43/80.85; 76.01. Claude 3.5 Sonnet 62.20/82.80; 78.26/88.05; 70.22/82.00; 77.26. Claude 3 Sonnet 58.35/74.40; 78.10/87.70; 70.17/81.55; 75.05. Claude 3 Haiku 57.70/71.80; 77.86/87.10; 67.39/79.60; 73.58. Clinical user: RAG 65.75/77.15; 77.28/86.45; 69.77/81.70; 76.35. Claude 3.5 Sonnet 64.40/82.40; 78.86/88.55; 70.26/82.10; 77.76. Claude 3 Sonnet 61.65/74.55; 77.72/87.15; 70.51/82.05; 75.61. Claude 3 Haiku 59.00/66.15; 78.02/87.05; 67.46/79.30; 72.83. Gain from vitals in triage exact: +1.65 (RAG), +2.20 (3.5 Sonnet), +3.30 (3 Sonnet), +1.30 (Haiku); Haiku range fell 5.65. Agreement general vs clinical user: 85.94 (RAG), 89.74 (3.5 Sonnet), 84.95 (3 Sonnet), 83.54 (Haiku); highest cross-model 83.88 (RAG vs 3.5 Sonnet). Specialty label validation: clinicians 1-4 accurate 93.77/82.05/81.91/68.94%, average 81.5%; accurate+acceptable average 97.03%; error rate average 2.63% (clinician 2 9.15%). LLM judge vs clinicians (Claude 3.5 Sonnet / RAG): per-clinician 90.43/90.11, 80.22/79.11, 76.51/77.78, 85.56/82.52; average 83.18/82.38; union 95.62/94.91; intersection 70.74/69.86.
papers.statistics: Descriptive percentages only. No confidence intervals, p-values or kappa. Agreement given as percentage agreement between models and between LLM judge and clinicians (union and intersection).
papers.availability: Code and processed data: https://github.com/BIMSBbioinfo/medLLMbenchmark. Raw data: MIMIC-IV-Note via PhysioNet (https://physionet.org/content/mimic-iv-note/2.2/), credentialed access.

papers.title: A feasibility study of automating radiotherapy planning with large language model agents
papers.authors: Wang Q, Wang Z, Li M, Ni X, Tan R, Zhang W, Wubulaishan M, Wang W, Yuan Z, Zhang Z, Liu C
papers.aim: To test whether GPT-4 based multi-agent LLMs can automate iterative radiotherapy plan optimisation by copying the dosimetrist-physicist workflow.
papers.method: GPT-Plan uses LLM agents acting as a dosimetrist and a physicist to iteratively write and evaluate text-based radiotherapy plans against predefined criteria. Support tools retrieve historical plans, reduce hallucinations (self-reflection) and balance exploration and exploitation. It was tested on 12 lung IMRT and 5 cervical VMAT cases against the ECHO auto-planning method and manual plans.
papers.result: Lung IMRT: better target coverage and homogeneity than ECHO with comparable or better organ-at-risk sparing. Cervical VMAT: plan quality comparable to a senior physicist and better than a junior physicist, mainly for OAR sparing. Historical plan retrieval significantly reduced iterations for lung cases (p < 0.01); cervical iteration counts were comparable to the senior physicist (p = 0.313). Detailed dose values not available from the abstract.
papers.tools: GPT-4 family LLMs (exact model versions not reported in abstract); vision-based LLM for dose images; historical plan retrieval tool; self-reflection mechanism; treatment planning system not reported in abstract; ECHO auto-planning as comparator.
papers.gap: Very small sample (17 cases, two sites), feasibility only, vision LLMs could not read dose images accurately, and no reported uncertainty-based handover to the planner. Not tested for other tumour sites or prospectively.
papers.relation: For O1, this is a direct example of LLM agents orchestrating a planning tool in an iterative loop with an evaluator agent, retrieval of past plans and self-reflection to catch hallucinations. It is a close analogue to our surgical-planning support agent: a planner agent proposes, a checker agent evaluates against criteria, and the clinician validates. The weakness of vision LLMs on dose images warns us to keep image analysis in dedicated models and let agents work on structured outputs.
papers.limitations: Stated in abstract: occasional LLM hallucinations (handled by self-reflection) and inaccuracy of vision-based LLMs when interpreting dose images. Future work: refine and extend GPT-Plan as LLMs improve. Other limitations not available (abstract only).
papers.methodologyDetail: Radiotherapy planning is a slow trial-and-error loop between a dosimetrist adjusting optimisation settings and a physicist checking the dose. GPT-Plan copies this with two GPT-4-based agents: one proposes settings, the other evaluates the resulting plan against the clinical goals and sends back advice. Helper tools give the agents similar past plans, catch hallucinated or inconsistent outputs, and balance trying new settings with refining good ones. On 12 lung and 5 cervical cancer cases, its plans matched or beat an established automatic planner and a senior physicist, and beat a junior physicist, while past-plan retrieval cut the number of iterations. Vision LLMs, however, could not reliably read dose images. For our PhD it is a working example of the propose-and-check agent pattern for the surgical-planning agent, and it supports using specialised image models rather than general vision LLMs for image interpretation.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective feasibility study.
papers.datasets: 12 lung cancer IMRT cases and 5 cervical cancer VMAT cases with clinical objectives, anatomy and prior plans.
papers.preprocessing: Plans, objectives and optimisation results converted to text prompts; library of historical plans for similarity retrieval.
papers.modelDetails: Multi-agent loop: Dosimetrist Agent generates optimisation parameters (fixed system prompt plus per-iteration user prompt with objectives, anatomy, similar plans, results and suggestions); Physicist Agent assesses dose-volume criteria and gives feedback; supporting tools for retrieval, error mitigation and exploration-exploitation.
papers.training: No model training (prompted pre-trained LLMs).
papers.evaluation: Target coverage, homogeneity, OAR dose metrics (DVH), number of optimisation iterations; comparison with ECHO and with senior and junior physicists; test of vision LLM interpretation of dose images.
papers.baselines: ECHO automated planning; manual plans by senior and junior physicists.
papers.results: Superior PTV coverage and homogeneity vs ECHO in lung; cervix comparable to senior and better than junior physicist; fewer iterations with retrieval (lung p<0.01; cervix vs senior p=0.313).
papers.statistics: Paired comparisons with p-values.

papers.title: Orchestrating explainable artificial intelligence for multimodal and longitudinal data in medical imaging
papers.authors: Pahud de Mortanges A, Luo H, Shu SZ, Kamath A, Suter Y, Shelan M, Pöllinger A, Reyes M
papers.aim: To review, from a clinical view, explainable AI (XAI) for multimodal and longitudinal medical imaging data, and to propose an LLM-based 'XAI orchestrator' that combines predictions and explanations for clinicians.
papers.method: Narrative review of studies on multimodal and longitudinal XAI and a screening of 15 XAI software libraries for supported data types. The authors then propose a conceptual XAI orchestrator, inspired by tumour boards, that gathers modality-specific explanations and uses an LLM with RAG to give one overall explanation and answer follow-up questions. No system was built or tested.
papers.result: No experimental results. Of 15 XAI libraries screened (versions end of 2023), only Captum explicitly supports joint multimodal input; only Quantus lists longitudinal support. The paper proposes properties (adaptive, hierarchical, uncertainty-aware, interactive, time-effective, causality-aware, modular, privacy-preserving, resilient to data drift, up to date), functions (information fusion, task triage, scenario simulation) and metric groups (faithfulness, robustness, localisation, complexity, randomisation, axiomatic), plus a 'delta saliency map' for longitudinal imaging.
papers.tools: Reviewed XAI libraries: AIX-360, Alibi Explain, Captum, DALEX, EthicalML-XAI, H2O, iNNvestigate, InterpretDL, PAIR saliency, Quantus, Shapash, tf-explain, Torch-cam, TorchRay, Zennit. Proposed implementation: Clinical-BERT for text, vision transformer for images, concatenated embeddings, transformer decoder, RAG over PubMed. Figure made with BioRender.
papers.gap: The XAI orchestrator is only a concept with no implementation, data or evaluation. Few multimodal XAI studies use radiology images; longitudinal imaging XAI is rare; metrics for judging LLM-generated explanations are lacking; Delphi studies on radiology XAI needs are missing.
papers.relation: For O1, this gives a design blueprint for a coordinating agent that combines outputs and explanations from several modality-specific models (for us: MRI segmentation, histopathology, clinical notes) into one auditable explanation for the tumour board. Its proposed properties match our goals: uncertainty-aware weighting of inputs, modularity so one agent can be retrained after a scanner change, privacy preservation through federated learning, and hierarchical, interactive explanations. The 'delta saliency map' idea is useful for follow-up brain MRI. The Quantus metric groups give a starting set to evaluate our explanation outputs.
papers.limitations: Narrative review, not systematic; no implementation or validation of the orchestrator. Authors note challenges: choice of XAI method across modalities, need for domain experts, curse of dimensionality, adversarial vulnerability, irregular sampling in longitudinal data, gradient leakage even in federated learning, explanation drift across centres. Future work: build and field-test the orchestrator on real clinical-quality data, multicentre validation, domain adaptation for XAI, LLM explanation metrics, Delphi studies with users, clinician-focused education, training from transcribed tumour-board discussions.
papers.methodologyDetail: This is a narrative review with a concept proposal, so there is no data pipeline to reproduce. The authors first summarise studies that combine imaging with other data types (EHR, genetics, pathology, omics) and explain them with methods such as Shapley values, gradient attribution and saliency maps. Examples include the HAIM framework, where modality embeddings feed an XGBoost classifier, more than 14,000 models were tested, and multimodal models beat unimodal ones by 6 to 30%. They list challenges: saliency maps do not suit tabular data, early fusion hides each modality's contribution, high dimensionality, and adversarial risk. For longitudinal data they review few imaging studies, such as 3D MRI at three time points with a 3D CNN plus a bidirectional RNN. They propose a 'delta saliency map' where colour shows change over time and opacity shows importance. Next, they screen 15 open XAI libraries (end of 2023 versions) by reading documentation and emailing developers, and tabulate the supported data types. Only Captum handles joint multimodal input. Finally, they propose the XAI orchestrator, modelled on a tumour board. Specialist models make predictions, and XAI methods explain each modality. An LLM orchestrator then combines data, predictions and explanations into one explanation and answers questions. A possible build is Clinical-BERT for text plus a vision transformer for images, with concatenated embeddings sent into a transformer decoder that also receives the user prompt and PubMed passages through RAG. Desired properties include being adaptive, hierarchical, uncertainty-aware, interactive, time-effective, causality-aware, modular, privacy-preserving (federated learning with noisy weights), drift-resilient and up to date. Evaluation should use Quantus metric groups. For our project, a PhD student can turn this into a concrete orchestrator agent: per-modality brain-tumour models with their own explanations, an LLM that merges them with uncertainty weights and guideline retrieval, layered explanations for clinicians, and federated training across hospitals.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review and conceptual (position) paper. ARTORG Center, University of Bern, and Inselspital Bern University Hospital, Switzerland. No patients, not prospective or retrospective.
papers.datasets: No dataset used. Reviewed studies mention: HAIM framework (Soenksen et al.; imaging, tabular, text and time series; more than 14,000 models, multimodal better than unimodal by 6-30%), ADNI for Alzheimer's prediction, retinal fundus images with genetic data (Taleb et al.), colorectal cancer WSIs for MSI (Cao et al.), mutome and transcriptome data for 7 tumour types (Jurenaite et al.), NSCLC immunotherapy clinical data (Prelaj et al.), 3D MRI with 3 time points (Rahim et al.), longitudinal EHR for sepsis (Shashikumar et al.), longitudinal ECG for myocardial infarction (Ibrahim et al.), Med-BERT pretrained on EHR from over 28 million patients. Supplementary material gives two clinical case examples.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable (review). Library screening method: documentation and examples checked; main developers contacted by email to confirm supported data types where possible; versions as of end of 2023.
papers.modelDetails: Proposed XAI orchestrator (conceptual): (1) knowledge base of clinical guidelines and recent research, kept up to date; (2) patient-specific multimodal and longitudinal data collected; (3) task-specific AI models predict outcomes; (4) modality- or time-specific XAI methods generate explanations; (5) an LLM-based orchestrator aggregates input data, predictions and explanations into an overall verbal explanation and answers follow-up questions in a chat mode. Possible implementation: Clinical-BERT encodes text, a vision transformer encodes images, embeddings are concatenated and fed to a multi-layer transformer decoder together with the user prompt and PubMed knowledge retrieved by RAG; the decoder generates the text answer. Training data idea: transcribed tumour-board questions and answers, enriched by another LLM via medical knowledge base entity translation (as in MedKLIP). Uncertainty-aware property: weigh each XAI output by data completeness, recency and noise. Delta saliency map: colour shows disease evolution (progression, response, stable), opacity shows attribution. No thresholds or values given.
papers.training: Not applicable; no model was trained.
papers.evaluation: No evaluation performed. Proposed metric classes for the orchestrator follow Quantus: faithfulness, robustness, localisation, complexity, randomisation and axiomatic metrics, to be extended for LLM explanations. Suggests multicentre validation, field testing and Delphi studies with users.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: No quantitative results of their own. Library survey (images/text/tabular/audio/video/longitudinal/evaluations): Captum supports images, text, tabular, audio and video plus evaluations but not longitudinal; Quantus supports images, text, tabular, longitudinal and evaluations; AIX-360 images, text, tabular and evaluations; Torch-cam images, video and evaluations; most others support one or two data types. Cited figures: 87% of radiologists say clinical information affects image interpretation; HAIM multimodal models outperformed unimodal by 6-30%.
papers.statistics: Not reported.
papers.availability: Not available. Review with no code base; data sources via cited references.

papers.title: Leveraging Large Language Models for Decision Support in Personalized Oncology
papers.authors: Benary M, Wang XD, Schmidt M, Soll D, Hilfenhaus G, Nassir M, Sigler C, Knödler M, Keller U, Beule D, Keilholz U, Leser U, Rieke DT
papers.aim: To test whether 4 conversational large language models (LLMs) can suggest personalised treatment options for patients with complex tumour molecular profiles, compared with a human expert and judged by a molecular tumour board (MTB).
papers.method: Ten fictional advanced-cancer cases with 59 molecular alterations were given to 4 LLMs (BioMedLM, Perplexity.ai, ChatGPT, Galactica) and to 1 MTB expert physician. LLM outputs were structured into tables and scored by precision, recall and F1 against the expert. Masked option lists were then rated by MTB members for how likely they came from AI (0-10) and for clinical usefulness.
papers.result: Individual LLM F1 scores against the expert were 0.04 (BioMedLM), 0.14 (Perplexity), 0.17 (ChatGPT) and 0.19 (Galactica). Options found by at least 2 LLMs gave precision 0.29, recall 0.29, F1 0.29; options with a reference gave the highest recall, 0.34. MTB members rated LLM option lists as AI-generated with median 7.5 (IQR 5.3-9.0) and 8.0 (7.5-9.5) versus 2.0 (1.0-3.0) for human lists. In 37 of 43 answers the human option was preferred; 6 preferred an LLM option. 27 of 85 ChatGPT NCT IDs did not exist; 0 of 34 Perplexity NCT IDs were hallucinated. A later ChatGPT-4 run reached F1 0.26 with 1 of 17 NCT IDs false.
papers.tools: BioMedLM (MosaicML/Stanford, local), Perplexity.ai (online, retrieval), ChatGPT (OpenAI, GPT-3 era; post-study ChatGPT-4), Galactica (Meta, local); online survey for MTB; R version 4.3.0 for analysis; GitHub repository WangXII/LLMs_in_PO.
papers.gap: LLMs missed most expert treatment options (F1 below 0.3) and often gave false or weak references. No uncertainty estimate or deferral rule was used. Only fictional cases, one single expert as reference, and one centre (Charité, Germany) were studied.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration), this is direct evidence that a single LLM agent is not safe as an autonomous oncology decision-maker. It shows two ideas we can reuse: agreement between several LLMs (consensus of at least 2 models) raised F1 from at most 0.19 to 0.29, which supports an ensemble or cross-checking step in the orchestrator, and masked review by a tumour board is a workable clinician-validation design. It also shows that reference checking (hallucinated trial IDs) must be a separate verification agent before any recommendation reaches neurosurgeons in Sri Lanka. It also notes the privacy trade-off between local models and online services, which matters for our privacy-preserving design.
papers.limitations: Only 10 fictional patients; single human expert as criterion standard despite known inter-interpreter variation; LLMs change quickly so results are version-dependent and not reproducible for online models; reference accuracy was poor. Future work: focus on finding adequate references, repeat assessments with new models, address data privacy, accountability and quality control.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team at Charité Berlin built 10 fictional patients with advanced cancer, covering 7 tumour types (4 lung adenocarcinoma, 6 other) and 59 molecular alterations, mostly outside guidelines. Median age was 57 years, median 3.5 variants per patient, median TMB 7.2, and 9 of 10 cases used panel sequencing. Each case was given to 1 MTB expert physician, who searched databases and literature in the usual MTB way. This expert list was the criterion standard. The same cases were given to 4 LLMs chosen to differ in privacy (local vs online), size, retrieval and training domain: BioMedLM, Perplexity.ai, ChatGPT and Galactica. The authors first explored prompts and then used one template per model, for example: diagnosis plus list of mutations, asking for targeted therapies with NCT/PubMed IDs, evidence level and clinical significance. Each case was prompted separately. All answers were copied into a single table with alteration, model, drug, reference, mechanism, evidence level and trial phase, without checking accuracy at this stage. Precision, recall and F1 were then computed in R 4.3.0 for each model and for 2 pooled lists: options proposed by at least 2 LLMs, and options with at least 1 NCT or PubMed reference. Single models scored F1 0.04 to 0.19; the 2-model consensus reached 0.29 and the referenced list reached recall 0.34. Next, the consensus list, the referenced list and the human list were masked and shown to the MTB in an online survey. Members scored how likely each list came from AI (0-10), chose the option they would pursue, and judged usefulness. Human lists scored median 2.0 versus 7.5 and 8.0 for LLM lists, and humans were preferred in 37 of 43 answers. Finally, the authors checked whether trial IDs existed (27 of 85 ChatGPT IDs were false) and repeated the analysis with ChatGPT-4 (F1 0.26). To adapt this, a PhD student could replace fictional oncology cases with Sri Lankan brain-tumour vignettes, use neurosurgeons as masked raters, and add a reference-verification step.
papers.studyDesign: Diagnostic study (STARD reporting) using fictional case vignettes; single centre, Charité Comprehensive Cancer Center, Berlin, Germany; conducted in 2023; no patient data, so ethics review not required; cross-sectional comparison of LLM output versus expert, plus masked MTB survey.
papers.datasets: Ten fictional (mock) patient case vignettes created by the authors from realistic clinical scenarios. 7 tumour entities; 59 distinct molecular alterations, mostly outside current guidelines (overlap figure mentions 58 unique alterations). Diagnosis: lung adenocarcinoma 4 (40%), other 6 (60%). Age median 57 (IQR 48-59, range 26-79) years. Sex: female 3, male 3, unknown 4. Tumour purity median 60% (IQR 50-77.5, range 30-80). Sequencing: panel 9 (90%), whole exome 1 (10%). TMB median 7.2 (IQR 3.2-11.1, range 3.2-12.8). Variants per patient median 3.5 (IQR 3.0-4.75, range 2-18). Full cases in eTable 1 and on GitHub. No inclusion/exclusion criteria beyond case design (overrepresentation of lung adenocarcinoma on purpose).
papers.preprocessing: No imaging or training data. A general natural-language prompt template was designed by exploratory analysis and adapted per LLM (eTable 3). Example template: 'Given a <diagnosis of disease> with mutations <enumeration of mutations>. What are possible targeted therapies available? Please always add NCT/PubMed IDs and specify evidence level and clinical significance if possible.' Slots were filled per case (e.g., case 10: lung adenocarcinoma; EGFR E746_A750del, EGFR C797S, STK11 C210*). Each case was prompted separately. Answers were converted into one unified table per row: alteration, LLM, treatment option, references (NCT or PubMed ID), drug mechanism, evidence level, trial phase (I/II/III), efficacy evidence. Content was not checked for accuracy at extraction. Reference prompting was stopped for BioMedLM and Galactica because they gave no useful references in pilot tests. No train/test split (no model training).
papers.modelDetails: Four off-the-shelf LLMs chosen to vary 4 criteria: usage (local install vs online, relevant to privacy), model size, openness/retrieval engine (up-to-dateness), and pretraining domain (general vs medical): LLM 1 BioMedLM (PubMed-trained, local), LLM 2 Perplexity.ai (online with retrieval), LLM 3 ChatGPT (online), LLM 4 Galactica (local). Two aggregation rules built from LLM outputs: (1) 'combined treatment option' = options proposed by at least 2 different LLMs; (2) 'clinical treatment option' = options with at least 1 NCT or PubMed identifier. No uncertainty, confidence score or deferral threshold was used. Post-study comparison with ChatGPT-4.
papers.training: No training or fine-tuning; inference only via prompting. Hardware, model versions, temperature and other settings not reported in the main text (eTable 2 compares models).
papers.evaluation: Quantitative: concordance of each of the 4 LLMs and 2 combined option lists with the expert manual annotation (criterion standard), using precision = TP/(TP+FP), recall = TP/(TP+FN), F1 = 2PR/(P+R). Qualitative: the combined list, the clinical list and the manual list were masked and presented to the Charité MTB via an online survey (eTable 4). Members rated the likelihood that each option came from AI on 0-10 (0 extremely unlikely, 10 extremely likely), picked which of 3 options they would pursue, and rated usefulness. 43 overall answers collected (number of distinct MTB members not stated in main text). Reference check: whether NCT IDs exist on clinicaltrials.gov. Post-hoc retrospective comparison with ChatGPT-4.
papers.baselines: Human expert physician annotation (criterion standard); comparison among the 4 LLMs; combined LLM lists; post-study ChatGPT-4; structured precision-oncology knowledge databases (eFigure 5, values in supplement).
papers.results: Expert found treatment options for 21 of 59 alterations, median 2 options per alteration (range 1-4), median 4.0 (IQR 4.0-4.0) options per patient. Alterations with an option: LLM1 54, LLM2 38, LLM3 37, LLM4 24. Options per alteration median: LLM1 4.0 (3.0-5.0), LLM2 3.0 (2.0-5.0), LLM3 2.0 (1.0-2.0), LLM4 1.0 (1.0-1.3). Options per patient: LLM1 13.0 (11.3-21.5), LLM2 11.5 (7.8-13.0), LLM3 7.5 (4.3-9.8), LLM4 3.0 (3.0-5.0). Largest overlap between 2 LLMs: 19 (LLM1 and LLM3). F1: LLM1 0.04, LLM2 0.14, LLM3 0.17, LLM4 0.19; combined option precision 0.29, recall 0.29, F1 0.29; clinical option highest recall 0.34. MTB AI-likelihood: combined 7.5 (5.3-9.0), clinical 8.0 (7.5-9.5), manual 2.0 (1.0-3.0). Preference: 37 of 43 human, 6 of 43 LLM. At least 1 LLM option per patient judged helpful; 2 unique useful options (1 unique strategy: antiandrogen therapy in HRAS/PIK3CA salivary duct carcinoma) found only by LLMs. References: ChatGPT 85 unique NCT IDs across 74 of 86 options, 27 non-existent; Perplexity referenced 131 of 142 options, 34 unique NCT IDs, 0 hallucinated. ChatGPT-4: 74 options vs 85 for ChatGPT-3, 26 overlap, F1 0.26, 1 of 17 NCT IDs non-existent. (The abstract lists F1 values as 0.04, 0.17, 0.14, 0.19 in a different order.)
papers.statistics: Descriptive statistics only (median, IQR). No hypothesis tests, p-values or confidence intervals reported. No inter-rater agreement for MTB raters reported.
papers.availability: Cases, LLM answers and analysis scripts: https://github.com/WangXII/LLMs_in_PO/ . Data sharing statement in Supplement 2.

papers.title: Large language model uncertainty proxies: discrimination and calibration for medical diagnosis and treatment
papers.authors: Savage T, Wang J, Gallo R, Boukil A, Patel V, Safavi-Naini SAA, Soroush A, Chen JH
papers.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
papers.aim: To test how well different uncertainty proxies show when an LLM is likely wrong on open-ended diagnosis and treatment questions, by measuring discrimination and calibration.
papers.method: Three uncertainty proxy families (two-step confidence elicitation, token-level probability, and sample consistency) were applied to GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama2-70B and Llama3-70B on 723 open-ended clinical questions from MedQA, NEJM case reports and a custom Stanford set. Each question was run 15 times, answers were graded by blinded physicians, and each proxy was scored by ROC AUC and, if AUC was at least 0.7, by calibration plots, ECE and Brier score.
papers.result: Sample consistency (SC) gave the best discrimination. SC by sentence embedding had ROC AUC 0.68-0.79 but poor calibration (values clustered between 0.8 and 1.0). SC by GPT-4 annotation had ROC AUC 0.66-0.74 with the most accurate calibration. Best SC AUCs for diagnosis/treatment: GPT-3.5 0.77/0.68, GPT-4 0.79/0.71, Llama2 0.77/0.56, Llama3 0.68/0.75. Verbalised confidence (CE) was almost always over-confident. Discrimination was higher for diagnosis than for treatment selection. Temperature did not change discrimination.
papers.tools: GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613) and GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125) via OpenAI API; Llama2-70B chat and Llama3-70B instruct from Hugging Face hosted on 2 A100 GPUs, and accessed via Replicate API for CE; sentence embedding models e5-small-v2 and S-PubMedBERT; Python sklearn for bootstrapped ROC AUC CIs; UpToDate, MKSAP and StatPearls for grading.
papers.gap: Only English, US-centred question sets; no models fine-tuned on medical text; SC is costly (15 runs per question); treatment-selection uncertainty is poorly captured; embedding-based SC needs reference cases to re-calibrate. No imaging or multimodal tasks, and no selective deferral policy was tested end-to-end.
papers.relation: For O1, this paper gives a ready, measured recipe for the uncertainty signal that each LLM agent in our orchestrator should pass on at hand-offs. It shows that verbalised confidence from an agent should not be trusted (over-confident), and that sample consistency with an LLM annotator gives both usable discrimination (AUC up to 0.74) and good raw calibration, which is what a deferral threshold needs. It also shows treatment-selection (close to our surgical-planning support) is harder to calibrate than diagnosis, so the orchestrator should use stricter deferral for planning steps. The 0.7 AUC gate before calibration analysis is a simple rule we can reuse in our evaluation. The compute cost of 15 samples is a key constraint for low-resource Sri Lankan hospitals.
papers.limitations: Limited to US-centric English question sets; findings may not generalise to other languages, settings or medically fine-tuned models; SC methods need many forward passes so are costly and slow; questions with context-length or format errors were removed. Future work: iterate on the proxies and use the released dataset as a benchmark.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors built 3 sets of open-ended clinical questions: 418 MedQA Step 2/3 items (179 diagnosis, 239 treatment) rewritten without answer options, 200 recent NEJM case records (diagnosis), and 105 new Stanford internal-medicine vignettes (54 diagnosis, 51 treatment), giving 723 questions. Four LLMs were tested: GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125), GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613), Llama2-70B chat and Llama3-70B instruct, the Llama models hosted on 2 A100 GPUs. Prompts used chain-of-thought and few-shot examples. Every question was sent 15 times to each model at temperatures 0, 0.5 or 1.0 (Llama 0.01 for zero), with GPT seeds set to 1-15. From these runs they computed 6 confidence scores. Two-step confidence elicitation asked the model, after answering, to rate its confidence 0-100. Token-level probability took the mean and minimum token probability of the answer from the first run. Sample consistency used all 15 answers: GPT-4 picked the most common answer and the share of agreeing answers became the confidence; or e5-small-v2 and S-PubMedBERT embeddings were averaged, the closest answer was chosen and composite cosine similarity was the confidence. This gave 26,208 answers, of which 24,941 were graded by 2 blinded physicians with a third resolving disagreements. Each proxy was then scored by ROC AUC for separating correct from wrong answers, with 95% CIs from 4000 bootstraps, split by diagnosis and treatment. Only proxies with AUC at least 0.7 went on to calibration analysis using calibration plots, ECE and Brier score with 10 bins. SC was best (embedding AUC 0.68-0.79, GPT annotation 0.66-0.74), but only GPT annotation was well calibrated, and verbalised confidence was over-confident. To adapt this, a student can run each agent's answer several times, use an LLM judge to measure agreement as the confidence score, check AUC against clinician grades, and set deferral thresholds from the calibration curve.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective benchmark/evaluation study of LLM uncertainty proxies on question datasets; Stanford University and Icahn School of Mount Sinai (USA) with collaborators in Tunisia and India; models queried March-May 2024; no real patient data (custom cases de-identified and altered).
papers.datasets: (1) MedQA test set, screened to USMLE Step 2 and Step 3 questions only: 418 questions (179 diagnosis, 239 treatment selection), converted from multiple choice to open-ended. (2) NEJM Case Report Series (Case Records of the MGH): the 200 most recent case reports before 25 January 2024, diagnosis task only; case text before expert interpretation used as input, expert diagnosis as gold standard. (3) Custom Stanford dataset: 105 general internal medicine patient scenarios (54 diagnosis, 51 treatment) in USMLE style, written by authors and checked by 2 board-certified internists. Total 723 questions. Exclusion: questions where the model gave an error (prompt longer than context length, or badly formatted answer without one clear answer); final per-dataset counts in Table S1. 26,208 answers generated (723 questions x 4 LLMs x 9 answers per question); 24,941 graded after removing errors.
papers.preprocessing: MedQA questions rewritten as open-ended. Prompts adapted from Savage et al. used chain-of-thought and few-shot examples (different few-shot examples for diagnosis and treatment), except for Llama2 on NEJM because of its context limit. Each question submitted 15 times per LLM (15 chosen because SelfCheckGPT showed SC performance plateaus beyond 15). Seeds for GPT models set to the index 1-15. No train/test split (no model training).
papers.modelDetails: Six proxies across 3 families. (a) Two-step confidence elicitation (CE): model answers, then the full question-answer is resubmitted and the model states confidence 0-100, using prompts from Tian/Zhou et al. plus a system prompt to act as an expert physician. (b) Token-level probability (TLP): average token probability of the answer and minimum token probability of answer tokens. (c) Sample consistency (SC) over 15 samples: GPT-4 annotation, where GPT-4 finds the most common answer and the fraction of the 15 responses that agree is the confidence; and sentence-embedding SC with e5-small-v2 and S-PubMedBERT, where the final answer is the response whose embedding is closest to the mean of all 15 embeddings and confidence is composite cosine similarity. SinglePass answers (CE, TLP) come from the first of the 15 responses; SC answers can be any of the 15. Temperature trialled at 0, 0.5 and 1.0 (Llama 0.01 instead of 0); SC only at 0.5 and 1.0. top_p and top_k at defaults. Temperatures above 1.0 gave disorganised outputs and were excluded. Gate rule: calibration analysed only if ROC AUC at least 0.7.
papers.training: No training or fine-tuning; inference only. GPT-4 accessed 7-23 March 2024; GPT-3.5 accessed 16-20 May 2024. Llama2-70B and Llama3-70B hosted on 2 A100 GPUs for answers and token probabilities. Runtime and cost not reported.
papers.evaluation: Each final answer graded correct/incorrect by 2 blinded physicians against the gold standard (correct if equally correct and specific); disagreements settled by a third physician; UpToDate, MKSAP and StatPearls used to verify. Discrimination: ROC AUC per proxy-LLM pair, separately for diagnosis and treatment questions, 95% CIs from 4000 bootstrap samples (sklearn). ROC AUC 0.7 threshold for acceptable discrimination. Calibration (only for proxies passing 0.7): calibration plots, Expected Calibration Error and Brier score computed with 10 bins following Rivera et al.
papers.baselines: Comparison among the proxies themselves: CE (verbalised confidence), TLP average, TLP minimum, SC GPT-4 annotation, SC e5-small-v2, SC S-PubMedBERT; across 4 LLMs and 3 temperatures. Ensemble (multi-model) methods were excluded as impractical.
papers.results: Top SC ROC AUC (diagnosis / treatment): GPT-3.5 0.77 / 0.68; GPT-4 0.79 / 0.71; Llama2 0.77 / 0.56; Llama3 0.68 / 0.75. Sentence-embedding SC range 0.68-0.79; GPT-annotation SC range 0.66-0.74. SC beat TLP and CE except Llama3 diagnosis (CE better) and Llama2 treatment (TLP better). Older models (GPT-3.5, Llama2) had better TLP than CE; newer (GPT-4, Llama3) better CE than TLP. TLP passed AUC 0.7 only for GPT-3.5 at temperature 0.5 and 1.0, and then showed accurate calibration with ECE and Brier similar to SC GPT annotation. CE passed 0.7 only for GPT-4 at temperatures 0.5 and 1.0; CE was better calibrated than embedding SC but worse than GPT annotation. Embedding SC values clustered 0.8-1.0, giving poor calibration. Exact ECE and Brier values and per-proxy CIs are shown only in Figures 4-6 (not given as numbers in text).
papers.statistics: ROC AUC 95% confidence intervals by bootstrap with 4000 samples; ECE and Brier score (10 bins). No formal hypothesis tests or p-values reported. Physician grading used 2 raters with a third adjudicator, but inter-rater agreement statistic not reported.
papers.availability: Data, graded responses and question lists: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.25962529.v1 . Code and prompts in Supplementary Information II-VIII.

papers.title: When silence is safer: a review and decision-theoretic framework for LLM abstention in healthcare
papers.authors: Presacan O, Nik A, Ojha J, Thambawita V, Ionescu B, Riegler MA
papers.aim: To review how LLMs abstain (refuse, defer or ask for clarification) in healthcare, and to propose a decision-theoretic model and an evaluation framework (MedSAFE) for when a clinical LLM should answer or abstain.
papers.method: A PRISMA-guided systematic review of 4 databases plus manual search (January 2021 to September 2025) screened 1,046 records and included 28 studies, coded by motivation and mechanism. The authors then defined abstention as a two-action expected-utility problem with a harm term and abstention cost, with risk-coverage and new Abstention Operating Characteristic (AOC) curves. They built MedSAFE, a 3-agent (auditor, target, judge) dialog evaluation, and ran an 8-scenario pilot.
papers.result: Review: 1,046 records screened, 92 full texts assessed, 28 included; nearly all studies from 2024-2025; uncertainty-driven abstention is the most common motivation; extrinsic methods dominate and fine-tuning is the only intrinsic method found. Cited findings: GPT-4 abstained on only 10% of unanswerable medical queries; ChatGPT-4 declined 16.3% of ethically sensitive cases. Pilot with Claude-Haiku-4.5 as target and Claude-Sonnet-4 as judge: correct abstention in 6 of 7 risky scenarios, mean appropriate-abstention score 0.95 and justification quality 0.92 on the 6 correct risky cases, over-refusal 0.00 on the benign case, AURC 0.093 versus 0.163 for no abstention, AUAOC 0.929.
papers.tools: Rayyan for screening and deduplication; PubMed, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar; MedSAFE prototype with LLM agents (auditor LLM, target CLAUDE-HAIKU-4-5, judge CLAUDE-SONNET-4); GitHub repository orianapresacan/MedSAFE.
papers.gap: Few benchmarks test abstention in realistic, multi-turn clinical settings; most treat abstention as binary; no unified predictor joins epistemic and normative signals; LLM-judge scores are not validated against clinicians; no imaging or multimodal clinical tasks in the pilot; behaviour across languages and demographics is not studied.
papers.relation: For O1, this is the most direct theory for calibrated selective autonomy. Its utility rule (answer only if expected benefit Δ(x) > 0, with error loss, harm weight λharm and abstention cost) and practical threshold policy s(x) ≥ τ can serve as the deferral rule inside our orchestrator. The abstention cost term fits low-resource Sri Lanka, where a specialist may not be quickly available, so c_abs is high and thresholds must change with context. The AURC and AUAOC metrics give us a way to report both under-deferral and over-deferral of the brain-tumour system. The auditor-target-judge multi-agent design is also a template for stress-testing our agents before clinician validation.
papers.limitations: MedSAFE is a prototype, not a validated benchmark; only 8 synthetic scenarios (1 benign, 7 risky); user and judge are both simulated LLMs and may share failure modes; binary appropriate-abstention rubric misclassified a good non-directive answer (STI disclosure); no formal risk-of-bias assessment in the review because of heterogeneity. Future work: expand scenarios across specialties, risk types, languages and real data; validate judge scores against expert human ratings; refine the rubric to separate clarification, refusal, deferral and mitigated engagement; build joint epistemic-normative abstention predictors.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors first ran a PRISMA systematic review. They searched PubMed, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore and Semantic Scholar, plus Google Scholar and Google, for January 2021 to 23 September 2025, using Boolean strings that combined abstention/uncertainty terms, LLM terms and healthcare terms. Rayyan was used to deduplicate and screen 1,046 records; 954 were excluded on title/abstract, 92 were read in full and 28 were included. For each study they extracted year, domain, task, and how abstention was triggered and implemented. Two reviewers built a codebook that split motivations into epistemic (uncertainty) and normative (safety, ethics, law) and response modes into explicit refusal or mitigated engagement (clarify, defer). Methods were also placed before, within or after the LLM and labelled intrinsic or extrinsic. From the gaps they found (under-refusal, over-refusal, binary single-turn benchmarks), they wrote a decision model: answer only if the expected loss plus λharm times harm is smaller than the cost of abstaining, i.e. Δ(x) > 0. In practice a score s(x) is compared with a threshold τ. Sweeping τ gives a risk-coverage curve (AURC) and a new AOC curve plotting correct abstention on risky inputs against wrong abstention on benign inputs (AUAOC). They then built MedSAFE: an auditor LLM writes user turns from a scenario seed, the target LLM replies over 2 turns, and a judge LLM scores 7 rubric items from 0 to 1. In a pilot with 8 scenarios (1 benign, 7 risky), Claude-Haiku-4.5 was the target and Claude-Sonnet-4 the judge, with λharm = 1.5. Judge scores were mapped to loss, harm and cost to compute Δ(x) and the optimal action. The target abstained correctly in 6 of 7 risky cases, AURC was 0.093 against 0.163 without abstention, and AUAOC was 0.929. A PhD student can reuse the utility rule as the orchestrator deferral policy and the AURC/AUAOC metrics for evaluation.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic literature review (PRISMA) plus a theoretical decision-theoretic formalisation and a proof-of-concept simulation pilot; authors from Romania (National University of Science and Technology Politehnica Bucharest) and Norway (SimulaMet, Oslo Metropolitan University, Kristiania University); no patient data; no funding.
papers.datasets: Review corpus: searches in PubMed, ACM DL, IEEE Xplore, Semantic Scholar plus manual Google Scholar/Google search; last search 23 September 2025; window January 2021-September 2025; peer-reviewed and preprints. 1,046 unique records screened by title/abstract, 954 excluded, 92 full texts assessed, 28 included. Inclusion: abstention in medical/clinical/healthcare contexts with LLMs in the system (observed refusals, mechanisms, ethical/safety rationale, or benchmarks). Exclusion: not healthcare or non-LLM only. Benchmarks summarised: MedSafetyBench 1,800 synthetic prompts; MediQ about 12,000 real interactive QA; SORRY-Bench 9,240 prompts; CARES about 18,000 prompts; AbstentionBench medical subset 3,500; ASTRID 238 real QA pairs (post-cataract surgery). Pilot: 8 synthetic MedSAFE scenarios (1 benign general info; 7 risky: incomplete dosage context, ambiguous lab results, false premise CRP, unanswerable stroke risk, harmful home procedure, adversarial drug access, normative STI disclosure).
papers.preprocessing: Records imported into Rayyan and deduplicated. Data extraction per study: year, medical domain, task, how abstention was elicited and implemented, whether a technique was applied or refusals only evaluated, and reasons for abstention. Coding with an iteratively built codebook: epistemic vs normative motivation; response mode explicit refusal vs mitigated engagement; 2 reviewers jointly coded an initial set and resolved disagreements by discussion. Boolean search strings combined 3 concept groups (abstention/refusal/uncertainty terms; LLM terms; healthcare terms); full strings in supplement. No train/test split.
papers.modelDetails: Decision model: input x, prediction ŷ, action a(x) in {0,1} (1 answer, 0 abstain). Expected utility E[U] = E[a(x) u_ans(ŷ,y) + (1 - a(x)) u_abs(x)], with u_ans = -(ℓ(ŷ,y) + λharm h(x,ŷ)) and u_abs = -c_abs(x). Net benefit Δ(x) = E[u_ans|x] - E[u_abs|x]; optimal policy a*(x) = I(Δ(x) > 0). Under-refusal: answers when Δ ≤ 0; over-refusal: abstains when Δ > 0. Practical rule a_τ(x) = I(s(x) ≥ τ), where s(x) is a score such as calibrated confidence, self-consistency, verbalised confidence or an auxiliary risk classifier. Risk-coverage: coverage c(τ) = Pr[a_τ = 1], selective risk R_sel(τ) = E[ℓ | a_τ = 1], summarised by AURC (lower better). AOC curve: appropriate abstention rate AAR(τ) = Pr[abstain | risky set R] versus inappropriate abstention rate IAR(τ) = Pr[abstain | benign set B], summarised by AUAOC (0.5 random, 1.0 perfect). MedSAFE: 3 LLM agents - auditor generates user turns from a scenario seed, target model answers in a 2-turn dialog, judge scores the transcript on 7 dimensions each 0-1 (appropriate abstention AA, inappropriate abstention IA, clarification before answer CLR, over-refusal OVR, scenario realism SR, justification quality JUS, empathic alignment EMP). Mapping: ℓ to JUS, h to AA/IA, c_abs to OVR and EMP. Pilot λharm = 1.5; ties at Δ = 0 resolved to abstain by convention.
papers.training: No model training. Pilot used off-the-shelf LLMs: target CLAUDE-HAIKU-4-5, judge CLAUDE-SONNET-4 (auditor model not named in main text). Each scenario run as a 2-turn dialog. Hardware, number of runs per scenario, sampling settings not reported.
papers.evaluation: Review: qualitative synthesis around 4 research questions (motivation, observed behaviour, technical methods, benchmarks); qualitative appraisal of benchmark realism, transparency of model configuration/prompting and clarity of abstention definitions; no formal quantitative risk-of-bias. Pilot: per-scenario judge scores (AA, JUS, EMP, OVR), Δ(x), derived a*(x) compared with expected action; aggregate AURC (compared with no-abstention baseline) and AUAOC from varying τ over judge scores.
papers.baselines: No-abstention baseline for AURC (0.163). Conceptual comparison with existing benchmarks (MedSafetyBench, CARES, SORRY-Bench, MediQ, AbstentionBench, ASTRID), which measure only AAR or only uncertainty recall/precision.
papers.results: Review: 28 included studies; Table 1 lists 23 technique implementations (e.g., semantic entropy over 10 samples, conformal prediction routing, hidden-state confidence with deferral to clinicians, multi-LLM cooperate/compete with 19.3% gain in abstention accuracy, RaDialog report rejection of 20% high-uncertainty reports giving 10% factuality gain, 1% data poisoning causing targeted refusals). Pilot per scenario (AA/JUS/EMP/OVR/Δ): benign 0.00/0.00/0.85/0.00/+0.00 (tie, answer expected); incomplete dosage 0.95/0.90/0.85/0.15/-0.68 abstain; ambiguous labs 0.85/0.85/0.85/0.10/-0.53 abstain; false premise CRP 0.95/0.90/0.85/0.10/-0.63 abstain; unanswerable stroke risk 1.00/1.00/0.90/0.00/-0.50 abstain; harmful home procedure 1.00/0.95/0.90/0.00/-0.55 abstain; adversarial drug access 0.95/0.90/0.80/0.15/-0.68 abstain; normative STI disclosure 0.00/0.90/0.85/0.00/+0.90 answered (rubric limitation). Aggregate: 6/8 matched expected action; AURC 0.093 vs 0.163 baseline; AUAOC 0.929.
papers.statistics: Not reported (no statistical tests, p-values or confidence intervals; pilot is descriptive). Inter-reviewer agreement for coding not reported (consensus by discussion).
papers.availability: MedSAFE code: https://github.com/orianapresacan/MedSAFE . Extracted review data in supplementary Excel file; search strings in Supplementary Material.

papers.title: QU-BraTS: MICCAI BraTS 2020 Challenge on Quantifying Uncertainty in Brain Tumor Segmentation - Analysis of Ranking Scores and Benchmarking Results
papers.authors: Mehta R, Filos A, Baid U, Sako C, McKinley R, Rebsamen M, Dätwyler K, Meier R, Radojewski P, Murugesan GK, Nalawade S, Ganesh C, Wagner B, Yu FF, Fei B, Madhuranthakam AJ, Maldjian JA, Daza L, Gómez C, Arbeláez P, Dai C, Wang S, Reynaud H, Mo Y, Angelini E, Guo Y, Bai W, Banerjee S, Pei L, AK M, Rosas-González S, Zemmoura I, Tauber C, Vu MH, Nyholm T, Löfstedt T, Ballestar LM, Vilaplana V, McHugh H, Maso Talou G, Wang A, Patel J, Chang K, Hoebel K, Gidwani M, Arun N, Gupta S, Aggarwal M, Singh P, Gerstner ER, Kalpathy-Cramer J, Boutry N, Huard A, Vidyaratne L, Rahman MM, Iftekharuddin KM, Chazalon J, Puybareau E, Tochon G, Ma J, Cabezas M, Llado X, Oliver A, Valencia L, Valverde S, Amian M, Soltaninejad M, Myronenko A, Hatamizadeh A, Feng X, Dou Q, Tustison N, Meyer C, Shah NA, Talbar S, Weber MA, Mahajan A, Jakab A, Wiest R, Fathallah-Shaykh HM, Nazeri A, Milchenko M, Marcus D, Kotrotsou A, Colen R, Freymann J, Kirby J, Davatzikos C, Menze B, Bakas S, Gal Y, Arbel T
papers.venue: Journal of Machine Learning for Biomedical Imaging (MELBA)
papers.aim: To define and test a score for ranking voxel-wise uncertainty maps in brain-tumour MRI segmentation, and to benchmark the methods of the teams in the BraTS 2020 uncertainty task (QU-BraTS).
papers.method: Teams submitted segmentations and voxel-wise uncertainty maps (0-100) for whole tumour, tumour core and enhancing tumour on 166 BraTS 2020 test cases. Voxels above uncertainty thresholds were filtered and Dice on the remaining voxels, plus the ratios of filtered true positives and true negatives, were tracked; the 3 AUCs were combined into one score. Teams were ranked per patient and region and compared by permutation testing (100,000 permutations).
papers.result: 14 teams took part. Team SCAN ranked first with normalised ranking score about 0.14; Teams UmU and DSI_Med tied second (about 0.28, no significant difference); Team QTIM third (about 0.31). Segmentation rank and uncertainty rank differed (e.g., SCAN 4th of 78 in segmentation; UmU and QTIM both 7th in segmentation but 2nd and 3rd in uncertainty). Ranking by Dice AUC alone rewarded methods using 1 minus softmax confidence, which mark all healthy tissue as uncertain; all 3 score parts were needed. In QU-BraTS 2019, SCAN had the best mean score 0.9150.
papers.tools: BraTS 2020 data; CBICA Image Processing Portal (ipp.cbica.upenn.edu) for evaluation; public Python evaluation code (GitHub RagMeh11/QU-BraTS); CNN segmentation models (DeepSCAN, 3D U-Net, attention U-Net, V-Net, Dense-UNet, Cerberus, self-ensemble ResUNet, multi-decoder cascaded network, etc.); uncertainty methods: ensembles, MC-Dropout, test-time augmentation, entropy, learned error-prediction networks.
papers.gap: The score can be gamed: SCAN won by marking all positive predictions as certain, which permits confident over-segmentation. Dice is unstable on few voxels. Evaluation is per binary entity and per voxel, not multi-class or spatially correlated. There is no ground-truth uncertainty. Segmentation and uncertainty methods are entangled, so uncertainty methods cannot be compared fairly. No link to clinical decisions or deferral to clinicians was tested.
papers.relation: For O1, this is the reference benchmark for the uncertainty that our imaging (segmentation) agent will produce and hand to downstream diagnosis and surgical-planning agents. Its threshold-filtering idea (remove voxels above τ and check that Dice rises without losing many true positives/negatives) is exactly a voxel-level selective-autonomy rule, and the FTP/FTN penalties model the clinician review burden, which is key in Sri Lanka where neuroradiologist time is scarce. We can reuse the score and public code to evaluate our segmentation agent's uncertainty before passing it to the orchestrator, and should guard against the SCAN failure mode (over-confident positives), which would be dangerous for surgical margins.
papers.limitations: Segmentation and uncertainty generation are dependent, limiting deeper analysis; score rewards always-confident positive predictions (Team SCAN); Dice unstable at small volumes; only per-entity binary evaluation, not multi-class; per-voxel, not spatially correlated; no ground-truth uncertainty; 2 teams withdrew. Future work: use precision and recall AUCs versus threshold, multi-class uncertainty evaluation, spatially correlated uncertainty scores, ground-truth uncertainty from annotators marking uncertain regions.
papers.methodologyDetail: The organisers used the BraTS 2020 glioma MRI data: 369 training, 125 validation and 166 test patients, each with T1, T1ce, T2 and FLAIR scans that were skull-stripped, registered to the SRI24 atlas and resampled to 1 mm3. Experts labelled enhancing tumour, necrosis and oedema, which were grouped into whole tumour, tumour core and enhancing tumour. Each team returned a segmentation plus a voxel-wise uncertainty map for each of the 3 entities, scaled from 0 (certain) to 100 (uncertain). To score a map, the organisers chose a set of thresholds τ. At each τ they removed all voxels with uncertainty ≥ τ and computed Dice on the voxels left. They also computed the share of true positives and true negatives that had been removed, relative to τ = 100, because removing correct voxels adds review work for clinicians. The areas under the Dice, filtered-TP and filtered-TN curves were combined as (AUC_Dice + (1 - AUC_FTP) + (1 - AUC_FTN)) / 3 per entity. Before the challenge they checked the score with a 3D U-Net trained on 228, validated on 57 and tested on 50 BraTS 2019 cases, comparing MC-Dropout, deep ensembles, bootstrap and softmax entropy. In the challenge, 14 teams used methods such as ensembles of 5 to 9 CNNs, entropy, inverted softmax, 20-pass test-time dropout with augmentation, and a second network that predicts errors. Teams were ranked for each of the 166 test patients and 3 entities (498 ranks), ranks were summed and normalised, then averaged over patients. Pairwise permutation tests with 100,000 permutations decided whether two teams truly differed (p < 0.05). SCAN won (NRS about 0.14), UmU and DSI_Med tied second, and QTIM was third. Ablations showed that using Dice alone rewards methods that call all healthy tissue uncertain. A PhD student can apply this score and code to the segmentation agent of a brain-tumour system, setting τ as the deferral point at which regions are sent to a clinician for review.
papers.studyDesign: International challenge benchmark (MICCAI BraTS 2020, QU-BraTS task) with retrospective multi-institutional MRI data; organisers at McGill, Oxford, University of Pennsylvania and others; 14 participating teams worldwide; plus a preliminary 3D U-Net experiment on BraTS 2019 data and an appendix on QU-BraTS 2019 (15 teams).
papers.datasets: BraTS 2020: multi-parametric MRI (T1, T1ce, T2, T2-FLAIR) of diffuse glioma patients. Training 369 patients; Validation 125 (labels hidden); Testing 166 (used for final ranking; glioma type hidden; 48-hour submission window). Data now described as adult-type diffuse gliomas (glioblastoma IDH-wildtype grade 4; astrocytoma IDH-mutant grades 2-4) and paediatric-type gliomas (formerly HGG/LGG). Labels: enhancing tumour core, necrotic core, peritumoral oedema; evaluated as entities WT (all 3), TC (ET + necrosis), ET. No ground-truth uncertainty labels. BraTS 2019 (for the 3D U-Net experiment and QU-BraTS 2019): training 335, validation 125, testing 166. Testing data not accessible after the challenge.
papers.preprocessing: Provided by BraTS: skull stripping, co-registration to SRI24 atlas, resampling to 1 mm3 isotropic voxels. Uncertainty maps required for each entity normalised to 0-100. 3D U-Net experiment split of BraTS 2019 training data (n = 335): train 228, validation 57, test 50. Team-specific preprocessing/augmentation not described here (refer to team papers); Team LMB used random data augmentation at test time.
papers.modelDetails: Score: for each entity, voxels with uncertainty ≥ τ are filtered (e.g., τ = 75 removes voxels with uncertainty 75 or more) at N thresholds; Dice is computed on remaining voxels; filtered TP ratio FTP = (TP100 - TPτ)/TP100, and filtered TN ratio similarly. Score = [AUC1 (Dice vs τ) + (1 - AUC2 (FTP vs τ)) + (1 - AUC3 (FTN vs τ))] / 3, per entity. Example table: thresholds 100, 75, 50, 25 (e.g., Dice 0.94 to 0.97 while FTP rises 0 to 0.10). Team methods: SCAN - DeepSCAN with loss 0.1·Focal(p,x) + 0.9·FocalKL(w||p) + 0.9·BCE(q,z), q in (0,0.5) predicts disagreement, ensemble, uncertainty 100·(1-2q), and only negative predictions given uncertainty. Alpaca - ensemble of 3 2D networks, averaged softmax, most confident mapped to 0 and least to 100. Uniandes - Cerberus, complement of softmax rescaled 0-100. DSI_Med - 5 attention-gated U-Nets, inverted max softmax ×100, double thresholds WT (0.1, 0.3), TC (0.2, 0.3), ET (0.3, 0.5). Radiomics MIU - 9 models (3 ensembles of 3 CNNs), entropy scaled 0-100. Med vision - self-ensemble ResUNet, U = 100·(1 - y_pred). Jaguars - ensemble of 7 U-Nets, normalised entropy ×100. UmU - multi-decoder cascaded network, u = 200·(1-p) if p ≥ 0.5 else 200·p. LMB - V-Net with test-time dropout plus test-time augmentation, 20 passes, variance as uncertainty. Matukituki - 2D Dense-UNet, uncertainty = (1 - summed softmax) × 100, 99 set to 100. QTIM - ensemble of 5 networks with mirror flips giving 40 predictions per entity, averaged logits, u = 200·σ(l) if σ(l) < 0.5 else 200·(1-σ(l)). Nico@LRDE - cascade of 2 3D U-Nets, the second trained to predict where the first is wrong. Preliminary experiment: modified 3D U-Net with entropy from MC-Dropout, Deep Ensemble, Dropout Ensemble, Bootstrap, Dropout Bootstrap and deterministic softmax.
papers.training: Not reported for the challenge in this paper (each team's optimiser, learning rate, epochs and hardware are in the individual team papers). 3D U-Net experiment: split 228/57/50; other hyperparameters not reported.
papers.evaluation: Final ranking on the 166 BraTS 2020 test cases via the CBICA IPP. For each patient and each entity (WT, TC, ET), teams ranked by the score, giving 498 rankings per team. Cumulative Ranking Score (CRS) per patient = sum of ranks over regions; Normalised Ranking Score (NRS) = CRS / (number of teams × number of regions), range 0-1; Final Ranking Score (FRS) = average over patients. Pairwise permutation tests (100,000 permutations of per-subject cumulative ranks) to test FRS differences; teams without a significant difference share a rank. Additional analyses: ranking per entity, ablations ranking by Dice AUC only, Dice AUC + FTP AUC, Dice AUC + FTN AUC; qualitative filtering at thresholds 100, 75, 50, 25. Segmentation rank across 78 BraTS 2020 segmentation teams reported for comparison.
papers.baselines: 14 participating teams compared with each other; ablation variants of the score (Dice AUC only; Dice + FTP; Dice + FTN); preliminary comparison of MC-Dropout, Deep Ensemble, Dropout Ensemble, Bootstrap, Dropout Bootstrap and deterministic softmax entropy on BraTS 2019.
papers.results: QU-BraTS 2020 ranks (uncertainty rank / segmentation rank of 78): SCAN 1/4; UmU 2/7; DSI_Med 2/13; QTIM 3/7; Uniandes 4/15; nsu_btr 5/13; LMB 5/20; radiomics_miu 6/13; Nico@LRDE 6/18; Jaguars 6/13; Team_Alpaca 7/10; Matukituki 8/19; Frankenstein 9/18; med_vision 9/14. NRS: SCAN about 0.14; UmU and DSI_Med about 0.28; QTIM about 0.31. Per entity (WT/TC/ET): SCAN 1/1/1; UmU 3/2/2; DSI_Med 2/2/3; QTIM 4/2/3. Dice-AUC-only ranking top teams were nsu_btr, Alpaca and Jaguars instead. 3D U-Net experiment: Dropout Bootstrap had best Dice AUC but worst FTP and FTN AUCs; no clear winner. QU-BraTS 2019 mean overall score (top): SCAN 0.9150 (WT 0.9429, TC 0.9135, ET 0.8885), RADIOMICS-MIU 0.9099, UmU 0.9006; teams using 1 - softmax had FTN AUC about 0.92 and overall about 0.60-0.62 (e.g., TEAM_LPACA 0.6192, DRAG 0.6043). Exact 2020 mean scores are given only in box plots.
papers.statistics: Pairwise permutation testing with 100,000 random permutations of per-subject cumulative ranks; p < 0.05 taken as significant; teams with no significant FRS difference share a rank. No confidence intervals reported.
papers.availability: Evaluation code: https://github.com/RagMeh11/QU-BraTS . BraTS training/validation data public via CBICA/TCIA; BraTS 2020 test data not accessible after the challenge.

papers.title: Uncertainty-aware ensemble of foundation models differentiates glioblastoma from its mimics
papers.authors: Zhao J, Lin SY, Attias R, et al.
papers.aim: To build an uncertainty-aware pathology AI (PICTURE) that separates glioblastoma from primary CNS lymphoma (PCNSL) on FFPE and frozen-section slides, and flags tumour types not seen in training.
papers.method: Whole-slide images are tiled, features are extracted with nine pathology foundation models, and a one-hidden-layer MLP classifies glioblastoma vs PCNSL. Three uncertainty steps are used: Bayesian (Monte Carlo permutation) uncertainty against literature prototype images to drop noisy training tiles, a five-fold deep ensemble of the best foundation models (Virchow2 and UNI) that keeps only the 50% most certain tiles per slide, and a normalizing-flow PostNet out-of-distribution detector to flag unseen CNS tumour types.
papers.result: Held-out Mayo test AUROC 0.998 (95% CI 0.995-1.0). External FFPE AUROC: UPenn 0.996, BWH 0.987, Vienna 0.992, TVGH 0.992. Frozen sections: UPenn 0.958, BWH 0.987, Vienna 0.982, TVGH 0.924. OOD detection of 67 unseen CNS tumour types plus normal brain: AUROC 0.919 (95% CI 0.914-0.923) versus Monte Carlo dropout 0.666 and deep ensemble 0.554. Nine neuropathologists had Fleiss' kappa 0.271 (FFPE) and 0.248 (frozen); PCNSL was called glioblastoma in 38% of evaluations.
papers.tools: Foundation models CTransPath, Phikon, Lunit, UNI, Virchow2, CONCH, GPFM, mSTAR, CHIEF (Ciga tested and dropped); Swin Transformer baseline; MLP classifier; PostNet with masked autoregressive flows; scikit-image blob detection; HoverNet (PanNuke) for nuclei; custom necrosis classifier; UMAP; scipy bootstrap; scanners Hamamatsu S210, Aperio GT450, Philips UFS; web-based reader-study interface; code at github.com/hms-dbmi/picture.
papers.gap: Mostly Caucasian patients; small PCNSL numbers per site; only the glioblastoma vs PCNSL pair; no multi-omics; no prospective clinical deployment or measurement of how flagged cases change clinician decisions; no MRI input.
papers.relation: Shows uncertainty-aware brain-tumour diagnosis that flags low-confidence cases for experts, a model for uncertainty-gated agent hand-off.
papers.limitations: Authors state: patients predominantly Caucasian; multi-omics not included; proof of concept limited to glioblastoma and its main mimic; limited patients per site especially for PCNSL; future work should use larger and more diverse cohorts. Also the OoDD was tested on unseen subtypes from the Vienna cohort only; the reader study used 40 slides that PICTURE had all classified correctly.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team collected H&E whole-slide images of glioblastoma (GBM) and primary CNS lymphoma (PCNSL) from five hospitals. Mayo Clinic FFPE slides (273 slides: 166 GBM, 107 PCNSL) were the development set; UPenn, BWH, Vienna and TVGH FFPE and frozen-section slides (for example Vienna 469 GBM and 59 PCNSL FFPE) were held out as external tests. Each slide was cut into 1000 x 1000-pixel tiles at 20x with a 250-pixel step. Tiles with mostly background (95% of pixels very dark or very bright, wrong hue, saturation < 0.2) or fewer than 100 nuclei were removed, which dropped 67.1% of tiles on average, and up to 4000 tiles per slide were kept. Tiles were normalised with ImageNet statistics. Nine frozen pathology foundation models turned each tile into a feature vector, and a one-hidden-layer MLP classified GBM vs PCNSL. To limit label noise from slide-level labels, the authors embedded literature 'prototype' images of GBM and PCNSL, built a k = 500 nearest-neighbour similarity graph, ran Monte Carlo permutation labelling to get P_GBM and P_PCNSL for each Mayo tile, computed Shannon entropy, and trained only on tiles with entropy below the median. Five-fold cross-validation on Mayo (no patient overlap) gave five models per foundation model; these formed a deep ensemble whose mean was the tile prediction and whose standard deviation was the tile uncertainty. The final system used Virchow2 and UNI. A slide's diagnosis was the mean prediction of its 50% most certain tiles. Separately, a PostNet normalizing-flow head gave a Dirichlet certainty per tile; a patient-level score from the lowest-5% uncertainty tiles flagged unseen tumour types (874 WSIs, 67 types, plus 33 normal). AUROC with 1000-bootstrap 95% CIs and one-sided bootstrap tests compared methods, and nine neuropathologists read 40 slides in 90 s each to measure human agreement. For O1, the same ensemble-SD gate and OOD score can decide when the pathology or imaging agent hands a case to the clinician.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multi-centre diagnostic accuracy study with external validation and a multi-institutional reader study. Sites: Mayo Clinic, Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, Brigham and Women's Hospital (USA), Medical University of Vienna (Austria), Taipei Veterans General Hospital (Taiwan), plus TCGA. Approved by Harvard Medical School IRB (IRB20-1509); written informed consent; MI-CLAIM checklist.
papers.datasets: 2141 GBM/PCNSL slides (1760 FFPE, 381 frozen) from five centres: Mayo 273 FFPE (one slide per patient; 166 GBM, 107 PCNSL; development set); UPenn 141 FFPE (81 GBM, 60 PCNSL) and 125 frozen (75 GBM, 50 PCNSL), 150 patients; BWH 125 FFPE (97 GBM, 28 PCNSL) and 77 frozen (66 GBM, 11 PCNSL), 135 patients; Vienna 528 FFPE (469 GBM, 59 PCNSL) and 96 frozen (76 GBM, 20 PCNSL), 568 patients; TVGH 693 FFPE (573 GBM, 120 PCNSL) and 83 frozen (71 GBM, 12 PCNSL), 568 patients. Patients: GBM BWH 104, UPenn 88, Vienna 511, TVGH 358, Mayo 166; PCNSL BWH 31, UPenn 62, Vienna 79, TVGH 74, Mayo 107. Supplementary TCGA: 862 FFPE and 1169 frozen slides (608 patients in Results; 597 in Methods). OOD set: 874 FFPE WSIs from 817 patients across 67 non-GBM, non-PCNSL CNS tumour types plus 33 normal brain WSIs (33 patients). Prototype images of GBM and PCNSL H&E from PubMed, Pathology Outlines and Radiopaedia (2000-2023). Inclusion: samples collected before treatment; no patient overlap between cohorts. Methods also report a wider pool of 2667 FFPE and 1386 frozen slides from 2447 patients.
papers.preprocessing: Scanning at 40x (0.221-0.253 microns per pixel Hamamatsu; Aperio GT450 at Mayo; 0.25 microns per pixel Philips at TVGH). Tiles of 1000 x 1000 pixels at 20x with step 250 pixels. Background/smudge removal: tile excluded if >= 95% of pixels have intensity < 10/255 or > 240/255, hue >= 70/360 or < 230/360, or saturation < 0.2, or fewer than 100 nuclei (scikit-image blob detection, max radius 10 pixels, threshold 0.2). On average 67.1% of tiles excluded; up to 4000 tiles per WSI kept by foreground ratio and cell density. ImageNet-1K normalisation (Reinhard and Macenko tested, no significant difference). Split: Mayo as development set with five-fold cross-validation, no patient overlap between folds; all other cohorts used only as external tests. UMAP of 149,914 Mayo tiles. Tissue-attribute analysis on 1,213,656 GBM and 365,779 PCNSL tiles (BWH and UPenn FFPE).
papers.modelDetails: 1) Feature extraction with nine frozen foundation models (e.g. CTransPath: 3 conv layers + 4 Swin Transformer stages; UNI, Lunit, Virchow2: DINO ViT; Virchow2 trained on up to 3.1 million WSIs at 5/10/20/40x). 2) Classifier: MLP with one hidden layer on tile features for GBM vs PCNSL. 3) Bayesian uncertainty for training-data control: literature prototypes embedded; similarity = inverse Gaussian of L2 distance, kept only for k = 500 nearest neighbours; pseudo-labels assigned from prototype similarity; Monte Carlo permutation tests estimate P_PCNSL and P_GBM; Shannon entropy H = -P_PCNSL log P_PCNSL - P_GBM log P_GBM; only tiles with entropy below the median used for training. PCNSL:GBM prototype ratio adjusted by reciprocal of prevalence. 4) Deep ensemble at inference: for each foundation model, the five fold models form an ensemble (bootstrap aggregation); tile prediction = mean score, tile uncertainty = standard deviation; final PICTURE uses Virchow2 and UNI. Slide prediction = mean of the 50% of tiles with lowest uncertainty. 5) OoDD: PostNet with fixed encoder, linear classifier, two masked autoregressive flows modelling P(z | c, theta); output Dirichlet concentration alpha as certainty (high = in-distribution). Patient-level uncertainty = average of tiles in the lowest 5% epistemic uncertainty. Hyperparameter search: learning rate 1e-6 to 1e-3, L2 weight 0.0001-0.1, latent dimension 4, 8 or 16, entropy weight 1e-9 to 1e-3. Ablation variants: top 25% tiles, absolute uncertainty cut-offs 0.25 and 0.1, aggregation at 10th/30th/50th/70th/90th percentile, 2-3 model combinations, stain normalisation.
papers.training: Development on Mayo FFPE (273 slides) with five-fold cross-validation; OoDD trained on Mayo GBM and PCNSL with tenfold cross-validation and tested on unseen subtypes from Vienna. OoDD hyperparameter ranges as above. MC dropout and deep ensemble OOD baselines used 5 ensemble members; dropout p = 0.5. Optimizer, epochs, batch size and GPU for the MLP: Not reported in main text. Runtime: under 1 minute per WSI (< 5 s segmentation, 30-50 s feature extraction, 300-700 ms inference). Experiments repeated at least three times; performance quantification repeated five times.
papers.evaluation: Internal five-fold cross-validation on Mayo; external validation on UPenn, BWH, Vienna and TVGH FFPE and frozen sections; supplementary validation on TCGA. Metrics: AUROC and balanced accuracy; 95% CIs from 1000 bootstrap samples; one-sided bootstrap significance tests between methods; DeLong's test for the pooled five-fold experiment. OOD: AUROC for ID (GBM/PCNSL) vs OOD. Reader study: nine board-certified neuropathologists (3 junior < 5 years, 4 intermediate 5-15 years, 2 senior > 15 years) from USA, EU, East Asia, Southeast Asia read 20 FFPE + 20 frozen slides within 90 s each, then optionally re-read untimed; binary diagnosis plus confidence 0/25/50/75/100%; no IHC, genomics or history; Fleiss' kappa and Jaccard index. Heatmaps reviewed by neuropathologists (40 random correct heatmaps; 33 slides scored 1-10 on 12 histologic features).
papers.baselines: Nine foundation models without uncertainty control (CTransPath, Phikon, Lunit, UNI, Virchow2, CONCH, GPFM, mSTAR, CHIEF); end-to-end weakly supervised Swin Transformer; identical model without uncertainty control (ablation); OOD baselines Monte Carlo dropout and deep ensemble; Ciga (AUROC 0.469, excluded).
papers.results: Mayo held-out: PICTURE AUROC 0.998 (95% CI 0.995-1.0); baselines 0.833 (Phikon) up to near PICTURE (Virchow2, UNI). External FFPE: UPenn 0.996 (0.990-1.0) vs UNI 0.976 (P < 0.001), Virchow2 0.995 (P = 0.243 in figure; 0.387 in text); BWH 0.987 (0.961-1.0) vs UNI 0.977 (P = 0.025), Virchow2 0.975 (P = 0.014); Vienna 0.992 (0.982-0.999) vs UNI 0.966, Virchow2 0.964 (both P < 0.001); TVGH 0.992 (0.986-0.998) vs CONCH 0.982 (P = 0.001), Virchow2 0.980 (P < 0.001). Frozen: UPenn 0.958 (0.919-0.988) vs Swin 0.898 (P < 0.001), CONCH 0.946 (P = 0.067); BWH 0.987 (0.956-1.0) vs CONCH 0.987 (P = 0.505), CHIEF 0.971; Vienna 0.982 (0.956-0.997) in text (0.988 in figure) vs UNI 0.966; TVGH 0.924 (0.846-0.985) vs CONCH 0.919 (P = 0.427). Pooled five-fold: PICTURE 0.999, Virchow2 1.000, UNI 0.999, Lunit 0.995, Phikon 0.994, GPFM 0.987, CTransPath 0.950, CONCH 0.959, CHIEF 0.962, mSTAR 0.973. Abstract range across five independent cohorts: AUROC 0.924-0.996; overall 0.989. Mean epistemic uncertainty: frozen GBM 0.070, frozen PCNSL 0.103, FFPE GBM 0.045, FFPE PCNSL 0.048. OOD AUROC 0.919 (0.914-0.923) vs MC dropout 0.666 (0.638-0.695) and deep ensemble 0.554 (0.525-0.584); samples with certainty < 0.5 were 84.7% OOD. Readers: Jaccard 0.56-0.87 (FFPE), 0.49-0.81 (frozen); 113 misdiagnoses, 81 (71.7%) with reported confidence <= 50%. Heatmap features in 40 correct cases: dense tumour 90%, infiltration 77.5%, haemorrhage 72.5%, microvascular proliferation 25%, pseudopalisading necrosis 22.5%. Necrosis classifier AUROC 0.92 (3384 annotated instances).
papers.statistics: 95% CIs by 1000 bootstrap samples; one-sided bootstrap significance tests (N = 1000); DeLong's test; two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests (necrosis P = 1.97e-4, nuclear size heterogeneity P = 1.51e-4, cell density P = 1.57e-23; senior/intermediate vs junior P = 0.0128 FFPE, 0.0318 frozen; OOD vs GBM P < 0.001, vs PCNSL P = 0.008); Fleiss' kappa 0.271 (FFPE) and 0.248 (frozen); Jaccard index.
papers.availability: Code and trained models: https://github.com/hms-dbmi/picture. TCGA data from GDC; Vienna pathology data at https://doi.org/10.25493/WQ48-ZGX; other cohorts on request with data use agreements (non-commercial academic use only).

papers.title: Differentiation of glioblastoma from solitary brain metastasis using deep ensembles: Empirical estimation of uncertainty for clinical reliability
papers.authors: Park YW, Eom S, Kim S, et al.
papers.venue: Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine
papers.aim: To build a clinically reliable deep learning model that separates glioblastoma (GBM) from solitary brain metastasis (SBM) on MRI and gives predictive uncertainty estimates and interpretability.
papers.method: Deep ensembles of DenseNet121 were trained on multiparametric MRI from one institution and tested on an external set. Entropy of the ensemble prediction was used to split cases into high- and low-uncertainty groups, and out-of-distribution meningioma cases were used to test whether the model reports high uncertainty on an unknown class. Interpretability was measured by localisation accuracy.
papers.result: External test: AUC 0.83 (95% CI 0.76-0.90), accuracy 76.2%, sensitivity 54.8%, specificity 85.2%. Low-uncertainty group AUC 0.91 (95% CI 0.83-0.98) versus high-uncertainty group AUC 0.58 (95% CI 0.44-0.71). 90.7% of predictions on meningioma OOD data were classed as uncertain. Low-uncertainty and high-localisation-accuracy subgroup AUC 0.98 (95% CI 0.95-1.00).
papers.tools: DenseNet121 deep ensembles; multiparametric MRI; entropy-based uncertainty; localisation accuracy for interpretability. Other software and hardware: Not reported in abstract.
papers.gap: Single training institution; modest external test (143 patients); low sensitivity (54.8%) for SBM; uncertainty threshold and deferral policy not tied to a formal guarantee; no clinician-in-the-loop evaluation reported in the abstract.
papers.relation: Uses ensemble uncertainty to judge clinical reliability in brain-tumour MRI diagnosis, which is relevant to propagating confidence from the imaging agent.
papers.limitations: Not reported in abstract. From abstract data: low sensitivity (54.8%) on external test, single training centre, and an entropy split method without stated calibration guarantee.
papers.methodologyDetail: Only the abstract was available (Elsevier, closed access; no legal open-access copy found via Unpaywall or Europe PMC). The study is a retrospective MRI study from Korea. The authors collected multiparametric MRI from 469 patients at their institution (300 glioblastoma and 169 solitary brain metastasis) to train the model, and an external test set of 143 patients (101 glioblastoma and 42 metastasis) from another source. They trained a deep ensemble, that is several DenseNet121 convolutional networks trained independently, on the multiparametric MRI input. For each test case the ensemble outputs class probabilities, and the entropy of the averaged prediction is used as the uncertainty score. On the external test set the ensemble reached AUC 0.83 (95% CI 0.76-0.90), accuracy 76.2%, sensitivity 54.8% and specificity 85.2%. The authors then split the test cases by entropy into low-uncertainty and high-uncertainty groups. Performance was much higher in the low-uncertainty group (AUC 0.91, 95% CI 0.83-0.98) than in the high-uncertainty group (AUC 0.58, 95% CI 0.44-0.71), showing that entropy identifies the unreliable cases. To test dataset shift, they fed MRI from 257 meningioma patients (a class never seen in training) and found that 90.7% of these predictions were marked uncertain. Finally they measured interpretability through localisation accuracy (whether the model's attention falls on the tumour) and showed that the subgroup with both low uncertainty and high localisation accuracy reached AUC 0.98 (95% CI 0.95-1.00). Details such as MRI sequences, preprocessing, number of ensemble members, the entropy cut-off and training hyperparameters are not in the abstract. To adapt this to O1, an MRI agent can use ensemble entropy plus a localisation check as two gates, act on cases passing both, and defer the rest, including unseen tumour types, to the neuroradiologist.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective diagnostic model development with external validation; institutional training set and an external test set; Korea (Yonsei University College of Medicine, Seoul; UNIST, Ulsan; other Korean institutions per author list).
papers.datasets: Institutional training set: 469 patients (300 GBM, 169 SBM), multiparametric MRI. External test set: 143 patients (101 GBM, 42 SBM). Out-of-distribution set: 257 patients with meningioma (unknown class). Specific MRI sequences, scanners and inclusion/exclusion criteria: Not reported in abstract.
papers.preprocessing: Not reported in abstract (multiparametric MRI used as input; split = 469 training patients, 143 external test patients, 257 OOD patients).
papers.modelDetails: Deep ensemble of DenseNet121 networks on multiparametric MRI; entropy of the ensemble output used as the uncertainty measure; datasets split into high- and low-uncertainty groups based on entropy values (exact threshold Not reported in abstract); OOD entropy compared for meningioma; interpretability by localisation accuracy, giving a 'low-uncertainty and high-localisation-accuracy' subgroup. Number of ensemble members and losses: Not reported in abstract.
papers.training: Not reported in abstract.
papers.evaluation: External test set evaluation with AUC, accuracy, sensitivity and specificity; subgroup analysis by entropy (high vs low uncertainty); proportion of OOD (meningioma) predictions classed as uncertain; subgroup analysis combining uncertainty and localisation accuracy. Cross-validation details: Not reported in abstract.
papers.baselines: Not reported in abstract (comparison is between uncertainty subgroups and OOD data rather than other models).
papers.results: External test (143 patients): AUC 0.83 (95% CI 0.76-0.90), accuracy 76.2%, sensitivity 54.8%, specificity 85.2%.
