Step 6 (round 5): manuscript drafting and feedback, adding method examples. Step 7 (round 6): 44 new external experts, chosen for diversity (patients, regulators, Africa, Latin America, Asia), voted agree/disagree/neutral. Step 8 (round 7): four online meetings in June 2023 settled wording. Step 9 (round 8): final vote by 117 experts from 50 countries; all 30 items passed with under 5% disagreement. The output is a phase-by-phase checklist (Tables 3-6). For a PhD orchestrator, the most useful items are: calibrated per-patient uncertainty and implausible-output checks (traceability 3), full logging of inputs, outputs and clinician decisions with anonymised IDs in encrypted logs (traceability 5), human override (usability 2), local validity and recalibration in low-resource settings (universality 1 and 4), and federated learning or differential privacy (general 2). A student can score their system against all 30 items as a compliance table.
papers.studyDesign: International expert consensus study (modified Delphi), 24 months, started 2021. FUTURE-AI Consortium led from Universitat de Barcelona (BCN-AIM) with experts from 50 countries on all continents; origin in five EU projects (EuCanImage, ProCAncer-I, CHAIMELEON, PRIMAGE, INCISIVE; AI4HI network). Funded by EU Horizon 2020 grant 952103 (EuCanImage). Not a patient study.
papers.datasets: No patient data. Participants: round 1, six working groups of 3 experts each (18 experts); rounds 2-5, 72 experts (AI scientists, clinicians, ethicists, social scientists, legal and industry experts); round 6, 44 additional external experts (patient advocates, social scientists, regulators, more from Africa, Latin America and Asia); round 8, final consortium of 117 experts from 50 countries. Literature review of trustworthy AI, reporting guidelines (TRIPOD+AI, CLAIM, CONSORT-AI, DECIDE-AI, PROBAST-AI, CLEAR) and EU, FDA and WHO documents.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable. Consensus process steps: literature review and thematic clustering of trustworthy AI requirements into 6 principles (Table 1); round 1 working groups proposed 6-10 best practices per principle, merged to 55 after removing overlap; round 2 survey kept items with >90% high agreement and discarded those with strong negative feedback (mostly method-specific ones), giving 22 items and 16 contentious points, plus a new general category; round 3 broadened scope from medical imaging to healthcare, giving 30 items; round 4 rated each item for research vs deployable tools; round 5 manuscript feedback; round 6 external feedback from 44 experts; round 7 four online meetings in June 2023; round 8 final online vote.
papers.modelDetails: Not an AI model. The framework structure: Fairness (define bias sources; collect individual and data attributes; evaluate fairness and correct bias). Universality (define clinical settings including low vs high resource; use standards such as SNOMED CT, OMOP, DICOM, FHIR/HL7, IEEE, ISO; evaluate on external/multisite data; evaluate local clinical validity with recalibration or fine-tuning). Traceability (risk management file; documentation such as AI information leaflet, model cards, AI passport; quality control of inputs and outputs with out-of-distribution detection, sanity checks and calibrated uncertainty per patient; periodic auditing, e.g. biannual or annual, with drift detection; logging of user actions, AI inputs, AI outputs, clinical decisions, timestamp, user ID, anonymised patient ID, in encrypted logs; governance with assigned roles and liability). Usability (user requirements; human-AI interaction and oversight with human-in-the-loop checks and ability to overrule AI; training materials; usability evaluation including automation bias; clinical utility and safety, e.g. randomised trial). Robustness (define data variations; train with representative real-world data; stress and repeatability tests). Explainability (define needs with users; evaluate explanations quantitatively and with users). General (stakeholder engagement; privacy and security incl. federated learning, differential privacy, encryption; risk mitigation; evaluation plan; regulatory compliance such as EU AI Act, MDR, FDA SaMD; ethical issues; social and environmental issues). Compliance levels: + recommended, ++ highly recommended, separately for research and deployable tools.
papers.training: Not applicable (no model training). Consensus process lasted 24 months over 8 rounds.
papers.evaluation: Quantitative analysis of voting patterns (consensus and disagreement levels) and qualitative synthesis of free-text feedback by recurring themes. Round 2 voting options: absolutely essential, very important, of average importance, of little importance, not important at all; plus keep/refine wording. Round 6 options: agree, disagree, neutral, did not understand, no opinion. Consensus threshold in round 2: >90% high agreement. Final approval: less than 5% disagreement.
papers.baselines: Compared conceptually with existing guidelines: FAIR data principles, TRIPOD+AI, CLAIM, CONSORT-AI, DECIDE-AI, PROBAST-AI, CLEAR, WHO ethics report, EU High-Level Expert Group checklist.
papers.results: Round 1: 55 preliminary recommendations from 6 groups of 3 experts. Round 2: 72 experts; 22 recommendations retained and 16 contentious points identified; seventh 'general' category added. Round 3: 30 recommendations (6 new general items). Round 6: 44 external experts gave feedback; most non-agreement due to unclear wording. Round 7: 4 online meetings, June 2023; adversarial-attack testing was merged into cybersecurity, and mandatory third-party clinical evaluation was dropped as impractical in resource-limited settings. Round 8: 117 experts, all 30 recommendations approved with <5% disagreement; remaining disagreement was mainly about 'recommended' vs 'highly recommended'. From Table 2, 26 of 30 items are highly recommended (++) for deployable tools and 13 of 30 for research tools.
papers.statistics: Descriptive consensus percentages only (>90% agreement threshold in round 2; <5% disagreement in final vote). No statistical tests.
papers.availability: Guideline and self-assessment checklist at www.future-ai.eu; appendix tables (glossary, stakeholders) online with the BMJ article. No code or data.

papers.title: Intricacies of human-AI interaction in dynamic decision-making for precision oncology
papers.authors: Niraula D, Cuneo KC, Dinov ID, et al.
papers.aim: To study how clinicians change their radiotherapy dose decisions when they see recommendations, outcome estimates and uncertainty from an AI decision-support tool (ARCliDS). The study looks at model-agnostic and model-specific collaborative behaviour.
papers.method: A two-phase within-subject reader study. Clinicians first chose a mid-treatment dose without AI (Unassisted) and then re-chose it after seeing ARCliDS recommendations (AI-assisted), and gave confidence (0-5) and an AI trust score (0-5). Decisions were analysed with matched-pair randomization t-tests, Spearman correlations and intraclass correlation coefficients.
papers.result: 144 evaluations (NSCLC 72 = 9 evaluators x 8 patients; HCC 72 = 8 evaluators x 9 patients). AI changed 41 (57%) NSCLC and 34 (47%) HCC decisions, but distribution-level tests were mostly not significant. Decision adjustment correlated with dissimilarity to AI (NSCLC rho=0.53, HCC rho=0.60, p<0.001). Agreement with AI correlated with AI trust (NSCLC rho=0.59, HCC rho=0.70, p<0.001). Inter-evaluator ICC rose with AI, e.g. NSCLC ICC(C,1) 0.135 to 0.216, HCC ICC(C,1) 0.163 to 0.264.
papers.tools: ARCliDS (model-based deep reinforcement learning, graph neural network radiotherapy environment, ensemble of 5 models for uncertainty); R Shiny, Plotly, reticulate, googlesheets4, shinyapps.io (Standard plan, max 5 instances, 8 GB each), Google Sheets storage; Python with pydicom, dicompylercore, NumPy (float16 arrays), scipy.ndimage.zoom; irr R package for ICC; randomization test code from David C Howell.
papers.gap: No ground truth for the continuous dose decisions; no external validation dataset; small sample; retrospective, simulated setting; no subgroup analysis by experience or specialty; effect of faulty AI not tested.
papers.relation: Studies how clinicians accept or override AI recommendations in oncology depending on AI confidence, which is relevant to logging and using clinician validations.
papers.limitations: Adaptive radiotherapy is not standard practice; patients came from the AI training data, not an external set; 144 evaluations give low inferential power; retrospective setting may differ from prospective behaviour; remarks were optional and uneven (48 total). Future work: prospective randomized study, larger sample, faulty-AI arms, varying explainability, time pressure, stratification by clinician characteristics, per-user online fine-tuning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors tested how clinicians work with ARCliDS, a reinforcement-learning tool that recommends a mid-treatment daily radiotherapy dose. ARCliDS was trained earlier on two retrospective trial cohorts: NSCLC patients from trial NCT01190527 (30 fractions, 13 multi-omics features chosen from 297) and HCC patients from three adaptive SBRT trials (3+2 fractions, 13 features chosen from 110). Its environment predicts TCP and NTCP, and its agent maximises a reward r = tcp(1-ntcp) with bonus points (+2 when tcp>0.70 and ntcp<0.172 for NSCLC, or tcp>0.90 and ntcp<0.25 for HCC; +1 when tcp>0.50 and ntcp<0.50). An ensemble of 5 models gives mean +/- SEM for the dose and outcomes. Cross-validated AUROC was 0.73 (TCP) and 0.79 (NTCP) for NSCLC and 0.74 and 0.68 for HCC. For the study, 8 NSCLC and 9 HCC patients were randomly picked. DICOM CT, structures and dose were converted to float16 NumPy arrays and shown as 2D slices in an R Shiny web app with Plotly viewers, auto-saving to Google Sheets. Each evaluator watched a 10-minute tutorial, then for each patient (random order) entered an unassisted dose (NSCLC 1.5-4 Gy/fx, HCC 1-15 Gy/fx) and confidence 0-5. Next they saw the AI dose, a TCP-NTCP outcome space with error bars and feature distribution plots, then re-entered dose and confidence and answered 4 items that sum to an AI trust score 0-5. They could not go back to the unassisted page. Thirteen clinicians from Moffitt and Michigan completed 17 evaluations, giving 144 paired decisions. Analysis used matched-pair randomization t-tests, Spearman correlations of derived values (adjustment aia-un, dissimilarity ai-un, agreement -|aia-ai|, closeness to standard of care), and McGraw-Wong ICC for inter-reader agreement. A PhD student can reuse this paired design, the 0-5 confidence and trust scales, and the derived quantities to measure clinician validation of a deferring AI.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective, two-phase sequential Human-AI interaction reader study (within-subject, each case: Unassisted then AI-assisted). Two institutions in the USA: Moffitt Cancer Center (Tampa, FL) and Michigan Medicine (University of Michigan). IRB Moffitt MCC# 20750. Two disease modules: NSCLC adaptive radiotherapy and HCC adaptive SBRT.
papers.datasets: (1) NSCLC: UMCC 2007-123 phase II dose-escalation trial NCT01190527; inoperable or unresectable NSCLC, 30 daily fractions (about 50 Gy EQD2 in evaluation phase, up to 92 Gy EQD2 total); endpoints local control (LC) and radiation pneumonitis grade >=2 (RP2); 297 multi-omics features reduced to 13 (cytokines pre-IL4, pre-IL15, slope-IP10; PET radiomics pre-MTV, RD-GLSZM-LZLGE, RD-GLSZM-ZSV; dosimetry tumour gEUD, lung gEUD; SNPs Cxcr1-Rs2234671, Ercc2-Rs238406, Ercc5-Rs1047768; miR-191-5p, miR-20a-5p). Training cohort size: Not reported in this paper (see Niraula et al. 2023). (2) HCC: adaptive arm of trials NCT01519219, NCT01522937, NCT02460835; adaptive SBRT 3+2 fractions with 1-month break; endpoints LC and liver toxicity (>=2 point Child-Pugh rise); 110 features reduced to 13 (sex, age, pre-cirrhosis, pre-ECOG-PS, active lesions, pre-albumin, GTV, Liver-GTV, GTV gEUD, Liver-GTV volume, RD-TGF-beta, RD-CD40L, RD-HGF); 95 of 99 HCC patients had local control. Reader study cases: 8 NSCLC and 9 HCC patients randomly selected from the training data based on imaging availability. Imaging shown: CT, RT structures, 3D dose, cumulative DVH; pre/mid PET for NSCLC; pre-treatment MRI and liver function for HCC. Readers: 20 volunteers, 13 completed, 4 did both modules, 17 completed evaluations (9 NSCLC, 8 HCC); physicians and residents of various specialties.
papers.preprocessing: DICOM CT, RT structure and 3D dose files converted with pydicom and dicompylercore: pixel-to-coordinate transform; select overlapping region between CT and dose; enlarge and interpolate dose to CT resolution with scipy.ndimage.zoom; merge all RT structures into one 3D grid using unique integer values; save as compressed float16 3D NumPy arrays. PET and MRI registered onto CT and RT structures with the same procedure. Cumulative DVH extracted. 2D axial, coronal and sagittal slices shown to reduce rendering time. AI recommendations and outcome estimates precomputed. ARTE validation used 80-20 split, 10-fold stratified shuffle cross-validation.
papers.modelDetails: ARCliDS has two parts. ARTE (artificial radiotherapy environment): radiobiologically constrained transition functions for patient state (graph of multi-omics features, graph neural network based), an RT outcome estimator (TCP and NTCP) and a reward function. ODM (optimal decision maker): agent trained with model-based deep reinforcement learning. Base reward r = tcp(1-ntcp). NSCLC reward: r+2 if tcp>0.70 and ntcp<0.172; r+1 if tcp>0.50 and ntcp<0.50; else r. HCC reward: r+2 if tcp>0.90 and ntcp<0.25; r+1 if tcp>0.50 and ntcp<0.50; else r. Dose range: NSCLC 1.5-4 Gy/fx; HCC 1-15 Gy/fx. Uncertainty: ensemble of 5 models, recommendation shown as mean +/- SEM daily dose plus EQD2; outcome space TCP vs NTCP with SEM error bars, colored by reward, green diamond for recommendation; population feature distribution plots. AI trust score (0-5) from 4 multiple-choice items: outcome reasonableness 1 pt, outcome uncertainty 1 pt, agreement with recommended dose range 2 pts, dose uncertainty 1 pt; only 'Reasonable' or 'Agree' scores points. No automatic deferral rule; the clinician always makes the final decision.
papers.training: ARCliDS modules were trained earlier on the retrospective trial cohorts (details in Niraula et al. 2023, Sci Rep); optimizer, learning rate, epochs and batch size: Not reported in this paper. Reader training: two 10-minute tutorial videos (one per disease), a pre-evaluation information session with demo and Q&A; evaluation designed to take under one hour; study ran a little over five months. Cyber security clearance took about 2 weeks (over 4 months total to reach the application).
papers.evaluation: Each evaluator saw patients in a randomized order; Unassisted phase locked once AI was seen and unassisted decision hidden on the AI page. Outcomes: unassisted decision (un), AI-assisted decision (aia), AI recommendation (ai), confidence (0-5) before and after, AI trust (0-5), free-text remarks. Derived: decision adjustment frequency, adjustment level (aia-un), dissimilarity (ai-un), agreement -|aia-ai|, closeness to standard of care -|d-SOC| with SOC 2 Gy/fx NSCLC and 10 Gy/fx HCC. Two-sided matched-pair randomization t-test on un-aia; Spearman correlations; Pearson for un vs aia; ICC (McGraw and Wong, two-way random effects, Consistency and Absolute agreement, single and average) via irr; toxicity-free local control score TCP(1-NTCP). AI model itself: 80-20 split 10-fold stratified shuffle CV, AUROC for TCP and NTCP; radiobiological self-evaluation of ODM. No external validation.
papers.baselines: Unassisted clinician decisions (Human only) versus AI-assisted decisions (Human + AI); standard of care dose (NSCLC 2 Gy/fx, HCC 10 Gy/fx); retrospective clinical decisions for the ODM self-evaluation.
papers.results: Adjusted decisions: NSCLC 41/72 (57%), HCC 34/72 (47%); 15/17 evaluations (88%) had at least 2 adjustments; NSCLC evaluators #7 and #8 made zero. Adjustment range: NSCLC 0-100% by evaluator, 44-78% by patient; HCC 22-67% by evaluator, 25-75% by patient. Adjustment vs dissimilarity: NSCLC rho=0.53, NSCLC excluding zero-adjusters rho=0.58, HCC rho=0.60 (all p<0.001). Trust vs agreement: 0.59, 0.69, 0.70 (p<0.001). aia confidence vs trust: NSCLC rho=0.14 (p=0.26), NSCLC excl. rho=0.34 (p=0.0094), HCC rho=0.47 (p<0.001). Change in confidence vs trust: HCC rho=0.32 (p=0.0055), NSCLC 0.11 (p=0.37), NSCLC excl. 0.19 (p=0.17). Change in confidence vs adjustment level: NSCLC rho=-0.24 (p=0.045), excl. -0.29 (p=0.028), HCC 0.28 (p=0.017). Confidence vs closeness to SOC: un NSCLC 0.15 (p=0.21), excl. 0.25 (p=0.059), HCC 0.32 (p=0.0056); aia NSCLC 0.092 (p=0.44), excl. 0.29 (p=0.029), HCC 0.48 (p<0.001). ICC unassisted to AI-assisted: NSCLC ICC(C,1) 0.135 [-0.005,0.507] to 0.216 [0.04,0.606]; ICC(A,1) 0.102 to 0.201; ICC(C,9) 0.584 to 0.713; ICC(A,9) 0.504 to 0.694; HCC ICC(C,1) 0.163 to 0.264; ICC(A,1) 0.117 to 0.195; ICC(C,8) 0.608 to 0.742; ICC(A,8) 0.515 to 0.659. NSCLC: 76% of adjustments raised TCP and NTCP; HCC: 74% (25/34) lowered TCP and NTCP. Score change aia-un: NSCLC mean 0.0011 (SD 0.0058); HCC mean 0.0059 (SD 0.0144), median 0.0034. ARTE AUROC: NSCLC TCP 0.73+/-0.15, NTCP 0.79+/-0.17; HCC TCP 0.74+/-0.27, NTCP 0.68+/-0.24. ODM reproduced 36% good / improved 74% bad decisions (NSCLC) and 50% / 30% (HCC). Remarks: 48 total (14, 14, 9, 11).
papers.statistics: Two-sided matched-pair randomization t-test (H0: un-aia=0), mostly not significant; Spearman rank correlation with two-sided p-values and 95% covariance ellipses; Pearson correlation for un vs aia (significant positive but not near 1); ICC with 95% CI and one-sided F-test p-values (e.g. NSCLC ICC(C,1) AI-assisted p=0.004; HCC ICC(C,1) AI-assisted p=0.001).
papers.availability: Evaluator decision source data provided with the paper. Patient clinical data restricted (University of Michigan data sharing application). ARCliDS code is proprietary (Moffitt and University of Michigan). Online tools: https://arclids.shinyapps.io/ARCliDS/, https://arclids.shinyapps.io/Eval_NSCLC_v2/, https://arclids.shinyapps.io/Eval_HCC_v2/.

papers.title: Human-AI interaction and collaboration in radiology: from conceptual frameworks to responsible implementation
papers.authors: Kocak B, Cuocolo R
papers.aim: To give a clear overview of how radiologists and AI interact and collaborate, where collaboration adds value or causes harm, and what is needed for responsible implementation.
papers.method: Narrative review based on targeted, topic-driven literature searches, expert knowledge and backward and forward reference chaining, without a formal systematic search. It builds conceptual models, a workflow taxonomy along an autonomy spectrum and design principles, and summarises evidence on cognitive effects, governance and emerging systems.
papers.result: The review proposes an eight-model workflow taxonomy from human-only reading to standalone AI, including an 'uncertainty-aware delegation and high-confidence filtering' model where AI auto-finalises normal cases and escalates uncertain or positive ones. It summarises evidence such as 'AI as supporting reader' cutting second human reads by up to 87% in more than 280,000 mammograms, prostate MRI AUC rising from 0.882 to 0.916 with AI (61 readers, 360 exams), trainee accuracy falling from about 80% to 20% with incorrect AI, and biased AI lowering clinician accuracy by about 9.1-11.3 percentage points.
papers.tools: Not applicable (review). Mentions vision-language models (e.g. Flamingo-CXR), saliency maps, NLP report-image discrepancy checking, active learning, FDA Predetermined Change Control Plan; figures made in Canva.com; language edited with ChatGPT 5.2 and Gemini 3 Pro.
papers.gap: Most studies evaluate algorithms alone, not the human-AI team in real workflows. Few prospective, multi-institutional studies of team performance, workload, equity and long-term learning. Explanation tools (saliency maps) are unstable; calibrated uncertainty for role arbitration is not yet well tested.
papers.relation: Reviews frameworks for dividing work between radiologists and AI, which guides where the orchestrator should hand control to clinicians.
papers.limitations: Narrative, non-systematic review, so study selection may be biased; no pooled quantitative analysis; workflow diagrams are simplified and focus on narrow task-specific AI. Future work: prospective multi-institutional studies of team performance, workload, equity and training outcomes; uncertainty-aware role arbitration; usable explanations; AI literacy.
papers.methodologyDetail: This is a narrative review, so there is no dataset or model to reproduce. The authors ran targeted, topic-driven literature searches, used their own expert knowledge, and followed references backward and forward. They did not use a formal systematic protocol, quality scoring or meta-analysis. They organised the material in five steps. First, they defined core terms (human-AI interaction, collaboration, team performance, diagnostic complementarity, automation bias, algorithmic aversion, cognitive offloading, trust calibration, physician-in-the-loop) in a table. Second, they built a workflow taxonomy of eight models along an autonomy spectrum, from human-only reading to standalone AI. For each model they listed the human role, the AI role, the output and the autonomy level. The 'uncertainty-aware delegation and high-confidence filtering' model lets the AI auto-finalise normal cases and escalate uncertain or positive ones, while the radiologist audits a sample of auto-finalised cases. Third, they gave six design principles (task allocation, workflow placement, interaction mode, trust calibration, learning and feedback, training and supervision) and a table of advantages and risks for five interaction setups. Fourth, they summarised evidence on cognitive effects using numbers from cited studies, for example trainee accuracy falling from about 80% to 20% with wrong AI, and biased AI lowering accuracy by 9.1-11.3 points. Fifth, they described governance (liability stays with the clinician, interdisciplinary committees, shadow then pilot deployment, drift monitoring, FDA change-control plans, EU AI Act literacy) and a five-step physician-in-the-loop active learning loop. For this PhD, the taxonomy and active learning loop can be used as the design template for when the orchestrator acts alone, when it defers, and how clinician corrections feed recalibration.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review (review article) by authors from Basaksehir Cam and Sakura City Hospital, Istanbul, Turkiye and University of Salerno, Italy. No primary data; not prospective or retrospective.
papers.datasets: No dataset used. Cited evidence includes: Lee et al. reader study, 30 radiologists and residents, 120 chest radiographs (60 with malignant nodules); Ng et al. simulation, more than 280,000 mammograms from two countries; prospective 'AI as additional reader' study, tens of thousands of screening exams; Zajac et al. qualitative study, 18 radiologists at 9 sites in Denmark and Kenya; PI-CAI consortium, 61 readers from 53 centres in 17 countries, 360 MRI exams; EuroAIM/EuSoMII survey of 572 ESR members; international survey of 1,041 radiologists; Chinese survey of 6,726 radiologists from 1,143 hospitals; prospective study of 18,680 chest radiographs.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable (review). Not reported.
papers.modelDetails: Conceptual frameworks, not a model. Diagnostic complementarity: human and AI errors only partly overlap, so the team can beat either alone. Autonomy spectrum with 8 workflow models: standard of care (human only); concurrent decision support (low); second reader and quality assurance (low to moderate); AI as supporting reader (moderate, AI acts as second reader only when it agrees with reader 1, discordant cases go to human reader 2); AI as additional reader (moderate, safety net on negative-consensus cases, arbitrator reviews flags); AI triage and worklist prioritisation (moderate to high); uncertainty-aware delegation and high-confidence filtering (high, AI auto-finalises normal cases, escalates uncertain or positive cases, radiologist audits a sample of auto-finalised normals); standalone AI reporting (autonomous, not clinically viable). Six design principles: task allocation, workflow placement, mode of interaction, trust calibration, learning and feedback, training and supervision. Physician-in-the-loop active learning loop in 5 steps: use in routine reporting; flag a subset (uncertain or discordant) for feedback; store in feedback set; periodic review, recalibration or retraining; redeploy and monitor drift and safety. No numeric thresholds given.
papers.training: Not applicable (review). Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable; no formal search protocol, quality appraisal or synthesis method reported. The review recommends phased deployment (shadow deployment, then scoped pilot, then full rollout), continuous post-market surveillance for drift, and evaluation frameworks such as Park et al., ECLAIR and RADAR.
papers.baselines: Not applicable (review).
papers.results: Reported evidence from cited studies: AI supporting reader reduced second human reads by up to 87% while maintaining screening performance; AI additional reader added 0.7-1.6 cancers per 1,000 women screened (83.3% invasive, 47.0% <=10 mm); prostate MRI with AI: AUC 0.882 to 0.916, sensitivity 94.3% to 96.8%, specificity 46.7% to 50.1% at PI-RADS >=3 (3 more true positives, 10 fewer false positives); AI triage cut critical chest radiograph reporting delay from 11.2 to 2.7 days and pneumothorax turnaround from 80.1 to 35.6 min; CTPA pulmonary embolism turnaround 59.9 to 47.6 min; trainee mammography accuracy about 80% with correct AI vs 20% with incorrect AI; biased AI reduced clinician accuracy by about 9.1-11.3 percentage points; saliency map localisation AUPRC 0.024-0.16; reading time 13.3 s vs 14.8 s overall, 10.8 s vs 13.1 s for normal-flag studies, 18.6 s vs 18.4 s for abnormal-flag studies; survey: 47.2% expected more workload, costs 49.5%, legal 43.7%, lack of validation 35.5%; 37% cited lack of trust (aOR 1.77, 95% CI 1.24-2.53, P=0.002 outside Europe); 98% said radiology teams should join AI development, 45% said radiologists should keep full responsibility; 64.8% of Singapore residents and faculty were AI novices, 59.2% said teaching was inadequate.
papers.statistics: No own statistical analysis. Cited: adjusted odds ratio 1.77 (95% CI 1.24-2.53; P=0.002) for lack-of-trust view outside Europe.
papers.availability: Not available (review; no code or data). Open-access article under CC BY-NC 4.0 at dirjournal.org.

heading: O2 - Calibrated uncertainty and escalation (when to defer to the clinician)

papers.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
papers.authors: Guo C, Pleiss G, Sun Y, Weinberger KQ
papers.aim: To check if the confidence scores of modern deep networks match their real accuracy.
papers.method: Measured calibration with ECE and reliability diagrams on many networks and datasets. Compared post-hoc fixes.
papers.result: Modern deep networks are over-confident. Depth, width, batch norm and less weight decay make it worse. Temperature scaling (one parameter) fixes most of it.
papers.tools: ResNet, DenseNet, Wide-ResNet; CIFAR, ImageNet, text datasets
papers.gap: Only tested on the same distribution as training.
papers.relation: Every agent in our system must be calibrated before we use its confidence for escalation. Temperature scaling is our first baseline.
papers.limitations: Calibration breaks when data shifts (new hospital). Future: shift-robust calibration.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors first measure calibration as the gap between confidence and accuracy. Test predictions are put into 15 equal-width confidence bins; for each bin they compare mean confidence with accuracy, and ECE is the weighted average gap (MCE is the largest gap). They then train modern networks (ResNets, Wide ResNets, DenseNets) and older LeNet-5 on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, SVHN, Birds, Cars and four text datasets, keeping the original papers' training recipes. Experiments on CIFAR-100 that vary depth, width, Batch Normalization and weight decay show that the changes that raise accuracy (more depth and width, BatchNorm, less weight decay) also make networks over-confident, and that NLL over-fits even when accuracy keeps improving. Next, they hold out a validation set (for example 5,000 images for CIFAR) and fit six post-hoc calibration methods on the network's logits. Temperature scaling divides all logits by one learned value T before the softmax, chosen to minimise NLL on the validation set. Across 17 model-dataset pairs it gives the lowest or near-lowest ECE, for example CIFAR-100 ResNet-110 from 16.53% to 1.26%, and it never changes accuracy. Matrix scaling over-fits with many classes. For our PhD this is the first calibration step for every agent: fit T on a hospital validation split, check ECE with 15 bins, then use the calibrated confidence in the escalation rule.
papers.studyDesign: Empirical study on public image and text classification benchmarks. First shows how modern network design affects calibration, then compares post-hoc calibration methods fitted on a held-out validation set.
papers.datasets: Image: Caltech-UCSD Birds (200 classes; 5,994/2,897/2,897 train/val/test), Stanford Cars (196 classes; 8,041/4,020/4,020), ImageNet 2012 (1,000 classes; 1.3M/25,000/25,000), CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (32x32; 45,000/5,000/10,000), SVHN (598,388/6,000/26,032). Text: 20 News (20 classes; 9,034/2,259/7,528), Reuters (8 classes; 4,388/1,097/2,189), Stanford Sentiment Treebank binary and fine-grained.
papers.preprocessing: Data preprocessing, training procedures and hyper-parameters as in each original architecture paper. Birds and Cars networks fine-tuned from ImageNet. A separate validation split is kept only for fitting the calibration method.
papers.modelDetails: Models: ResNet (50, 110, 152), ResNet with stochastic depth, Wide ResNet-32, DenseNet-40/161, LeNet-5, DAN (text) and TreeLSTM (SST). Calibration methods compared: histogram binning, isotonic regression, Bayesian Binning into Quantiles (BBQ), and Platt-scaling variants: matrix scaling (W z + b), vector scaling (diagonal W) and temperature scaling (softmax(z/T), one scalar T > 0 fitted by minimising NLL on the validation set). Temperature scaling does not change the predicted class, so accuracy is unchanged.
papers.training: Networks trained with the settings of their original papers. Calibration parameters (T, W, b, bins) fitted on the validation split by NLL. Also studied how depth, width, Batch Normalization and weight decay (10^-5 to 10^-2) change calibration on CIFAR-100.
papers.evaluation: Expected Calibration Error (ECE) with M = 15 equal-width confidence bins as the main metric; Maximum Calibration Error (MCE); negative log-likelihood (NLL); reliability diagrams; test error.
papers.baselines: Uncalibrated network vs histogram binning, isotonic regression, BBQ, temperature scaling, vector scaling and matrix scaling.
papers.results: ECE (%) before -> after temperature scaling: CIFAR-100 ResNet-110 16.53 -> 1.26; CIFAR-100 Wide ResNet-32 15.0 -> 2.32; CIFAR-100 DenseNet-40 10.37 -> 1.18; Birds ResNet-50 9.19 -> 1.85; ImageNet DenseNet-161 6.28 -> 1.99; ImageNet ResNet-152 5.48 -> 1.86; CIFAR-10 ResNet-110 4.6 -> 0.83; 20 News DAN 8.02 -> 4.11. Matrix scaling made calibration worse with many classes (CIFAR-100 ResNet-110 25.49%). Deeper and wider networks and Batch Normalization increased miscalibration; more weight decay reduced it.
papers.statistics: Not reported (single runs; no confidence intervals or significance tests).

papers.title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
papers.authors: Gal Y, Ghahramani Z
papers.aim: To get model uncertainty from normal deep networks without changing them much.
papers.method: Showed dropout training is approximate Bayesian inference. Keep dropout on at test time and run many forward passes (MC dropout).
papers.result: Better predictive log-likelihood and RMSE on regression tasks, and useful uncertainty in classification and RL.
papers.tools: Dropout networks, Bayesian approximation
papers.gap: Uncertainty quality depends on dropout rate, and is often still too low.
papers.relation: Cheap way to get epistemic uncertainty for our MRI segmentation and classification agents on modest hardware.
papers.limitations: Several forward passes needed, so slower at inference. Future: better approximations.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors prove that minimising the usual dropout training loss with L2 weight decay is the same as variational inference in a deep Gaussian process, so a dropout network already holds an approximate posterior over weights. At test time they keep dropout on and run the network T times; the mean of the outputs is the prediction and their spread is the model uncertainty. For regression they add the inverse precision tau^-1, where tau comes from the prior length-scale, dropout rate and weight decay. They test this on the Mauna Loa CO2 series with 4-5 layer networks of 1,024 units (ReLU or TanH, dropout 0.1-0.2), training on the first part and predicting the rest: normal dropout gives a confident wrong value far from the data, while MC dropout widens its uncertainty. On rotated MNIST digits, 100 passes show that a digit can be classed as 5 while the spread of outputs is very large, so uncertainty flags the error. For a fair numeric test they copy the 10-dataset UCI protocol (20 random splits, 50-unit network, dropout 0.05 or 0.005, tau chosen by Bayesian optimisation, Adam, batch 32) and beat VI and PBP on RMSE and log-likelihood on 9 of 10 datasets. For our PhD, MC dropout is the cheapest way to get an uncertainty value from an existing segmentation or classification agent without retraining.
papers.studyDesign: Theory plus benchmark experiments. Shows that a network trained with dropout is an approximate Bayesian model (a deep Gaussian process), then tests the uncertainty it gives on regression, classification and reinforcement learning tasks.
papers.datasets: Regression: Mauna Loa CO2 (about 200 points, extrapolation) and reconstructed solar irradiance (interpolation). Classification: MNIST (rotated digit test). Predictive performance: 10 UCI regression sets - Boston Housing (N=506, 13 inputs), Concrete (1,030, 8), Energy (768, 8), Kin8nm (8,192, 8), Naval (11,934, 16), Power Plant (9,568, 4), Protein (45,730, 9), Wine Red (1,599, 11), Yacht (308, 6), Year MSD (515,345, 90).
papers.preprocessing: CO2 and solar data centred and normalised; model trained on the left part of the series and tested on all of it (extrapolation). UCI: set-up of Hernandez-Lobato and Adams (2015), averaged over 20 random train/test splits (5 for Protein, 1 for Year).
papers.modelDetails: MC dropout: keep dropout switched on at test time, run T stochastic forward passes, and use the mean as the prediction and the variance (plus inverse model precision tau^-1) as predictive uncertainty. Dropout probability and weight decay correspond to a prior length-scale and model precision. CO2: 4 or 5 hidden layers of 1,024 units, ReLU or TanH, dropout 0.1 or 0.2. UCI: one hidden layer of 50 units, dropout 0.05 or 0.005. MNIST: LeNet with dropout; 100 forward passes shown.
papers.training: UCI: prior length-scale 10^-2; tau found by Bayesian optimisation over validation log-likelihood (40 iterations, then 10x more iterations for the final model); mini-batch 32; Adam optimiser. CO2 plots used T = 1,000 passes; T = 10 already gives a reasonable estimate.
papers.evaluation: Test RMSE and test predictive log-likelihood (mean and standard error over splits); qualitative uncertainty plots far from the training data; softmax input/output spread for rotated MNIST digits.
papers.baselines: Variational inference for Bayesian NNs (VI, Graves 2011), Probabilistic Back-propagation (PBP), standard dropout with weight averaging, Gaussian process with squared-exponential kernel.
papers.results: Test RMSE (VI / PBP / MC dropout): Boston 4.32 / 3.01 / 2.97; Concrete 7.19 / 5.67 / 5.23; Energy 2.65 / 1.80 / 1.66; Protein 4.84 / 4.73 / 4.36; Yacht 6.89 / 1.02 / 1.11. Test log-likelihood: Boston -2.90 / -2.57 / -2.46; Concrete -3.39 / -3.16 / -3.04; Protein -2.99 / -2.97 / -2.89. Dropout was best on all datasets except Yacht RMSE. Boston median RMSE 2.68 (IQR 2.45-3.35). On CO2, standard dropout predicted a far-away point confidently, while MC dropout showed large uncertainty there.
papers.statistics: Mean +/- standard error over 20 random splits; medians and IQR reported for Boston. No hypothesis tests.

papers.title: Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles
papers.authors: Lakshminarayanan B, Pritzel A, Blundell C
papers.aim: To give a simple, non-Bayesian way to estimate predictive uncertainty.
papers.method: Train several networks with different random starts, using proper scoring rules (and optional adversarial training), then average.
papers.result: Well-calibrated predictions and higher uncertainty on out-of-distribution samples, often better than MC dropout.
papers.tools: Deep ensembles, MNIST, SVHN, ImageNet
papers.gap: Training and running many models costs a lot.
papers.relation: Strong UQ baseline to compare with MC dropout for our agents. Cost matters in low-resource hospitals.
papers.limitations: Compute and memory cost. Future: lighter ensembles.
papers.methodologyDetail: Instead of a Bayesian network, the authors train several ordinary networks and average them. Each of M networks (default 5) is trained from a different random start on the whole training set and outputs a full predictive distribution - for regression a mean and a variance, trained with Gaussian negative log-likelihood, so the network learns its own noise level. Optionally each training batch is extended with adversarial examples made by the fast gradient sign method with step 1% of the input range, which smooths the predictive distribution. At test time the M outputs are combined as an equal-weight mixture; its spread shows where the members disagree. They evaluate on the 10-dataset UCI benchmark against PBP and MC dropout (best NLL on most sets, e.g. Energy 1.38 vs 1.99), on MNIST (3x200 MLP) and SVHN (VGG-style net), where the ensemble beats MC dropout with the same number of samples on error, NLL and Brier score, and on ImageNet with an Inception network. Finally, a model trained on MNIST is tested on NotMNIST letters: the ensemble's entropy rises clearly on these unseen classes, so its uncertainty can flag inputs outside its training data. For our PhD, a 5-member ensemble per imaging agent is a simple, strong source of uncertainty for escalation, at 5x the training cost.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with benchmark experiments on regression, image classification and out-of-distribution detection.
papers.datasets: 10 UCI regression sets (Boston, Concrete, Energy, Kin8nm, Naval, Power Plant, Protein, Wine, Yacht, Year MSD; same splits as PBP); MNIST; SVHN; ImageNet ILSVRC-2012; NotMNIST test split as unseen classes for out-of-distribution testing.
papers.preprocessing: UCI: protocol of Hernandez-Lobato and Adams (2015). Each ensemble member trained on the full training set (no bagging - bagging made results worse because a bootstrap sample only has about 63% unique points). Diversity comes from random initialisation and random shuffling.
papers.modelDetails: Train M networks independently. Each network outputs a predictive distribution (mean and variance for regression, softmax for classification) and is trained with a proper scoring rule (NLL or Brier). Optional adversarial training with the fast gradient sign method, epsilon = 1% of the input range. Prediction = uniform mixture of the M members; for regression the mixture mean and variance are combined into one Gaussian. Recommended default M = 5. MNIST: MLP with 3 hidden layers of 200 units, ReLU, batch normalisation. SVHN: VGG-style convolutional network. ImageNet: Inception network.
papers.training: Defaults M = 5 networks and adversarial epsilon = 1% of input range (for example 2.55 for 0-255 images). MC-dropout comparison used dropout 0.1 after each non-linearity (0.5 performed worse). Networks trained in parallel.
papers.evaluation: Regression: test RMSE and NLL over 20 splits. Classification: error, NLL and Brier score as ensemble size M grows; ImageNet single-crop accuracy and calibration; predictive entropy on known (MNIST) vs unknown (NotMNIST) classes.
papers.baselines: Probabilistic Back-propagation (PBP), MC dropout (same number of samples M), ensembles without adversarial training, ensembles with random-direction perturbation.
papers.results: UCI NLL (PBP / MC-dropout / Deep Ensembles): Boston 2.57 / 2.46 / 2.41; Energy 2.04 / 1.99 / 1.38; Naval -3.73 / -3.80 / -5.63; Protein 2.97 / 2.89 / 2.83; Yacht 1.63 / 1.55 / 1.18. RMSE sometimes slightly worse (Boston 3.01 / 2.97 / 3.28) because the method optimises NLL. On MNIST and SVHN, ensembles beat MC-dropout on error, NLL and Brier score at every M; adversarial training helped on MNIST and on SVHN only at M = 1. On ImageNet both accuracy and uncertainty quality improved as M increased. Ensembles gave higher predictive entropy on unseen NotMNIST letters than on MNIST digits.
papers.statistics: Mean +/- standard deviation over splits; no hypothesis tests.
papers.availability: Not available (no official code link in the paper).

papers.title: Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks
papers.authors: Geifman Y, El-Yaniv R
papers.aim: To let a network refuse to predict on uncertain inputs while guaranteeing a chosen error rate.
papers.method: Selection with Guaranteed Risk (SGR): pick a confidence threshold on held-out data so the error on accepted cases stays under a target, with high probability. Tested softmax response and MC dropout.
papers.result: On ImageNet they could guarantee 2% top-5 error while still covering about 60% of images.
papers.tools: VGG / ResNet, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet
papers.gap: Single model, single decision, same cost for every mistake.
papers.relation: The risk-coverage trade-off is basically our escalation threshold. We need to extend it to asymmetric error cost and to a chain of agents.
papers.limitations: Guarantee assumes test data like calibration data. Future: training models for selection.
papers.methodologyDetail: The method takes any trained network and adds a reject option with a guaranteed error rate. First a confidence score is chosen for each input: the maximum softmax probability (SR) or the variance of MC-dropout outputs. A labelled hold-out set is sorted by this score. The SGR algorithm then runs a binary search over thresholds: for a candidate threshold it keeps only cases above it, counts their errors, and computes the tightest binomial upper bound on the true error of the kept cases at confidence delta divided by the number of search steps. It moves the threshold until the bound just meets the target risk r* set by the user, so the final rule is: answer if confidence >= theta, otherwise abstain. The authors test this on CIFAR-10/100 with a VGG-16 trained with augmentation and dropout (93.54% accuracy on CIFAR-10) and on ImageNet with VGG-16 and ResNet-50, using one half of the validation data to set theta and the other half to check the guarantee, with delta = 0.001. On CIFAR-10 a 1% error target is met with 78.6% of images answered; on ImageNet top-5 a 2% target keeps 53.5% coverage, and the measured test error never exceeded the bound. For our PhD this is the template for the escalation threshold: a clinician sets the acceptable error (for example 2% wrong tumour grades), the threshold is fitted on a local validation set, and every case below it is referred to the clinician.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with risk-control experiments on image classification benchmarks. A trained classifier is wrapped with a reject option whose error rate is guaranteed with high probability.
papers.datasets: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (half of the 10,000-image validation set, about 5,000 images, used to fit the selector; the other half, about 5,000, used for testing), ImageNet ILSVRC (about 25,000 images to fit and 25,000 to test), top-1 and top-5 tasks.
papers.preprocessing: CIFAR: data augmentation with horizontal flips, vertical and horizontal shifts and rotations. The validation set is randomly split in two equal halves: one to run the selection algorithm, one to test the guaranteed risk.
papers.modelDetails: Selective classifier (f, g): f predicts, g decides to answer or say 'don't know'. Two confidence-rate functions: softmax response (SR, the maximum softmax probability) and MC-dropout variance. The SGR algorithm (Selection with Guaranteed Risk) sorts samples by confidence and does a binary search over the threshold theta; for each candidate it computes a tight binomial upper bound on the selective risk (Gascuel and Caraux) with confidence delta / ceil(log2 m), and keeps the lowest-coverage-loss threshold whose bound is below the target risk r*. Networks: VGG-16 with heavy dropout (CIFAR), pre-trained VGG-16 and ResNet-50 (ImageNet).
papers.training: CIFAR-10 VGG-16: SGD, momentum 0.9, initial learning rate 0.1, weight decay 0.0005, learning rate halved every 25 epochs, 250 epochs; validation accuracy 93.54%. Same recipe for CIFAR-100. Confidence level delta = 0.001 for all SGR runs.
papers.evaluation: Risk-coverage curves; for each target risk r*: train/test selective risk, train/test coverage and the risk bound b*.
papers.baselines: SR vs MC-dropout as the confidence function; full-coverage classifier (no rejection).
papers.results: CIFAR-10 (delta 0.001): target 1% error -> test risk 0.92% at 78.6% coverage (bound 0.99%); target 2% -> 1.49% at 84.7%; target 6% -> 5.72% at 97.8%. CIFAR-100: target 2% -> test risk 1.87% at 21.3% coverage. ImageNet VGG-16 top-1: target 10% -> test risk 9.48% at 59.5% coverage; target 25% -> 24.45% at 91.2%. ImageNet VGG-16 top-5: target 2% -> 1.79% at 53.5% coverage. ResNet-50 top-1: target 10% -> 9.88% at 65.0%. The test risk never exceeded the bound. SR was clearly better than MC-dropout on ImageNet (top-1 at 60% coverage: about 10% vs more than 20% error).
papers.statistics: High-probability guarantee: P(selective risk > b*) < delta = 0.001 (numerical binomial bound with union bound over log2 m search steps). No Bonferroni correction across table rows.

papers.title: Consistent Estimators for Learning to Defer to an Expert
papers.authors: Mozannar H, Sontag D
papers.aim: To train a classifier and a 'defer to the expert' decision together, with a sound loss.
papers.method: Adds an extra 'defer' class and a consistent surrogate loss based on cross-entropy, taking expert accuracy into account.
papers.result: Beat confidence-based and earlier L2D baselines on CIFAR-10 with synthetic experts, CIFAR-100, CheXpert and hate-speech data.
papers.tools: Surrogate loss, WideResNet, CheXpert
papers.gap: Needs expert labels on training data. Does not limit how many cases go to the expert.
papers.relation: Core method for O2. We need to add the limit of clinician review time and the clinical cost of each error type.
papers.limitations: One expert, one decision. Future: multiple experts and budget constraints.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors frame deferral as cost-sensitive learning: for each training case the cost of predicting class j is the classifier's error, and the cost of the extra 'defer' class is the expert's error on that case (known from the expert's recorded label). They add one output unit to an ordinary network, so it has K class outputs plus a defer output, and train it with a new surrogate loss that reduces to cross-entropy when the expert is ignored and is proven consistent, so with enough data it learns the best possible rule for when to hand a case to the expert. At test time the case goes to the expert when the defer output is the largest. They test it with a WideResNet-28 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 using simulated experts that are perfect on only some classes, on CIFAR10H with 50 real human labels per image when expert labels exist for only part of the data, on hate-speech text and on chest X-rays. The joint training beats the common approach of training the model alone and then comparing its confidence with the expert's (+6.39 points on synthetic data). For our PhD this is the core learning-to-defer recipe: each agent gets a 'refer to clinician' output trained on recorded clinician decisions, and our work adds limits on clinician time and different costs for different clinical errors.
papers.studyDesign: Theory (consistent surrogate loss and generalisation bound) plus experiments with synthetic and real human experts on image, text and chest X-ray classification.
papers.datasets: Synthetic mixture data (logistic regression test); CIFAR-10 (50,000 train / 10,000 test, 32x32, 10 classes); CIFAR-100; CIFAR10H (50 crowdworker labels for each of the 10,000 CIFAR-10 test images, used as a real human expert with limited labels); hate speech and offensive language tweets; chest X-rays with synthetic experts.
papers.preprocessing: Synthetic expert k: perfect on the first k classes, uniform random on the rest (CIFAR-100 expert correct with probability 0.94 on its classes). CIFAR-10 model deliberately trained without augmentation to leave room for the expert. Limited-expert setting: only part of the data has expert labels; missing expert labels imputed.
papers.modelDetails: Learn a classifier h and a rejector r together. One network with K+1 outputs: the first K are class scores, the extra unit is the 'defer' score. Trained with the proposed surrogate loss L_CE^alpha, a cost-sensitive generalisation of cross-entropy that is consistent (minimising it gives the Bayes-optimal defer rule). alpha in {0, 0.5, 1} weights how much the model still fits the true label on deferred cases. Defer when the defer score is larger than every class score.
papers.training: CIFAR-10: WideResNet-28, SGD with momentum, cosine annealing learning rate, 200 epochs; plain model 90.47% test accuracy. CIFAR-100: WideResNet-28 with random crops and flips, 79.28% accuracy.
papers.evaluation: System accuracy (model + expert), coverage (share of cases the model handles), classifier accuracy on non-deferred cases; difference vs baselines with 95% confidence intervals; varying expert competence k and training-set size.
papers.baselines: Confidence baseline (Raghu et al. 2019: defer if expert confidence > model confidence), learned oracle rejector, mixture-of-experts loss (Madras et al. 2018).
papers.results: Synthetic data: L_CE (alpha=0) beat the confidence baseline by 6.39 accuracy points (95% CI 3.71-9.06), matched the oracle (+0.22, CI -1.71 to 2.15) and beat mixture-of-experts by 2.01 (CI 0.14-4.06). CIFAR-100: +1.60 points over the confidence baseline on average for 30 <= k <= 90. CIFAR10H with limited expert labels: L_CE impute system accuracy 96.29 +/- 0.25% at 51.67% coverage (classifier accuracy 99.2% on kept cases); L_CE 2-step 96.03% at 60.81% coverage.
papers.statistics: 95% confidence intervals for accuracy differences; mean +/- standard deviation over repeated runs.

papers.title: Predict Responsibly: Improving Fairness and Accuracy by Learning to Defer
papers.authors: Madras D, Pitassi T, Zemel R
papers.aim: To show that a model should defer by thinking about who will receive the case, not only its own confidence.
papers.method: Learning-to-defer model that is trained with the downstream decision maker in mind, compared with simple reject option.
papers.result: Better accuracy and fairness of the whole system on COMPAS and Heritage Health data.
papers.tools: Neural networks, fairness metrics
papers.gap: Decision makers were simulated.
papers.relation: Supports our idea that deferral depends on the clinician (radiologist, pathologist, neurosurgeon) who will review it.
papers.limitations: Not tested in medicine. Future: real human decision makers.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors model a decision pipeline where an automated model can either decide or pass the case to a human decision-maker who has extra information but may be biased or inconsistent. Classic rejection learning passes a case whenever the model is unsure, using a fixed cost per pass, and ignores who receives the case. Learning to defer adds the decision-maker's prediction into the training loss: on each training case, passing costs whatever error the decision-maker would make, so the model learns to keep the cases where the human is weak or biased and pass the cases where the human is strong. A fairness term can be added so the whole system treats groups (race in COMPAS, age in Health) more equally. Because real joint human-model data is rare, they simulate the human with a second two-layer network trained with extra features, and test three humans: very accurate, biased and inconsistent. Sweeping the pass penalty and fairness weight traces accuracy-fairness curves; the deferring model dominates rejection learning in every scenario. For our PhD this shows that the escalation rule must be learned with respect to the specific clinician who will review the case (radiologist, pathologist, neurosurgeon), not only from the model's own confidence.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with semi-synthetic experiments: real datasets, and a simulated downstream decision-maker (DM) trained under different conditions with extra information the model does not see.
papers.datasets: COMPAS (predict a defendant's recidivism without discriminating by race) and Heritage Health (predict a patient's Charlson comorbidity index without discriminating by age).
papers.preprocessing: Simulated DMs are separate classifiers given extra information in training: violent recidivism for COMPAS, primary condition group for Health. Three DM scenarios: highly accurate DM, biased DM, inconsistent DM (random errors on subgroups).
papers.modelDetails: Two-stage system: model either predicts or says 'pass' and the DM decides. Rejection learning uses a fixed penalty gamma_reject for each pass. Learning to defer instead includes the DM's own prediction in the loss, so the pass decision adapts to where the DM is accurate or biased. Two versions: post-hoc (pass decision from model outputs) and end-to-end (pass network also sees the input X). A fairness regulariser alpha_fair penalises disparate impact between groups. All models and DMs are fully-connected two-layer neural networks.
papers.training: Hyper-parameter sweeps over gamma_reject / gamma_defer and alpha_fair; further details in the appendix (not reported in the main text).
papers.evaluation: System accuracy against fairness (disparate impact between subgroups) and against deferral rate, for each DM scenario.
papers.baselines: Binary classifier optimised for accuracy only; binary classifier with fairness penalty; fair rejection learning; DM alone.
papers.results: Results are given as accuracy-fairness and accuracy-deferral curves (no single summary numbers in the main text). Learning to defer gave higher system accuracy and lower unfairness than rejection learning in all three DM scenarios, including with biased and inconsistent DMs; with an inconsistent DM, only the end-to-end deferring model adapted, because the post-hoc model cannot see X.
papers.statistics: Not reported.

papers.title: The Algorithmic Automation Problem: Prediction, Triage, and Human Effort
papers.authors: Raghu M, Blumer K, Corrado G, Kleinberg J, Obermeyer Z, Mullainathan S
papers.aim: To decide which cases an algorithm should handle and which should go to humans, to use human effort well.
papers.method: Triage using predicted human error / disagreement plus model uncertainty. Tested on medical data like diabetic retinopathy grading.
papers.result: Mixing algorithm and human by triage did better than full automation or full human review.
papers.tools: Deep learning, uncertainty estimation, triage
papers.gap: Workflow and time cost of humans not modelled in detail.
papers.relation: Our case: specialist time is the scarcest thing. This paper frames the problem in the same way.
papers.limitations: Preprint, retrospective only. Future: prospective test.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors ask how to split cases between an algorithm and doctors when the algorithm is better on average. They train a CNN on a large fundus photograph set to predict the 5 diabetic retinopathy grades, using the spread of doctor grades as a soft target, and turn its output into a referable / non-referable decision (grade 3 or more). On a small adjudicated test set with many doctor grades per image, they show that per-image errors of doctors and algorithm vary a lot: on some images doctors are more reliable, on others the model is. They then train two more networks to predict, for each image, the chance that the model is wrong and the chance that a doctor is wrong (the latter learned from how much doctors disagree). Images are ranked by this triage score; the easiest share is automated and the remaining images get the available doctor time. Error falls from about 5.5% (doctors) and 4% (full automation) to about 3.5% with triage. For our PhD this supports routing per case on both AI error risk and clinician error risk, and treating clinician review time as a fixed budget in the escalation policy.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective study on a real medical imaging task (diabetic retinopathy grading from fundus photographs), comparing full automation, human-only review and optimal triage between algorithm and doctors.
papers.datasets: Large fundus photograph training set, each image sparsely graded by 1-3 doctors on the 5-point diabetic retinopathy (DR) scale; a smaller gold-standard evaluation set where each image has many individual doctor grades plus a single adjudicated grade (from doctor discussion) used as ground truth; a second dataset in the appendix with the same findings.
papers.preprocessing: DR graded as 5 classes for training; for triage the task is binary: referable DR (grade >= 3) vs non-referable. Multiple doctor grades per image are aggregated and thresholded.
papers.modelDetails: A convolutional neural network outputs a distribution over the 5 DR grades, trained with the empirical distribution of doctor grades as target. Two auxiliary networks predict, per image, (i) the algorithm's error probability Pr[M_i] and (ii) the human error probability Pr[H_i] (built on direct prediction of doctor disagreement). A triage score from these ranks images; the top alpha*N go to the algorithm and the rest share the human effort budget B = cN equally.
papers.training: Model development details given in the paper's appendix (not in the main text).
papers.evaluation: Error rate against the adjudicated grade for: doctors alone, full automation (alpha = 1), equal human coverage (alpha = 0), and triage at intermediate alpha.
papers.baselines: Full automation; equal human effort on all instances; individual doctors.
papers.results: Doctors alone about 5.5% error; full automation about 4%; automation with optimal triage about 3.5%. Human and algorithm error differ strongly from image to image, and this difference is partly predictable, which is why triage beats full automation even though the algorithm is better on average.
papers.statistics: Not reported as formal tests in the main text.

papers.title: Enhancing the reliability and accuracy of AI-enabled diagnosis via complementarity-driven deferral to clinicians (CoDoC)
papers.authors: Dvijotham K, Winkens J, Barsbey M, et al., Karthikesalingam A
papers.aim: To learn when to trust a predictive AI and when to defer to the clinician, in real screening.
papers.method: CoDoC uses only the AI confidence score, the clinician's read and ground truth from past data to learn deferral regions. Does not need access to the model inside.
papers.result: In breast cancer screening data it cut false positives (around 25% in the UK set) at the same false negatives and reduced clinician workload a lot. Also tested on TB screening.
papers.tools: Density estimation on confidence scores, mammography and chest X-ray AI
papers.gap: Single AI model and single decision. Retrospective.
papers.relation: The closest prior work to our O2. Our difference: a chain of agents, brain MRI + pathology, and small Sri Lankan data.
papers.limitations: Needs enough labelled past cases with clinician opinion. Future: prospective use.
papers.notes: Same paper as O1-P46 (CoDoC); PDF and methodology under O1-P46
papers.methodologyDetail: CoDoC treats the diagnostic AI as a frozen black box and learns only when to defer. For each case in a tuning set the authors stored three numbers: the AI confidence score (mean softmax from an ensemble), the binary clinician decision, and the ground truth (biopsy for breast cancer, Xpert MTB/RIF for TB). The AI operating point theta was set halfway between the thresholds that match the clinician on sensitivity and on specificity. They then estimated, with kernel density estimation, the distribution of AI scores in four groups (disease present or absent, crossed with clinician correct or wrong). From these they computed an advantage function over the score axis, weighted by lambda to trade sensitivity against specificity. Score intervals where the advantage is positive become deferral regions: cases there go to the clinician workflow, all others are decided by thresholding the AI score. Smoothing (KDE bandwidth) removes the underspecification of raw threshold search; the bandwidth and model choice were picked on a separate validation split, and the test set was used once. Data: UK mammography tuning 60,755 cases (1,198 cancers) with 12,169 used for fitting and the rest for validation; UK test 25,856 women (414 cancers, 39-month follow-up); US NYU set 7,074 train / 7,074 test (only 26 tuning cancers); a new US population with 4,392 / 4,391 / 8,981 cases; TB 23,954 Bangladeshi adults split 50/50 with 3 radiologists and 5 commercial AIs. Evaluation compared CoDoC to AI-only and clinician-only with McNemar (superiority, alpha 0.05) and Wald (non-inferiority, margin 0.05) tests, reported 95% CIs, reads per case, recall rates and Xpert tests saved. Stress tests covered new population, unseen readers, subgroups, and an oracle upper bound (up to 10 regions, fit on test data) showing when confidence-only deferral cannot help. To adapt: collect a local tuning set of agent scores, clinician reads and confirmed diagnoses for brain-tumour MRI, fit deferral regions per agent, and validate on a held-out Sri Lankan set.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective, multi-dataset simulation study of human-AI deferral. Settings: UK breast screening (two screening centres in England, double reading with arbitration), US breast screening (NYU Langone Health; a US community screening centre), and TB triage at 3 screening centres in Dhaka, Bangladesh (Stop TB Partnership / icddr,b). Industry-led (Google, DeepMind) with NYU and Stop TB collaborators.
papers.datasets: (1) UK Mammography: CoDoC tuning data = 60,755 cases (1,198 biopsy-confirmed cancers) from the diagnostic AI's hyperparameter-tuning subset, split into a deferral training subset of 12,169 cases (243 cancers) and a validation subset (remaining cases). UK held-out test set: screening mammograms from 25,856 women, 2012-2015, two English screening centres (10% random sample), ground truth by biopsy-confirmed follow-up over 39 months, 414 cancers; historical First reader and Double read (with arbitration) decisions. (2) US Mammography Dataset 2 (NYU): CoDoC trained on 7,074 exams and tested on 7,074 exams of women aged 27-92 (May-August 2017); cancer = positive biopsy within 120 days; combined, 307 benign-only, 40 malignant-only, 21 benign and malignant, 13,780 not biopsied; lesions split evenly across sets. Only 26 positive cancers available for tuning. (3) New-population study (Mammography AI 1 on a new US community centre with yearly screening and DBT-assisted single reader): tuning 8,783 cases (139 cancers) from 2,926 women, split 4,392 training / 4,391 model selection; test 8,981 cases (174 cancers). (4) TB: individuals aged 15+ at 3 TB centres in Dhaka, May 2014-Oct 2016, digital PA chest X-ray plus Xpert MTB/RIF; 23,954 included after excluding under-15s and missing valid CXR or Xpert; split evenly into CoDoC training and test sets. Read by 3 registered radiologists (dichotomised possible TB vs not TB) and 5 commercial AI systems with no site training. Reference standard: Xpert.
papers.preprocessing: No image preprocessing by CoDoC: each case is reduced to a 3-tuple (average softmax score from an ensemble of diagnostic AI models, clinician/reader binary opinion, ground truth label) stored as 'DeferralData'. Radiologist TB reads were dichotomised (highly suggestive/possibly TB = positive; abnormal not TB/normal = negative). Splits: all data split into training and a held-out test set touched once; training further split into a tuning set (fits deferral AI) and a validation set (chooses smoothing hyperparameters / model). UK: 12,169 training vs remaining ~48,586 validation; US Dataset 2: 7,074 train / 7,074 test; new US population: 4,392 / 4,391 / 8,981 test; TB: 50/50 train/test. AI operating point set as the mean of the thresholds matching the clinical workflow on sensitivity and on specificity.
papers.modelDetails: Step 1: the locked diagnostic AI outputs a confidence score z per case. Step 2: an operating point theta turns z into an AI opinion (positive if z above theta). Step 3: from the tuning set, estimate four conditional densities of z given ground truth (positive/negative) and clinician correct/incorrect using kernel density estimation. Step 4: with a trade-off weight lambda in [0,1] between sensitivity and specificity, compute an advantage function A(z) = expected gain in the weighted objective from deferring at score z versus using the AI. Step 5: defer to the clinician workflow wherever the smoothed A(z) > 0; the zero crossings of the smoothed function give unique deferral intervals (unlike plain threshold search, which is underspecified). This is proved optimal for a given theta (Appendix A.1.1.1). Step 6: KDE smoothing hyperparameters are chosen on the validation set. Deployment: if z is inside a deferral region, the clinical workflow decides; otherwise threshold z (green region = no disease, red = disease). Clinical workflows deferred to: single first reader, double reading with arbitration, single US reader, TB radiologist. Upper-bound analysis: up to 10 deferral regions found by dynamic programming and trained on the test set to estimate the best possible confidence-based deferral. Optimised either for higher sensitivity at non-inferior specificity or vice versa (operating points OP1-OP4).
papers.training: Non-iterative fitting (density estimation plus search over thresholds and smoothing parameters); no optimizer, learning rate, epochs or batch size are reported. Hardware and training time: Not reported. The diagnostic AI models were pretrained and frozen; they are not retrained.
papers.evaluation: Held-out test sets used once. Comparison of CoDoC vs standalone AI and vs clinician workflow on sensitivity and specificity at matched operating points. Superiority tested with McNemar test (alpha 0.05) and non-inferiority with Wald test (margin 0.05). Workload measured as human reads per case. Clinical translation measured as recall-to-assessment rate per 1000 cases and proportion of Xpert tests avoided. Generalisation stress tests: new population (US community centre), unseen readers (per-reader analysis on UK test set), different AI manufacturers, different workflows; subgroup analysis by age and breast density; comparison with threshold search; theoretical upper bound of confidence-based deferral; summary ROC curves for Pareto front.
papers.baselines: Standalone diagnostic AI (Mammography AI 1, Mammography AI 2, TB AI manufacturers 1-5); clinician-only workflows (UK first reader, UK double reading with arbitration, US single reader, Bangladesh radiologists); threshold-search deferral (Leibig et al. 2022).
papers.results: Table 1 (sensitivity/specificity %, CoDoC vs clinician vs AI). UK, defer to first reader OP1: CoDoC 72.6/91.8, reader 62.7/92.8, AI 64.9/93.9; OP2: 64.4/96.5. UK, defer to double read OP3: CoDoC 71.0/95.1, double read 67.6/96.1; OP4: 68.3/96.9. US Dataset 1 (AI 1), defer to single reader OP1: 56.9/87.5 vs reader 50.0/88.0 vs AI 48.3/86.3; OP2: 50.0/91.2. US Dataset 2 (AI 2): CoDoC 96.7/90.9, reader 96.7/84.5, AI 86.7/70.0. TB CoDoC vs AI (reader 89.4/62.4): M1 90.5/68.3 vs 90.9/65.6; M2 89.3/64.2 vs 89.5/62.5; M3 89.2/67.7 vs 89.7/62.7; M4 90.6/70.8 vs 91.9/67.9; M5 91.8/71.7 vs 92.8/69.1. UK single reader: specificity +2.6% (95% CI 2.3-2.9, P=0.005) or sensitivity +7.7% (95% CI 4.5-10.7, P<0.001) vs AI at 0.15 and 0.34 extra reads/case; recall rate 70 to 44 per 1000 using 15% of one reader's workload. UK double reading: recall 48 to 41 per 1000, reads 2.1 to 0.7 per case. US Dataset 2: recall 159 to 88 per 1000; one read every 2.1 cases. TB: Xpert tests avoided +5.2%, +3.3%, +9.5% (M1-M3), one human read per 2.9, 3.7, 3.8 cases. New US population: sensitivity +6.9% (95% CI 0.4-13.2, P=0.033) or specificity +3.2% (95% CI 2.6-3.7, P=0.037) vs reader with 55% fewer reads; vs AI specificity +4.9% (95% CI 4.1-5.6) or sensitivity +8.6% (95% CI 1.9-15.2, P=0.011); recall 127 to 96 per 1000. Unseen readers: mean +5.4% sensitivity (2.5-8.2) and +0.9% specificity (0.6-1.1). CoDoC beat threshold search when tuning sets were small (<1000 samples); nearly identical on large sets. Worked with only 40 local tuning cases.
papers.statistics: McNemar test for superiority (significance 0.05) and Wald test for non-inferiority (margin 0.05); 95% confidence intervals for absolute sensitivity/specificity differences; P values reported (e.g. P=0.005, P<0.001, P=0.019, P=0.033, P=0.037, P=0.011). Inter-rater agreement: Not reported.
papers.availability: Code, trained deferral models and the tuning/test data needed to reproduce results (AI scores, clinician opinions, labels) at https://github.com/google-research/codoc. Raw images not public (OPTIMAM access by application; NYU, Northwestern, St Clair, Stop TB/icddr,b under licence).

papers.title: A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification
papers.authors: Angelopoulos AN, Bates S
papers.aim: To explain conformal prediction in a practical way.
papers.method: Tutorial with code: split conformal, adaptive sets, conformal risk control, examples on images and medicine.
papers.result: Shows how to turn any model output into prediction sets with a guaranteed coverage.
papers.tools: Conformal prediction, Python examples
papers.gap: Guarantee needs exchangeable data, which is not true across hospitals.
papers.relation: For tumour type we can give a set of likely classes with a coverage guarantee. A large set = escalate. Works with small calibration sets.
papers.limitations: Coverage only on average, not per patient. Future: shift-aware conformal.
papers.methodologyDetail: Conformal prediction turns any model's heuristic confidence into a set of answers that contains the truth with a user-chosen probability, for example 90%. The recipe needs only a labelled calibration set the model has not seen. For each calibration case a score measures how wrong the model is on the true answer (for classification, one minus the softmax probability of the true class). The (n+1)(1-alpha)/n quantile of these scores becomes a threshold; for a new case every label scoring below the threshold goes into the prediction set. If calibration and new cases come from the same distribution, the set contains the true label at least 1-alpha of the time, whatever the model. The guide then shows better scores (APS, which adds sorted softmax probabilities until the true class, giving larger sets for hard inputs), conformalised quantile regression for continuous outputs, group-wise and class-wise calibration, risk control for losses other than coverage, and weighting for distribution shift, and explains how to test an implementation by repeating calibration on 100+ random splits. For our PhD, the set size from conformal prediction is a direct escalation signal: if the set for a tumour grade or diagnosis has more than one label at the chosen error level, the case goes to the clinician.
papers.studyDesign: Tutorial / methods guide with worked examples and Python pseudocode. No new clinical study.
papers.datasets: Worked examples on ImageNet classification (prediction sets), regression with quantile regression, and other examples (tumour segmentation, time series, outliers) in later sections.
papers.preprocessing: Split conformal prediction: keep a calibration set of n labelled examples that the model never trained on; the model itself is trained on separate data.
papers.modelDetails: Any pre-trained model f. Steps: (1) choose a score s(x, y) that is large when the model is wrong, e.g. 1 minus the softmax probability of the true class; (2) compute the score on the n calibration points; (3) take q-hat = the ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))/n quantile of the scores; (4) for a new input, the prediction set is all labels whose score <= q-hat. Variants: Adaptive Prediction Sets (APS, sum sorted softmax until the true label), conformalised quantile regression (score = distance from y to the nearest fitted quantile), class-conditional and group-conditional conformal, conformal risk control for other losses, handling of distribution shift (weighted conformal).
papers.training: No training of the predictor; calibration only needs the quantile step. Evaluation requires repeating calibration over at least 100 random splits.
papers.evaluation: Marginal coverage P(Y_test in C(X_test)) >= 1 - alpha; set size (smaller = more useful); conditional coverage checks across groups and set sizes (size-stratified coverage); coverage fluctuation follows a Beta distribution that depends on n.
papers.baselines: Naive softmax thresholding (which does not guarantee coverage).
papers.results: Theorem: with exchangeable data, split conformal gives coverage of at least 1 - alpha for any model and any score. The usefulness (set size and conditional coverage) depends on the score function. The guide gives formulas to choose the calibration size n so that coverage of a single calibration run stays close to 1 - alpha.
papers.statistics: Finite-sample coverage guarantee; distribution of realised coverage is Beta(n + 1 - l, l) with l = floor((n+1) alpha), used to check implementations.

papers.title: Can You Trust Your Model's Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift
papers.authors: Ovadia Y, Fertig E, Ren J, Nado Z, Sculley D, Nowozin S, Dillon JV, Lakshminarayanan B, Snoek J
papers.aim: To compare uncertainty methods when test data is shifted from training data.
papers.method: Large benchmark of methods (vanilla, temperature scaling, dropout, ensembles, SVI, last-layer) under increasing shift and OOD data.
papers.result: Calibration gets worse as shift grows. Temperature scaling on clean validation does not hold. Deep ensembles were the most robust.
papers.tools: Images, text, genomics; ResNet, LSTM
papers.gap: No method was good under strong shift.
papers.relation: Sri Lankan scanners and protocols are a dataset shift from BraTS. We must test calibration on local data, not just public data.
papers.limitations: Not medical imaging. Future: shift-robust methods.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors train seven uncertainty methods - plain softmax, temperature scaling, MC dropout, a 10-network deep ensemble, full SVI and last-layer SVI or dropout - on five problems: MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet, 20 Newsgroups text and the 37-million-example Criteo ad data, with standard splits and Bayesian-optimised hyper-parameters. Besides the usual test set, they build test sets with growing shift (rotated or translated digits, 16 kinds of image corruption at 5 intensities, randomised ad features) and fully out-of-distribution sets (for example SVHN for a CIFAR model). On each they measure accuracy, NLL, Brier score and ECE, plus how predictive entropy behaves on OOD inputs and how accuracy changes when keeping only predictions above a confidence threshold. All methods lose calibration as shift grows; temperature scaling, which looks perfect on the clean test set, degrades sharply; deep ensembles hold up best overall. The lesson for our PhD is that calibration checked only on the development set is not enough: the escalation thresholds must be re-checked on data from each Sri Lankan hospital and scanner, and ensembles are a strong default when data shift is expected.
papers.studyDesign: Large-scale benchmark of uncertainty methods on images, text and tabular ad data, tested on the normal test set, on increasingly shifted data, and on out-of-distribution (OOD) data.
papers.datasets: MNIST (LeNet; rotated 15-180 degrees and translated 2-14 px); CIFAR-10 with corruptions (CIFAR-10-C, increasing intensity) and SVHN as OOD; ImageNet with ImageNet-C corruptions; 20 Newsgroups text with OOD text; Criteo display ads (37 million examples) with randomised features as shift.
papers.preprocessing: Standard training/validation/test protocols for each dataset; shifted test sets made by applying corruptions or rotations of increasing intensity; OOD sets from unrelated datasets.
papers.modelDetails: Methods compared: Vanilla (maximum softmax probability), Temperature scaling (fitted on the validation set), MC Dropout, Deep Ensembles (M = 10 networks), stochastic variational inference (SVI), and last-layer-only variants (LL-SVI, LL-Dropout). Architectures: LeNet (MNIST), ResNet-20 (CIFAR-10), ResNet-50 (ImageNet), LSTM (text), fully connected nets (Criteo).
papers.training: Hyper-parameters tuned for all methods with Bayesian optimisation (except ImageNet); details in the appendix.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy; negative log-likelihood; Brier score; Expected Calibration Error; for OOD inputs, distribution of predictive entropy and confidence-vs-accuracy curves (accuracy on examples above a confidence threshold).
papers.baselines: All methods compared with each other; vanilla softmax is the reference.
papers.results: Calibration of every method gets worse as shift increases. Temperature scaling works in-distribution but falls short under shift. Deep ensembles were the most robust across most tasks and shift levels; last-layer methods and SVI were less consistent (SVI good on MNIST, hard to scale). Good calibration on the i.i.d. test set did not predict good calibration under shift. Most numerical results are shown as box plots over shift intensities rather than tables.
papers.statistics: Distributions over corruption types shown as box plots; no hypothesis tests.

papers.title: Confidence Calibration and Predictive Uncertainty Estimation for Deep Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Mehrtash A, Wells WM, Tempany CM, Abolmaesumi P, Kapur T
papers.aim: To study calibration and uncertainty of segmentation networks in medical images.
papers.method: Compared Dice vs cross-entropy loss, model ensembles, and proposed segment-level uncertainty. Datasets incl. prostate, heart and brain tumour MRI.
papers.result: Dice-trained models are badly calibrated. Ensembles improve calibration. Segment-level uncertainty relates to how good the Dice is, so it can flag bad segmentations.
