papers.tools: FCN / U-Net style models, ensembles, MRI
papers.gap: Ensembles are costly, and no link to a decision (accept or refer).
papers.relation: Direct use in our MRI agent: give a per-tumour uncertainty that is passed to the next agent and used for escalation.
papers.limitations: Few datasets. Future: cheaper UQ.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors train U-Net-style networks on three public MRI tasks - BraTS 2017 brain tumours (trained on 66 CBICA patients, tested on 102 multi-centre TCIA patients), ACDC heart ventricles and PROSTATEx prostate - with either cross-entropy or soft Dice loss, after resampling and cropping slices to 224x224 and normalising intensities. For each they compare a single network, MC dropout, and ensembles of up to 50 independently trained networks. Calibration is measured only near the structure (inside a bounding box) using NLL, Brier score and ECE, and segmentation with Dice and Hausdorff distance, with 95% confidence intervals. Dice-loss training gives good overlap but over-confident voxel probabilities; ensembling both improves Dice and brings ECE down (brain 8.11% to 3.28%; prostate to 2.82%). They then average voxel entropy over each predicted segment and show it tracks segmentation quality (r = 0.77-0.92 with logit Dice), and that high entropy picks out cases from a different hospital or coil. For our PhD this gives a ready recipe for the MRI segmentation agent: train an ensemble, compute segment-level entropy, and escalate cases whose entropy predicts a poor Dice.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective experimental study on three public MRI segmentation tasks (brain tumour, heart, prostate), comparing loss functions and uncertainty methods, with out-of-distribution test sets.
papers.datasets: Brain: MICCAI BraTS 2017 multiparametric MRI (T1, T1-Gd, T2, FLAIR); CBICA subset 66 train / 22 validation patients, TCIA multi-institution subset 102 patients as test. Heart: ACDC 2017 cine MRI end-diastole, 40 / 10 / 50. Prostate: PROSTATEx T2 (16 / 4 / 20, single institution) and PROMISE12 (35 multi-scanner cases, out-of-distribution test only).
papers.preprocessing: Resampled to 1x1x2 mm (brain), 2x2 mm in-plane (heart), 0.5x0.5 mm (prostate); axial slices centre-cropped to 224x224; intensities normalised to [0, 1].
papers.modelDetails: 2D U-Net-style fully convolutional networks with batch normalisation (plus 3D FCN for prostate). Trained with cross-entropy (L_CE) or soft Dice loss (L_DSC). Uncertainty / calibration methods: MC dropout (MCDO) and deep ensembles (EN) with M up to 50 models. Segment-level uncertainty = average voxel entropy over the predicted segment.
papers.training: Mini-batch 16 (prostate) or 32 (brain, heart); initial learning rate 0.005, reduced by a factor 0.5-0.8 if validation Dice did not improve by 0.001 within 10 epochs; up to 1,000 epochs with early stopping; checkpoint at best validation Dice.
papers.evaluation: Calibration: NLL, Brier score, ECE (computed inside bounding boxes around the structure), reliability diagrams. Segmentation: Dice and 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance. Correlation between segment-level entropy and Dice; out-of-distribution detection with average entropy. 95% confidence intervals and significance tests.
papers.baselines: Single models trained with cross-entropy or Dice loss; MC dropout; ensembles of sizes M = 2, 10, 50.
papers.results: Brain tumour: ECE 8.11% (CE) vs 13.41% (MC dropout CE) vs 3.28% (ensemble CE); ensembles also raised mean Dice (e.g. segment I 0.37 -> 0.49). Prostate 3D: ECE 8.25% (CE), 5.32% (Dice loss), 2.82% (ensemble with Dice loss); Dice 0.84 -> 0.90; 95% HD 9.25 -> 4.61 mm. Dice-loss models were poorly calibrated alone but ensembling fixed this. Segment-level average entropy correlated strongly with the logit of Dice (r = 0.77-0.92), and high entropy flagged out-of-distribution PROMISE12 cases (e.g. endorectal coil scans).
papers.statistics: 95% confidence intervals for all metrics; statistical significance testing of best results.
papers.availability: Not reported in the main text.

papers.title: QU-BraTS: MICCAI BraTS 2020 Challenge on Quantifying Uncertainty in Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.authors: Mehta R, Filos A, Baid U, Sako C, McKinley R, Rebsamen M, et al., Arbel T
papers.aim: To create a fair way to score uncertainty maps in brain tumour segmentation and compare methods.
papers.method: New score that rewards confidence on correct voxels and uncertainty on wrong ones, and penalises throwing away too many correct voxels. Used to rank challenge teams.
papers.result: Ranked many teams. Ensemble and test-time augmentation methods were common among top teams.
papers.tools: BraTS 2020 multi-parametric MRI, 3D CNNs, ensembles, TTA
papers.gap: Voxel-level score only, not linked to clinical decisions.
papers.relation: Ready-made metric to evaluate our MRI agent uncertainty in a brain tumour setting.
papers.limitations: Only BraTS (adult glioma) data. Future: link uncertainty to clinical use.
papers.methodologyDetail: QU-BraTS asked segmentation teams to output, for each voxel of each tumour region, an uncertainty value from 0 to 100 alongside the BraTS segmentation. To score these maps the organisers remove voxels above a sweep of uncertainty thresholds and track three curves: Dice on the voxels that remain, the fraction of correctly segmented tumour voxels thrown away, and the fraction of correct background voxels thrown away. A good uncertainty map should raise Dice quickly while throwing away few correct voxels, so the final score combines the area under the Dice curve with one minus the two filtered-voxel areas. Fourteen teams were tested on 166 hidden test patients and ranked case by case and region by region (498 rankings each), with significance testing; the paper also studies how each part of the score changes the ranking. Methods included ensembles, test-time augmentation and dropout, and networks that directly predict where they are likely wrong. For our PhD this gives a validated way to score the voxel-level uncertainty of the MRI segmentation agent, and supports the idea that the most uncertain regions should be shown to the clinician for review.
papers.studyDesign: International challenge (QU-BraTS 2019 preliminary, 2020 ranked) benchmarking uncertainty estimates for multi-region brain tumour segmentation; proposes and analyses a score for ranking uncertainty maps.
papers.datasets: BraTS multiparametric MRI (T1, T1-Gd, T2, FLAIR) of glioma patients; BraTS 2019: 335 training, 125 validation, 166 test patients; QU-BraTS 2020 test set of 166 cases (glioma type hidden from teams). Tumour regions: whole tumour (WT), tumour core (TC), enhancing tumour (ET).
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS preprocessing (co-registration to the same anatomical template, resampling to 1 mm isotropic, skull stripping). Teams submit, per case and region, a segmentation and an uncertainty map scaled 0-100.
papers.modelDetails: Evaluation score: voxels with uncertainty above a threshold tau (tau = 0-100) are filtered out; for each tau compute Dice on the remaining voxels, the ratio of filtered true positives (FTP) and the ratio of filtered true negatives (FTN). The score combines the area under the Dice-vs-threshold curve with one minus the areas for FTP and FTN, so it rewards uncertainty that removes errors without removing correct voxels. 14 participating teams used methods such as ensembles, test-time augmentation, MC dropout and directly learned error probabilities (e.g. Team SCAN: DeepSCAN with focal loss plus a KL term; output q predicts the chance the classifier disagrees with the ground truth; Team LMB: V-Net with 20 passes of test-time dropout + augmentation).
papers.training: Each team trained on the BraTS training set with its own settings; test results uploaded within a 48-hour window to the CBICA Image Processing Portal.
papers.evaluation: Per-case, per-region ranking of each team by the overall uncertainty score; 166 cases x 3 regions = 498 rankings per team; ranks summed and compared with permutation-based statistical significance testing; ablation of score components; comparison with segmentation-task ranking.
papers.baselines: Teams compared with each other; ablation versions of the score (Dice-only, without FTP / FTN terms).
papers.results: Filtering uncertain voxels raised Dice for good uncertainty methods, but methods that marked many correct voxels as uncertain were penalised by the FTP/FTN terms. The uncertainty ranking differed from the segmentation ranking, showing uncertainty quality is a separate property. (Per-team scores are given in figures; exact values not extracted.)
papers.statistics: Rank-based scheme with statistical significance analysis of team rankings (permutation testing).

papers.title: Second opinion needed: communicating uncertainty in medical machine learning
papers.authors: Kompa B, Snoek J, Beam AL
papers.aim: To argue why medical ML must show uncertainty and be able to say 'I don't know'.
papers.method: Perspective paper with examples and overview of UQ methods.
papers.result: Recommends that models abstain when uncertain and that uncertainty is reported in medical ML studies.
papers.tools: Perspective / review
papers.gap: No new method or experiment.
papers.relation: Good motivation reference for our problem statement and O2.
papers.limitations: Opinion piece. Future: standards for reporting uncertainty.
papers.methodologyDetail: This is a perspective rather than an experimental study. The authors argue that every clinical ML prediction should come with a measure of how sure the model is, and that the system should be able to say 'I don't know' and ask for a human second opinion, just as clinicians do. They explain the two kinds of uncertainty - noise in the data (aleatoric) and lack of knowledge in the model (epistemic, which grows on unfamiliar patients) - and review practical methods: Bayesian neural networks and cheap approximations such as MC dropout, ensembles of independently trained networks, post-hoc calibration, conformal prediction sets, and selective prediction with an abstain option. They link these to failure modes seen in medical AI, especially loss of accuracy when a model moves to a new hospital or patient group, and recommend measuring calibration, behaviour under shift and the trade-off between accuracy and how often the model abstains. For our PhD this paper supports the core design choice: each agent reports a calibrated uncertainty, and high-uncertainty cases are routed to a clinician as a second opinion rather than being answered automatically.
papers.studyDesign: Perspective / narrative review (npj Digital Medicine 2021). No new data or experiments.
papers.datasets: Not applicable (perspective). Discusses published examples such as dataset shift in medical imaging and clinical risk models.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Reviews ways to get per-patient uncertainty: Bayesian neural networks and approximations (MC dropout, variational inference), deep ensembles, calibration (temperature scaling), conformal prediction, and selective prediction / abstention where the model says 'I don't know' and the case goes to a human. Separates aleatoric (data) and epistemic (model) uncertainty and explains why each matters clinically.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Recommends evaluating calibration, performance under dataset shift and out-of-distribution inputs, and the accuracy-vs-abstention trade-off; argues uncertainty should be communicated to clinicians with each prediction.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Main conclusions: medical ML should be able to abstain when uncertain; uncertainty estimates protect against known failure modes such as dataset shift and out-of-distribution patients; communicating uncertainty can build clinician trust; deployment should include abstention and second-opinion workflows.
papers.statistics: Not applicable.

papers.title: Calibrated Learning to Defer with One-vs-All Classifiers
papers.authors: Rajeev Verma, Eric Nalisnick
papers.aim: To build a learning-to-defer (L2D) system whose probability that the human expert is correct is properly calibrated, without losing accuracy.
papers.method: Shows that the softmax-based L2D loss of Mozannar and Sontag (2020) does not give valid or calibrated expert-correctness probabilities. Proposes a one-vs-all (OvA) surrogate loss with K+1 independent sigmoid outputs, which is still consistent for L2D and gives calibrated probabilities.
papers.result: On CIFAR-10 with a simulated expert, ECE of the expert-correctness estimate fell from 7.58% (softmax) to 3.01% (OvA). Accuracy was equal or better than the softmax method on hate speech, galaxy zoo, HAM10000 skin lesions and CIFAR-10.
papers.tools: WideResNet-28 (CIFAR-10), ResNet-34 (HAM10000), PyTorch, SGD with cosine annealing, Adam; code: https://github.com/rajevv/OvA-L2D
papers.gap: Single expert; simulated experts on most datasets; does not handle a budget on expert time or different error costs.
papers.relation: Gives a consistent learning-to-defer loss whose deferral probabilities are calibrated, directly supporting a calibrated defer-to-clinician rule.
papers.limitations: Authors note that calibration under distribution shift and with multiple experts is not studied.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors start from the standard learning-to-defer network with K class outputs plus one 'defer' output trained with a softmax loss, and show that the implied probability that the expert is correct is not a valid probability and is poorly calibrated (ECE 7.58% in a CIFAR-10 test). They replace the softmax with K+1 separate one-vs-all logistic losses, so the defer output becomes a direct sigmoid estimate of whether the expert will be right on this case, and prove the loss still leads to the optimal defer rule. They test calibration on CIFAR-10 with simulated experts who are good on some classes and guess on others, varying how useful the data and the expert are; on HAM10000 skin-lesion images with a ResNet-34 classifier and a separate network simulating a dermatologist who also sees patient metadata; and on hate speech and Galaxy Zoo with real human labels under a limit on how many cases can be deferred. OvA cuts ECE by more than half and shrinks the gap between predicted and real expert error from about 27 to 8 points, with no loss of accuracy. For our PhD this is the loss we plan to use when training each agent's 'refer to clinician' output, because the escalation rule must compare calibrated AI and clinician success probabilities.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with theory (consistency proof) and experiments on simulated and real expert data.
papers.datasets: CIFAR-10 with a simulated expert (correct with probability 0.70-0.75 on some classes, random on the others); HAM10000 dermoscopy images with a simulated dermatology expert model that also sees metadata (74% accuracy); hate speech tweets and Galaxy Zoo with real human labels (budgeted deferral set-up of Okati et al. 2021).
papers.preprocessing: HAM10000: random cropping, reflection and horizontal flipping; expert model gets image metadata in its final layer. CIFAR-10 experts vary k = 2-8 classes on which they are competent.
papers.modelDetails: Classifier and rejector share one network with K+1 outputs. Softmax L2D estimates expert correctness as p_m = g_bot / (1 - max softmax), which can exceed 1. OvA replaces softmax with K+1 binary (sigmoid) logistic losses: each class output is a one-vs-all classifier, and the defer output is trained to predict whether the expert is correct. Defer when the defer probability is larger than the best class probability.
papers.training: CIFAR-10: 28-layer WideResNet, SGD with momentum, cosine annealing, early stopping after 20 epochs without validation improvement. HAM10000: fine-tuned ResNet-34. Surrogate models: Adam, cosine-annealed learning rate, 5 warm-up epochs.
papers.evaluation: ECE and reliability diagrams for the expert-correctness probability; system accuracy and coverage (share not deferred) against k; accuracy against deferral budget.
papers.baselines: Softmax L2D (Mozannar and Sontag 2020), a proxy estimator, Okati et al. (2021) triage methods, confidence baseline.
papers.results: CIFAR-10 ECE (%) OvA / softmax / proxy: random expert 0.68 / 3.72 / 2.83; random data 2.05 / 2.07 / 39.06; both useful 1.68 / 3.32 / 37.15. Main simulation ECE 3.01% (OvA) vs 7.58% (softmax). HAM10000: gap between predicted and true expert error 8.02 +/- 1.37 (OvA) vs 26.72 +/- 1.77 (softmax). OvA system accuracy slightly higher than softmax for all k and competitive at every deferral budget.
papers.statistics: Mean +/- standard deviation over repeated runs.

papers.title: Sample Efficient Learning of Predictors that Complement Humans
papers.authors: Mohammad-Amin Charusaie, Hussein Mozannar, David Sontag, Samira Samadi
papers.aim: To show, in theory and practice, when learning a classifier that complements the human expert beats training the classifier alone, and how to learn deferral with few expert labels.
papers.method: Compares joint learning (classifier and rejector trained together) with staged learning (classifier first, rejector after). Gives generalisation bounds, a family of consistent surrogate losses L_CE^alpha, and active-learning schemes that ask the expert to label only the most useful cases.
papers.result: The accuracy gap between joint and staged learning shrinks as the classifier gets more complex, as the theory predicts. When only a small part of the data has expert labels, staged and semi-supervised joint learning can be more sample-efficient; active learning needs fewer expert labels to reach good deferral accuracy.
papers.tools: Small CNN (2 convolutional + 2 fully connected layers), CIFAR-10, PyTorch; code: https://github.com/clinicalml/active_learn_to_defer
papers.gap: Experiments use simulated experts on CIFAR-10 only; no medical data, no workload limit.
papers.relation: Studies learning deferral policies when expert (clinician) labels are scarce, which fits a low-resource setting.
papers.limitations: Mainly theoretical; small model and simulated expert.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors study when it is worth training the AI specifically to complement a human, rather than training it for best average accuracy and adding a deferral rule afterwards. They prove that joint training of classifier and rejector has an advantage when the classifier is simple, which shrinks as the classifier becomes more powerful, and that staged training can use data without expert labels more efficiently. They propose a family of consistent surrogate losses and active-learning schemes that only ask the human for labels on cases that matter for the deferral decision. To illustrate, they train a small CNN on CIFAR-10 with a simulated expert who is perfect on half the classes and guesses on the rest, vary network size and the share of expert-labelled data, and repeat each setting 10 times. Results match the theory: the joint-vs-staged gap shrinks with model size, and with little expert data the staged approach is competitive. For our PhD, clinician-labelled cases will be few, so we plan to train each agent on all available data first and then learn the escalation rule from a small, actively chosen set of cases reviewed by clinicians.
papers.studyDesign: Theory paper (sample-complexity bounds, surrogate-loss consistency, active learning) with an illustrative experiment.
papers.datasets: CIFAR-10 (32x32, 10 classes) with the simulated expert of Mozannar and Sontag (2020): perfect on the first 5 classes, random on the other 5. Settings where only a subset of data has expert labels (S_l) and the rest only has true labels (S_u).
papers.preprocessing: Data split into expert-labelled and expert-unlabelled parts; validation set used to choose alpha and model settings.
papers.modelDetails: Classifier h and rejector r. Joint learning minimises the 0-1 deferral loss on expert-labelled data using surrogate L_CE^alpha. Staged learning: train h on all data, then train r (a network predicting expert error) and defer by comparing classifier confidence with predicted expert accuracy (Raghu et al. 2019). Joint-SemiSupervised: pre-train on unlabelled data then train deferral on expert-labelled data. Active learning schemes choose which cases to ask the expert to label.
papers.training: CNN with two convolutional and two feed-forward layers; model complexity varied by filter size and number of units; alpha chosen on validation data; 10 trials per setting.
papers.evaluation: System accuracy of the classifier-plus-expert; gap between joint and staged learning vs model complexity and vs amount of expert-labelled data (mean +/- SD over 10 trials).
papers.baselines: Staged learning (Raghu et al. confidence comparison), joint learning, Joint-SemiSupervised.
papers.results: Gap in system accuracy (joint minus staged) fell from about 5% to about 1% as the classifier's parameter count grew (shown in figure). With few expert labels, staged learning closed or reversed the gap; active learning reduced the number of expert labels needed. Exact numbers are reported in figures only.
papers.statistics: Mean and standard deviation over 10 trials.

papers.title: Learning to Defer to a Population: A Meta-Learning Approach
papers.authors: Dharmesh Tailor, Aditya Patra, Rajeev Verma, Putra Manggala, Eric Nalisnick
papers.aim: To build a learning-to-defer system that works with experts it has never seen before, without retraining for each new expert.
papers.method: L2D-Pop: meta-learning over a population of experts. A small context set of the new expert's past decisions is embedded and fed to the rejector, so the deferral policy adapts at test time. Two variants: fine-tuning (optimisation-based) and a neural-process model with attention over similar context points.
papers.result: Across Traffic Signs, CIFAR-10 and HAM10000, L2D-Pop raised the expert's accuracy on deferred cases and overall system accuracy compared with a single-expert L2D model; the gain grew as experts differed more. Cross-attention further improved selection of fine-grained expert strengths on CIFAR-100.
papers.tools: CNN / ResNet base networks, neural process with multi-head attention (8 heads), PyTorch.
papers.gap: Experts simulated from class-wise skills; real clinicians' changing behaviour not tested.
papers.relation: Lets a deferral system adapt to new or changing clinicians at test time, which matters when the pool of available specialists varies.
papers.limitations: Needs a context set of labelled decisions for each new expert; simulated experts.
papers.methodologyDetail: Ordinary learning-to-defer trains the deferral rule for one specific expert. Here the authors simulate a population of experts, each skilled on a random subset of classes (with an overlap probability controlling how similar they are), and meta-train a deferral network over many such experts. For each expert the model sees a small 'context set' of past cases with the expert's answer and the true label (50-140 cases), embeds it, and combines this with the image features to decide whether to defer. A neural-process version uses attention so that, for a new image, it looks at the most similar past cases to judge whether this expert is likely to be right. Tested on traffic signs, CIFAR-10 and HAM10000 skin lesions, the population-aware model sends more of the right cases to each expert, raising both the expert's accuracy on deferred cases and overall accuracy compared with a model trained for an average expert; the benefit grows as experts become more different. For our PhD this suggests keeping a short log of each clinician's recent validated decisions, so the escalation rule can adapt to the specific reviewer and hospital.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with experiments on synthetic 2D data and three image classification benchmarks using simulated populations of experts.
papers.datasets: Synthetic 2D clusters; Traffic Signs (GTSRB, train set down-sampled to 10,000); CIFAR-10; HAM10000 skin lesion images; CIFAR-100 merged into 20 superclasses for the attention ablation (experts strong on 12 random sub-classes).
papers.preprocessing: Random horizontal flipping and random cropping. Context sets: 50 cases per expert (Traffic Signs, CIFAR-10), 140 (HAM10000), 100 (CIFAR-100 ablation); at evaluation context sets come from a 20% split of validation/test data.
papers.modelDetails: One base network (Mozannar and Sontag style) with K class outputs and a defer output. For L2D-Pop, penultimate features are concatenated with an embedding of the expert's context set (pairs of input, expert prediction, true label). NP variant: deterministic Attentive Neural Process with self-attention then cross-attention (8-head multi-head attention) so each test case looks at similar context cases. Finetune variant: adapt the rejector by a few gradient steps on the context set.
papers.training: Meta-training over sampled experts from the population; hyper-parameters (epochs, learning rates, weight decay, context size, MLP depths) per dataset in the appendix; warm-start from a pre-trained base network.
papers.evaluation: System accuracy and expert accuracy on deferred examples as the overlap probability between experts' skills varies from 0 to 1; runtime comparison.
papers.baselines: Single-L2D trained on the 'marginal' (average) expert; fine-tuning a marginal-expert model.
papers.results: Reported in figures: L2D-Pop (both variants) gave higher expert accuracy on deferred examples and higher system accuracy than single-L2D on all three datasets, with the largest gap when experts' skills overlapped least. NP with cross-attention beat vanilla NP and fine-tuning on the CIFAR-100 superclass task.
papers.statistics: Mean and spread over repeated runs shown in figures.
papers.availability: Not stated in the extracted text.

papers.title: Post-Hoc Estimators for Learning to Defer to an Expert
papers.authors: Harikrishna Narasimhan, Wittawat Jitkrittum, Aditya Krishna Menon, Ankit Singh Rawat, Sanjiv Kumar
papers.relation: Shows how to add deferral to an already-trained classifier after training, a practical route for adding escalation to existing diagnostic agents.

papers.title: Principled Approaches for Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
papers.authors: Anqi Mao, Mehryar Mohri, Yutao Zhong
papers.venue: ISAIM 2024 (Lecture Notes in Computer Science, Springer)
papers.aim: To design surrogate losses with strong theoretical guarantees for learning to defer when there are several experts, each with its own cost.
papers.method: Adds one output per expert to the label set and learns prediction and deferral together with a new family of surrogate losses (built from comp-sum and sum losses) that have H-consistency bounds. Cost of deferring to expert j can include its error and a fixed per-expert cost.
papers.result: System accuracy rose as more experts were available: CIFAR-10 73.31% (1 expert), 77.12% (2), 78.71% (3); SVHN 92.08%, 93.18%, 93.46%.
papers.tools: Base CNN classifiers with small / medium / large model experts; SVHN, CIFAR-10.
papers.gap: Experts are other models, not humans; mainly theoretical; no workload limit.
papers.relation: Gives consistent surrogate losses for routing a case to one of several experts, such as a radiologist or neurosurgeon, with costs included.
papers.limitations: Main focus is theory; experiments are small-scale with model experts.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors extend learning to defer from one expert to many. The model's output layer covers every class plus one extra output per expert, and the prediction is whichever output scores highest - a class, or 'send to expert j'. Each expert has a cost on each case, either just whether that expert would be wrong, or that error plus a fixed charge reflecting how expensive the expert is. They build a family of surrogate losses for training this, combining a standard multi-class loss with expert terms weighted by how good each expert would be, and prove H-consistency bounds, meaning that reducing the surrogate loss provably reduces the true deferral loss for the chosen model class. Experiments on SVHN and CIFAR-10 use a base network with one, two or three larger networks as experts and show accuracy rising with more experts (CIFAR-10 from 73.3% to 78.7%), while adding per-expert costs makes the system use costly experts less. For our PhD the same structure can route a case to the most suitable reviewer - radiologist, pathologist or neurosurgeon - with a cost that reflects each clinician's scarce time.
papers.studyDesign: Theory paper (H-consistency bounds for multi-expert deferral surrogates) with experiments on two image benchmarks.
papers.datasets: SVHN and CIFAR-10 image classification.
papers.preprocessing: Not detailed in the main text (appendix B).
papers.modelDetails: Augmented label set [n + n_e]: n classes plus n_e experts. Hypothesis h scores all n + n_e outputs; predicting a class or deferring to expert j is the argmax. Surrogate: a multi-class loss on the true label plus, for each expert, a term weighted by (1 - c_j(x, y)), using comp-sum losses (logistic, exponential, square-hinge, rho-margin) with explicit H-consistency bounds. Experts: a larger model (1 expert); small + large (2); small + medium + large (3).
papers.training: Three random seeds per setting; setup in appendix B.
papers.evaluation: Overall system accuracy (mean +/- SD over 3 seeds) for 1, 2 and 3 experts under two cost types: (1) c_j = expert misclassification; (2) c_j = misclassification + base cost beta_j (larger expert = higher beta).
papers.baselines: Comparison across numbers of experts; single-expert deferral.
papers.results: Cost type 1 - SVHN: 92.08 +/- 0.15, 93.18 +/- 0.18, 93.46 +/- 0.12 (1/2/3 experts); CIFAR-10: 73.31 +/- 0.21, 77.12 +/- 0.34, 78.71 +/- 0.43. Cost type 2 - SVHN: 92.36, 93.23, 93.36; CIFAR-10: 73.70, 76.29, 76.43. More experts gave higher accuracy; base costs reduced the gain for CIFAR-10.
papers.statistics: Mean +/- standard deviation over three random seeds.

papers.title: Two-Stage Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
papers.authors: Anqi Mao, Christopher Mohri, Mehryar Mohri, Yutao Zhong
papers.relation: Learns a deferral rule on top of a fixed pretrained predictor using cost-sensitive losses, which fits a modular multi-agent pipeline.

papers.title: Learning to Defer to Multiple Experts: Consistent Surrogate Losses, Confidence Calibration, and Conformal Ensembles
papers.authors: Rajeev Verma, Daniel Barrejon, Eric Nalisnick
papers.aim: To extend learning to defer to many experts with consistent losses, calibrated estimates of each expert's correctness, and a principled way to ask a subset of experts.
papers.method: Derives two consistent multi-expert surrogates (softmax and one-vs-all), analyses how well each estimates P(expert j is correct | x), and proposes conformal inference to choose a set of experts to query when the system defers, then combines their answers.
papers.result: OvA never fell below the single-classifier baseline as experts were added on HAM10000 and Galaxy-Zoo, while softmax and mixture-of-experts sometimes did. Softmax mis-calibration spreads across experts; OvA does not (with some practical trade-offs). Conformal expert sets improved accuracy over querying only the single most confident expert.
papers.tools: Base CNN / ResNet classifiers, simulated and real annotators, conformal prediction, PyTorch.
papers.gap: Most experts simulated; querying several experts costs more clinician time, which is not limited in the model.
papers.relation: Combines calibration and conformal sets for deferral among several experts, linking uncertainty calibration directly to escalation.
papers.limitations: Simulated experts; conformal step assumes exchangeable data.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors give the model one output for every class and one for every available expert, and derive two training losses - a softmax version and a one-vs-all version with separate sigmoids - proving both lead to the best possible routing of cases. They then study the implied probability that each expert will be right, showing that with softmax a calibration error in one expert's estimate leaks into the others, while the one-vs-all version keeps them separate. Finally, when the system decides to defer, instead of sending the case to just one expert it uses conformal prediction to pick a small set of experts that, with high probability, includes a correct one, and combines their answers. They test on hate-speech tweets and Galaxy-Zoo images with real annotators, on HAM10000 skin lesions with simulated dermatologists whose accuracy is set from published clinical figures (for example 80% on their speciality), and on CIFAR-10, adding experts one by one from a random guesser up to an experienced specialist. The OvA model stays above the classifier-only baseline as experts are added and is better calibrated. For our PhD this supports routing uncertain cases to one or more specific clinicians and estimating each clinician's likely accuracy on that case.
papers.studyDesign: Theory plus experiments on three classification tasks with pools of 2 to 10 experts.
papers.datasets: Hate Speech (tweets with real annotator labels), Galaxy-Zoo (real volunteer annotations), HAM10000 dermoscopy images (7 diagnostic categories; simulated dermatologists), CIFAR-10 (10 class-specific oracle experts).
papers.preprocessing: Expert pools built by adding increasingly accurate experts. HAM10000 simulated dermatologists: correct with probability p_in on their speciality and p_out otherwise (e.g. malignant specialist 25/15%, melanoma specialist 75/15%, experienced dermatologist 80/60%), based on reported clinical accuracy (unaided ~60%, dermoscopy 75-84%); an MLP-Mixer model is also one expert. Hate Speech / Galaxy-Zoo: random, probabilistic, label-flipping (20-50%) and real human experts.
papers.modelDetails: One network with K class outputs and J expert outputs. Softmax surrogate (generalises Mozannar-Sontag) and OvA surrogate (generalises Verma-Nalisnick, J+K sigmoids). Expert-correctness estimates from each parameterisation. Conformal ensembles: on deferral, build a conformal set of experts likely to be correct and aggregate their predictions (e.g. majority vote).
papers.training: Base model fixed across runs except added output dimensions; 3 random seeds per pool size; details in appendix.
papers.evaluation: System accuracy vs number of experts (mean +/- standard error); ECE of expert-correctness estimates; accuracy and expert-set size for conformal ensembles.
papers.baselines: Single classifier, best single expert, mixture-of-experts of Hemmer et al. (2022), softmax vs OvA, querying the top-1 expert.
papers.results: Reported in figures: on Hate Speech all methods similar; on HAM10000 and Galaxy-Zoo OvA accuracy stayed above the single-classifier line for every pool size while softmax and MoE dipped below it. Calibration of expert-correctness was better with OvA in most settings. Conformal expert sets gave higher accuracy than single-expert deferral at modest set sizes.
papers.statistics: Mean and standard error over 3 seeds.

papers.title: Cost-Sensitive Learning to Defer to Multiple Experts with Workload Constraints
papers.authors: Jean V. Alves, Diogo Leitao, Sergio Jesus, Marco O. P. Sampaio, Javier Liebana, Pedro Saleiro, Mario A. T. Figueiredo, Pedro Bizarro
papers.venue: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (arXiv preprint)
papers.aim: To make learning to defer practical by handling different costs for false positives and false negatives, needing only one human decision per training case, and respecting each human's work capacity.
papers.method: DeCCaF: (1) an ML classifier; (2) a human expertise model that predicts each expert's probability of being correct, trained with supervised learning from only one expert decision per case; (3) an assigner that uses constraint programming to send each batch of cases to the classifier or to experts so the expected misclassification cost is minimised under capacity limits.
papers.result: Across fraud-detection scenarios with teams of 9 synthetic analysts and individual capacity limits, DeCCaF significantly beat the baselines, with an average 8.4% reduction in misclassification cost.
papers.tools: LightGBM-type classifiers, constraint programming solver, Python; code: https://github.com/feedzai/deccaf
papers.gap: Fraud data and synthetic experts, not clinical; static capacity per batch.
papers.relation: Builds error costs and limited expert capacity into deferral, which matters where specialist time is scarce.
papers.limitations: Synthetic experts; assumes capacity is known in advance; tabular domain.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors design deferral for a real operations setting: a fraud team of 9 analysts, each able to review only a limited number of cases per batch, and errors that cost different amounts. They use a public dataset of one million synthetic bank-account applications (1.1% fraud, changing over time) and create 9 simulated analysts whose chance of error depends on the case features and on the model score they see. DeCCaF has three parts: a classifier that estimates fraud probability; a 'human expertise model' that learns, from historical data where each case was seen by only one analyst, the probability that each analyst would decide correctly; and an assigner that, for each batch, solves a constraint-programming problem to give every case either to the model or to an analyst so that total expected cost (false positives weighted by lambda plus false negatives) is minimal and nobody exceeds capacity. They test six scenarios of alert rate and cost ratio, each with 25 variations of training seed and capacity, and compare with one-vs-all learning to defer and simpler assignment rules. DeCCaF lowers misclassification cost by 8.4% on average. For our PhD this is the template for capacity-aware escalation: clinician review slots per day act as constraints, and missed tumours are weighted more heavily than unnecessary referrals.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with simulation experiments on a large tabular fraud-detection dataset and synthetic expert teams.
papers.datasets: Bank Account Fraud dataset (version 1): 1 million synthetic bank-account applications based on anonymised real data, 1.1% fraud prevalence, with concept drift over time.
papers.preprocessing: Synthetic analysts generated with instance-dependent noise: each label is flipped with a probability depending on pre-processed features and the alert model's score. Scenarios defined by alert rate ar (0.05 or 0.15) and cost ratio lambda (0.0114, 0.057, 0.285). Test capacity per expert sampled from N(N_test/10, N_test/50); 5 training seeds x 5 capacity settings = 25 test variations per scenario.
papers.modelDetails: Human expertise model (HEM) estimates P(correct | x, expert); classifier h estimates P(y = 1 | x). For each batch, the assigner solves a constraint program that minimises the expected cost lambda*FP + FN, subject to each expert's capacity H_b,j. Compared with OvA learning to defer (Verma et al.), which needs all experts' predictions for training.
papers.training: Classifier and HEM trained on historical data where each case has one expert decision; 5 random seeds.
papers.evaluation: Expected misclassification cost on test sets; ROC-AUC and ECE of the classifier and of the expert-correctness models; comparison across 6 (ar, lambda) scenarios.
papers.baselines: OvA multi-expert L2D with greedy capacity handling; random assignment of cases to experts; rejection learning.
papers.results: Average 8.4% lower misclassification cost than baselines. Classifier h: ROC-AUC 0.70-0.76 and ECE 1.1-4.8% across scenarios. Expert-correctness models had similar ROC-AUC for HEM and OvA, but HEM needs far fewer human labels. Expert decision outcomes per scenario: e.g. ar 0.05, lambda 0.0114: 30.2% FP, 0.3% FN, 11.1% TP, 58.4% TN.
papers.statistics: Results over 25 test variations per scenario with error bars; significance of improvement reported as significant in most scenarios.

papers.title: Towards Unbiased and Accurate Deferral to Multiple Experts
papers.authors: Vijay Keswani, Matthew Lease, Krishnaram Kenthapadi
papers.venue: AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2021)
papers.aim: To learn a classifier and a deferral system together that can defer to one or more of several experts, each with its own expertise and biases, while improving accuracy and fairness.
papers.method: Joint learning of classifier and a deferrer that outputs weights over the classifier and the experts for each input; final prediction is a weighted combination. Variants with expert costs, sparsity (defer to few experts) and fairness constraints across groups.
papers.result: On synthetic data the deferrer learned which expert to trust for which input cluster; on a crowd-sourced (MTurk) offensive-language dataset it improved accuracy and reduced dialect-group disparity compared with baselines such as single-expert deferral and crowd-label aggregation.
papers.tools: Neural classifier and deferrer, Amazon Mechanical Turk survey (170 workers), Python.
papers.gap: Text moderation, not medicine; experts' availability and workload not modelled.
papers.relation: Optimises a classifier and a deferral system together for accuracy and fairness across a set of human experts.
papers.limitations: Missing expert predictions handled approximately; small real-expert dataset.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors consider a system that can ask several human experts, each good on different kinds of input and possibly biased against some groups. They train a classifier and a 'deferrer' together: for each input the deferrer outputs weights over the classifier and every expert, and the final answer is their weighted vote, so it can send hard cases to one or several experts. Extra terms add a cost for each expert consulted, encourage consulting only a few experts, and constrain the accuracy gap between demographic groups. In a synthetic test the experts secretly know which cluster a point belongs to; the deferrer learns to pick the right expert per cluster, beating crowd-aggregation baselines (67% and 83%). In a real test, 170 crowd workers labelled 1,471 tweets for offensive language (about 10 labels per tweet, each worker seeing 50), with tweets balanced across two dialect groups; the joint method improved both accuracy and fairness between dialects. For our PhD this shows how to choose which clinician or combination of clinicians to escalate to, and to audit escalation for unequal treatment of patient groups.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with a synthetic simulation and a real crowd-worker experiment.
papers.datasets: Synthetic clustered data where cluster identity is known only to experts; 1,471 Twitter posts (subset of Davidson et al. offensive-language data, balanced across classes and two dialect groups) labelled by 170 MTurk workers (about 10 labels per post).
papers.preprocessing: Each MTurk participant labelled 50 posts into 5 options (threat/insult to group, to individual, other, profanity, none) and saw the predicted dialect label; treated as data with missing expert predictions. Workers paid $4 (about $16/hour).
papers.modelDetails: Classifier f and deferrer d; d(x) gives a distribution over {classifier, expert 1..m}; prediction = weighted vote. Loss includes per-expert costs; sparse variant limits how many experts are consulted; fair variant adds a constraint on accuracy difference between dialect groups.
papers.training: Joint gradient-based training of classifier and deferrer; details in the paper's appendix.
papers.evaluation: Overall and group-specific (dialect) accuracy with standard errors; fairness gap between groups.
papers.baselines: Classifier only; experts' majority vote; LL (learning from crowds, Raykar et al.); CrowdSelect; single-expert deferral (Madras et al.).
papers.results: Synthetic: baseline LL about 67% accuracy, CrowdSelect about 83%; the joint deferrer chose experts per input cluster and did better, with the non-sparse variant more accurate than the sparse one unless expert costs were added. MTurk: joint framework and its fair variants improved accuracy and reduced the dialect accuracy gap over baselines (Table 2).
papers.statistics: Mean accuracy with standard error over repeated runs.

papers.title: Differentiable Learning Under Triage
papers.authors: Nastaran Okati, Abir De, Manuel Gomez-Rodriguez
papers.aim: To understand when a model benefits from algorithmic triage (sending some cases to humans) and to train the model and triage policy together for a given triage level.
papers.method: Proves that the optimal triage policy is a deterministic threshold on the per-instance difference between model error and human error, and that models trained for full automation are sub-optimal under triage. Proposes a gradient-based algorithm that alternately trains the model on the cases it will keep and updates the triage policy, with guaranteed improvement.
papers.result: Synthetic regression: average loss 0.0053 for full automation, 0.0020 with optimal triage of the same model, and lower again when the model is trained under triage. On Hatespeech and Galaxy Zoo, models trained under triage beat confidence-based and surrogate-based triage baselines across triage levels.
papers.tools: Sigmoid regression (synthetic), fastText features + neural classifier (Hatespeech), CNN on pixel maps (Galaxy Zoo).
papers.gap: Needs per-instance human error estimates at training time; triage level b fixed by user; no medical data.
papers.relation: Learns a triage policy that splits cases between the model and humans, the core decision O2 must make.
papers.limitations: Human predictions simulated by sampling from crowd label distributions.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors ask how a model should be trained if a set share of cases will go to humans. They prove that, for any model and a limit b on the share of cases sent to humans, the best routing rule is simple: send a case to the human when the model's expected error minus the human's expected error is above a threshold. They also prove a model trained for full automation is not the best model once triage is used, because it wastes capacity on cases humans will handle. Their algorithm alternates between training the model only on the cases it will keep and recomputing the threshold rule, and learns a separate network to apply the rule to new cases. In a small synthetic regression with 72 points and region-dependent human noise, triage cut the loss from 0.0053 to 0.0020, and training under triage reduced it further. On 24,783 crowd-labelled tweets and 10,000 crowd-labelled galaxy images, with human answers sampled from annotator distributions, the method beat confidence-based and surrogate-loss baselines across triage levels. For our PhD this supports training each agent jointly with the escalation rule and setting the share of escalated cases from available clinician capacity.
papers.studyDesign: Theory plus experiments on synthetic regression and two real crowd-labelled classification datasets.
papers.datasets: Synthetic: 72 samples, x ~ U[-3, 3], y from two sigmoids, human noise variance 1-8 x 10^-3 by region. Hatespeech: 24,783 tweets, each labelled by 3-5 Crowdflower annotators (hate speech / offensive / neither). Galaxy Zoo: 10,000 galaxy images, each labelled by 30+ volunteers (early type vs spiral).
papers.preprocessing: Hatespeech tweets embedded as 100-dimensional fastText vectors; Galaxy Zoo pixel maps as input. Human prediction distribution P(h | x) from annotator counts; true label = most common label; at test time a human answer is sampled from P(h | x).
papers.modelDetails: Triage policy pi(x) in {0 (model), 1 (human)} with at most a fraction b of cases sent to humans. Optimal policy: send x to the human when loss(model) - loss(human) exceeds a threshold t_P,b,m. Algorithm: iterate (i) fit the model on cases assigned to it, (ii) recompute the optimal threshold policy; a second network approximates the policy for unseen data.
papers.training: Gradient-based training with squared-error loss (synthetic) or cross-entropy (classification); maximum triage level b varied (e.g. 0.4 for Hatespeech, 1.0 for Galaxy Zoo in the illustrated runs).
papers.evaluation: Average loss / misclassification error as a function of triage level b; per-instance model vs human losses during training.
papers.baselines: Full automation; confidence-based triage (Raghu et al. 2019); surrogate-loss deferral (Mozannar and Sontag 2020); score-based triage (De et al. 2020).
papers.results: Synthetic losses: 0.0053 (no triage), 0.0020 (optimal triage with automation-trained model), lower still with triage-trained model. Real data: the proposed method gave the lowest misclassification error across most triage levels on both Hatespeech and Galaxy Zoo (figures).
papers.statistics: Not reported beyond averages over runs.

papers.title: Combining Human Predictions with Model Probabilities via Confusion Matrices and Calibration
papers.authors: Gavin Kerrigan, Padhraic Smyth, Mark Steyvers
papers.aim: To combine a model's probability output with a human's class label so the combination is more accurate than either alone, using very few labelled examples.
papers.method: Bayesian combination: calibrate the model with temperature scaling, model the human with a class confusion matrix (Dirichlet prior), and multiply the two to get combined class probabilities. Variants include a single-parameter confusion model and an unsupervised EM version.
papers.result: Combinations beat both human and model alone: e.g. CIFAR-10H ResNet-110 6.10% error and human 4.62% -> combined 2.85%; ImageNet-16H VGG-19 11.1% and human 9.99% -> 6.62%. Parameters could be estimated well with as few as 10 labelled points.
papers.tools: ResNet-110/164, PreResNet-164, DenseNet (CIFAR-10H); VGG-19 and GoogLeNet (ImageNet-16H); temperature scaling; MAP and EM inference.
papers.gap: Single human per case, crowd workers not clinicians; image classification only.
papers.relation: Shows how calibrated model probabilities can be combined with clinician labels, an alternative to full deferral.
papers.limitations: Assumes human errors independent of the model given the class; one human label per image.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors treat combining a human's answer with a model's probabilities as Bayesian updating. First the model's probabilities are calibrated with temperature scaling on a small labelled set. The human is described by a confusion matrix - how often they say class i when the truth is j - estimated with a Dirichlet prior so a handful of examples is enough. For each new case the calibrated model probability for each class is multiplied by the chance that the human would give their observed answer if that class were true, and the result is renormalised. They test on CIFAR-10H and ImageNet-16H, where real crowd workers labelled the images, with CNNs ranging from worse to better than humans, splitting data into model-training, combination-fitting and test sets. The combination always beat both partners (CIFAR-10H 2.85% vs 4.62% human), stayed calibrated, and needed only about 10 labelled cases. For our PhD this gives a principled way to merge clinician validation with AI output, and shows why calibration of each agent matters even when a clinician reviews the case.
papers.studyDesign: Method and theory paper with experiments on two image datasets that include real human crowd labels.
papers.datasets: CIFAR-10H: 10-way human labels for the 10,000 CIFAR-10 test images. ImageNet-16H: 16-way human labels for ImageNet test images distorted with four levels of phase noise (80, 95, 110, 125). Human labels from Amazon Mechanical Turk; one human label sampled per image.
papers.preprocessing: Each dataset split into a model training set, a combination training set (to fit calibration and confusion parameters) and an evaluation set.
papers.modelDetails: Methods: logistic regression on concatenated outputs (k^2 + 2k params); calibrated machine probabilities + single-parameter confusion (SP, 2 params); machine labels + human labels (L+L); calibrated probabilities + human confusion matrix (P+L, k^2 + 1 params); unsupervised P+L-EM. Combined posterior proportional to calibrated p_model(y | x) x P(human label | y). Dirichlet prior with diagonal gamma and off-diagonal beta set from classifier accuracy.
papers.training: Four CNNs on CIFAR-10 and eight (four VGG-19, four GoogLeNet) of varying accuracy on ImageNet-16H, chosen to span below- to above-human accuracy; details in the appendix. Combination parameters fitted by MAP on the combination set with sizes down to 10 points.
papers.evaluation: Classification error and calibration (ECE) of model, human and combinations as a function of combination-set size.
papers.baselines: Model alone, human alone, logistic regression combiner, label-only combination.
papers.results: Combined error lower than either human or model across all models; e.g. 2.85% (CIFAR-10H) and 6.62% (ImageNet-16H) vs 4.62% / 9.99% human and 6.10% / 11.1% model. Combinations also better calibrated. Calibrated-probability methods (P+L) needed far fewer labelled points than logistic regression.
papers.statistics: Mean and spread over repeated random splits.

papers.title: Learning-to-defer for sequential medical decision-making under uncertainty
papers.authors: Shalmali Joshi, Sonali Parbhoo, Finale Doshi-Velez
papers.aim: To decide when to hand control to a clinician in multi-step treatment decisions, taking long-term outcomes and future deferrals into account rather than deciding each step in isolation.
papers.method: Sequential Learning-to-Defer (SLTD): model-based reinforcement learning. Learns the environment dynamics, samples K plausible models to capture model uncertainty, and at each time step compares the value of deferring now versus delaying deferral, giving a pre-emptive deferral policy with a deferral cost.
papers.result: SLTD achieved higher expected value than baselines on synthetic, diabetes and HIV simulators while deferring less often than most baselines; modelling uncertainty (K > 1) mattered most in the HIV simulator.
papers.tools: Model-based RL, Bayesian / bootstrapped dynamics models, simulators (synthetic MDP, UVA/Padova-type diabetes simulator, HIV treatment simulator).
papers.gap: Simulated environments; assumes the expert policy is known and good; no real clinician data.
papers.relation: Extends learning to defer to multi-step clinical decisions, which resemble staged diagnosis and surgical planning.
papers.limitations: Relies on accurate dynamics models; tested only in simulation.
papers.methodologyDetail: Most learning-to-defer work decides one case at a time. In treatment, however, a poor action now can cause harm several steps later, and repeatedly calling a clinician is costly. The authors treat deferral as a sequential decision: they learn a model of how a patient's state evolves, draw several plausible versions of that model to represent uncertainty, and at every time step estimate whether handing over to the expert now would lead to a better long-term outcome than waiting, given that deferral may still happen later. This lets the system defer early, before entering states where the ML policy is known to fail. They test it in a designed synthetic environment where the risky region is known, and in diabetes and HIV treatment simulators, comparing with myopic and stationary deferral rules. SLTD reaches the highest expected outcome while deferring fairly rarely, and correctly defers early in the risky region. For our PhD this supports propagating uncertainty along the brain-tumour pathway and escalating at an earlier stage (for example at segmentation) when downstream steps such as grading or surgical planning are likely to be unreliable.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with simulation experiments in three sequential decision environments.
papers.datasets: Synthetic MDP (8 states, binary actions, episode length 15, low-reward state 6 = -5, others +1, dynamics change for 5 <= t <= 12); a diabetes (glucose control) simulator; an HIV treatment simulator.
papers.preprocessing: Target ML policy pi_tar fixed and known to be sub-optimal in some regions; expert policy pi_0 available; deferral cost c varied.
papers.modelDetails: Learn a dynamics model; draw K sampled MDPs to propagate model uncertainty; at each state and time compute whether deferring now gives higher value than waiting (accounting for possible later deferrals); deferral probability g(s, t) depends on time (non-stationary). Variants: SLTD-Stationary, SLTD-One-Step, K = 1 (no model uncertainty).
papers.training: Hyper-parameters tuned per environment (appendix); best policy after tuning reported.
papers.evaluation: Expected (true) value of the combined system without subtracting deferral cost; deferral frequency; time of first deferral; decomposition of uncertainty (model vs total variance).
papers.baselines: Augmented-MDP deferral, one-step (myopic) deferral, stationary deferral, ML policy alone, always defer.
papers.results: Table 1: SLTD had the best expected value on all three environments with a lower (though not lowest) deferral rate; myopic one-step deferral missed pre-emptive deferral in the region where the target policy fails. Ignoring model uncertainty (K = 1) changed little for synthetic and diabetes data but hurt in HIV. Stochastic dynamics, not model error, was the main source of uncertainty in the trajectories examined.
papers.statistics: Expected values averaged over simulated episodes (error bars in figures).

papers.title: Incorporating uncertainty in learning to defer algorithms for safe computer-aided diagnosis
papers.authors: Jessie Liu, Blanca Gallego, Sebastiano Barbieri
papers.aim: To defer to human experts the patients whose computer-aided diagnosis is uncertain, by feeding uncertainty measures into a learning-to-defer network.
papers.method: Learning to defer with uncertainty (LDU), two stages: (1) a deep ensemble gives the diagnosis plus uncertainty measures (entropy of ensemble probabilities and of predicted labels); (2) a learning-to-defer network takes these as input and outputs a diagnosis or 'defer'. Defer-loss weight alpha sets the accuracy-vs-deferral trade-off.
papers.result: LDU reached the same F1 as learning to defer without uncertainty (LD) while deferring far fewer patients, e.g. pleural effusion F1 0.96 with 36% vs 69% deferral; MI F1 0.88 with 38% vs 55% deferral; 17% F1 increase for any-comorbidity diagnosis where direct triage by uncertainty was not applicable.
papers.tools: MIMIC-III notes, structured EHR data, MIMIC-CXR chest X-rays; text CNN/NLP model, fully connected net, DenseNet-121; deep ensembles; Adam optimiser.
papers.gap: Retrospective, simulated deferral (human assumed correct); no real clinician workload measurement.
papers.relation: Combines uncertainty estimates with learning to defer for safer computer-aided diagnosis, which is close to the O2 mechanism.
papers.limitations: Assumes the human expert is always correct; single centre (MIMIC); fixed thresholds per task.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors combine two ideas: ensembles that measure how uncertain a diagnosis is, and a learned rule that decides whether to defer. For four tasks - myocardial infarction from 13,805 MIMIC-III discharge summaries, any comorbidity from structured ICU data, and pleural effusion and pneumothorax from MIMIC-CXR chest X-rays - they first train a deep ensemble (text network, a 2-layer 200-node network, or DenseNet-121, all with Adam) and compute for each patient the predicted diagnosis plus entropy-based uncertainty. A second small network takes these values and outputs either a diagnosis or 'defer', trained with a loss whose defer weight alpha controls how readily it defers. Deferred patients are assumed to be diagnosed correctly by an expert. Compared with learning to defer without uncertainty and with simple thresholding of uncertainty, LDU reaches the same F1 with many fewer referrals (pleural effusion 36% vs 69%) and still works when the model is confidently wrong, where thresholding fails. For our PhD this is a medical example of exactly our two-stage design: ensemble uncertainty from each agent feeding a learned escalation rule whose referral rate is tuned to clinician capacity.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective evaluation on public ICU and chest X-ray datasets for four diagnostic tasks.
papers.datasets: Myocardial infarction (MI): 13,805 MIMIC-III discharge summaries (6,183 MI positive by ICD 410*; negatives down-sampled from 51,093 to 7,622). Any comorbidity: structured MIMIC data, Charlson Index positive vs not. Pleural effusion and pneumothorax: chest X-rays from MIMIC-CXR.
papers.preprocessing: Down-sampling of the negative MI class to balance admissions; X-ray images transformed and normalised; train / validation / test splits per task.
papers.modelDetails: Stage 1: deep ensemble of networks with different random initialisations; epistemic uncertainty from entropy of the ensemble's continuous probabilities and of its predicted labels. Comorbidity model: 2 hidden layers of 200 nodes (sigmoid after the first), softmax outputs. X-ray: DenseNet-121. Stage 2: LDU network takes predicted diagnoses + uncertainty measures; loss = -log softmax(target) - alpha * log softmax(defer).
papers.training: Adam optimiser; MI text model learning rate 1e-4, weight decay 0; comorbidity model 4 epochs, learning rate 9e-4, weight decay 0; DenseNet-121 with Adam. alpha swept (e.g. 1.23-1.31 for MI, 0.77-0.80 for pleural effusion).
papers.evaluation: F1 on non-deferred patients, overall F1 (deferred patients assumed correctly diagnosed by experts), defer rate; accuracy, sensitivity and specificity at selected F1 levels.
papers.baselines: Learning to defer without uncertainty (LD); direct triage by uncertainty threshold (DT); diagnostic network without deferral.
papers.results: MI: base F1 0.74; all methods reached F1 >= 0.90 by deferring; LDU deferred 49% vs DT 51%; for F1 0.88, LDU 38% vs LD 55% deferral; reducing alpha from 1.31 to 1.23 raised defer rate from 38% to 56%. Pleural effusion: F1 0.96 with 36% (LDU) vs 69% (LD) deferral; LDU found 18-30% of patients whose automated diagnosis had error probability within 1%. Any comorbidity: +17% F1 with LDU; DT not applicable because many errors were confident.
papers.statistics: Performance curves over alpha; no formal hypothesis tests reported.

papers.title: Combining the strengths of radiologists and AI for breast cancer screening: a retrospective analysis
papers.authors: Christian Leibig, Moritz Brehmer, Stefan Bunk, Danalyn Byng, Katja Pinker, Lale Umutlu
papers.relation: Gives clinical-scale evidence that confidence-based referral of uncertain cases to radiologists beats both the AI alone and the radiologist alone.

papers.title: Calibrated Selective Classification
papers.authors: Adam Fisch, Tommi Jaakkola, Regina Barzilay
papers.aim: To abstain on cases whose uncertainty estimates are unreliable, so that the confidence of the accepted cases is well calibrated (selective calibration), not just more accurate.
papers.method: Trains a separate selector network g on top of a fixed, temperature-scaled classifier f, using meta-features (confidence, entropy, class information, outlier scores, last-layer features) and a new trainable selective calibration loss (S-MMCE, based on maximum mean calibration error) with distributionally robust training over perturbed versions of the data.
papers.result: On CIFAR-10-C, ImageNet-C and lung-cancer CT risk prediction (NLST and MGH), the selector achieved lower calibration error on accepted cases than confidence-based selection at the same coverage, including under unseen corruptions and a new hospital.
papers.tools: WideResNet-40-2 (CIFAR), ResNet-50 (ImageNet), 3D CNN (Sybil-type lung CT model), AugMix perturbations, One-Class SVM / Isolation Forest outlier scores, MLP selector.
papers.gap: Selector needs perturbation family T similar to real shifts; binary medical task only.
papers.relation: Makes sure the predictions a selective model does not abstain on are also well calibrated, which matches the 'calibrated selective autonomy' goal.
papers.limitations: Performance depends on chosen perturbation family; selector input features fixed and simple.
papers.methodologyDetail: Ordinary selective classification keeps the cases the model is most confident about, but confidence itself can be wrong under shift. The authors keep a fixed, temperature-scaled classifier and train a separate selector that looks at many 'meta' signals about each case - confidence, entropy, predicted class, novelty scores from One-Class SVM and Isolation Forest, and last-layer features - and decides whether to accept the case. The selector is trained so that, among accepted cases, predicted probabilities match observed frequencies, using a differentiable calibration loss (S-MMCE). To make this hold under shift, training uses perturbed copies of the data (AugMix image augmentations, or re-weighting CT scans by the hospital they came from across 33 NLST sites) and focuses each update on the worst perturbations. They test on CIFAR-10-C and ImageNet-C, whose corruptions were never seen in training, and on 6-year lung-cancer risk from CT, training the selector on 6,282 NLST scans and testing at MGH. The selector gives better-calibrated accepted cases than confidence thresholding at every coverage level. For our PhD this supports a second gate in escalation: even if an agent is confident, the case is escalated when signs of shift (new scanner, unusual image) suggest its confidence cannot be trusted.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with experiments on two corrupted image benchmarks and a real clinical lung-cancer screening task with external hospital testing.
papers.datasets: CIFAR-10 (50k train / 10k test; 5k removed each for validation and for selector training); CIFAR-10-C (15 corruption types x 5 intensities, 50k images per split); ImageNet (1.2M images) and ImageNet-C; lung cancer: 3D CNN trained on NLST CT scans (33 hospitals), selector trained on a separate 6,282 NLST scans, tested on MGH data; outcome = biopsy-confirmed lung cancer within 6 years.
papers.preprocessing: Perturbation family T: AugMix chains of augmentations (contrast, rotate, shear, ...) for images; for NLST, random re-weighting of scans by hospital to simulate site shift. Temperature scaling of f on clean validation data. ImageNet features projected from 2048 to 128 dimensions with SVD.
papers.modelDetails: Selector g(x) in [0, 1] decides accept / abstain; trained to minimise the S-MMCE selective calibration error on the kappa-worst perturbed batches (distributionally robust optimisation). Input meta-features: top-label confidence, entropy, full confidence vector, predicted class one-hot (omitted for ImageNet), outlier/novelty scores, last-layer features (128 or 256 dims).
papers.training: Base models fixed (WideResNet-40-2, off-the-shelf ResNet-50, NLST 3D CNN); selector MLP trained on perturbed validation splits; ablations on perturbations, DRO and feature groups.
papers.evaluation: Selective calibration error (ECE / Brier on accepted cases) and selective accuracy across coverage levels; evaluation on unseen corruptions and on an external hospital (MGH).
papers.baselines: Confidence-based selection (max softmax), outlier-score selection, selective classification trained for accuracy (SelectiveNet-style), full coverage.
papers.results: Reported in figures and appendix tables: S-MMCE selectors gave the lowest selective calibration error across coverage levels on all three tasks; confidence features helped most at high coverage and outlier scores at low coverage; DRO over perturbations improved robustness to unseen corruptions.
papers.statistics: Results averaged over perturbation types and repeated runs with error bars.

papers.title: Towards Better Selective Classification
papers.authors: Leo Feng, Mohamed Osama Ahmed, Hossein Hajimirsadeghi, Amir Abdi
papers.aim: To test whether special selection heads or abstain logits really help selective classification, and to propose a simpler, better selection method.
papers.method: Shows that methods like SelectiveNet, Deep Gamblers and Self-Adaptive Training work because they train a better classifier, not because of their selection head. Proposes selecting with the classifier's own softmax response (SR) and adds an entropy-minimisation regulariser during training.
papers.result: Using softmax response instead of each method's own selection head lowered selective error at all coverages on all datasets; adding entropy minimisation further improved results, giving new state-of-the-art selective classification without extra compute.
papers.tools: ResNet-34 (StanfordCars, Food101, ImageNet100, ImageNetSubset), VGG-16 (CIFAR-10), PyTorch.
papers.gap: Natural images only; no calibration or deferral to humans.
papers.relation: Proposes better selection mechanisms for selective classification, a baseline for the abstain-or-predict component.
papers.limitations: Selective performance depends on classifier quality; not tested under distribution shift.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors re-examine three popular selective classifiers that add a special component to decide when to abstain: a selection head (SelectiveNet), an abstention logit (Deep Gamblers) or an extra class (Self-Adaptive Training). Training these on ImageNet100 shows they also produce slightly better base classifiers (about 86.2-86.5% vs 85.7% accuracy). When the authors keep the trained networks but select cases using the plain softmax response - the highest class probability - instead of the special component, selective error drops at every coverage level, meaning the extra components add a failure mode rather than value. They then propose training an ordinary classifier with cross-entropy plus a small entropy-minimisation term (beta tuned from 0.0001 to 0.1), which makes confidence more decisive, and selecting by softmax response. Experiments with ResNet-34 and VGG-16 on ImageNet subsets, Food101, StanfordCars and CIFAR-10, over 3-5 seeds, show this simple recipe performs best. For our PhD it sets the baseline every escalation method must beat: a well-trained, calibrated agent thresholded on its own confidence.
papers.studyDesign: Empirical study plus new regulariser, on five image classification datasets.
papers.datasets: ImageNet100 and ImageNetSubset; Food101 (75,750 train / 25,250 test, 101 classes); StanfordCars (8,144 train / 8,041 test, 196 classes, trained from scratch); CIFAR-10 (50,000 / 10,000).
papers.preprocessing: Standard augmentation per dataset (details in appendix).
papers.modelDetails: Selective methods: SelectiveNet (separate selection head), Deep Gamblers (extra abstention logit), Self-Adaptive Training (extra class). Selection mechanisms compared: original head/logit vs softmax response (max class probability). Proposed: train with cross-entropy + beta * entropy minimisation, select by softmax response.
papers.training: Entropy regulariser beta tuned in {0.1, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0001}; 5 seeds for CIFAR-10, Food101, StanfordCars; 3 seeds for ImageNet experiments; official implementations adapted.
papers.evaluation: Selective classification error at fixed coverage levels (100% down to low coverage); accuracy at full coverage.
papers.baselines: Vanilla classifier with softmax response, SelectiveNet, Deep Gamblers, Self-Adaptive Training (with their own and with SR selection).
papers.results: ImageNet100 accuracy at 100% coverage: vanilla 85.68 +/- 0.14, SelectiveNet 86.23, Deep Gamblers 86.51, Self-Adaptive Training 86.40 - i.e. these methods train better classifiers. Replacing their selection head by SR lowered selective error at every coverage (Table 2). Entropy-minimisation + SR gave the best results across coverages and datasets.
papers.statistics: Mean +/- standard deviation over 3-5 seeds.
papers.availability: Code linked in the paper (Borealis AI GitHub).

papers.title: Deep Neural Network Benchmarks for Selective Classification
papers.authors: Andrea Pugnana, Lorenzo Perini, Jesse Davis, Salvatore Ruggieri
papers.venue: Journal of Data-centric Machine Learning Research
papers.aim: To fairly compare existing selective classification methods on many datasets so practitioners know which to use.
papers.method: Benchmarks 18 selective classification baselines (learn-to-abstain, learn-to-select and score-based) on 44 image and tabular datasets with the same architectures, evaluating selective error, empirical coverage, which classes get rejected, and behaviour on out-of-distribution data.
papers.result: No single method wins everywhere; the best choice depends on the user's goal (target coverage, class balance of rejections, robustness to OOD). Ensembles plus softmax response and score-based methods were often strong but costly (ensembles need ~10x training).
papers.tools: ResNet-34 / VGG-16 for images; revised tabular DNNs (Gorishniy et al., Grinsztajn et al.); bootstrap evaluation.
papers.gap: No medical imaging datasets specifically; single train-test split; no text or 3D data.
papers.relation: Benchmarks many selective-classification methods on risk-coverage trade-offs, which guides the choice of method for the escalation module.
papers.limitations: One architecture per dataset; datasets up to ~300k instances; running times not compared.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors collect 44 public datasets (20 image, 24 tabular) and implement 18 selective classification methods with the same backbone per dataset - ResNet-34 or VGG-16 for images and recent tabular deep networks - training and tuning each from scratch. For each method and target coverage level they measure the error on accepted cases, how close the achieved coverage is to the target, which classes end up rejected, and how the method behaves on out-of-distribution inputs, using bootstrap resampling of the test set to estimate variability. The main finding is that no method dominates: some are more accurate, some hit coverage targets more reliably, some reject minority classes more often, and ensembles are strong but about ten times more expensive. For our PhD this means escalation methods must be compared on our own data and goals, and we must check that escalation does not mostly reject rare tumour types or particular patient groups.
papers.studyDesign: Large benchmark study (comparative evaluation), no new method.
papers.datasets: 44 benchmark datasets from finance, healthcare and other real-life domains: 20 image and 24 tabular; binary and multi-class; 13 used in original papers of the baselines; sizes up to about 300,000 instances.
papers.preprocessing: Single train-test split per dataset; models trained and tuned from scratch; test-set bootstrap to measure variability.
papers.modelDetails: 18 baselines: DG (Deep Gamblers), SAT, SAT+EM (learn-to-abstain); SELNET, SELNET+EM (learn-to-select); SR, SAT+SR, SAT+EM+SR, SELNET+SR, SELNET+EM+SR, ENS, ENS+SR, CONFIDNET, REG, SELE, SCROSS, PLUGINAUC, AUCROSS (score-based). Same backbone per dataset (ResNet-34 or the original paper's architecture for images; modern tabular DNNs for tabular data).
papers.training: Network-specific hyper-parameters (layers, learning rate) and loss-specific ones (e.g. beta for SAT+EM) tuned per dataset; ensembles of 10 networks.
papers.evaluation: Selective error rate at target coverages, empirical coverage vs target coverage, distribution of rejected instances across classes, performance on out-of-distribution instances; ranking across datasets with bootstrap variability.
papers.baselines: All 18 methods compared against each other.
papers.results: Results tables in the paper/appendix: no clear overall winner; methods differ in how well they hit the target coverage, in whether they reject minority classes disproportionately, and in OOD behaviour. Users must choose by objective.
papers.statistics: Bootstrap of the test set; rank-based comparisons across 44 datasets.

papers.title: A Call to Reflect on Evaluation Practices for Failure Detection in Image Classification
papers.authors: Paul F. Jaeger, Carsten T. Luth, Lukas Klein, Till J. Bungert
papers.aim: To unify how misclassification detection, selective classification and out-of-distribution detection are evaluated, and to test methods under a realistic range of failure sources.
papers.method: Proposes the FD-Shifts benchmark: confidence scoring functions (CSFs) are evaluated by the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC) on i.i.d. data and on many shifts (sub-class shift, image corruptions, new-class shift semantic and non-semantic), with CNN and Vision Transformer classifiers.
papers.result: None of the evaluated literature methods beat the simple maximum softmax response (MSR) baseline across realistic failure sources; MSR or MC-dropout MSR was best or near-best on all i.i.d. and most shifted test sets except new-class shifts. Vision Transformers gave better failure detection than CNNs. CSFs beyond MSR can be calibrated with Platt scaling.
papers.tools: CNNs and ViT classifiers; MSR, MC dropout, DeepGamblers, DeVries confidence, ConfidNet, Mahalanobis, energy scores; FD-Shifts code.
papers.gap: Natural and some medical-domain images (CAMELYON pathology); no 3D MRI; no human deferral.
papers.relation: Sets a unified evaluation protocol (AURC) for confidence scoring functions that decide which predictions to trust.
papers.limitations: Classification only; selected shifts may not cover all clinical shifts.
papers.methodologyDetail: Three research communities - misclassification detection, selective classification and out-of-distribution detection - all try to flag when a classifier will fail, but each tests methods differently. The authors argue that what matters in practice is whether the confidence score ranks wrong predictions below correct ones under every realistic kind of failure, and propose evaluating this with the area under the risk-coverage curve. They build FD-Shifts: seven datasets, including CAMELYON-17 histopathology with hospital shift and iWildCam/BREEDS with population shift, each tested on clean data, sub-class shift, image corruptions at five intensities, and images from new classes. Many published scoring methods are re-implemented on the same CNN and Vision Transformer classifiers, with 5-10 runs per setting. The plain maximum softmax probability (with or without MC dropout) is best or close to best almost everywhere except new-class shift, and specialised methods fail to generalise. For our PhD this sets the evaluation protocol for escalation signals: AURC on i.i.d. data, on scanner or hospital shift, on corrupted images, and on unseen tumour types.
papers.studyDesign: Large-scale benchmark study with a proposed unified evaluation protocol.
papers.datasets: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, TinyImageNet, iWildCam (Wilds), BREEDS (ImageNet sub-population shift), CAMELYON-17-Wilds (histopathology, hospital shift); with i.i.d. test, sub-class shift, 5-level corruptions, and semantic / non-semantic new-class shift sets.
papers.preprocessing: Standard splits; corruptions averaged over 5 intensities; 5 runs per experiment (10 for CAMELYON-17-Wilds due to volatility, 2 for BREEDS).
