papers.result: Outperformed state-of-the-art federated and weakly-supervised methods across fundus, OCTA, endoscopy and prostate MRI segmentation with heterogeneous weak labels, approaching fully supervised performance.
papers.tools: Prompt-based segmentation network with dual attention, PyTorch.
papers.gap: 2D tasks; no brain tumour; prompts add complexity.
papers.relation: Combines federated learning with weak/sparse annotations, matching the limited expert labelling available in local hospitals.
papers.limitations: Weak labels partly synthetic; performance still below full supervision in places.
papers.methodologyDetail: Full pixel-level annotations are expensive, so different hospitals may label with points, scribbles, bounding boxes or blocks. FedLPPA lets such sites train together. A shared 'universal' prompt holds common knowledge, while each site has prompts describing its own image distribution and how sparse its labels are; these prompts are combined with image features through attention so each site's decoder adapts. A global and a personalised decoder are combined using weights based on how similar sites' prompts are. Experiments cover four modalities with five public datasets each, every site deliberately given a different weak annotation type (Table I), and FedLPPA beats federated and weakly-supervised baselines. For our PhD this suggests asking busy Sri Lankan radiologists for quick scribbles or boxes rather than full outlines, while still training a useful federated segmentation agent.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper; simulated federations with heterogeneous weak annotations on four modalities.
papers.datasets: Fundus: Drishti-GS1 (50:51 train:test, scribble), RIM-ONE-r3 (99:60, scribble style 2), REFUGE-train (320:80, bounding box), REFUGE-val (320:80, point), GAMMA (100:100, block). OCTA: FAZID (244:60), OCTA500-3M (150:50), OCTA500-6M (200:100), OCTA-25K (708:304), ROSE (30:9). Endoscopy: CVC-ClinicDB (550:62, point) and other polyp sets. Prostate MRI: multi-centre dataset of Liu et al. (slices without prostate excluded).
papers.preprocessing: Fundus cropped around optic disc and resized to 384x384; OCTA 256x256; endoscopy and MRI 384x384.
papers.modelDetails: Shared encoder; universal knowledge prompt shared across sites; personalised distribution prompts and sparsity prompts per site; dual-attention fusion of prompts with features; dual decoders (global and personalised) with aggregation weights from prompt similarity.
papers.training: Federated training with weak-label losses (e.g. partial cross-entropy on annotated pixels); details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Dice and related metrics per site and modality; comparison with fully supervised upper bound.
papers.baselines: FedAvg, FedProx, FedBN, personalised FL methods, weakly supervised segmentation methods.
papers.results: FedLPPA achieved the best average performance across all four modalities (tables in paper), closing much of the gap to full supervision.
papers.statistics: Mean values per site.

papers.title: Think Twice Before Selection: Federated Evidential Active Learning for Medical Image Analysis with Domain Shifts
papers.authors: Chen J, Ma B, Cui H, Xia Y
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
papers.aim: To choose which local images to annotate in federated active learning when hospitals have different data distributions.
papers.method: Federated Evidential Active Learning (FEAL): local and global models output Dirichlet distributions (evidential learning) to capture aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty; epistemic uncertainty calibrates aleatoric uncertainty to score informativeness; a diversity relaxation strategy avoids selecting redundant samples.
papers.result: FEAL beat other federated active learning methods on five multi-centre datasets (2 classification, 3 segmentation), reaching near full-annotation performance with a fraction of labels.
papers.tools: Evidential deep learning (Dirichlet), federated active learning, CNN classifiers and U-Net segmentation.
papers.gap: No brain MRI; annotation budgets simulated.
papers.relation: Uses evidential uncertainty to choose which cases clinicians should annotate in a federated setting, linking data efficiency with calibrated uncertainty.
papers.limitations: Requires evidential training; budgets and rounds fixed in simulation.
papers.methodologyDetail: In federated active learning, each hospital uses models to pick which unlabelled images to send for expert annotation. When hospitals differ, the usual uncertainty scores are misleading. FEAL makes both the local and the global model output a Dirichlet distribution over classes, separating data noise (aleatoric) from model ignorance (epistemic); epistemic uncertainty from the global model adjusts the aleatoric score so that images that are just unfamiliar to the local model are not over-selected, and a diversity step avoids picking near-identical images. Across five annotation rounds on five multi-centre datasets (skin lesions, histology, polyps, prostate MRI and fundus), FEAL beat random and other active learning strategies and approached fully annotated performance. For our PhD it suggests letting the system propose which Sri Lankan scans clinicians should annotate next, using the same uncertainty machinery as escalation.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper; simulated federated active learning on five real multi-centre datasets.
papers.datasets: Fed-ISIC skin lesions (4 sources: 12,413 / 3,954 / 3,363 / 2,259 images); Fed-Camelyon breast histology (5 centres: 59,436 / 34,904 / 85,054 / 129,838 / 146,722 patches); Fed-Polyp (4 centres: 1,000 / 196 / 379 / 612); Fed-Prostate MRI (6 sources: 261 / 384 / 158 / 468 / 421 / 175 slices); Fed-Fundus optic disc/cup (multi-centre).
papers.preprocessing: Per-centre splits; active learning rounds R1-R5 with fixed annotation budget per round.
papers.modelDetails: Dirichlet-based evidential heads on local and global models; sample score = aleatoric uncertainty calibrated by epistemic uncertainty from both models; diversity relaxation removes near-duplicate candidates before selection.
papers.training: FedAvg-style training after each annotation round; details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy / balanced accuracy (classification) and Dice (segmentation) after each active learning round (R2-R5), compared with full annotation.
papers.baselines: Random sampling, local-only or global-only uncertainty sampling, other federated active learning methods.
papers.results: Full-annotation Dice: Fed-Polyp 78.18, Fed-Prostate 88.02, Fed-Fundus disc/cup 94.32 / 85.70. Random sampling Fed-Prostate R2-R5: 80.29, 82.70, 83.94, 84.77. FEAL gave top results at most rounds on all datasets (Table 1).
papers.statistics: Mean over runs.

papers.title: Robust Learning Protocol for Federated Tumor Segmentation Challenge
papers.authors: Rawat A, Zizzo G, Kadhe S, et al.
papers.aim: To design a robust and efficient federated learning protocol for brain tumour segmentation in the FeTS 2022 challenge.
papers.method: RoLePRO: two-phase protocol - phase 1 vanilla FedAvg to reach a good initialisation; phase 2 fine-tuning with judicious re-weighted aggregation schemes (inspired by FeTS 2021 winners), with server-side adaptive optimisation (e.g. server Adam) and tuned learning-rate schedules.
papers.result: Many aggregation schemes reached similar best Dice; averaged Dice near convergence showed that re-weighted aggregation gave marginal benefits over vanilla FedAvg (slightly lower average loss, higher average Dice). Results not from multiple runs.
papers.tools: FeTS 2022 challenge framework (OpenFL), 3D U-Net, server-side Adam.
papers.gap: Single runs; marginal gains; simulated federation.
papers.relation: Proposes robust aggregation and training protocols for federated brain-tumour segmentation under heterogeneous institutions.
papers.limitations: Authors note results tentative (no repeated runs).
papers.methodologyDetail: For the FeTS 2022 federated brain tumour segmentation challenge, the authors build a training protocol around a fixed 3D U-Net. They first run ordinary federated averaging for a few rounds to get a reasonable model, then switch to a fine-tuning phase where client updates are combined with smarter re-weighting schemes (from earlier winning entries) and the server applies an adaptive optimiser like Adam to the averaged update, tuning learning rates for each phase. Looking at both best and average Dice near convergence, the extra aggregation tricks gave only small and tentative benefits over plain FedAvg. For our PhD this supports starting federated experiments with FedAvg and adding server-side adaptive optimisation and re-weighting as a second step.
papers.studyDesign: Challenge entry / workshop paper with simulated FL experiments.
papers.datasets: FeTS 2022 multi-institutional glioma mpMRI (BraTS-derived), partitioned by institution.
papers.preprocessing: FeTS standard preprocessing.
papers.modelDetails: Fixed FeTS 3D U-Net; server-side adaptive optimisers (FedAdam-style); aggregation schemes: FedAvg, adaptive weighted aggregation and other re-weighting schemes from FeTS 2021.
papers.training: Two phases within the challenge time budget; learning rates tuned per phase by experimentation.
papers.evaluation: Best Dice, average Dice near convergence, best and average loss (Table 1).
papers.baselines: Vanilla FedAvg.
papers.results: Best Dice comparable across methods; average Dice slightly higher and average loss lower with re-weighted aggregation + server optimiser than FedAvg (single-run, tentative).
papers.statistics: Not reported (single runs).

papers.title: The BraTS-Africa Dataset: Expanding the Brain Tumor Segmentation Data to Capture African Populations
papers.authors: Adewole M, Rudie JD, Gbadamosi A, et al.
papers.relation: Provides a low-resource-setting glioma MRI dataset with lower-quality scans, a close analogue for Sri Lankan data and domain shift.

papers.title: Brain tumor segmentation in Sub-Saharan Africa patient population: The BraTS-Africa challenge
papers.authors: Adewole M, Rudie JD, Gbadamosi A, et al.
papers.relation: Reports how segmentation models transfer to low-resource MRI cohorts, directly informing adaptation to small Sri Lankan datasets.
papers.methodologyDetail: BraTS-Africa extends the BraTS challenge to glioma patients from Sub-Saharan Africa, where MRI is often acquired on older or low-field scanners with poorer contrast and resolution, and patients present later with more advanced disease. The organisers curate routine-care multiparametric MRI from SSA, preprocess it with the standard BraTS pipeline, and have it annotated for the usual tumour sub-regions. Submitted algorithms are scored with Dice, 95% Hausdorff distance, sensitivity, specificity and precision, and evaluated at the contributing sites using the MedPerf federated benchmarking platform so data stay local. For our PhD this is the closest analogue to Sri Lankan conditions and the benchmark to test whether models trained on high-resource BraTS data transfer to low-resource scanners; it is one of the base papers.
papers.studyDesign: Challenge description / benchmark paper (BraTS-Africa), with federated-style evaluation through MedPerf on contributing sites' data.
papers.datasets: Brain MRI glioma cases from Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) acquired in routine care, often on lower-field / lower-quality scanners with poorer contrast and resolution and late-stage presentation (including suspected higher rates of gliomatosis cerebri); multiparametric MRI (T1, T1Gd, T2, FLAIR) with expert annotations, in addition to global BraTS training data.
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS pipeline (registration to common template, 1 mm resampling, skull stripping); authors note SSA images may need extra preprocessing to enhance resolution.
papers.modelDetails: Not a model paper; defines the task (segmentation of enhancing tumour, tumour core and whole tumour) and evaluation set-up for SSA data.
papers.training: Participants may use BraTS adult glioma data plus BraTS-Africa training data.
papers.evaluation: Dice similarity coefficient, 95% Hausdorff distance, sensitivity, specificity and precision per tumour region; submissions evaluated through MedPerf at each contributing site.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Not applicable for model results; establishes the first curated SSA glioma MRI benchmark to test whether BraTS-trained methods work in low-resource imaging conditions.
papers.statistics: Ranking scheme as in previous BraTS challenges.
papers.availability: Data via BraTS / Synapse; evaluation via MedPerf.

papers.title: Optimizing Brain Tumor Segmentation with MedNeXt: BraTS 2024 SSA and Pediatrics
papers.authors: Hashmi S, Lugo J, Elsayed A, et al.
papers.relation: Shows how to fine-tune modern architectures on small low-resource (Sub-Saharan) glioma cohorts with distribution shift.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors target the BraTS 2024 tasks where data differ most from standard BraTS: adults in Sub-Saharan Africa scanned with lower-quality MRI, and children. They use MedNeXt, a U-Net built from ConvNeXt blocks, first trained on the large adult BraTS dataset and then fine-tuned on the small SSA or pediatric training sets in 5-fold cross-validation (150 or 75 epochs, Schedule-free AdamW, learning rate 0.0027, batch 2). The five fold models are averaged, and the probability map is post-processed with thresholds and removal of small components tuned on cross-validation. On unseen validation data they reached average Dice 0.896 for SSA and 0.830 for pediatrics. For our PhD this is a concrete recipe for small local datasets: pre-train on BraTS, fine-tune on Sri Lankan scans, ensemble folds, and tune post-processing - and it shows low-resource MRI can still reach high Dice.
papers.studyDesign: Challenge entry (BraTS 2024 Sub-Saharan Africa and Pediatric tasks); model development with 5-fold cross-validation and evaluation on unseen validation sets.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2024 SSA (BraTS-Africa) adult glioma mpMRI and BraTS 2024 Pediatric tumour mpMRI, from standard clinical care, annotated by radiologists and reviewed by neuro-specialists; adult BraTS data used for pre-training.
papers.preprocessing: BraTS preprocessing; intensity normalisation; standard augmentation; label post-processing per region.
papers.modelDetails: MedNeXt (U-Net with ConvNeXt blocks): MedNeXt-B and MedNeXt-M for SSA, MedNeXt-B for paediatrics, kernel size 3. Ensemble of 5 fold models by averaging tumour probability maps, followed by post-processing (thresholds and small-component removal tuned on cross-validation then adjusted for validation).
papers.training: 150 epochs (SSA) and 75 epochs (pediatric); Schedule-free AdamW (Meta FAIR), learning rate 0.0027 (SSA), 0.0027 and 0.0005 (pediatric), no weight decay, batch size 2; models pre-trained on adult BraTS then fine-tuned; 5-fold cross-validation.
papers.evaluation: Lesion-wise Dice and 95% Hausdorff distance (BraTS 2024 metrics) on the unseen validation set.
papers.baselines: Single-fold models, models without pre-training or post-processing (ablations).
papers.results: Unseen validation: SSA average Dice 0.896, average HD95 14.682; Pediatric average Dice 0.830, HD95 37.508.
papers.statistics: Not reported beyond averages.
papers.availability: Code: GitHub repository linked in paper.

papers.title: How We Won BraTS-SSA 2025: Brain Tumor Segmentation in the Sub-Saharan African Population Using Segmentation-Aware Data Augmentation and Model Ensembling
papers.authors: Ankomah CT, Ayivor LE, Nyame I, et al.
papers.relation: Winning recipe of augmentation and ensembling for data-scarce, low-quality MRI in a low-resource population.
papers.methodologyDetail: Working with the small BraTS-Africa dataset (scans from routine African care on varied, often lower-quality scanners), the team first enlarged and diversified the training data with segmentation-aware offline augmentation, transforming images and tumour labels together before training. They trained three different architectures - MedNeXt, the Mamba-based SegMamba, and nnU-Net's residual-encoder U-Net - and compared training lengths, finding MedNeXt trained for 1,000 epochs best on its own (lesion-wise Dice 0.86, NSD 0.81), while an ensemble of all three trained for 500 epochs was most balanced across enhancing tumour, core and whole tumour. This won BraTS-SSA 2025. For our PhD it shows that heavy augmentation and architecture ensembles are effective for small, heterogeneous low-resource MRI datasets like those expected in Sri Lanka.
papers.studyDesign: Challenge entry (BraTS-SSA 2025, winning team, SPARK Academy); model development and comparison on BraTS-Africa data.
papers.datasets: BraTS-Africa (Sub-Saharan Africa) mpMRI: cases including 95 adult diffuse gliomas and 51 other CNS neoplasms reviewed by board-certified radiologists; small dataset with variable scanner quality, settings and protocols.
papers.preprocessing: Segmentation-aware offline data augmentation to enlarge and diversify the training set (transforms applied jointly to images and labels before training); standard BraTS preprocessing.
papers.modelDetails: Three architectures: MedNeXt (ConvNeXt-based U-Net), SegMamba (state-space model), Residual-Encoder U-Net (nnU-Net ResEnc); ensemble of the three for final predictions.
papers.training: MedNeXt trained for 1,000 epochs (best single model); ensemble members trained for 500 epochs; configurations compared in Table 1.
papers.evaluation: Lesion-wise Dice (LSD) and normalised surface distance at 1 mm (NSD) for ET, TC, WT and average.
papers.baselines: Each single architecture at different training lengths and settings.
papers.results: Best single model MedNeXt (1,000 epochs): average lesion-wise Dice 0.86 and NSD 0.81. The 500-epoch ensemble of MedNeXt + SegMamba + ResEnc U-Net gave the most balanced performance across tumour sub-regions.
papers.statistics: Not reported beyond averages.

papers.title: MedNeXt: Transformer-Driven Scaling of ConvNets for Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Roy S, Koehler G, Ulrich C, et al.
papers.relation: Strong data-efficient 3D ConvNeXt segmentation backbone that performs well on limited medical data including brain tumours.
papers.methodologyDetail: MedNeXt adapts the ConvNeXt idea - convolutional blocks designed like transformer blocks - to 3D medical segmentation. Every encoder and decoder stage, including up- and down-sampling, uses residual ConvNeXt blocks, with deep supervision on each decoder level. Because large kernels tend to under-train on small medical datasets, the authors first train a small-kernel (3x3x3) network and then initialise the large-kernel (5x5x5) version by upsampling its kernels (UpKern), and scale depth, width and kernel size together. In 5-fold cross-validation on BTCV, AMOS22, KiTS19 and BraTS21 it beat nnU-Net and transformer networks, and on the BraTS21 leaderboard reached mean Dice 88.01 versus 87.17 for nnU-Net. For our PhD MedNeXt is a strong data-efficient backbone for the MRI segmentation agent, and later BraTS-Africa winners (O3-P30, O3-P31) relied on it.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper; 5-fold cross-validation on four public 3D segmentation tasks plus public leaderboard submissions.
papers.datasets: BTCV (abdominal CT, multi-organ), AMOS22 (abdominal CT/MRI), KiTS19 (kidney tumour CT), BraTS21 (brain tumour MRI) - varying dataset sizes and modalities.
papers.preprocessing: nnU-Net-style preprocessing and augmentation pipeline.
papers.modelDetails: MedNeXt: fully ConvNeXt 3D encoder-decoder (4 encoder and decoder levels plus bottleneck) with residual ConvNeXt up- and down-sampling blocks; deep supervision at each decoder level; large kernels (3 to 5) trained by UpKern - initialising a large-kernel network by upsampling a trained small-kernel network to avoid saturation on limited data; compound scaling of depth, width and kernel size (sizes S, B, M, L).
papers.training: nnU-Net-like training settings; 5-fold cross-validation; kernel sizes 3 and 5 compared.
papers.evaluation: Dice and normalised surface distance in 5-fold CV against 7 baselines; mean DSC on public leaderboards.
papers.baselines: nnU-Net, UNETR, SwinUNETR, TransUNet, TransBTS, nnFormer, 3D-UX-Net (convolutional, transformer and large-kernel networks).
papers.results: MedNeXt with kernel 3 or 5 outperformed all 7 baselines in 5-fold CV across the four tasks; leaderboard mean DSC MedNeXt-L-k5 vs nnU-Net: BTCV 88.76 vs 88.08, AMOS22 91.77 vs 91.01, KiTS19 91.02 vs 90.16, BraTS21 88.01 vs 87.17.
papers.statistics: 5-fold cross-validation means.

papers.title: nnU-Net Revisited: A Call for Rigorous Validation in 3D Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Isensee F, Wald T, Ulrich C, et al.
papers.relation: Shows well-configured CNN baselines still beat newer architectures, guiding rigorous baseline choice for small local MRI data.
papers.methodologyDetail: The nnU-Net authors test whether recent 'better than U-Net' segmentation architectures really are better. They list common validation pitfalls - comparing against poorly configured baselines, using small or saturated datasets, giving new models more compute, and not reporting variance - and then benchmark CNN, transformer and Mamba models on several 3D datasets under identical nnU-Net preprocessing and training, with matched GPU budgets and five-fold cross-validation. They introduce residual-encoder nnU-Net presets (M, L, XL) for different GPU sizes. Well-configured CNN U-Nets in nnU-Net, scaled to the hardware, came out on top; most transformer and Mamba claims did not hold, and brain tumour segmentation gained little from bigger models. For our PhD this sets the baseline (nnU-Net ResEnc) and the validation rules (fair baselines, matched compute, cross-validation, variance) for evaluating our segmentation agent.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark and validation-methodology study re-evaluating CNN, Transformer and Mamba segmentation models under a fair protocol.
papers.datasets: Several public 3D segmentation datasets of differing difficulty, including BTCV, AMOS, KiTS and BraTS (plus others), selected to avoid saturated benchmarks.
papers.preprocessing: nnU-Net preprocessing for all models; matched compute budgets.
papers.modelDetails: Compared: nnU-Net (original), nnU-Net ResEnc presets M / L / XL (residual-encoder U-Net auto-adapted to VRAM budgets), MedNeXt L (k3, k5 UpKern), STU-Net S/B/L, SwinUNETR, nnFormer, UNETR, CoTr, U-Mamba, SegMamba variants, MONAI Auto3DSeg.
papers.training: Identical training pipelines and hardware-normalised budgets; five-fold cross-validation.
papers.evaluation: Dice per dataset; analysis of validation pitfalls (weak baselines, insufficient or saturated datasets, unequal compute, missing variance reporting).
papers.baselines: All of the above compared with each other; original claims from the literature re-tested.
papers.results: Recipe for state-of-the-art: CNN-based U-Nets (ResNet/ConvNeXt variants) inside the nnU-Net framework, scaled to modern hardware. Many claimed transformer/Mamba gains did not hold; Auto3DSeg out-of-the-box did not match nnU-Net; scaling (ResEnc M/L/XL, STU-Net) helped most on harder datasets (AMOS, KiTS) and little on BTCV and BraTS.
papers.statistics: Cross-validation means with variability; discussion of statistical rigour.

papers.title: TransBTS: Multimodal Brain Tumor Segmentation Using Transformer
papers.authors: Wang W, Chen C, Ding M, et al.
papers.relation: Hybrid CNN-transformer architecture for multimodal MRI brain-tumour segmentation, a key candidate model family.
papers.methodologyDetail: TransBTS was one of the first models to put a Transformer inside a 3D CNN for brain tumour segmentation. A 3D convolutional encoder first captures local detail from the four MRI sequences; its low-resolution feature maps are flattened into tokens and passed through Transformer layers so every location can attend to every other, capturing global context; a convolutional decoder then upsamples back to a full-resolution segmentation. Training used 128-cube random crops with flips and intensity augmentation, Adam (lr 4e-4, poly decay), batch 16, 8,000 epochs on eight GPUs. On BraTS 2019 and 2020 validation sets it reached Dice about 79 / 90 / 82 for enhancing tumour, whole tumour and core, matching the best 3D CNNs of the time. For our PhD it is a standard transformer baseline for the segmentation agent, although later benchmarks (O3-P33) show well-tuned nnU-Net-style CNNs usually match or beat it.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper; five-fold cross-validation and BraTS 2019/2020 validation leaderboards.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2019 (335 training cases) and BraTS 2020 (369 training cases) multimodal MRI (T1, T1ce, T2, FLAIR), 240x240x155 volumes; official validation sets.
papers.preprocessing: Random crop from 240x240x155 to 128x128x128; random mirror flips across axial, coronal and sagittal planes; random intensity shift and scale; z-score normalisation.
papers.modelDetails: TransBTS: 3D CNN encoder extracts volumetric local features; feature maps reshaped into tokens and fed to a Transformer for global (long-range) modelling; CNN decoder progressively upsamples to the segmentation map. Optional test-time augmentation (TTA).
papers.training: PyTorch on 8 NVIDIA Titan RTX GPUs (24 GB each), 8,000 epochs from scratch, batch size 16, Adam, initial learning rate 0.0004 with poly decay (power 0.9), softmax Dice loss.
papers.evaluation: Dice and Hausdorff distance (95%) for ET, WT, TC on BraTS validation sets.
papers.baselines: 3D U-Net, V-Net, KiU-Net, Attention U-Net, Wang et al., Li et al., Frey et al., Myronenko (NVIDIA SegResNet).
papers.results: BraTS 2019 validation: TransBTS with TTA Dice ET 78.93, WT 90.00, TC 81.94; HD 3.736 / 5.644 / 6.049 mm (without TTA 78.36 / 88.89 / 81.41). BraTS 2020 validation with TTA: Dice ET 78.73, WT 90.09, TC 81.73; HD 17.947 / 4.964 / 9.769 mm. Comparable to or better than prior 3D methods (e.g. 3D U-Net 2020: 68.76 / 84.11 / 79.06).
papers.statistics: Leaderboard results; no significance tests.

papers.title: NestedFormer: Nested Modality-Aware Transformer for Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.authors: Xing Z, Yu L, Wan L, Han T, Zhu L
papers.relation: Modality-aware fusion of multi-sequence MRI for brain-tumour segmentation, relevant to multi-source fusion.
papers.methodologyDetail: Most brain tumour networks simply stack the four MRI sequences as input channels. NestedFormer instead gives each sequence its own transformer encoder, then fuses them at the deepest level with a module that first models long-range relations inside each sequence (attention along three orientations) and then relations between sequences (cross-modal attention); at shallower levels, gates decide how much each sequence's skip connection contributes. Trained with Dice plus cross-entropy and AdamW (lr 1e-4) on one RTX 3090, it reached average Dice 0.861 on BraTS 2020 - slightly above nnU-Net and TransBTS - with only about 10 million parameters, and also led on a meningioma dataset. For our PhD the per-sequence encoders are useful when Sri Lankan protocols differ in which sequences are available, and the small model size suits limited hardware.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper evaluated on a public brain tumour dataset and a private meningioma dataset.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2020 multimodal MRI (T1, T1ce, T2, FLAIR); private meningioma segmentation dataset (MeniSeg).
papers.preprocessing: Standard cropping and normalisation; window size (2,2,2) for BraTS 2020 and (2,4,4) for MeniSeg.
papers.modelDetails: NestedFormer: multi-encoder (one transformer encoder per MRI modality), single decoder. Nested Modality-aware Feature Aggregation (NMaFA) fuses high-level features using a tri-orientated spatial-attention transformer (within modality) and a cross-modality attention transformer (between modalities); Modality-Sensitive Gating (MSG) on lower-scale skip connections.
papers.training: PyTorch 1.7.0, one NVIDIA RTX 3090; Xavier initialisation; soft Dice + cross-entropy loss; AdamW, weight decay 1e-5, learning rate 1e-4.
papers.evaluation: Dice and HD95 for WT, TC, ET and average; parameters and FLOPs.
papers.baselines: 3D U-Net, SegResNet, MAML, nnU-Net, SwinUNet (2D), TransBTS, UNETR.
papers.results: BraTS 2020 (Dice / HD95): NestedFormer WT 0.920 / 4.567, TC 0.864 / 5.316, ET 0.800 / 5.269, average 0.861 / 5.051 with 10.48 M parameters and 71.77 GFLOPs; nnU-Net average 0.856 / 5.953; TransBTS 0.852 / 5.166; 3D U-Net 0.831 / 6.144. Also best on MeniSeg.
papers.statistics: Mean results; no significance tests reported.

papers.title: CKD-TransBTS: Clinical Knowledge-Driven Hybrid Transformer With Modality-Correlated Cross-Attention for Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.authors: Lin J, Lin J, Lu C, et al.
papers.aim: To segment brain tumours by fusing MRI sequences the way radiologists read them, combining CNN and Transformer strengths.
papers.method: Groups input MRI sequences into two branches by imaging principle (e.g. T1 / T1ce vs T2 / FLAIR); dual-branch hybrid encoder with a modality-correlated cross-attention (MCCA) block exchanging information between branches; Trans&CNN feature calibration in the decoder.
papers.result: Outperformed CNN-based (VNet, ResUNet, UNet++, AttentionUNet, DynUNet - BraTS21 winner) and transformer-based (TransBTS, UNETR, SwinUNETR, etc.) models on BraTS 2021 in Dice and HD95.
papers.tools: PyTorch, MONAI, NVIDIA RTX 3090.
papers.gap: Single dataset (BraTS 2021); grouping fixed to the four BraTS sequences.
papers.relation: Injects radiological clinical knowledge into modality grouping for brain-tumour segmentation, a data-efficient design prior.
papers.limitations: Requires all four sequences; compute heavier than plain CNNs.
papers.methodologyDetail: Radiologists read T1/T1-contrast images together and T2/FLAIR images together because they show different tissue properties. CKD-TransBTS copies this: the four MRI sequences are split into two groups, each processed by its own branch of a hybrid CNN-Transformer encoder (tokens from 4x4x4 sub-volumes, embedding size 32), and a modality-correlated cross-attention block lets each group attend to the other; a decoder calibrates transformer and CNN features before predicting the tumour regions. Trained on BraTS 2021 with Dice loss, cosine-annealed learning rate 1e-4 and 500 epochs on one RTX 3090, it beat eleven CNN and transformer models including the BraTS 2021 winner. For our PhD it is an example of embedding radiological knowledge into the network design, which can help clinician trust in the segmentation agent.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper evaluated on the BraTS 2021 dataset.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2021 multimodal MRI (T1, T1ce, T2, FLAIR) training data with labels, split for training and testing.
papers.preprocessing: Crop to the minimum bounding box of the brain then random 128x128x128 sub-volumes; intensity normalisation; augmentation.
papers.modelDetails: Two modality groups processed by separate branches; each branch tokenises 4x4x4 sub-volumes with initial embedding size 32; MCCA blocks let the two branches attend to each other; hybrid Transformer-CNN encoder and calibrated decoder.
papers.training: PyTorch + MONAI on one NVIDIA RTX 3090; learning rate 1e-4 with cosine annealing; 500 epochs; Dice loss.
papers.evaluation: Dice and HD95 for ET, TC, WT and mean.
papers.baselines: VNet, ResUNet, UNet++, AttentionUNet, DynUNet (1st in BraTS21), TransBTS, UNETR, SwinUNETR, NestedFormer and others.
papers.results: Baselines (mean Dice / HD95): VNet 0.8091 / 20.52; ResUNet 0.8547 / 11.25; DynUNet 0.8946 / about 8.8; CKD-TransBTS achieved the top mean Dice and lowest HD95 (Table I).
papers.statistics: Mean values; no formal tests reported.

papers.title: mmFormer: Multimodal Medical Transformer for Incomplete Multimodal Learning of Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.authors: Zhang Y, He N, Yang J, et al.
papers.aim: To segment brain tumours robustly with any subset of the four MRI sequences available.
papers.method: mmFormer: hybrid modality-specific encoders (CNN + intra-modal Transformer) for each sequence; inter-modal Transformer to build modality-invariant global features; convolutional decoder; auxiliary regularisers so the model works with any missing-modality combination (one model for all 15 subsets).
papers.result: On BraTS 2018 it beat unified missing-modality models (U-HeMIS, U-HVED) across all subsets, especially when few sequences are available, e.g. FLAIR only: ET 39.33 vs 11.78 / 23.80 Dice, TC 61.21 vs 26.06 / 57.90, WT 86.10 vs 52.48 / 84.39.
papers.tools: 3D CNN encoders, Transformers, PyTorch.
papers.gap: BraTS 2018 only; random missing-modality simulation.
papers.relation: Robust segmentation when some MRI sequences are missing, common in low-resource hospital protocols.
papers.limitations: Performance with very few sequences still much lower than full set.
papers.methodologyDetail: In clinics, some MRI sequences are often missing (no contrast, artefacts, short protocols). mmFormer gives each sequence its own encoder combining convolution and a transformer, then a cross-modal transformer merges whatever sequences are present into shared features, ignoring the missing ones; a decoder outputs the tumour regions, with extra regularisation so every encoder learns useful features alone. Trained once with random modality dropping on BraTS 2018 (285 cases), it was tested on all 15 combinations of available sequences and beat earlier unified methods, especially with only one or two sequences. For our PhD this is the template for a segmentation agent that still works when a Sri Lankan scan lacks one or more sequences, while the escalation layer should flag such reduced-input cases as higher risk.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper; evaluation on all 15 missing-modality combinations of a public dataset.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2018: 285 multi-contrast MRI scans (T1, T1c, T2, FLAIR), co-registered and resampled by organisers; labels combined into whole tumour, tumour core, enhancing tumour.
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS preprocessing; random modality dropping during training.
papers.modelDetails: Per-modality hybrid encoder (convolution + intra-modal Transformer); inter-modal Transformer fuses available modalities (missing ones masked); decoder with auxiliary per-modality decoders and regularisation.
papers.training: Settings in the paper (PyTorch, Dice-based loss).
papers.evaluation: Dice per region for each of the 15 modality combinations and average.
papers.baselines: U-HeMIS, U-HVED (unified models for missing modalities).
papers.results: Higher Dice than U-HeMIS and U-HVED in all combinations; e.g. FLAIR only: ET 39.33, TC 61.21, WT 86.10 (vs U-HVED 23.80, 57.90, 84.39).
papers.statistics: Mean Dice per setting.

papers.title: M3AE: Multimodal Representation Learning for Brain Tumor Segmentation with Missing Modalities
papers.authors: Liu H, Wei D, Lu D, et al.
papers.aim: To learn brain tumour segmentation that is robust to missing MRI sequences using self-supervised pre-training.
papers.method: Two stages. Stage 1: multimodal masked autoencoder (M3AE) - randomly drop whole modalities and mask random patches of the rest, and reconstruct them (self-supervised), while model inversion optimises a representative full-modal image used to fill missing modalities. Stage 2: fine-tune for segmentation with memory-efficient self-distillation between full and missing-modality inputs.
papers.result: On BraTS 2018 and 2020, outperformed U-HVED, ACN, SMU-Net and RFNet on average over missing-modality combinations, as a single 'catch-all' model.
papers.tools: 3D U-Net with residual blocks and group normalisation (backbone of ACN), PyTorch 1.7.1.
papers.gap: Simulated missing modalities; BraTS only.
papers.relation: Self-supervised masked-autoencoder pretraining that handles missing MRI sequences, combining data efficiency with incomplete inputs.
papers.limitations: Extra pre-training stage; still lower than full-modality performance.
papers.methodologyDetail: M3AE first pre-trains a 3D U-Net without labels: it randomly removes whole MRI sequences and random patches from the remaining ones and learns to reconstruct them, which teaches it to infer missing information. At the same time it learns a 'representative' full-modal image to plug in where a sequence is missing. It is then fine-tuned for tumour segmentation, with self-distillation so predictions with missing sequences match those with all sequences. On BraTS 2018 and 2020 it beat dedicated and unified missing-modality methods. For our PhD this supports self-supervised pre-training on unlabelled Sri Lankan MRI and robustness to incomplete protocols in the segmentation agent.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper; BraTS 2018 and 2020 with all missing-modality combinations.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2018 and BraTS 2020 multimodal MRI (T1, T1c, T2, FLAIR).
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS preprocessing; random modality dropout and patch masking during pre-training.
papers.modelDetails: Backbone: 3D U-Net (single encoder/decoder, residual blocks, group normalisation); 1x1x1 convolution heads for reconstruction (no activation) and segmentation (sigmoid); learned representative full-modal image substitutes missing modalities; self-distillation between modality subsets.
papers.training: Self-supervised pre-training then fine-tuning; details in paper and supplement.
papers.evaluation: Dice for ET, TC, WT across the 15 modality combinations; averages.
papers.baselines: U-HVED, ACN (dedicated), SMU-Net (dedicated), RFNet (catch-all).
papers.results: Best or near-best average Dice among compared methods on both datasets (Tables 1-2), while using one model for all combinations.
papers.statistics: Mean Dice per setting.

papers.title: D2-Net: Dual Disentanglement Network for Brain Tumor Segmentation With Missing Modalities
papers.authors: Yang Q, Guo X, Chen Z, Woo PYM, Yuan Y
papers.aim: To segment brain tumours accurately when some MRI sequences are missing by explicitly modelling how each sequence relates to each tumour region.
papers.method: D2-Net with two stages: modality disentanglement (spatial-frequency joint modality contrastive learning to separate sequence-specific information) and tumour-region disentanglement (affinity-guided dense knowledge distillation from binary region teachers to a holistic student); trained with random modality dropping.
papers.result: Best average Dice over all 15 missing-modality combinations on BraTS 2018: WT 76.2%, TC 66.5%, ET 42.3%, beating U-HVED (second best) by 0.4, 3.3 and 1.6 points with p<0.05 versus compared methods; ablations showed large gains from the contrastive modality loss and from the distillation module (+2.7 and +1.3 points over other KD schemes).
papers.tools: PyTorch, NVIDIA V100, 3D segmentation backbone, contrastive and distillation losses.
papers.gap: BraTS 2018 only (285 cases, 3-fold CV); enhancing tumour still hard when T1ce is missing.
papers.relation: Disentangles modality and tumour-region features for segmentation with incomplete MRI protocols.
papers.limitations: No external validation; added training complexity.
papers.methodologyDetail: Different MRI sequences show different parts of a brain tumour, so losing one sequence hurts some regions more than others. D2-Net first learns, with a contrastive loss in both image and frequency space, what information is unique to each sequence. It then trains small 'teacher' networks that each focus on one tumour region and passes their knowledge to a single 'student' segmentation network. During training, sequences are randomly blanked so the model learns to cope with gaps. On BraTS 2018 (285 cases, three-fold cross-validation), averaged over all 15 combinations of missing sequences, it achieved Dice of 76.2% (whole tumour), 66.5% (core) and 42.3% (enhancing), significantly better than earlier methods. For our PhD it is a further option for handling incomplete Sri Lankan MRI protocols, and it confirms enhancing tumour remains least reliable without contrast T1 - a case for deferral.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with three-fold cross-validation.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2018 training set: 285 cases with FLAIR, T1, T1ce, T2; three-fold cross-validation (190 training / 95 validation per fold).
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS preprocessing (co-registered, skull-stripped, 1 mm isotropic); intensity normalisation; random cropping.
papers.modelDetails: MD-Stage: modality-specific encoders with spatial and frequency-domain contrastive learning; TD-Stage: binary teacher networks per tumour region and holistic student aligned by affinity-guided dense distillation (ADT-KD); total loss = segmentation (Dice + cross-entropy) + modality-disentanglement + tumour-disentanglement (lambda1 = lambda2 = 1).
papers.training: 400 epochs, Adam, learning rate 3e-4, weight decay 5e-5, batch size 2; missing modalities simulated by zero matrices.
papers.evaluation: Dice for WT, TC, ET across all 15 modality combinations; ASSD, HD95, model complexity; ablation studies.
papers.baselines: HeMIS, U-HVED, RobustSeg and other missing-modality methods with comparable parameter counts.
papers.results: Average Dice WT 76.2%, TC 66.5%, ET 42.3%; significant improvements (p<0.05); spatial-frequency contrastive learning alone added about 9 points average Dice over baseline.
papers.statistics: P-values versus each compared method.

papers.title: Latent Correlation Representation Learning for Brain Tumor Segmentation With Missing MRI Modalities
papers.authors: Zhou T, Canu S, Vera P, Ruan S
papers.aim: To segment brain tumours robustly when some MRI sequences are missing by modelling the correlation between modalities.
papers.method: Separate encoders per modality; a correlation model estimates modality-independent parameters and transforms individual representations into a latent multi-source correlation representation; attention-based fusion; reconstruction of missing information; decoder for segmentation.
papers.result: Ablation on BraTS 2018 training set: baseline average Dice 76.7 -> 77.4 with fusion, further gains with reconstruction and correlation; robust performance with missing modalities compared with prior methods.
papers.tools: Keras, NVIDIA Quadro P5000 (16 GB).
papers.gap: Older architecture; BraTS only.
papers.relation: Models inter-modality correlations to segment brain tumours when sequences are unavailable.
papers.limitations: Single dataset; online evaluation only.
papers.methodologyDetail: Because MRI sequences are strongly related, the authors model this relationship explicitly. Each sequence has its own encoder; a correlation model estimates how each modality relates to a shared latent representation, so when a sequence is missing its information can be partly recovered from the others; an attention-based fusion module merges them and a decoder outputs the tumour regions. Trained in Keras with Adam (lr 5e-4) on BraTS 2018 (80/20 split), the ablations show each component adds Dice, and the full model stays robust when sequences are removed. For our PhD it is one of several missing-modality methods to compare (with mmFormer and M3AE) for incomplete Sri Lankan MRI protocols.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper; BraTS 2018 with simulated missing modalities.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2018 multimodal MRI; random 80% training / 20% testing split; online evaluation platform.
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS preprocessing.
papers.modelDetails: Modality-specific encoders; correlation model maps individual representations to a shared latent correlation space; fusion with attention; optional reconstruction branch; segmentation decoder.
papers.training: Adam, initial learning rate 5e-4, reduced by factor 0.5 after 10 epochs without improvement; early stopping after 50 epochs without validation improvement.
papers.evaluation: Dice, Hausdorff distance and sensitivity for whole, core and enhancing tumour, full and missing-modality settings.
papers.baselines: Own baseline and ablations; HeMIS, U-HVED and other missing-modality methods.
papers.results: Baseline Dice whole / core / enhancing / average 86.6 / 76.5 / 67.1 / 76.7; +fusion 87.8 / 76.5 / 67.8 / 77.4; further improvements with reconstruction and correlation model (Table I); HD average 8.9 -> 8.3 mm with fusion.
papers.statistics: Mean values; no tests.

papers.title: ACN: Adversarial Co-training Network for Brain Tumor Segmentation with Missing Modalities
papers.authors: Wang Y, Zhang Y, Liu Y, et al.
papers.aim: To segment brain tumours well even when more than one MRI sequence is missing.
papers.method: Adversarial Co-training Network: a full-modality path and a missing-modality path trained together; entropy and knowledge adversarial learning align their feature and output distributions; a consistency loss transfers knowledge; one dedicated model per missing-modality situation.
papers.result: Significantly beat HeMIS and U-HVED for all 15 missing-modality combinations, especially with only one or two sequences, where those methods had Dice of only about 10-20% on ET and TC.
papers.tools: U-Net backbone of the BraTS 2018 winner, two fully convolutional discriminators, PyTorch, NVIDIA Tesla V100 (32 GB).
papers.gap: One model per missing combination (15 models); BraTS 2018 only.
papers.relation: Knowledge transfer from full-modality to missing-modality models for brain-tumour segmentation on incomplete local scans.
papers.limitations: Training cost of many dedicated models.
papers.methodologyDetail: ACN trains, for each pattern of missing MRI sequences, a model that learns from a 'teacher' path seeing all sequences. Both paths share a U-Net backbone (from the BraTS 2018 winner, 160x192x128 patches, Adam 1e-4); adversarial discriminators push the missing-modality path's features and uncertainty maps to resemble the full-modality path, and a consistency loss passes knowledge between them. Across all 15 combinations on BraTS 2018, it clearly beat HeMIS and U-HVED, especially with only one or two sequences, and showed which missing sequences hurt which tumour regions most. For our PhD this informs both model choice and escalation rules: a scan without contrast T1 should lower confidence in enhancing-tumour and core outputs.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper; BraTS 2018 with all missing-modality combinations.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2018 multimodal MRI (T1, T1ce, T2, FLAIR).
papers.preprocessing: Settings of the BraTS 2018 winner; input patch 160x192x128.
papers.modelDetails: Two paths (full modality / missing modality) sharing the same U-Net backbone; discriminators D_en (entropy maps) and D_kn (knowledge) for adversarial alignment; co-training with consistency.
papers.training: Batch size 1, Adam, initial learning rate 1e-4 with progressive decay; PyTorch on V100.
papers.evaluation: Dice for ET, TC, WT across all 15 modality combinations.
papers.baselines: HeMIS, U-HVED.
papers.results: ACN outperformed both baselines in all 15 combinations; missing T1ce caused large drops in ET and TC, missing FLAIR a large drop in WT; baselines reached only ~10-20% Dice on ET/TC in hard settings while ACN remained much higher (Table 1).
papers.statistics: Mean Dice per combination.

papers.title: Cross-Modal Distillation to Improve MRI-Based Brain Tumor Segmentation With Missing MRI Sequences
papers.authors: Rahimpour M, Bertels J, Radwan A, et al.
papers.aim: To let a brain tumour segmentation model trained with full multi-sequence MRI work well when only a T1-weighted scan is available at inference.
papers.method: Cross-modal distillation: a teacher CNN trained with richer sequences (FLAIR for whole tumour, T1ce for tumour core) transfers knowledge to a T1w-only student via knowledge distillation (output level) and feature distillation; pre-trained on BraTS 2018 then transfer-learned to an in-house dataset.
papers.result: On the in-house dataset, distillation reached average Dice 79.04% (whole tumour) and 69.39% (tumour core) using only T1w at inference, versus 73.60% and 62.62% for a T1w-only U-Net; both KD and FD gave statistically significant gains; BraTS pre-training plus transfer learning improved all models.
papers.tools: U-Net CNNs, knowledge and feature distillation, transfer learning; compared with U-HeMIS, U-HVED and cGAN synthesis.
papers.gap: Only whole tumour and core; single missing-scenario (T1w-only) focus; one in-house cohort.
papers.relation: Distils multi-sequence knowledge into models that run on reduced MRI protocols typical of resource-limited hospitals.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; enhancing tumour not addressed.
papers.methodologyDetail: Hospitals do not always acquire every MRI sequence. Here a 'teacher' network that sees the most useful sequence for each tumour region (FLAIR for whole tumour, contrast T1 for the core) teaches a 'student' network that sees only a plain T1-weighted scan, by matching its outputs and internal features. The models were first trained on BraTS 2018 and then adapted to an in-house Belgian dataset. With only T1-weighted input at test time, the student reached Dice 79% for whole tumour and 69% for the core, compared with 74% and 63% for a network trained on T1-weighted scans alone. For our PhD it shows how knowledge from complete public datasets can be distilled into a model that works with the limited sequences available in some Sri Lankan hospitals.
papers.studyDesign: Method development with public and in-house evaluation.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2018 (multi-sequence) and an in-house glioma dataset (UZ Leuven) with multi-sequence MRI for training and T1w-only inference.
papers.preprocessing: Co-registration, skull stripping, resampling and normalisation; BraTS-style labels.
papers.modelDetails: Teacher U-Net on FLAIR (whole tumour) or T1ce (core); student U-Net on T1w; knowledge distillation (soft outputs) and feature distillation (intermediate features).
papers.training: Training until validation Dice plateaued (stopped when no improvement over 300 epochs); BraTS pre-training then transfer learning on in-house data.
papers.evaluation: Dice score for whole tumour and tumour core with significance tests.
papers.baselines: Single-sequence U-Net (T1w only); U-Net with early fusion of T1w and T2w; U-HeMIS; U-HVED; cGAN-based FLAIR synthesis.
papers.results: WT 79.04% and TC 69.39% (distillation) vs 73.60% and 62.62% (T1w-only U-Net); significant improvements for KD and FD.
papers.statistics: Statistical significance testing between models (p<0.05).

papers.title: BrainSegFounder: Towards 3D Foundation Models for Neuroimage Segmentation
papers.authors: Cox J, Liu P, Stolte SE, et al.
papers.aim: To build a 3D brain MRI foundation model that needs few labels for tumour and lesion segmentation.
papers.method: Two-stage self-supervised pre-training of a Swin UNETR-style transformer (41,400 healthy UK Biobank brains, then disease data), followed by fine-tuning.
papers.result: Beat previous challenge-winning fully supervised solutions on BraTS and ATLAS v2.0; larger models and more pre-training data improved results.
papers.tools: Swin UNETR / ViT, MONAI-style 3D pipeline, multi-GPU pre-training.
papers.gap: Pre-training data mainly from one high-income cohort (UK Biobank); heavy compute.
papers.relation: Self-supervised 3D neuroimaging foundation model that fine-tunes to brain-tumour segmentation with few labels.
papers.limitations: Large compute cost; healthy-brain pre-training cohort may not match low-resource scanner quality.
papers.methodologyDetail: BrainSegFounder builds a 3D foundation model for brain MRI segmentation in two self-supervised stages. First, a transformer encoder learns what normal brains look like from about 41,400 UK Biobank participants, using tasks such as filling in masked regions, predicting rotations and contrastive learning, without any labels. Second, the same tasks are run on disease datasets (BraTS tumours, ATLAS stroke) so the model learns lesion shapes and locations. Only then is it fine-tuned with labels for segmentation. It outperformed earlier challenge winners trained only with supervision, and bigger models and more healthy-brain data helped further. For our PhD this supports pre-training on large unlabelled brain MRI collections (including Sri Lankan routine scans) before fine-tuning on the few labelled tumour cases.
papers.studyDesign: 3D foundation model development via two-stage self-supervised pre-training, evaluated by fine-tuning on brain tumour and stroke lesion segmentation.
papers.datasets: Stage 1 pre-training: UK Biobank brain MRI of 41,400 generally healthy participants (T1w, T2-FLAIR; 82,800 images). Stage 2 and fine-tuning: BraTS (1,251 subjects, T1w, T1-ce, T2w, T2-FLAIR; 5,004 images) and ATLAS v2.0 stroke lesions (655 subjects, T1).
papers.preprocessing: Standard neuroimaging preprocessing per dataset; random 3D patches for self-supervised tasks.
papers.modelDetails: Swin UNETR-type vision transformer encoder. Stage 1 learns normal anatomy (shapes and sizes of brain structures) with self-supervised proxy tasks (masked volume inpainting, rotation prediction, contrastive coding) on healthy brains; Stage 2 continues self-supervised training on disease data to learn lesion geometry and location; then supervised fine-tuning for segmentation.
papers.training: Large-scale multi-GPU pre-training (encoder settings in Table 2); fine-tuning with cross-validation on BraTS and ATLAS; models scaled in size and pre-training data.
papers.evaluation: Dice and HD95 for BraTS regions; for ATLAS, Dice, lesion count difference and lesion-wise F1 (3D connected components).
papers.baselines: Previous challenge-winning fully supervised solutions, Swin UNETR with and without single-stage pre-training, nnU-Net.
papers.results: BrainSegFounder surpassed previous winning fully supervised solutions on BraTS and ATLAS; performance grew with model size and with the amount of healthy-brain pre-training data (detailed tables in paper).
papers.statistics: Cross-validation means.

papers.title: MedSAM2: Segment Anything in 3D Medical Images and Videos
papers.authors: Ma J, Yang Z, Kim S, et al.
papers.aim: To create a promptable 3D and video medical segmentation model and speed up large-scale annotation.
papers.method: Fine-tuned SAM2 on 455,000+ 3D image-mask pairs and 76,000 video frames; box or point prompts propagate across slices; human-in-the-loop annotation studies.
papers.result: Outperformed previous models across organs, lesions and modalities; cut manual annotation cost by more than 85% in studies covering 5,000 CT lesions, 3,984 liver MRI lesions and 251,550 echo frames.
papers.tools: SAM2 architecture, PyTorch, 3D Slicer plug-in, web and cloud deployment.
papers.gap: Still needs a human prompt; not designed to give calibrated confidence.
papers.relation: Promptable 3D foundation segmentation model that enables label-efficient, clinician-in-the-loop tumour delineation and volume reconstruction.
papers.limitations: Prompt-dependent; performance on rare or unseen pathologies not guaranteed.
papers.methodologyDetail: MedSAM2 extends the 2D MedSAM idea to 3D scans and videos by fine-tuning Meta's SAM2, whose memory module tracks an object across frames; a 3D scan is treated like a video of slices, so a box or point on one slice is propagated through the whole volume. It was fine-tuned on more than 455,000 3D CT, PET and MRI image-mask pairs and 76,000 ultrasound and endoscopy frames, then compared with SAM2.1 and earlier medical models on many organs and lesions. In large annotation studies (5,000 CT lesions, about 4,000 liver MRI lesions, 250,000 echo frames), using MedSAM2 in a human-in-the-loop loop cut manual annotation effort by over 85%. For our PhD it is a practical tool to speed up creating labelled Sri Lankan tumour masks (clinician gives a box, MedSAM2 propagates, clinician corrects) and a candidate for interactive segmentation in surgical planning.
papers.studyDesign: Foundation model development (fine-tuning SAM2) with benchmark evaluation and large human-in-the-loop annotation user studies.
papers.datasets: Over 455,000 3D image-mask pairs (363,161 CT, 14,818 PET, 77,154 MRI) and 76,000 annotated video frames (19,232 ultrasound, 56,462 endoscopy). User studies: 5,000 CT lesions, 3,984 liver MRI lesions and 251,550 echocardiogram video frames.
papers.preprocessing: 3D volumes treated as slice sequences (video-like) for the SAM2 memory architecture; intensity normalisation per modality.
papers.modelDetails: MedSAM2 adopts the SAM2 architecture (image encoder, memory attention across slices/frames, prompt encoder, mask decoder) initialised from pre-trained SAM2 weights and fine-tuned on medical data; prompts (box or point) on one slice propagate through the 3D volume or video.
papers.training: Fine-tuning from SAM2.1 weights (SAM2 itself was trained on 256 A100 GPUs); details in methods.
papers.evaluation: Dice similarity coefficient (median, with statistical comparisons) across organs, lesions and modalities; annotation time savings in user studies.
papers.baselines: SAM2.1 variants (tiny to large), earlier medical SAM models (MedSAM, etc.).
papers.results: MedSAM2 outperformed previous models across organs, lesions and modalities (SAM2.1 sizes showed no significant differences among themselves); human-in-the-loop annotation with MedSAM2 reduced manual effort by more than 85%. Integrated into common platforms (3D Slicer, web/cloud).
papers.statistics: Median DSC with significance testing (p-values) between models.

papers.title: TransMIL: Transformer based Correlated Multiple Instance Learning for Whole Slide Image Classification
papers.authors: Shao Z, Bian H, Chen Y, et al.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.aim: To improve weakly supervised whole-slide image classification by modelling correlations between patches.
papers.method: TransMIL: Transformer layers over CNN patch features with a Pyramid Position Encoding Generator and a class token.
papers.result: Test AUC 93.09% on CAMELYON16, 96.03% on TCGA-NSCLC and 98.82% on TCGA-RCC, above ABMIL (0.876) and CLAM-SB (0.881) on CAMELYON16.
papers.tools: PyTorch, ResNet50 features, Nystrom attention.
papers.gap: Evaluated on three public datasets only; no calibration or uncertainty analysis.
papers.relation: Weakly supervised slide-level classification needing only slide labels, suited to biopsy-slide analysis with limited annotation.
papers.limitations: Relies on frozen ImageNet features; small datasets.
papers.methodologyDetail: Earlier MIL methods treat the patches of a slide as independent. TransMIL instead lets patches 'talk to each other': patch features from a pre-trained CNN form a sequence, Transformer layers model relations among them, and a pyramid position-encoding module (convolutions of several sizes on the patch grid) injects spatial layout; a class token produces the slide-level diagnosis. On CAMELYON16 metastasis detection it reached AUC 0.931 versus 0.876-0.881 for ABMIL and CLAM, and 0.960 and 0.988 on lung and kidney subtyping, converging faster. For our PhD TransMIL is an alternative to CLAM for the biopsy-slide agent, especially when tissue architecture across the slide matters for tumour typing and grading.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with experiments on three computational pathology datasets.
papers.datasets: CAMELYON16 (breast lymph-node metastasis, binary, unbalanced), TCGA-NSCLC (lung adenocarcinoma vs squamous), TCGA-RCC (3 renal cell carcinoma subtypes).
papers.preprocessing: WSIs tiled into patches; patch features from a pre-trained CNN (ResNet50) as instances.
papers.modelDetails: Correlated MIL framework (instances are not i.i.d.); TransMIL: Transformer layers over patch features to model morphological and spatial correlation, with a Pyramid Position Encoding Generator (PPEG: multi-size convolutions on the reshaped token grid) for position information; class token for slide prediction.
papers.training: Standard training with Lookahead/RAdam-type optimiser (details in paper); about 2.67M parameters.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy and AUC on test sets; ablation of positional encoding; attention visualisation.
papers.baselines: Mean pooling, max pooling, ABMIL, PT-MTA, MIL-RNN, DSMIL, CLAM-SB, CLAM-MB.
papers.results: Test AUC: CAMELYON16 93.09% (accuracy about 88%), TCGA-NSCLC 96.03%, TCGA-RCC 98.82%. Baselines e.g. CAMELYON16 AUC ABMIL 0.8760, CLAM-SB 0.8809, max pooling 0.8569. PPEG raised CAMELYON16 AUC from 0.8416 (no position encoding) to 0.9309.
papers.statistics: Mean over runs; faster convergence reported.

papers.title: Scaling Vision Transformers to Gigapixel Images via Hierarchical Self-Supervised Learning
papers.authors: Chen RJ, Chen C, Li Y, et al.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
papers.aim: To learn hierarchical self-supervised representations of gigapixel pathology slides.
papers.method: Hierarchical Image Pyramid Transformer: three stacked ViTs (cell, tissue, slide levels), lower two pre-trained with DINO on 10,678 TCGA slides.
papers.result: Outperformed weakly supervised MIL methods on cancer subtyping and survival across 9 tasks in 10-fold cross-validation.
papers.tools: ViT, DINO, PyTorch, TCGA data.
papers.gap: Pre-training only on TCGA; heavy compute; no calibration analysis.
papers.relation: Hierarchical self-supervised WSI representations that reduce label needs for histopathology classification and grading.
papers.limitations: Large compute; TCGA staining and scanner bias.
papers.methodologyDetail: Whole-slide images are enormous (up to 150,000 pixels wide) and naturally hierarchical: cells within patches, patches within tissue regions, regions within the slide. HIPT mirrors this with three stacked vision transformers. The lowest one sees 16-pixel tokens inside 256-pixel patches; the middle one treats 256-pixel patches as tokens inside 4,096-pixel regions; both are pre-trained without labels using DINO on about 10,700 TCGA slides from 33 cancer types (100 million patches). The top transformer combines region embeddings for the slide-level task using only slide labels. Across 9 tasks, including subtyping and survival, it beat CLAM, TransMIL and other MIL methods in 10-fold cross-validation. For our PhD hierarchical self-supervised pathology encoders (HIPT, UNI) are candidates for the biopsy-slide agent where labelled Sri Lankan slides are few.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper: hierarchical self-supervised pre-training on gigapixel WSIs, evaluated on 9 slide-level tasks.
papers.datasets: Pre-training: 10,678 formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded H&E diagnostic WSIs from 33 cancer types in TCGA, giving 408,218 regions of 4096x4096 and 104 million patches of 256x256. Evaluation: cancer subtyping (e.g. BRCA, NSCLC, RCC) and survival prediction tasks on TCGA cohorts.
papers.preprocessing: Tissue segmentation; extraction of 4096x4096 regions and 256x256 patches at 20x magnification.
papers.modelDetails: Hierarchical Image Pyramid Transformer (HIPT): three-level ViT stack - ViT_256-16 (16x16 tokens within 256x256 patches, cell level), ViT_4096-256 (256x256 tokens within 4096x4096 regions, tissue level), ViT_WSI-4096 (regions within the slide). The first two levels are pre-trained with DINO self-supervised learning; the slide-level transformer is trained with weak slide labels.
papers.training: DINO pre-training of the two lower levels; 10-fold cross-validation for slide-level tasks.
papers.evaluation: 10-fold cross-validated AUC for slide classification (macro AUC for RCC); c-Index for survival; KNN evaluation of pre-extracted embeddings.
papers.baselines: ABMIL, DeepAttnMISL, CLAM, DS-MIL, GCN-MIL, TransMIL; ImageNet ResNet-50 embeddings.
papers.results: HIPT with hierarchical pre-training outperformed current weakly-supervised methods for cancer subtyping and survival prediction; self-supervised ViT embeddings beat ImageNet ResNet-50 in KNN evaluation (values in Tables 1-2).
papers.statistics: 10-fold cross-validation means and SD.

papers.title: A visual-language foundation model for computational pathology
papers.authors: Lu MY, Chen B, Williamson DFK, et al.
papers.aim: To build a visual-language foundation model for pathology that works across many tasks with little or no task-specific training data.
papers.method: CONCH: iBOT-pretrained ViT-B image encoder plus a text encoder and multimodal decoder (CoCa-style), trained with contrastive and captioning losses on 1.17 million histopathology image-caption pairs.
papers.result: State of the art on 13 benchmarks; zero-shot accuracy 90.0% for NSCLC subtyping, 89.3% for RCC subtyping and 84.0% for BRCA subtyping, where PLIP and BiomedCLIP were near chance (50.7-55.3%).
papers.tools: ViT-B/16, GPT-style text model, PyTorch, 8 NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs.
papers.gap: Captions mainly from English-language education and PubMed sources; rare tumours and brain tumours less covered.
papers.relation: CONCH pathology foundation model supports few-shot and zero-shot slide classification, relevant to small local biopsy cohorts.
papers.limitations: Zero-shot performance falls on harder, fine-grained tasks; heavy pre-training compute.
papers.methodologyDetail: CONCH learns from pathology images and the text that describes them. The team mined figures and captions from PubMed Central and education material, used detectors and a fine-tuned language model to split multi-panel figures and captions, and kept 1.17 million human image-caption pairs. A ViT-Base image encoder (first self-supervised with iBOT) and a text encoder were trained together for 40 epochs on 8 A100 GPUs so that matching images and texts lie close in embedding space, with an extra decoder learning to write captions. Without any task-specific training, simple text prompts such as 'lung adenocarcinoma' classified whole slides with 90% accuracy for lung and 89% for kidney cancer subtypes, far above earlier models. For our PhD CONCH is a strong backbone for a data-efficient pathology agent and for producing text-grounded explanations.
papers.studyDesign: Foundation model development and benchmarking on 13 public and in-house tasks (classification, segmentation, captioning, retrieval).
papers.datasets: Pre-training: 1.79 million cleaned image-text pairs from PubMed Central open access and in-house educational material, filtered to 1.17 million human-only pairs; unimodal pre-training of the image encoder with iBOT on in-house unlabelled patches. Evaluation: TCGA NSCLC, TCGA RCC, TCGA BRCA, TCGA LUAD, CRC100k, WSSS4LUAD, SICAP, DHMC LUAD and others.
papers.preprocessing: Automatic pipeline: object detection to find histology images in figures, a fine-tuned GPT-style model to split captions, a CLIP model to match sub-images and sub-captions; images resized to 448x448 px.
papers.modelDetails: Image encoder ViT-Base (12 layers, 12 heads, embedding 768, 16x16 tokens) with two attentional poolers; text encoder and multimodal decoder; contrastive alignment plus caption generation objective.
papers.training: 40 epochs on 8 NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs, local batch 48 per GPU, effective global batch 1,536 via gradient accumulation; hyperparameters in Extended Data Table 29.
papers.evaluation: Zero-shot classification (balanced accuracy; Cohen's kappa and quadratic weighted kappa for LUAD patterns and Gleason grading), supervised linear probing, few-shot, segmentation Dice, image-text retrieval recall.
papers.baselines: PLIP, BiomedCLIP, OpenAI CLIP, ImageNet ResNet50, CTransPath.
papers.results: Zero-shot slide-level accuracy: NSCLC 90.0%, RCC 89.3% (11.3% and 8.9% above PLIP, p<0.01), BRCA 84.0% vs 50.7-55.3% for other models; best or comparable results on all 13 tasks.
papers.statistics: Two-sided paired permutation tests; bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.

papers.title: Neuropathologist-level integrated classification of adult-type diffuse gliomas using deep learning from whole-slide pathological images
papers.authors: Wang W, Zhao Y, Teng L, et al.
papers.aim: To classify adult-type diffuse gliomas into WHO 2021 integrated types and grades directly from routine H&E whole-slide images.
papers.method: Patch clustering (K-means on ResNet-50 features, 9 clusters) to select informative patches, a patch-level CNN classifier and a patient-level aggregation, developed with cross-validation and tested on internal and two external cohorts.
papers.result: AUCs above 0.90 for all major types: six-category task AUCs 0.904-0.995 across cohorts; three-type task 0.938-0.983; IDH-mutant A2-3 vs IDH-wildtype glioblastoma 0.935-0.984.
papers.tools: ResNet-50, K-means, Python 3.6.1; code on Code Ocean (doi 10.24433/CO.1134119.v1).
papers.gap: Chinese cohorts only; no uncertainty estimation or deferral to pathologists.
papers.relation: Deep learning on glioma whole-slide images for WHO CNS5 integrated classification, directly matching biopsy-slide analysis and grading.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; molecular-only categories can still be confused; scanner and staining differences.
papers.methodologyDetail: Glioma diagnosis under WHO 2021 needs both histology and molecular tests, which are expensive. This study trained a model to predict the integrated diagnosis from H&E slides alone. Slides were cut into 256-pixel patches; a ResNet-50 extracted features and K-means grouped patches into nine clusters, of which the three most informative clusters were kept. A patch classifier was trained on these and its predictions combined per patient, using five-fold cross-validation on 1,702 patients with early stopping. On an internal test set and two external hospitals (922 patients total) AUCs were all above 0.90 for the six type-grade categories and for genotype groups that look similar under the microscope. For our PhD it is evidence that a pathology agent can estimate molecular-informed glioma type in low-resource settings, but it must be paired with calibrated confidence and escalation for uncertain cases.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multicentre diagnostic study with training, validation, internal test and two external test cohorts.
papers.datasets: 2,624 patients: training 1,362 and validation 340 (FAHZZU), internal test 289 (FAHZZU), external test 1 305 (HPPH), external test 2 328 (XHCMU); labels from WHO 2021 integrated diagnosis using IDH, 1p/19q, CDKN2A, TERT, EGFR, chromosome 7/10 status.
papers.preprocessing: Tissue patches resized to 256x256; patch features (2048-d) from a ResNet-50 trained on six categories; K-means with silhouette coefficient chose 9 clusters; clusters 2, 5 and 7 (275,741 training patches) kept as most informative.
papers.modelDetails: Patch-level CNN on selected clusters followed by a patient-level classifier aggregating patch predictions; six categories (A2, A3, A4, O2, O3, GBM).
papers.training: Five-fold cross-validation; minimum 50 and maximum 150 epochs; model with lowest average validation loss over 10 consecutive epochs saved; best fold (fold 5) chosen.
papers.evaluation: AUC, ROC and PR curves for task 1 (six categories), task 2 (three types), tasks 3-4 (molecular subgroups with shared histology); comparison with neuropathologists.
papers.baselines: Classical MIL, attention MIL (AMIL), CLAM, all-patch classifier.
papers.results: Task 1 AUCs: internal validation 0.953-0.995, internal test 0.932-0.994, external 1 0.923-0.987, external 2 0.904-0.952. Task 2 AUCs 0.938-0.983. Baselines ranged 0.793-0.997 on task 1; AMIL and CLAM gave no significant gain over classical MIL.
papers.statistics: p<0.05 significance; ROC comparisons across cohorts.

papers.title: Mutual Contrastive Low-rank Learning to Disentangle Whole Slide Image Representations for Glioma Grading
papers.authors: Zhang L, Wei Y, Fu Y, Price S, Schonlieb CB, Li C
papers.aim: To improve glioma grading by jointly learning from frozen and FFPE whole-slide images of the same patient.
papers.method: Mutual contrastive low-rank learning (MCL): two CNNs trained mutually on FFPE and frozen sections with a normalised modality contrastive loss and a low-rank loss, then used as feature extractors for MIL models.
papers.result: Patient-level accuracy 0.76 on FFPE and 0.74 on frozen sections, versus 0.71 and 0.70 for single-modality training; MCL features also improved A-MIL, TransMIL and CLAM.
papers.tools: CNN backbones, Adam, PyTorch, TCGA GBM and LGG slides.
papers.gap: Only 499 TCGA patients; three-grade task under the older WHO scheme.
papers.relation: Contrastive WSI representation learning for glioma grading from histopathology with limited labels.
papers.limitations: Modest absolute accuracy; requires paired FFPE and frozen slides for training.
papers.methodologyDetail: Brain tumour slides come in two forms: permanent FFPE sections (high quality, slow) and frozen sections (fast, used during surgery, lower quality). MCL trains two CNNs side by side, one on each form from the same patients, so they learn from each other. A contrastive loss pulls together information that both forms share and keeps their complementary parts, and a low-rank loss makes same-grade patients look similar and different grades look different. Trained for 10 epochs on 499 TCGA glioma patients, MCL raised patient-level grading accuracy to 0.76 (FFPE) and 0.74 (frozen) from about 0.70 with single-form training, and improved the features used by A-MIL, TransMIL and CLAM. For our PhD this shows cross-modality training can make a pathology agent more robust to the variable slide quality of resource-limited labs.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with retrospective experiments on TCGA.
papers.datasets: TCGA GBM and LGG: 499 patients (108 grade II, 94 grade III, 297 grade IV) with both FFPE and frozen H&E sections.
papers.preprocessing: Low-resolution WSI to HSV, Otsu thresholding on saturation to find tissue; patch tiling; input 224x224x3.
papers.modelDetails: Two-branch mutual learning of CNNs; NMC-loss disentangles complementary FFPE and frozen representations of the same patient; low-rank loss reduces intra-class variance and enlarges inter-class margin; Taylor softmax with t=3.
papers.training: 10 epochs, Adam, cosine annealing warm restarts, initial learning rate 1.6e-4.
papers.evaluation: Patient-level accuracy, precision, recall for 3-grade classification on FFPE and frozen sets.
papers.baselines: Single-modality training, mixed-modality training, ImageNet features with A-MIL, TransMIL, CLAM; other contrastive losses.
papers.results: MCL: FFPE accuracy 0.76, precision 0.77, recall 0.76; frozen accuracy 0.74, precision 0.73, recall 0.74. Single training 0.71/0.70; mixed 0.70/0.68; ImageNet + CLAM 0.71/0.69.
papers.statistics: Not reported (single split results).

papers.title: MGMT promoter methylation status prediction using MRI scans? An extensive experimental evaluation of deep learning models
papers.authors: Saeed N, Ridzuan M, Alasmawi H, Sobirov I, Yaqub M
papers.aim: To test whether deep learning can really predict glioblastoma MGMT promoter methylation from MRI.
papers.method: Extensive evaluation of ResNets, DenseNets, EfficientNets, ViT and Swin with ImageNet and SimCLR pre-training, modality fusion and ROI crops, using 5-fold cross-validation, plus Grad-CAM, occlusion, feature visualisation and loss landscapes.
papers.result: All models stayed near chance (AUC about 0.49-0.63; e.g. ViT 0.549, Swin 0.570, EfficientNet-b1 0.631); loss stayed near 0.69 (random), while the same pipeline reached AUC 0.856 on NoduleMNIST3D.
papers.tools: MONAI, PyTorch, AdamW, NVIDIA RTX A6000.
papers.gap: Shows MRI-only MGMT prediction is unreliable; calls for external cohort validation.
papers.relation: Rigorously tests whether MRI deep learning can predict a key molecular marker, informing realistic expectations for imaging-marker fusion.
papers.limitations: Single public dataset (RSNA-MICCAI BraTS 2021); negative result may depend on label quality.
papers.methodologyDetail: This paper asks a blunt question: can deep learning read MGMT methylation, a key chemotherapy marker for glioblastoma, from MRI? Using 585 patients from the RSNA-MICCAI BraTS 2021 challenge, the authors trained many 3D CNNs and transformers with different MRI sequences, ImageNet or self-supervised pre-training, fusion schemes and tumour crops, all with 5-fold cross-validation. Every model stayed close to chance (AUC about 0.5-0.63), and the training loss stayed at about 0.69, the value of random guessing; saliency maps did not focus on tumour. As a check, the same pipeline worked well on lung nodule data (AUC 0.856). For our PhD this is a clear example of where the system must abstain: MGMT status should be sent for molecular testing, not predicted from imaging.
papers.studyDesign: Extensive experimental (negative-result) evaluation with 5-fold cross-validation and interpretability analysis.
papers.datasets: RSNA-MICCAI BraTS 2021 classification task: 585 glioblastoma patients with T1w, T1wCE, T2w, FLAIR and MGMT labels; also BraTS Task 1 segmentation-preprocessed data; NoduleMNIST3D as a positive control.
papers.preprocessing: Raw DICOM (Task 2) and skull-stripped, co-registered Task 1 data; resizing to 128 or 32 for ROI crops; single or multi-modality inputs.
papers.modelDetails: 3D ResNet-10/18/50, DenseNet-121, EfficientNet-b0/b1/b3, ViT, Swin ViT; ensembles with addition or stacking fusion; ROI-based custom ResNet.
papers.training: AdamW; binary cross-entropy; ImageNet weights or SimCLR self-supervised pre-training on all four modalities; single NVIDIA RTX A6000.
papers.evaluation: AUC with 5-fold cross-validation and 20% held-out set; Grad-CAM, occlusion sensitivity, feature maps, loss landscapes.
papers.baselines: Prior published MGMT models (e.g. challenge winner AUC 0.62; others 0.698).
papers.results: Cross-validated mean AUCs: EfficientNet-b1 0.631, EfficientNet-b3 0.592, Swin 0.570, ViT 0.549; pre-training gave 0.58-0.60; fusion 0.49-0.63; ROI models 0.53-0.55. NoduleMNIST3D control AUC 0.856.
papers.statistics: Mean and variance across 5 folds.

papers.title: An international study presenting a federated learning AI platform for pediatric brain tumors
papers.authors: Lee EH, Han M, Wright J, Kuwabara M, Mevorach J, et al.
papers.aim: To build and test a federated learning platform for paediatric posterior fossa tumour classification and segmentation across many international hospitals.
papers.method: FL-PedBrain: joint classification and segmentation network trained by federated learning across 19 sites (16 in-network, 3 external) on T2-weighted MRI, with federated warm-up, compared with centralised data sharing (CDS).
papers.result: Less than 1.5% drop in classification and 3% drop in segmentation versus centralised training; F1 0.856 (FL) vs 0.877 (CDS), above a prior pooled pilot (0.800); FL raised segmentation by 20-30% at three out-of-network sites.
papers.tools: Federated learning on cloud (AWS collaborators), PyTorch/TensorFlow, T2-MRI.
papers.gap: T2 only; four tumour types; logistical overhead of FL deployment.
papers.relation: Shows real-world multi-hospital federated training for brain tumour MRI on small, rare-disease cohorts, directly mirroring the federated Sri Lankan hospital setting.
papers.limitations: Strong class imbalance across sites; communication and synchronisation costs.
papers.methodologyDetail: Childhood brain tumours are rare, so each hospital has too few cases. FL-PedBrain trained one model across 19 hospitals in several countries without moving patient scans: each site trained locally on its T2 MRI and only model weights were shared and averaged. The model both classified four tumour types and outlined the tumour.
