With 1,468 children, federated training was within 1.5% of pooling all data centrally for classification and 3% for segmentation, and it improved segmentation at three outside hospitals by 20-30%. Starting with a 'warm-up' on the two largest centres made training up to 10 times faster. For our PhD it is the closest blueprint for federating brain tumour models across Sri Lankan hospitals with uneven case numbers.
papers.studyDesign: International retrospective multicentre study comparing federated and centralised training.
papers.datasets: 1,468 children (mean age 7.6 years; 48% female) with posterior fossa tumours from 19 institutions: 596 medulloblastoma, 210 ependymoma, 335 pilocytic astrocytoma, 327 DIPG; pre-treatment axial T2-weighted MRI.
papers.preprocessing: Tumour segmentation masks by experts; T2-MRI normalisation; exclusion of non-diagnostic scans.
papers.modelDetails: Joint tumour-type classification and tumour segmentation deep network trained with federated averaging; federated warm-up on the two largest centres first.
papers.training: Federated rounds across 16 in-network sites; warm-up on two largest sites; without warm-up training took up to 10 times longer.
papers.evaluation: F1 score (worst-class accuracy focus), per-class accuracy, Dice; external out-of-network testing at 3 sites; site-only models for comparison.
papers.baselines: Centralised data sharing (CDS), 16 independently trained site-specific models, prior pilot study.
papers.results: Classification F1 0.856 FL vs 0.877 CDS (no significant difference); segmentation DSC about 3% lower than CDS; site-only models were poor; FL improved external-site segmentation by 20-30%; warm-up on two centres alone gave >70% accuracy and DSC except for ependymoma.
papers.statistics: Comparison of FL and CDS without statistically discernible difference; per-example Dice distributions.

papers.title: The federated tumor segmentation (FeTS) tool: an open-source solution to further solid tumor research
papers.authors: Pati S, Baid U, Edwards B, Sheller MJ, Foley P, et al.
papers.relation: Provides an open-source clinical tool for federated brain tumour segmentation that could be deployed across local hospitals.

papers.title: Federated benchmarking of medical artificial intelligence with MedPerf
papers.authors: Karargyris A, Umeton R, Sheller MJ, Aristizabal A, et al.
papers.aim: To provide an open platform for federated evaluation (benchmarking) of medical AI models on private data at many sites.
papers.method: MedPerf: a server that registers benchmarks, models, data and results, plus MLCube containers that carry data preparation, model and metric code to each data owner, who runs them locally and approves sharing of results only.
papers.result: Used in the MICCAI FeTS 2022 challenge to benchmark 41 models across 32 hospitals on six continents, and in pilot studies on brain tumour segmentation, pancreas segmentation and surgical phase recognition.
papers.tools: MLCube (Docker/Singularity), Python CLI, web server and database, Hugging Face Hub integration; supports cloud and on-premises.
papers.gap: Evaluation only (not training); sending models to sites carries its own risk; requires local IT effort.
papers.relation: Offers a privacy-preserving federated evaluation framework (piloted on brain tumour segmentation) for validating models on local hospital data without sharing it.
papers.limitations: Platform description rather than a controlled experiment; quantitative pilot results in supplementary material.
papers.methodologyDetail: MedPerf turns the usual approach around: instead of collecting hospital data into one place to test an AI model, the model travels to each hospital. A benchmark committee defines the task, a reference data-preparation step and the metrics; each step is packaged as an MLCube container. Hospitals register their data locally, run the containers on their own machines, look at the results and approve what is sent back to the MedPerf server. The platform was used in the FeTS 2022 brain tumour challenge to test 41 models at 32 hospitals in six continents, and in pilots on brain tumour and pancreas segmentation and surgical videos. For our PhD it offers a privacy-preserving way to measure how well, and how well-calibrated, our agents are at each Sri Lankan hospital.
papers.studyDesign: Platform design paper with real-world deployment (FeTS challenge) and three academic pilot studies.
papers.datasets: FeTS 2022 brain tumour MRI data held at 32 hospitals worldwide; pilot datasets for brain tumour segmentation, pancreas segmentation and surgical workflow video (public and private).
papers.preprocessing: Benchmark-specific data preparation MLCube that validates and converts local data to a common format before evaluation.
papers.modelDetails: Not a model; benchmark components: MedPerf server, client, MLCubes (data preparator, model, metrics).
papers.training: Not applicable (federated evaluation).
papers.evaluation: Model metrics defined by each benchmark (e.g. Dice and Hausdorff distance for FeTS); usability and scalability of the platform.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: 41 models evaluated across 32 sites in FeTS 2022; pilots ran successfully across institutions on brain, pancreas and surgical video tasks in cloud and on-premises setups.
papers.statistics: Not reported in main text.

papers.title: Swarm learning for decentralized artificial intelligence in cancer histopathology
papers.authors: Saldanha OL, Quirke P, West NP, James JA, Loughrey MB, et al.
papers.aim: To show that decentralised swarm learning can train pathology AI across hospitals without a central coordinator.
papers.method: Swarm learning (HPE, blockchain-coordinated peers) trained attention-free MLP classifiers on ResNet-18 tile features to predict BRAF mutation and MSI from colorectal cancer H&E slides at three physically separate sites; external validation in two UK cohorts.
papers.result: Weighted swarm model AUROC 0.7736 for BRAF, significantly above every local model and the merged model (p=0.0374); for MSI swarm models reached 0.8001 and 0.8151 vs 0.7884 (Epi700) and 0.7639 (TCGA) local models.
papers.tools: HPE Swarm Learning (Docker, SPIRE identity), ResNet-18, OpenCV, Python.
papers.gap: Only three training peers; weak-label biomarker tasks; no uncertainty estimation.
papers.relation: Demonstrates decentralised privacy-preserving training of whole-slide pathology models across centres, applicable to federated biopsy-slide analysis.
papers.limitations: With 200 or fewer patients per site the merged (central) model beat swarm models; proprietary HPE software.
papers.methodologyDetail: Swarm learning is a form of federated learning without a central server: each hospital trains the model on its own computer and the peers exchange and average weights through a blockchain-coordinated network, so no one party controls the model. Here three cohorts (Northern Ireland 661, Germany 2,448, USA 632 patients) each trained a classifier on ResNet-18 features from 150 colour-normalised tiles per slide to predict BRAF mutation and MSI in colorectal cancer. Tested on two independent UK cohorts, the swarm models beat every single-site model and were on par with, or better than, pooling all data (BRAF AUROC 0.774 vs merged model). When sites had very few patients (200 or fewer), central pooling was still better. For our PhD this supports a decentralised federation among Sri Lankan hospitals and shows the gain expected for smaller sites.
papers.studyDesign: Multicentre retrospective study comparing local, merged (centralised) and swarm learning models with external validation.
papers.datasets: Training: Epi700 (661 patients, Northern Ireland), DACHS (2,448 patients, Germany), TCGA (632 patients, USA). External test: QUASAR (UK; MSI 1,477, BRAF 1,774) and YCR BCIP (UK; MSI 805). Over 5,000 patients in total.
papers.preprocessing: Tessellation into 512 px tiles resized to 224 px, Macenko colour normalisation, removal of blurry tiles with Canny edge threshold (mean < 4), 150 random tiles per patient, class balancing by undersampling.
papers.modelDetails: ResNet-18 feature extractor (512-d per tile) with a fully connected classification network on patient-level labels; swarm learning merges weights among peers via blockchain-based coordination; basic and weighted (by cohort size) checkpoints.
papers.training: Each peer trains locally on its own server; weights synchronised at sync intervals; experiments repeated with random seeds.
papers.evaluation: AUROC on external cohorts with mean and SD over repeats; experiments with reduced patient numbers per site (down to 100-400).
papers.baselines: Local single-cohort models and a merged model trained on pooled data.
papers.results: BRAF: b-chkpt2 AUROC 0.7621, w-chkpt 0.7736 (better than local and merged models). MSI: swarm 0.8001 and 0.8151 vs Epi700 0.7884 and TCGA 0.7639. DACHS BRAF fell from 0.7339 to 0.6626 when patients were restricted; swarm models partly rescued small-site losses.
papers.statistics: Two-sided tests (P-values reported, e.g. P=0.0374 vs merged); mean +/- SD over repeated runs.
papers.availability: Code on GitHub (KatherLab swarm-learning-hpe); data from cohort owners on request.

papers.title: Gradient Matching Federated Domain Adaptation for Brain Image Classification
papers.authors: Zeng LL, Fan Z, Su J, Gan M, Peng L, Shen H, Hu D
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
papers.relation: Addresses site heterogeneity in federated brain MRI classification through federated domain adaptation, a core problem for multi-hospital local data.

papers.title: Integrated approach of federated learning with transfer learning for classification and diagnosis of brain tumor
papers.authors: Albalawi E, T R M, Thakur A, Kumar VV, Gupta M, et al.
papers.aim: To classify brain tumours on MRI with federated learning combined with transfer learning while keeping data private.
papers.method: Modified ImageNet-pretrained VGG16 (adjusted filters, extra dropout) trained with federated averaging across simulated clients on a 4-class MRI dataset.
papers.result: Overall accuracy 98%; precision 0.99 glioma, 0.95 meningioma, 1.00 no tumour, 0.98 pituitary.
papers.tools: VGG16, TensorFlow/Keras-style CNN, simulated federated clients.
papers.gap: Simulated clients split from one public 2D dataset; no real multi-hospital heterogeneity; no external test.
papers.relation: Combines transfer learning with federated training for brain tumour MRI classification, matching the data-efficient federated approach of O3.
papers.limitations: 2D slices, possible leakage and duplicates in the public dataset; communication overhead acknowledged but not measured on real networks.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors pooled 7,023 public 2D brain MRI images (figshare, SARTAJ, Br35H) into four classes and resized them to 224x224. They adapted an ImageNet-trained VGG16 with adjusted filters and extra dropout, split the data across simulated clients and trained with federated averaging, where each client trains locally and only weight updates are combined. The model reached 98% accuracy with per-class precision from 0.95 (meningioma) to 1.00 (no tumour). Because the clients were simulated from one public dataset and there was no external test, these numbers are likely optimistic. For our PhD it is a simple baseline for FL with transfer learning, but our evaluation must use real site splits, external testing and calibration.
papers.studyDesign: Experimental method paper with simulated federated clients.
papers.datasets: 7,023 brain MRI images in 4 classes (glioma, meningioma, no tumour, pituitary) combined from figshare, SARTAJ and Br35H; SARTAJ glioma images replaced by figshare images because of label concerns.
papers.preprocessing: Resize to 224x224; normalisation to VGG16 input range; augmentation.
papers.modelDetails: Modified VGG16 with ImageNet weights, tuned convolution filter sizes and added dropout layers; softmax over 4 classes; FedAvg aggregation of client updates.
papers.training: Batch training over epochs and federated rounds (exact values in paper tables); clients train locally and send weight updates to a server.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, confusion matrix on the held-out test split.
papers.baselines: Previously published CNN methods on the same public datasets.
papers.results: Accuracy 98%; per-class precision 0.99, 0.95, 1.00, 0.98 with similar recall and F1; outperformed compared methods.
papers.statistics: Not reported (single split).

papers.title: Stepwise Transfer Learning for Expert-level Pediatric Brain Tumor MRI Segmentation in a Limited Data Scenario
papers.authors: Boyd A, Ye Z, Prabhu SP, Tjong MC, Zha Y, et al.
papers.aim: To build expert-level paediatric low-grade glioma segmentation on T2 MRI when only small paediatric datasets exist.
papers.method: In-domain stepwise transfer learning with nnU-Net: train on adult BraTS 2021, fine-tune on paediatric data, then fine-tune again with the encoder or decoder frozen; external validation and blinded expert review (Likert ratings and Turing test).
papers.result: Best model (Transfer-Encoder) median Dice 0.877 vs 0.812 baseline (p<0.05); external test Dice 0.834 vs inter-expert 0.861 (p=0.13); AI segmentations acceptable in 80.2% vs 65.4% for experts; experts identified AI segmentations only 26% of the time.
papers.tools: nnU-Net (default settings, built-in ensembling), BraTS 2021, CBTN data.
papers.gap: T2-only; low-grade glioma only; small external set (60).
papers.relation: Shows clinically validated expert-level segmentation from very small datasets via stepwise transfer learning, a key data-efficient strategy.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; two US datasets; single sequence.
papers.methodologyDetail: Paediatric low-grade gliomas are rare, so there is too little data to train a segmentation model from scratch. The authors used nnU-Net in steps: first train on 1,251 adult glioma scans (BraTS 2021), then fine-tune on paediatric T2 MRI, then fine-tune once more while freezing either the encoder or decoder so fewer parameters change and the model overfits less. The encoder-frozen model reached median Dice 0.877 versus 0.812 for the plain model, matched inter-expert agreement on 60 external scans, and in blinded tests experts rated its outlines as acceptable more often than other experts' outlines (80% vs 65%) and could rarely tell they were AI-made. For our PhD this stepwise transfer recipe is a practical plan for adapting public brain tumour models to the small Sri Lankan dataset.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective development and external validation study with randomized, blinded clinical benchmarking.
papers.datasets: Children's Brain Tumor Network (CBTN) consortium (n=184) and a paediatric cancer centre (n=100) T2-weighted MRI of pLGG; external test n=60; clinical benchmark 100 scans with 300 expert segmentations; adult BraTS 2021 (1,251 scans) for pre-training.
papers.preprocessing: De-identified PACS exports; nnU-Net automatic preprocessing (resampling, normalisation); T2-weighted input chosen because many pLGGs do not enhance.
papers.modelDetails: nnU-Net 3D models: Scratch (paediatric only), BraTS (adult only), Transfer (adult then paediatric fine-tune), Transfer-Encoder and Transfer-Decoder (further fine-tune with decoder or encoder frozen).
papers.training: nnU-Net defaults; early stopping after 50 epochs without validation improvement, maximum 1,000 epochs; built-in ensembling.
papers.evaluation: Dice similarity coefficient (median, IQR); external validation; 10-point Likert acceptability ratings by three experts; Turing test.
papers.baselines: Model trained from scratch on paediatric data; adult BraTS model applied directly; inter-expert agreement.
papers.results: Transfer-Encoder Dice 0.877 [IQR 0.715-0.914] vs baseline 0.812 [0.559-0.888]; external Dice 0.834 [0.726-0.901] vs inter-expert 0.861 [0.795-0.905]; median Likert 9 vs 7 for experts; acceptability 80.2% vs 65.4%; Turing test accuracy 26%.
papers.statistics: Wilcoxon-type comparisons, p<0.05 significance; medians with IQR.

papers.title: Multi-class glioma segmentation on real-world data with missing MRI sequences: comparison of three deep learning algorithms
papers.authors: Pemberton HG, Wu J, Kommers I, Muller DMJ, Hu Y, et al.
papers.aim: To test how well three top BraTS segmentation models generalise to real-world multicentre clinical MRI with missing sequences.
papers.method: DeepMedic, nnU-Net and NVIDIA-net trained on BraTS 2021 plus clinical data from 12 hospitals with sparsified training (randomly dropping sequences); internal and external testing.
papers.result: All models' median Dice within or above human inter-rater range (0.74-0.85); nnU-Net best with Dice 0.86 internal and 0.93 external and lowest Hausdorff distances (10.07 and 13.87 mm), p<0.001; missing sequences did not significantly reduce performance.
papers.tools: DeepMedic, nnU-Net, NVIDIA-net (SegResNet), ANTs registration, SRI24 atlas, N4 bias correction.
papers.gap: Preoperative adult glioma only; no uncertainty output.
papers.relation: Evaluates glioma segmentation on real-world clinical scans with missing sequences, typical of low-resource hospital protocols.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; manual reference segmentations from different raters across sites.
papers.methodologyDetail: BraTS challenge models are trained on clean data where every patient has all four MRI sequences, but real hospital scans are often incomplete and of variable quality. This study retrained three leading BraTS models (DeepMedic, nnU-Net, NVIDIA-net) on BraTS 2021 plus 480 clinical glioma scans from 12 hospitals, using 'sparsified training' in which sequences are randomly dropped so the model learns to cope with missing inputs. After registration to an atlas and bias correction, all models reached Dice within the range of human agreement; nnU-Net was best (0.86 internal, 0.93 on an external set of 227 patients) and missing sequences did not significantly harm results. For our PhD this supports nnU-Net with sparsified training as the default segmentation agent for incomplete Sri Lankan MRI.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multicentre comparison of three algorithms with internal and external test sets.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2021 (1,251) plus PICTURE clinical data: 275 GBM and 205 LGG from 12 hospitals; split 80% train, 5% validation, 15% internal test; external test set 158 GBM and 69 LGG from other hospitals; some cases missing T1w, T2w or FLAIR.
papers.preprocessing: T1w, T2w and FLAIR rigidly registered to T1c; T1c affinely registered to SRI24 atlas; 1 mm isotropic resampling in one interpolation step (ANTs); N4 bias field correction; skull stripping.
papers.modelDetails: DeepMedic (multi-scale 3D CNN), nnU-Net (self-configuring U-Net), nv-Net (NVIDIA encoder-decoder with VAE branch); sparsified training replaces missing sequences with empty channels during training.
papers.training: Each model trained with its published default settings on the combined training set with sparsified inputs.
papers.evaluation: Dice similarity coefficient and Hausdorff distance for enhancing tumour, tumour core and whole tumour; subgroup analysis by missing sequence.
papers.baselines: Comparison among the three models; human inter-rater agreement (0.74-0.85).
papers.results: nnU-Net median DSC 0.86 (internal) and 0.93 (external), HD 10.07 and 13.87 mm, best for all classes (p<0.001); DeepMedic and nv-Net also within inter-rater range; no significant effect of missing sequences.
papers.statistics: Non-parametric tests with p<0.001 for model differences; medians with IQR.

papers.title: Generative Adversarial Networks to Synthesize Missing T1 and FLAIR MRI Sequences for Use in a Multisequence Brain Tumor Segmentation Model
papers.authors: Conte GM, Weston AD, Vogelsang DC, Philbrick KA, et al.
papers.relation: Uses sequence synthesis to make segmentation robust to incomplete MRI protocols common in resource-limited hospitals.

papers.title: Handling missing MRI sequences in deep learning segmentation of brain metastases: a multicenter study
papers.authors: Grovik E, Yi D, Iv M, Tong E, Nilsen LB, et al.
papers.aim: To segment brain metastases reliably when one of the MRI sequences used in training is missing at test time.
papers.method: Input-level dropout (ILD): a 2.5D network trained on four MRI sequences while randomly dropping whole sequences, so it learns all subsets; compared with DeepLab V3 on a multicentre test set missing one sequence.
papers.result: AUC 0.989 for both models (p=0.62); ILD had higher Dice (0.795 vs 0.774, p=0.017), higher IoU (0.561 vs 0.492, p<0.001) and fewer false positives (3.6 vs 7.0 per patient, p<0.001).
papers.tools: 2.5D DeepLab V3-based CNN with input-level dropout; Wilcoxon rank sum test.
papers.gap: Small test set (55); only one specific sequence missing in testing.
papers.relation: Multicentre validation of brain tumour segmentation robust to heterogeneous and missing inputs across sites.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; two centres; metastases rather than primary tumours.
papers.methodologyDetail: Hospitals do not always acquire the same MRI sequences. This study trained a 2.5D segmentation network for brain metastases on four sequences but randomly 'switched off' whole sequences during training (input-level dropout), so the network learned to work with any combination. Trained on 100 patients from Stanford and tested on 55 patients from Oslo whose scans lacked one of the four sequences, it matched DeepLab V3 in detection (AUC 0.989) but gave better outlines (Dice 0.795 vs 0.774) and half as many false positives (3.6 vs 7.0 per patient). For our PhD input-level dropout is an easy way to make the segmentation agent robust to missing sequences in Sri Lankan scans.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multicentre study (Stanford, USA and Oslo University Hospital, Norway).
papers.datasets: 165 patients with brain metastases: training 100, validation 10, test 55. Training sequences: pre- and post-gadolinium T1 3D fast spin echo, post-Gd T1 inversion-recovery prepped fast spoiled gradient echo, 3D FLAIR; test set lacked the IR-prepped series.
papers.preprocessing: Co-registration of sequences; 2.5D input stacks of neighbouring slices per sequence; ground truth by experienced neuroradiologists.
papers.modelDetails: 2.5D DeepLab V3-style segmentation network with an input-level dropout layer that zeroes all slices of a sequence together (never all four at once).
papers.training: Trained on the full set and all possible sequence subsets via input dropout; details in Methods.
papers.evaluation: Precision, recall, IoU, Dice, ROC AUC, false positives per patient with 10 mm3 lesion-size limit; Wilcoxon rank sum test.
papers.baselines: Standard DeepLab V3 trained on full inputs.
papers.statistics: Wilcoxon rank sum test; mean +/- SD.

papers.title: 2.5D and 3D segmentation of brain metastases with deep learning on multinational MRI data
papers.authors: Ottesen JA, Yi D, Tong E, Iv M, Latysheva A, et al.
papers.aim: To compare 2.5D and 3D deep learning segmentation of brain metastases on MRI from two countries with different protocols.
papers.method: HRNetV2-based 2.5D and 3D networks with mixup, input-level dropout and deep supervision, trained on Stanford data only and tested on Stanford and Oslo cohorts; nnU-Net as benchmark.
papers.result: Centre 1: 2.5D, 3D and nnU-Net detected 79%, 71% and 65% of metastases with 6.2, 3.2 and 1.7 false positives per patient; centre 2: 88%, 86% and 78% with 1.0, 0.4 and 0.1 false positives.
papers.tools: HRNetV2, nnU-Net, MONAI augmentation, AdamW, PyTorch.
papers.gap: Accuracy falls for very small metastases; two centres only.
papers.relation: Assesses generalisation of brain tumour detection and segmentation across multinational scanner heterogeneity.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; trained on one centre; small lesions remain hard.
papers.methodologyDetail: This study trained two versions of the high-resolution network HRNetV2 - one working on stacks of neighbouring slices (2.5D) and one on whole volumes (3D) - to find and outline brain metastases. Both were trained only on Stanford data, using mixup and input-level dropout so they cope with missing sequences, and tested on Stanford and on Oslo scans acquired with different protocols, with nnU-Net as a comparison. The 2.5D model found the most metastases (79% and 88%) but made more false alarms, while nnU-Net made the fewest false alarms but missed more lesions; the 3D model was in between. Small metastases remained the main weakness. For our PhD it shows that architecture choice moves the balance between missed lesions and false alarms, which our calibration and deferral rules must take into account.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multinational study with training at one centre and testing at two.
papers.datasets: Stanford cohort (training 100 patients, validation 10, plus test patients) and Oslo University Hospital cohort (external test); sequences 3D BRAVO/T1 pre- and post-contrast, 3D T1 CUBE/SPACE, 3D FLAIR.
papers.preprocessing: Skull stripping, co-registration, z-score standardisation of brain voxels (non-brain set to zero); input-level dropout of sequences (25%) so missing sequences are handled; metastasis slices weighted ten-fold in 2.5D sampling.
papers.modelDetails: 2.5D HRNetV2 for slice-wise segmentation and 3D HRNetV2 encoder with U-Net-like decoder; deep supervision; mixup augmentation (2.5D).
papers.training: 2.5D: 150 epochs of about 12,000 slices, AdamW lr 5e-4, 10-epoch warm-up then cosine annealing, weight decay 0.01, AMSGrad, batch 16. 3D: 1,000 epochs of 95 volumes, AdamW lr 5e-3, 50-epoch warm-up then cosine annealing, batch 2.
papers.evaluation: Dice score, lesion-wise detection rate, per-patient sensitivity and false positives per patient, by lesion size.
papers.baselines: nnU-Net; previously published models on the same cohorts.
papers.results: Centre 1: detection 79% / 71% / 65%, per-patient sensitivity 0.88 / 0.84 / 0.76, false positives 6.2 / 3.2 / 1.7 (2.5D / 3D / nnU-Net). Centre 2: 88% / 86% / 78%, sensitivity 0.92 / 0.91 / 0.85, false positives 1.0 / 0.4 / 0.1.
papers.statistics: Descriptive per-patient means.

papers.title: Development and validation of a deep-learning model for detecting brain metastases on 3D post-contrast MRI: a multi-center multi-reader evaluation study
papers.authors: Yin S, Luo X, Yang Y, Shao Y, Ma L, et al.
papers.aim: To develop and validate a deep learning system that detects brain metastases on 3D contrast T1 MRI and to measure how it helps radiologists.
papers.method: Multi-scale cascaded convolutional network trained on 950 patients; prospective internal and three external validation sets; multi-reader study of 6 radiologists reading with and without the system after a 3-week washout.
papers.result: Sensitivity 95.8% with 0.39 false positives per patient on test, 96.0% / 0.27 internal, 88.9-95.5% / 0.29-0.66 external; system sensitivity 93.2% vs 68.5-80.4% for unaided radiologists (p<0.001); aided readers reached 92.7-95.0% and reading time fell by 47% (trainees) and 32% (experts).
papers.tools: 3D cascaded CNN, SPSS 25.0.
papers.gap: Single sequence; Chinese hospitals only; excluded leptomeningeal disease and >50 metastases.
papers.relation: Provides a multi-reader clinician validation design for MRI tumour detection that informs the clinician-validation protocol.
papers.limitations: Within-patient correlation ignored; exclusions limit generalisability.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team trained a multi-scale cascaded CNN on contrast T1 MRI from 950 patients (573 with over 10,000 metastases, 377 without) to find brain metastases of all sizes. They then tested it prospectively on 300 new patients from their own and three other hospitals. The system found about 96% of metastases internally and 89-96% externally with fewer than one false alarm per patient. Six radiologists read the same 300 scans with and without the system, separated by three weeks: alone they found 69-80% of lesions; with the system 93-95%, and they read 32-47% faster. For our PhD it is a clear example of the 'AI as second reader' workflow and of the multi-reader evaluation design we can adapt for clinician evaluation in O4.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective development with prospective multicentre validation and a multi-reader multi-case study.
papers.datasets: Development: 573 consecutive patients with newly diagnosed brain metastases (10,448 lesions) and 377 without. Validation (n=300): internal 46 patients with 349 lesions and 44 controls; three external hospitals 102 patients with 717 lesions and 108 controls.
papers.preprocessing: 3D contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images; exclusions for prior brain surgery, primary brain tumour, artefacts, leptomeningeal disease and more than 50 metastases; ground truth by 3 experts from 3 hospitals.
papers.modelDetails: Multi-scale cascaded convolutional network for candidate detection and false-positive reduction across lesion sizes.
papers.training: Trained on the development set with a held-out test set (details in supplementary material).
papers.evaluation: Lesion-based sensitivity, false positives per patient, sensitivity by lesion size; reader sensitivity, patient-level AUC and reading time with and without the system.
papers.baselines: Three trainees and three experienced radiologists reading without AI.
papers.results: Test 95.8% / 0.39 FP; internal 96.0% / 0.27 FP; external 88.9-95.5% / 0.29-0.66 FP. System 93.2% (95% CI 91.6-94.7) vs readers 68.5-80.4% unaided; 92.7-95.0% aided; reading time -47% trainees, -32% experts.
papers.statistics: McNemar test (sensitivity), Z test (AUC), Wilcoxon signed-rank (reading time), logistic regression; two-sided, 95% CIs.

papers.title: Automated segmentation of brain metastases with deep learning: A multi-center, randomized crossover, multi-reader evaluation study
papers.authors: Luo X, Yang Y, Yin S, Li H, Shao Y, et al.
papers.aim: To develop a brain metastasis segmentation system and test, in a randomized crossover multi-reader study, whether it improves radiologists' contours and speed.
papers.method: VB-Net-based segmentation system (BMSS) trained on 488 patients; prospective 5-centre test set; 5 residents and 5 attending radiologists contoured the same cases with and without AI in randomized crossover order.
papers.result: BMSS alone median Dice 0.91 (95% CI 0.90-0.92), similar in internal and external sets (p=0.67); with AI readers' Dice rose from 0.87 to 0.92 (p<0.001) and contouring time fell by 42% per lesion; residents improved more (+0.05 vs +0.03 Dice).
papers.tools: VB-Net (V-Net with bottleneck), 3D contrast-enhanced T1 MRI.
papers.gap: Metastases only; single sequence; Chinese centres.
papers.relation: Randomised crossover evaluation of AI-assisted brain tumour segmentation by clinicians, a model for validating outlining tools in practice.
papers.limitations: Small prospective test set (50 patients); contouring task only.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors trained a VB-Net segmentation system on contrast T1 MRI from 488 patients with more than 10,000 metastases. They then prospectively collected 50 new patients from five hospitals and ran a randomized crossover study: ten radiologists (five residents, five attendings) outlined every metastasis once with the AI's draft and once without, in random order. The AI alone reached median Dice 0.91, equally good inside and outside the training hospital. With AI help, radiologists' contours improved from Dice 0.87 to 0.92 and took 42% less time; juniors gained most in accuracy. For our PhD this randomized crossover reader design is a template for O4, and the result supports offering AI drafts that clinicians edit rather than replacing them.
papers.studyDesign: Model development plus prospective multicentre randomized crossover multi-reader multi-case (MRMC) study.
papers.datasets: Development: 488 patients with 10,338 brain metastases (Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center, Aug 2019 - Nov 2020, from 624 consecutive patients). Prospective test: 50 patients with 203 metastases from 5 centres.
papers.preprocessing: 3D contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging; resampling and intensity normalisation; expert reference contours.
papers.modelDetails: VB-Net deep segmentation network (V-Net with bottleneck blocks) for 3D lesion delineation.
papers.training: Trained on the development cohort with internal validation (details in supplement).
papers.evaluation: Dice, average surface distance, relative volume difference; reader Dice and contouring time per lesion with and without assistance.
papers.baselines: Unassisted residents and attending radiologists; internal vs external performance.
papers.results: BMSS Dice 0.91 (0.90-0.92); readers 0.87 (0.87-0.88) unaided vs 0.92 (0.92-0.92) aided, p<0.001; time saving 42% (40-45%); residents +0.05 Dice and 44% time saving, attendings +0.03 and 40%.
papers.statistics: Medians with 95% CI; randomized crossover analysis; p-values.

papers.title: Fully automated hybrid approach to predict the IDH mutation status of gliomas via deep learning and radiomics
papers.authors: Choi YS, Bae S, Chang JH, Kang SG, Kim SH, et al.
papers.relation: Externally validated MRI-based molecular marker prediction combining segmentation and classification, relevant to marker fusion and grading.

papers.title: Diagnostic performance of deep learning for predicting glioma isocitrate dehydrogenase and 1p/19q co-deletion in MRI: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Farahani S, Hejazi M, Tabassum M, Di Ieva A, et al.
papers.aim: To pool the diagnostic accuracy of deep learning MRI models for predicting glioma IDH mutation and 1p/19q co-deletion and find what drives differences between studies.
papers.method: PRISMA systematic review of 5 databases to March 2025; quality by Radiomics Quality Score and QUADAS-2; bivariate random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression.
papers.result: 104 studies reviewed, 72 meta-analysed. Test-cohort IDH: sensitivity 0.80 (0.77-0.83), specificity 0.85 (0.81-0.87). 1p/19q: sensitivity 0.75 (0.65-0.82), specificity 0.82 (0.75-0.88). Segmentation method and degree of DL integration explained heterogeneity.
papers.tools: Bivariate meta-analysis model, meta-regression, RQS, QUADAS-2.
papers.gap: Few studies with true external or prospective validation; heterogeneous MRI protocols.
papers.relation: Summarises the evidence on MRI deep learning for WHO-relevant molecular marker classification, including external validation gaps.
papers.limitations: Publication bias and high risk of bias in many included studies; mostly retrospective single-centre data.
papers.methodologyDetail: This review collected every study up to March 2025 that used deep learning on MRI to predict two key glioma markers, IDH mutation and 1p/19q co-deletion. From 1,517 papers, 104 met the criteria and 72 had enough data to pool. Quality was scored with the Radiomics Quality Score and QUADAS-2, and a bivariate model combined sensitivity and specificity across studies. On test data, models found IDH-mutant tumours about 80% of the time with 85% specificity, and 1p/19q co-deletion 75% / 82%. How the tumour was segmented and how fully deep learning was used explained much of the variation. The authors call for data harmonisation, automatic segmentation, multicentre external and prospective validation. For our PhD it sets a realistic ceiling for imaging-based molecular prediction and supports showing such predictions with uncertainty and confirming them with laboratory tests.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis.
papers.datasets: 1,517 unique publications screened from PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science and Google Scholar; 104 included, 72 in meta-analysis (many using TCGA/TCIA and institutional cohorts).
papers.preprocessing: Data extraction of 2x2 tables from test cohorts; classification of studies by segmentation method (manual, semi-automatic, automatic) and DL role (feature extractor vs end-to-end).
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable (review); included models were CNNs, transformers and hybrid DL-radiomics pipelines.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Pooled sensitivity and specificity with 95% CI; heterogeneity and meta-regression; RQS and QUADAS-2 quality ratings.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: IDH: sensitivity 0.80 (95% CI 0.77-0.83), specificity 0.85 (0.81-0.87). 1p/19q: sensitivity 0.75 (0.65-0.82), specificity 0.82 (0.75-0.88). Significant moderators: tumour segmentation method and extent of DL integration.
papers.statistics: Bivariate random-effects model; meta-regression; 95% confidence intervals.

papers.title: Artificial-intelligence-based molecular classification of diffuse gliomas using rapid, label-free optical imaging
papers.authors: Hollon T, Jiang C, Chowdury A, Nasir-Moin M, et al.
papers.aim: To predict glioma molecular markers (IDH, 1p19q, ATRX) during surgery in under 90 seconds from label-free optical images.
papers.method: DeepGlioma: ResNet50 encoder trained on stimulated Raman histology (SRH) with patch contrastive learning, plus a transformer genetic embedding learned from public genomic data, for multi-label molecular classification; prospective international test.
papers.result: Mean molecular classification accuracy 93.3% (+/-1.6) across IDH, 1p19q and ATRX in 153 prospective patients; molecular subgroup accuracy 91.5% (95% CI 86.0-95.4), +4.6% over a multiclass baseline.
papers.tools: SRH microscope, ResNet50, contrastive learning, transformer label embedding, PyTorch.
papers.gap: Requires SRH hardware; ATRX prediction least stable.
papers.relation: Clinically validated intraoperative AI for molecular glioma classification from tissue, relevant to biopsy analysis and surgical support.
papers.limitations: Specialised imaging device; training data from one centre (Michigan).
papers.methodologyDetail: DeepGlioma works on a tiny piece of fresh tumour removed during surgery, imaged in about 90 seconds with stimulated Raman histology (a stain-free optical microscope). A ResNet50 learned image features with patch contrastive learning on 373 Michigan patients, while a transformer learned how glioma mutations co-occur from large public genomic datasets; together they predict IDH, 1p19q and ATRX status at once. In a prospective test of 153 patients at four hospitals in the USA and Europe, mean accuracy was 93% and the WHO molecular subgroup was right 92% of the time, better than a standard classifier. For our PhD it shows how rapid AI-based molecular screening could support surgical decisions where sequencing takes weeks, and its use of label relations is a useful idea for the pathology agent.
papers.studyDesign: Model development with prospective multicentre international testing and leave-one-institution-out cross-validation.
papers.datasets: Training: SRH images from 373 adult diffuse glioma patients at University of Michigan (Nov 2015 - Nov 2021): 61.9% IDH-wildtype, 17.2% IDH-mutant 1p19q-codeleted, 21% IDH-mutant 1p19q-intact; public genomic data (TCGA and others) for genetic embedding. Prospective test: 153 patients from NYU, UCSF, University Hospital Cologne and Medical University of Vienna.
papers.preprocessing: 3x3 mm fresh biopsy imaged at two Raman shifts; images split into patches; patch-level representations averaged per patient.
papers.modelDetails: ResNet50 SRH visual encoder trained with patch contrastive learning; transformer encoder for genetic embedding with masked label training; multi-label classifier for IDH, 1p19q and ATRX; rule-based assignment of WHO molecular subgroup.
papers.training: Fixed number of epochs without hyperparameter tuning in leave-one-institution-out cross-validation.
papers.evaluation: Mean label accuracy, mean AUROC, mean average precision, subset accuracy, F1 scores; molecular subgroup accuracy with 95% CI.
papers.baselines: ResNet50 multiclass SRH classifier with cross-entropy.
papers.results: Mean molecular accuracy 93.3% (+/-1.6); subgroup accuracy 91.5% (86.0-95.4); +4.6% over multiclass baseline; LIOCV accuracy SD 2.75-6.06%; ATRX mAUROC variance +/-9.10% vs IDH +/-2.73%; correct zero-shot classification of non-canonical IDH and H3 K27M cases.
papers.statistics: 95% confidence intervals; leave-one-institution-out variability.

papers.title: Ultra-fast deep-learned CNS tumour classification during surgery
papers.authors: Vermeulen C, Pages-Gallego M, Kester L, Kranendonk MEG, et al.
papers.aim: To classify CNS tumours during surgery from sparse methylation profiles obtained by rapid nanopore sequencing.
papers.method: Sturgeon: a small fully connected network trained on millions of simulated sparse nanopore runs generated from 2,801 reference methylation array profiles, calibrated with temperature scaling and used with a 0.95 confidence cut-off that abstains below threshold.
papers.result: Correct diagnosis within 40 minutes of sequencing in 45 of 50 retrospective samples (abstained on 5); in 25 live surgeries turnaround under 90 minutes with 18 (72%) correct and 7 below the confidence threshold (no wrong confident calls); ECE fell from 0.025 to 0.002.
papers.tools: Oxford Nanopore MinION, PyTorch, temperature scaling, expected calibration error.
papers.gap: Some rare classes do not reach target true-positive rate; needs sequencing hardware and bioinformatics.
papers.relation: Shows data-efficient deep learning on sparse methylation data for intraoperative CNS tumour classification, informing marker-based diagnosis.
papers.limitations: Small prospective series (25 surgeries); reference classes from the Capper classifier only.
papers.methodologyDetail: Surgeons often do not know the exact brain tumour type during an operation, yet it changes how aggressively they should resect. Sturgeon reads a very sparse DNA methylation profile obtained from 20-40 minutes of portable nanopore sequencing. Because real sparse training data do not exist, the team simulated tens of millions of sparse runs from 2,801 reference methylation arrays and trained a small neural network on them. They then calibrated its scores with temperature scaling (calibration error dropped from 0.025 to 0.002) so that a score of 0.95 really means about 95% correct, and only reported a diagnosis above 0.95. In 50 stored samples it was correct for 45 and abstained for 5; during 25 live surgeries it gave 18 correct diagnoses within 90 minutes and abstained on 7, with no confident wrong answers. For our PhD this is the clearest real-world proof that calibrated confidence plus abstention makes AI safe to use in neurosurgery.
papers.studyDesign: Model development on simulated data with retrospective validation and prospective intra-operative use.
papers.datasets: 2,801 labelled Infinium 450K methylation profiles of CNS tumours and control tissue (Capper et al., 91 classes) for simulation (50% train, 25% validation, 25% test; 4-fold rotation; 36.8 million training simulations); 94 paediatric EPIC array profiles (Princess Maxima Center); 50 retrospectively sequenced samples; 25 live surgeries.
papers.preprocessing: Binarisation of array beta values to methylated or unmethylated; simulation of non-uniform nanopore coverage, read lengths and sample purity at 12 sparsity levels; 428,643 CpG sites as inputs.
papers.modelDetails: Fully connected network: input of 428,643 CpG nodes, hidden layers of 256 and 128 nodes, softmax output per tumour class; ensemble across folds; temperature scaling on validation folds.
papers.training: Training on simulated sparse profiles; best state selected on validation; temperature scaling fitted with learning rate 0.01, max 500 iterations.
papers.evaluation: Top-1 and top-3 F1 per class over 500 simulated runs per test sample; true positive rate at 0.95 and 0.8 cut-offs; ECE with 10 bins; real-time turnaround and accuracy in surgery.
papers.baselines: Array-based reference classification and final pathological diagnosis.
papers.results: ECE 0.025 to 0.002 after calibration; at 0.95 cut-off 80 of 91 classes had TPR > 0.95; retrospective 45/50 correct within 40 min, 5 abstentions; prospective 18/25 correct, 7 below threshold, turnaround < 90 min.
papers.statistics: Expected calibration error; per-class TPR and F1 across simulations.

papers.title: A multi-center performance assessment for automated histopathological classification and grading of glioma using whole slide images
papers.authors: Jin L, Sun T, Liu X, Cao Z, Liu Y, et al.
papers.aim: To test whether an automated glioma histopathology classification and grading system keeps its accuracy on whole-slide images from other hospitals.
papers.method: Subtask-guided image-to-label multiple instance learning (HAS-Bt) with 'patch prompting' (patch proposals from a pre-trained patch classifier) for end-to-end training; trained at one centre and tested on four centres.
papers.result: Overall accuracy 0.79 on internal validation and 0.73 on the multi-centre test set for 5 common glioma types under WHO CNS5.
papers.tools: SE-DenseNet patch feature extractor, MIL, HAS-Bt system.
papers.gap: Moderate accuracy; small external sets; histology only without molecular data.
papers.relation: Multicentre validation of whole-slide glioma classification and grading that quantifies cross-site generalisation.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; class imbalance; Chinese centres only.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team had built a glioma pathology assistant (HAS-Bt) that classifies H&E slides into five common glioma types under the 2021 WHO scheme, but it had only been tested at one hospital. Here they retrained it on 456 slides with an end-to-end multiple-instance learning pipeline, in which a pre-trained patch classifier proposes the most useful patches ('patch prompting') so training stays affordable. On 150 internal slides it was 79% accurate, and on 127 slides from four hospitals 73% accurate. For our PhD it gives a realistic picture of how much a pathology model loses at new sites, which is why our biopsy agent needs per-site calibration and should defer uncertain slides to a neuropathologist.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multicentre development and external validation study.
papers.datasets: 733 WSIs from four centres (institutes A-D): 456 training, 150 internal validation, 127 multi-centre testing; 5 common glioma types.
papers.preprocessing: Slide digitisation; tissue tiling into patches; patch proposals selected by a pre-trained patch-level classifier.
papers.modelDetails: Patch-level feature extractor (SE-DenseNet from prior work) with slide-level multiple-instance learning changed from two-stage image-to-feature-to-label into an end-to-end image-to-label process with online feature extraction; subtask guidance for classification and grading.
papers.training: End-to-end MIL training with patch prompting to reduce computation (details in STAR Methods).
papers.evaluation: Class-wise and overall accuracy on internal validation and multi-centre test; confusion matrices.
papers.baselines: Prior single-centre model (patient-level accuracy 87.5% on 56 patients).
papers.results: Overall accuracy 0.79 internal and 0.73 multi-centre; described as a minor, acceptable decline.
papers.statistics: Descriptive accuracy per class and overall.

papers.title: A Multicenter Study on Intraoperative Glioma Grading via Deep Learning on Cryosection Pathology
papers.authors: Liu X, Sun T, Chen H, Wu S, Cheng H, et al.
papers.relation: Validates deep-learning glioma grading on frozen-section slides across centres to support intraoperative decisions.

papers.title: Pediatric brain tumor classification using digital pathology and deep learning: Evaluation of SOTA methods on a multi-center Swedish cohort
papers.authors: Tampu IE, Nyman P, Spyretos C, Blystad I, Shamikh A, et al.
papers.aim: To evaluate state-of-the-art weakly supervised pathology methods and foundation-model features for classifying paediatric brain tumours on a national multicentre cohort.
papers.method: Patch features from ResNet50, UNI and CONCH aggregated with ABMIL or CLAM for three hierarchical tasks (category, family, type); generalisation tested by training on 2 centres and testing on 4 others; attention maps for interpretability.
papers.result: Best: UNI + ABMIL with MCC 0.76 +/- 0.04 (category), 0.63 +/- 0.04 (family), 0.60 +/- 0.05 (type); UNI and CONCH beat ResNet50 out-of-site, but the in-site to out-of-site drop was similar for all extractors.
papers.tools: CLAM framework, UNI, CONCH, ResNet50, AdamW, scikit-learn, NVIDIA RTX 4090.
papers.gap: Rare tumour types have few cases; scanner variability remains a source of error.
papers.relation: Evaluates foundation-model and MIL pathology pipelines on a small multicentre national cohort, analogous to limited Sri Lankan slide data.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; Swedish population; five scanners at 20x or 40x.
papers.methodologyDetail: Paediatric brain tumours are many and rare, so pathology datasets are small. This study gathered 1,449 slides from 540 children at all six Swedish university hospitals, digitised on five different scanners. Each slide was cut into patches, features were extracted with a classic ResNet50 or with the pathology foundation models UNI and CONCH, and an attention-based MIL model (ABMIL or CLAM) combined them into a patient diagnosis at three levels of detail. UNI features with ABMIL worked best (MCC 0.76 for broad category down to 0.60 for exact type). When trained on two hospitals and tested on four others, foundation features stayed better than ResNet50, but every model lost about the same amount out-of-site. For our PhD it supports using UNI/CONCH features with ABMIL for the biopsy agent and shows that site shift persists, so calibration per site is still needed.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective national multicentre evaluation of computational pathology pipelines.
papers.datasets: 1,449 H&E WSIs from 540 children and young adults (age 8.5 +/- 4.9 years; 284 male, 253 female) from six Swedish university hospitals (2013-2023), after excluding 62 cases / 128 WSIs; five scanners at 20x or 40x.
papers.preprocessing: Tissue segmentation and patching with CLAM; patch features from ResNet50 (ImageNet), UNI and CONCH foundation models.
papers.modelDetails: Attention-based MIL (ABMIL) and clustering-constrained attention MIL (CLAM) aggregators for patient-level classification at three hierarchical levels.
papers.training: AdamW, initial learning rate 1e-4 with cosine annealing; 10-20 epochs with early stopping (patience 5) on validation loss; NVIDIA RTX 4090 24 GB.
papers.evaluation: Matthews correlation coefficient, balanced accuracy, weighted F1, AUROC; in-site vs out-of-site testing; attention heatmaps.
papers.baselines: ResNet50 ImageNet features; CLAM vs ABMIL; UNI vs CONCH.
papers.results: UNI + ABMIL MCC 0.76 / 0.63 / 0.60 for category / family / type; foundation features better than ResNet50 out-of-site; similar relative generalisation drop for all extractors.
papers.statistics: Mean +/- SD over repeated splits.
papers.availability: Code on GitHub (IulianEmilTampu); data access via the Swedish Childhood Tumor Biobank.

papers.title: Streamlined Intraoperative Brain Tumor Classification and Molecular Subtyping in Stereotactic Biopsies Using Stimulated Raman Histology and Deep Learning
papers.authors: Reinecke D, Ruess D, Meissner AK, Furtjes G, et al.
papers.relation: Applies deep learning to stereotactic biopsy tissue for tumour classification and molecular subtyping in a surgical workflow.

papers.title: Multimodal fusion of pathology and radiology foundation models for WHO 2021 glioma subtyping
papers.authors: Saueressig C, Scholz D, Raffler P, Delbridge C, et al.
papers.aim: To classify WHO 2021 glioma subtypes by fusing histopathology and MRI foundation-model features, even without patient-paired training data.
papers.method: Frozen pathology and MRI foundation models as unimodal experts producing patch tokens; three fusion classifiers (late fusion, early fusion, mixture of experts), each with a linear patch-mean or Mamba patch-sequence expert; trained on unpaired WSI and MRI datasets with random label-pairing.
papers.result: Mixture-of-experts model best: AUC 0.98 on validation and 0.94 on an independent 171-patient matched test set; multimodal models beat unimodal ones and still matched unimodal baselines when only one modality was available.
papers.tools: Pathology and MRI foundation models (frozen), Mamba sequence model, UMAP, PyTorch.
papers.gap: Only three WHO subtypes; TCGA is the only paired test cohort.
papers.relation: Fuses MRI and histopathology foundation-model features for WHO glioma subtyping, directly matching the multi-source fusion goal.
papers.limitations: Retrospective public datasets; class imbalance (few oligodendrogliomas in UCSF MRI).
papers.methodologyDetail: Doctors decide glioma subtype in a tumour board where radiologists and pathologists each give an opinion. This study mimics that: a pathology foundation model turns slide patches into tokens and an MRI foundation model does the same for scan patches, and a small classifier learns to combine them by late fusion, early fusion or a mixture of experts. Because few patients have both MRI and slides, the authors paired a random MRI and a random slide with the same subtype label during training, using 772 slide cases and 959 MRI cases. Tested on 171 TCGA patients with both, the mixture-of-experts model reached AUC 0.94 and outperformed single-modality models, while still working when only one modality was available. For our PhD it supports combining the MRI and pathology agents through a learned gating step and shows training is feasible without paired Sri Lankan data.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multimodal model development with independent paired test set.
papers.datasets: WSI: EBRAINS (497 glioblastoma, 132 astrocytoma, 157 oligodendroglioma). MRI: UCSF-PDGM (398 / 84 / 15) and EGD (249 / 62 / 58). Paired test: TCGA (86 / 55 / 30; 171 patients). Total 1,731 unique training patients (772 WSI, 959 MRI).
papers.preprocessing: WSIs tiled and embedded with a pathology foundation model; mpMRI preprocessed (registration, skull stripping) and embedded with an MRI foundation model; one token per patch.
papers.modelDetails: MM-LF (late fusion of unimodal predictions), MM-EF (early fusion of tokens), MM-MoE (mixture of experts gating unimodal experts); experts are linear patch-mean or Mamba-based patch-sequence models; random label-paired training samples an MRI and a WSI of the same subtype.
papers.training: Random label-pairing creates tens of thousands of multimodal pairs; unpaired alternate training also tested (details in Methods).
papers.evaluation: AUC, accuracy and further metrics (Table S1) on validation and TCGA holdout; comparison with initial pathologist diagnosis (70% accurate vs WHO 2021 labels); attention maps and UMAP of embeddings.
papers.baselines: Unimodal MRI and WSI models; naive ensembling; patient-matched training on TCGA.
papers.results: MM-MoE AUC 0.98 (validation), 0.94 (test); random label-pairing equivalent to patient-matched training and better than naive ensembling; unpaired training equivalent except for late fusion; all models at least matched the 70% initial pathologist accuracy.
papers.statistics: Bootstrap confidence intervals and significance tests between architectures.

papers.title: Towards consistency in pediatric brain tumor measurements: Challenges, solutions, and the role of artificial intelligence-based segmentation
papers.authors: Familiar AM, Fathi Kazerooni A, Vossough A, et al.
papers.relation: Discusses clinical requirements and validation of AI segmentation for consistent tumour measurement in neuro-oncology practice.

papers.title: Enhancing efficiency in pediatric brain tumor segmentation using a pathologically diverse single-center clinical dataset
papers.authors: Piffer A, Buchner JA, Gennari AG, Grehten P, et al.
papers.aim: To test deep learning segmentation across diverse paediatric brain tumour types and MRI sequence combinations using a single-centre clinical dataset.
papers.method: 3D nnU-Net trained on 121 and tested on 53 paediatric patients for four subregions (whole tumour, T2-hyperintensity, enhancing tumour, cystic component); compared with intra- and inter-rater variability; sequence ablations; clinical 4-level usability rating and contouring-time comparison.
papers.result: Mean Dice 0.85 for whole tumour and T2-hyperintensity (human variability 0.86), 0.75 enhancing tumour, 0.26 cystic component; T1 + T1-C + T2 nearly matched the full protocol; manual contouring time reduced by up to 83%.
papers.tools: nnU-Net 3D, connected-component size filtering, publicly released model.
papers.gap: Cystic components poorly segmented; single centre (Zurich).
papers.relation: Shows how a modest single-centre clinical dataset can train useful segmentation models, relevant to small local hospital data.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; small test set (53); rare tumour types underrepresented.
papers.methodologyDetail: Childhood brain tumours vary widely in type and appearance. Using 174 children from one Zurich hospital, the authors trained nnU-Net to outline four tumour parts and compared it with how consistently human experts outline the same tumours. Whole tumour and T2-bright regions were outlined as well as humans (Dice 0.85 vs 0.86), enhancing tumour moderately (0.75), and cysts poorly (0.26). Using only T1, contrast T1 and T2 gave almost the same results as all four sequences, and AI drafts cut manual outlining time by up to 83%. For our PhD it shows that confidence should be judged per tumour subregion and that shorter MRI protocols can still support reliable segmentation.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective single-centre development and evaluation study with clinical usability rating.
papers.datasets: 174 paediatric patients (0-18 years) at University Children's Hospital Zurich, 2014-2022, pre-treatment MRI (T1, T1-C, T2, FLAIR); HGG, LGG, medulloblastoma, ependymoma and rarer types; split 121 train / 53 test.
papers.preprocessing: Registration and skull stripping; manual expert annotation of 4 subregions; post-processing removing small isolated components in ET and CC channels.
papers.modelDetails: 3D full-resolution nnU-Net; models trained on different sequence combinations for ablation.
papers.training: nnU-Net default training with 5-fold cross-validation on the training set.
papers.evaluation: Dice and volume difference per subregion, by tumour type, location and sequence combination; intra- and inter-rater Dice; clinicians' 4-level usability rating; contouring time.
papers.baselines: Human intra- and inter-rater variability; full 4-sequence protocol.
papers.results: WT and T2H mean Dice 0.85 vs human 0.86; ET 0.75; CC 0.26; T1+T1-C+T2 close to full protocol; up to 83% time reduction.
papers.statistics: Mean Dice with comparisons across subgroups (non-parametric tests).

papers.title: Deep Learning-Based Glioma Segmentation of 2D Intraoperative Ultrasound Images: A Multicenter Study Using the Brain Tumor Intraoperative Ultrasound Database (BraTioUS)
papers.authors: Cepeda S, Esteban-Sinovas O, Singh V, Shetty P, et al.
papers.aim: To develop a CNN that segments gliomas on 2D intraoperative ultrasound images using a multicentre database.
papers.method: nnU-Net 2D trained from scratch (1,000 epochs, 5-fold CV, Dice + cross-entropy) on manually segmented largest-diameter B-mode slices from BraTioUS and ReMIND; stratified 70/30 split by centre; external validation on RESECT-SEG and Imperial College NHS cohorts.
papers.result: Hold-out test median Dice 0.90, ASSD 8.51, HD95 29.08; external RESECT-SEG Dice 0.65 (ASSD 14.14, HD95 44.02) and Imperial-NHS Dice 0.93 (ASSD 8.58, HD95 28.81).
papers.tools: nnU-Net (default hyperparameters), BraTioUS, ReMIND, RESECT-SEG datasets.
papers.gap: 2D single-slice only; large drop on one external cohort; not yet real-time.
papers.relation: Multicentre segmentation on low-cost intraoperative ultrasound, a modality relevant to surgical planning in low-resource settings.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; only pre-resection images; operator-dependent image quality.
papers.methodologyDetail: Intraoperative ultrasound is portable and cheap but its images are noisy and hard to read. The authors pooled glioma ultrasound images from several hospitals in Europe and the USA (BraTioUS) and a public dataset (ReMIND), outlined the tumour on the slice where it looked largest, and trained a 2D nnU-Net from scratch for 1,000 epochs. On held-out patients it matched expert outlines well (Dice 0.90) and on a London cohort even better (0.93), but on another external set (RESECT-SEG) only 0.65. For our PhD it shows ultrasound-based tumour guidance is a realistic low-cost option, but performance can swing between sites, so the surgical-planning agent must estimate its own reliability on each new site.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multicentre development with internal hold-out and two external validation cohorts.
papers.datasets: BraTioUS (centres in Spain, France, USA incl. MGH; surgeries 2018-2023) plus public ReMIND: 197 subjects in training cohort, 56 in hold-out test; external validation 53 subjects (RESECT-SEG and Imperial College NHS Trust London).
papers.preprocessing: Histologically confirmed gliomas (WHO 2021); pre-resection B-mode images only; manual segmentation on the slice with largest tumour diameter; exclusion of poor-quality images.
papers.modelDetails: 2D nnU-Net with default configuration.
papers.training: From scratch, 1,000 epochs, 5-fold cross-validation, loss = soft Dice + cross-entropy.
papers.evaluation: Dice similarity coefficient, average symmetric surface distance, 95th percentile Hausdorff distance.
papers.baselines: Not reported (feasibility study).
papers.results: Hold-out: Dice 0.90, ASSD 8.51, HD95 29.08. RESECT-SEG: Dice 0.65, ASSD 14.14, HD95 44.02. Imperial-NHS: Dice 0.93, ASSD 8.58, HD95 28.81.
papers.statistics: Medians with IQR.
papers.availability: BraTioUS database; code based on public nnU-Net.

papers.title: A Transfer Learning-Based Active Learning Framework for Brain Tumor Classification
papers.authors: Hao R, Namdar K, Liu L, Khalvati F
papers.aim: To cut MRI annotation cost for brain tumour grading by combining transfer learning with active learning.
papers.method: ImageNet-pretrained AlexNet fine-tuned on 2D T1/T1C/T2 slices for HGG vs LGG, with active learning that queries the most informative unlabelled slices using uncertainty sampling plus query-by-committee.
papers.result: Test AUC 82.89% on 66 patients, 2.92 points above the baseline, while saving at least 40% of labelling; on a balanced dataset AUC 82% vs 78.48% baseline.
papers.tools: AlexNet (ImageNet), active learning (uncertainty sampling, query by committee), BraTS 2019.
papers.gap: Simple 2D slice model; binary grading only; older backbone.
papers.relation: Reduces annotation needs for brain tumour MRI classification through active and transfer learning, a data-efficient strategy for scarce labels.
papers.limitations: Slice-level labels from patient grade; single public dataset; modest AUC.
papers.methodologyDetail: Labelling medical images is the most expensive part of building AI. This study starts from an AlexNet already trained on everyday photos and fine-tunes it to tell high-grade from low-grade glioma on 2D MRI slices from BraTS 2019 (335 patients). Instead of labelling everything, an active learning loop repeatedly picks the slices the model is least sure about - judged by its own uncertainty and by disagreement between several models - asks for their labels, and retrains. With at least 40% fewer labels the model reached AUC 0.829 on 66 test patients, slightly better than training on all labels (about 0.80), and the gain held on a balanced dataset. For our PhD active learning is a practical way to decide which Sri Lankan cases clinicians should annotate first, using the same uncertainty signals that drive deferral.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective method study on a public dataset with train/validation/test split by patient.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2019: 335 patients (259 HGG, 76 LGG); 20 tumour-containing axial slices per patient giving 6,700 2D slices; split 203 train, 66 validation, 66 test patients with the same HGG/LGG ratio; also a balanced subset.
papers.preprocessing: BraTS preprocessing (skull stripping, 1 mm isotropic, SRI24 registration, 240x240x155); 3 channels (T1, T1C, T2) chosen to fit AlexNet; resize 240 to 224 pixels.
papers.modelDetails: Pretrained AlexNet fine-tuned for binary HGG/LGG slice classification; committee of models for query-by-committee; uncertainty sampling of unlabelled slices.
papers.training: Iterative active learning rounds: train on labelled pool, score unlabelled slices, add most informative to labelled pool, fine-tune again.
papers.evaluation: Patient-level and slice-level ROC AUC on held-out test set; labelling cost saved versus full-data baseline; repeated on balanced data.
papers.baselines: Same network trained on the full labelled training set (validation set baseline); random sampling.
papers.results: AUC 82.89% (+2.92 points over baseline) with at least 40% less labelling; balanced data AUC 82% vs 78.48%.
papers.statistics: Not reported beyond point estimates.

papers.title: Analyzing magnetic resonance imaging data from glioma patients using deep learning
papers.authors: Menze B, Isensee F, Wiest R, Wiestler B, Maier-Hein K, et al.
papers.relation: Reviews the clinical use of deep learning for glioma MRI detection, segmentation and outcome prediction, framing O3 tasks.

papers.title: The 2024 Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge Meningioma Radiotherapy (BraTS-MEN-RT) dataset
papers.authors: LaBella D, Schumacher K, Mix M, Leu K, et al.
papers.aim: To provide a large public multi-institutional dataset of meningioma radiotherapy-planning MRI with expert gross tumour volume labels for automated segmentation research.
papers.method: Data descriptor: retrospective collection from 7 US/UK centres; native-resolution T1 post-contrast MRI, AFNI defacing (no skull stripping), nnU-Net pre-segmentation (trained on 1,000 BraTS-MEN cases, iteratively retrained) followed by expert correction to RT protocols; slice-by-slice QC.
papers.result: 750 RT planning MRIs from 747 patients (500 training with GTV labels, plus validation and test sets); 570 scans public with 500 annotated; intact and postoperative meningiomas; used for the BraTS 2024 MEN-RT challenge.
papers.tools: AFNI defacing, ITK-SNAP, nnU-Net, Synapse challenge platform.
papers.gap: Single sequence (T1c); GTV only, no clinical target volume or organs at risk.
papers.relation: Extends benchmark data to meningioma with treatment-planning MRI, useful for pretraining and evaluating models across tumour types.
papers.limitations: Imaging parameters partly missing; label style follows US/UK RT guidelines.
papers.methodologyDetail: Planning radiotherapy for meningioma requires a specialist to outline the tumour (gross tumour volume) on MRI, which is slow and varies between experts. The BraTS-MEN-RT dataset gathers 750 real radiotherapy planning scans from seven hospitals in the USA and UK. Unlike earlier BraTS sets, the scans are kept in their original resolution and are not skull-stripped, because frames and surrounding anatomy matter for treatment; faces are removed with AFNI for privacy. An nnU-Net trained on 1,000 earlier meningioma cases drew first-pass outlines that experts then corrected to standard radiotherapy protocols, with the model retrained as more cases were finished. For our PhD it is a public resource for the planning agent and a working example of AI-assisted annotation to create labels efficiently.
papers.studyDesign: Dataset descriptor for a public segmentation challenge.
papers.datasets: 750 RT planning MRI exams from 747 patients at Duke, UCSF, SUNY Upstate, University of Washington, University of Missouri, King's College London and UC San Diego: training 500 (66.7%), validation and test sets; treatments included Cobalt-60, photon EBRT, SRS and proton therapy.
papers.preprocessing: DICOM to NIfTI at original orientation and voxel size; no skull stripping or resampling (to keep headframes and extracranial anatomy); AFNI automated defacing; manual QC in ITK-SNAP.
papers.modelDetails: nnU-Net trained on T1c and tumour-core labels of 1,000 BraTS-MEN cases (1,000 epochs, default settings) to propose preliminary GTV masks; retrained as RT cases accumulated.
papers.training: Pre-label model: default nnU-Net hyperparameters and augmentation, 1,000 epochs; iterative retraining.
papers.evaluation: Challenge metrics: lesion-wise Dice and 95% Hausdorff distance on hidden test set.
papers.baselines: Not applicable (dataset paper).
papers.results: Largest public meningioma RT planning MRI set: 570 public scans with 500 expert GTVs; heterogeneous acquisition parameters across and within sites.
papers.statistics: Descriptive dataset statistics.

papers.title: Effectiveness of Federated Learning and CNN Ensemble Architectures for Identifying Brain Tumors Using MRI Images
papers.authors: Islam M, Reza MT, Kaosar M, Parvez MZ
papers.aim: To test whether federated learning with a CNN ensemble can detect brain tumours on MRI without sharing patient images.
papers.method: Six ImageNet-pretrained CNNs compared; the best three (VGG16, InceptionV3, DenseNet121) combined as an averaged model and a voting ensemble; the averaged ensemble used as the global model in a federated client-server setup; repeated on a second, larger dataset.
papers.result: Federated ensemble accuracy 91.05% versus 96.68% for the centrally trained ensemble - a small loss for full data privacy; similar behaviour on the larger dataset.
papers.tools: Keras/TensorFlow, VGG16, VGG19, InceptionV3, ResNet50, Xception, DenseNet121, federated averaging.
papers.gap: Binary tumour/no-tumour on small public 2D Kaggle datasets; simulated clients; no external validation.
papers.relation: Compares federated and centralised ensemble CNNs for brain tumour MRI classification, showing the accuracy cost of privacy-preserving training.
papers.limitations: Simple task; possible data leakage in public sets; no calibration or uncertainty.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors first fine-tuned six well-known ImageNet CNNs on a public brain MRI dataset to say whether a tumour is present, then combined the best three (VGG16, InceptionV3, DenseNet121) by averaging their outputs or by majority vote. The averaged ensemble was then trained in a federated way: each simulated client trained on its own images and only sent weights to a central server for averaging. The federated version reached 91% accuracy versus 97% when all data were pooled, and similar results on a second dataset. For our PhD it is a simple reference for the accuracy cost of FL, but its simulated clients and binary task mean our own evaluation must use real hospitals and report calibration.
papers.studyDesign: Experimental comparison of centralised and federated training on public datasets.
papers.datasets: Public brain MRI tumour / no-tumour image dataset (Kaggle) converted to PNG and split into train, validation and test; a second slightly larger public dataset to test scalability.
papers.preprocessing: Conversion to PNG, resizing for each pretrained CNN, labelling (No_Tumor 0, Yes_Tumor 1), augmentation.
papers.modelDetails: Transfer-learned CNNs; averaged model of VGG16, InceptionV3 and DenseNet121 outputs; majority voting ensemble (tumour if two or more models say yes); federated global model = averaged ensemble.
papers.training: Local training on simulated clients, weights sent to central server for averaging over communication rounds.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, confusion matrix on the test set.
papers.baselines: Individual CNNs; centrally trained averaged and voting ensembles.
papers.results: Central ensemble 96.68% accuracy; federated ensemble 91.05%; individual models lower than ensembles.
papers.statistics: Not reported (single runs).

heading: O4 - Clinical evaluation: performance, escalation appropriateness, workload, usability, trust and safety

papers.title: Reporting guideline for the early-stage clinical evaluation of decision support systems driven by artificial intelligence: DECIDE-AI
papers.authors: Vasey B, Nagendran M, Campbell B, Clifton DA, Collins GS, et al., McCulloch P
papers.aim: To give a reporting guideline for the first live clinical studies of AI decision support.
papers.method: International Delphi consensus with experts and stakeholders.
papers.result: Checklist of 17 AI-specific items and 10 generic items, covering human factors, safety, and user interaction.
papers.tools: Reporting guideline
papers.gap: Guideline only, it does not say which metrics to use for deferral.
papers.relation: Our O4 study is exactly this early stage. We should design and report it using DECIDE-AI.
papers.limitations: Needs adoption by journals. Future: updates as field changes.
papers.methodologyDetail: DECIDE-AI is a reporting checklist for the early, small-scale clinical evaluation of AI decision support - the stage after lab validation and before large trials, which is exactly the stage of our O4 study. It was built with a two-round modified Delphi survey of 123 and 138 experts from 20 stakeholder groups (clinicians, engineers, regulators, patients, journal editors and others), a consensus meeting of 16 people and a qualitative check by 16 more. It asks studies to report, for example, who the users were and how they were trained, the exact AI version, how inputs were obtained and handled when missing, how outputs were shown, human factors such as usability and trust, errors and safety events, and how often users agreed with or overrode the AI. For our PhD this is the main reporting standard for the clinician evaluation in O4.
papers.studyDesign: Consensus-based reporting guideline development (modified Delphi, consensus meeting, qualitative evaluation).
papers.datasets: Expert panel from 20 pre-defined stakeholder categories: 123 experts in Delphi round 1, 138 in round 2, 16 at the virtual consensus meeting and 16 in the qualitative evaluation.
papers.preprocessing: Initial candidate item list from literature review and steering group; items added after round 1 feedback.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable (guideline). Output: DECIDE-AI checklist of 17 AI-specific items (28 subitems) and 10 generic items, each with an Explanation & Elaboration paragraph.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Delphi agreement thresholds on importance of each item; consensus meeting voting; qualitative evaluation of clarity and usability.
papers.baselines: Existing guidelines (TRIPOD, STARD, CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT-AI, IDEAL) - DECIDE-AI covers the early clinical stage between them.
papers.results: Final guideline with 17 AI-specific reporting items (28 subitems) and 10 generic items covering intended use, users and their training, AI system version and inputs/outputs, human factors (usability, learning curve, user trust), safety and errors, and human-AI agreement.
papers.statistics: Delphi consensus percentages.
papers.availability: Checklist and E&E published open access (Nature Medicine 2022; BMJ).

papers.title: Reporting guidelines for clinical trial reports for interventions involving artificial intelligence: the CONSORT-AI extension
papers.authors: Liu X, Cruz Rivera S, Moher D, Calvert MJ, Denniston AK; SPIRIT-AI and CONSORT-AI Working Group
papers.aim: To extend CONSORT for randomised trials that test AI interventions.
papers.method: Delphi process and consensus meeting.
papers.result: 14 new items, for example describing the AI version, input data, how humans interact with the output, and error analysis.
papers.tools: Reporting guideline
papers.gap: For RCTs, which come after early-stage studies.
papers.relation: Our study is not an RCT, but these items help us describe AI version, input and human interaction. Useful for future trial.
papers.limitations: Not for early studies. Future: updates.
papers.methodologyDetail: CONSORT-AI extends the standard checklist for reporting randomized trials so that trials testing AI tools describe the AI clearly. Candidate items were rated by 103 international experts over two Delphi rounds, agreed at a two-day meeting of 31 experts and piloted with 34 users, producing 14 new items. Trials must state which AI version was used, how input data were collected and what happened with poor-quality or missing inputs, how clinicians interacted with the AI and what skills they needed, how its output fed into decisions, and how errors were analysed. For our PhD it defines what a later randomized evaluation of the system must report, and several items (input quality handling, human-AI interaction, error analysis) should already be built into our O4 study design.
papers.studyDesign: Consensus-based extension of the CONSORT 2010 reporting guideline for randomized trials of AI interventions.
papers.datasets: 29 candidate items assessed by 103 international stakeholders in a two-stage Delphi survey; 31 stakeholders at a two-day consensus meeting; checklist pilot with 34 participants. Ethics approval University of Birmingham (ERN_19-1100).
papers.preprocessing: Literature review and steering group consultation to generate candidate items (developed together with SPIRIT-AI).
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable (guideline). Output: 14 new AI-specific items (extensions and elaborations) added to CONSORT 2010.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Delphi rating and consensus meeting agreement on each item; pilot testing.
papers.baselines: CONSORT 2010 core items.
papers.results: 14 new items, including: state the AI intervention and its intended use; inclusion criteria at participant and input-data level; how the AI was integrated in the trial setting; AI version; how input data were acquired and handled when poor or missing; human-AI interaction and user skills; output of the AI and how it was used in decisions; analysis of performance errors; and access to the AI code.
papers.statistics: Delphi consensus percentages.
papers.availability: Published open access in Nature Medicine, BMJ and Lancet Digital Health (2020).

papers.title: TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction models that use regression or machine learning methods
papers.authors: Collins GS, Moons KGM, Dhiman P, Riley RD, Beam AL, et al., Logullo P
papers.aim: To update TRIPOD for prediction models built with machine learning.
papers.method: Delphi survey and consensus meeting.
papers.result: 27-item checklist covering fairness, data, model development, evaluation and open science.
papers.tools: Reporting guideline
papers.gap: Covers model development and validation, not live human use.
papers.relation: Use when we report the O3 models (segmentation, classification, fusion).
papers.limitations: Reporting only. Future: wider use.
papers.methodologyDetail: TRIPOD+AI updates the main reporting standard for studies that build or test prediction models so that it covers machine learning and AI as well as regression. Starting from items in the original TRIPOD and other AI guidelines, the team ran two international Delphi survey rounds (170 then 200 respondents from 22 countries), added a patient and public involvement meeting, and agreed the final list at a consensus meeting. The result is a 27-item checklist plus a 13-item checklist for abstracts.
