It asks authors to report, for example, where the data came from and how representative they are, sample size reasoning, handling of missing data, how the model was tuned, discrimination and calibration with confidence intervals, fairness across patient groups, and whether code and data are shared. For our PhD it is the reporting standard for the model-development parts of O2 and O3, especially calibration and subgroup performance.
papers.studyDesign: Consensus-based reporting guideline update (two-round Delphi, patient and public involvement meeting, consensus meeting).
papers.datasets: Delphi round 1: 170 of 292 invited completed (22 countries; mainly UK 52, US 31, Netherlands 23, Canada 20); round 2: 200 of 395 invited completed; additional online PPIE meeting with 9 members of HDR UK's patient and public group (8 April 2022); ethics approval University of Oxford (R73034/RE001).
papers.preprocessing: Candidate items drafted from TRIPOD 2015, TRIPOD-Cluster, TRIPOD for Abstracts, CAIR, MI-CLAIM, CLAIM, MINIMAR, SPIRIT-AI and CONSORT-AI plus literature; 70% agreement threshold for inclusion.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable (guideline). Output: TRIPOD+AI 27-item checklist with expanded recommendations and a 13-item TRIPOD+AI for Abstracts checklist, applicable to regression and machine learning prediction models.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Delphi agreement (>=70%) and consensus meeting decisions.
papers.baselines: TRIPOD 2015 statement.
papers.results: 27-item checklist covering, among others: data sources and representativeness, sample size, handling of missing data, model development and tuning, calibration and discrimination with uncertainty, fairness across subgroups, open science (code and data availability), patient and public involvement, and model updating.
papers.statistics: Delphi consensus percentages (e.g., patient and public involvement item 69%, retained for discussion).

papers.title: Does the Whole Exceed its Parts? The Effect of AI Explanations on Complementary Team Performance
papers.authors: Bansal G, Wu T, Zhou J, Fok R, Nushi B, Kamar E, Ribeiro MT, Weld DS
papers.aim: To test if AI explanations help humans and AI together do better than either alone.
papers.method: User studies on text tasks with AI recommendations, with and without explanations and confidence.
papers.result: Explanations made people accept AI advice more, even when the AI was wrong. Team performance was not better than just showing confidence.
papers.tools: Human-subject experiments, explanation methods
papers.gap: Non-medical tasks with crowd workers.
papers.relation: Warning for our UI: showing explanations may cause over-reliance. Calibrated confidence and deferral may matter more.
papers.limitations: Lay users, not experts. Future: domain experts.
papers.methodologyDetail: This study asked whether AI explanations help people and AI do better together than either alone. Crowd workers (about 1,100 in the main review tasks) labelled the sentiment of beer and book reviews, or answered LSAT logic questions, with help from an AI that was about as accurate as they were. Conditions showed only the AI's confidence, or added highlighted explanations for one or both answers, an adaptive explanation that argued for the alternative when the AI was unsure, or explanations written by experts. Teams did beat both humans and AI alone, but explanations added nothing beyond confidence and made people accept the AI more even when it was wrong. For our PhD this is key evidence that showing calibrated confidence matters more than adding explanations, and that explanations can cause over-reliance - which O4 must measure.
papers.studyDesign: Mixed-methods randomized user studies (crowdsourced) comparing AI assistance conditions.
papers.datasets: Three tasks: sentiment of beer reviews (Beer) and Amazon book reviews (Amzbook), and LSAT logical reasoning questions; 50 test examples per domain chosen so AI accuracy matched unassisted human accuracy (about 85-87%). Participants: 566 (Beer) and 552 (Amzbook) Amazon Mechanical Turk workers (US, >=97% approval, >=1,000 tasks); 84% passed quality checks; plus LSAT study.
papers.preprocessing: 80/20 data split, minority-class oversampling; removal of participants with median labelling time < 2 s or constant labels.
papers.modelDetails: Fine-tuned RoBERTa text classifiers (AllenNLP) for the review tasks; explanation conditions: AI confidence only, Explain-Top-1 (saliency for predicted class), Explain-Top-2 (both classes), Adaptive (explain alternative when AI is unsure), expert-written explanations.
papers.training: Hyperparameters selected on validation split.
papers.evaluation: Team accuracy versus human alone and AI alone (complementary performance), agreement with AI when AI was right vs wrong, qualitative feedback.
papers.baselines: Human alone; AI alone; team with confidence display but no explanation.
papers.results: Complementary performance (team better than either alone) appeared on all tasks, but explanations did not improve it over just showing AI confidence; explanations increased acceptance of the AI's recommendation whether it was correct or not. Adaptive explanations shifted agreement in the desired direction without significant accuracy gains.
papers.statistics: Bootstrap / regression comparisons of conditions with significance testing.
papers.availability: Study materials released by the authors.

papers.title: Human-Centered Tools for Coping with Imperfect Algorithms during Medical Decision-Making
papers.authors: Cai CJ, Reif E, Hegde N, Hipp J, Kim B, Smilkov D, Wattenberg M, Viegas F, Corrado GS, Stumpe MC, Terry M
papers.aim: To give pathologists tools to refine and control a similar-image search algorithm.
papers.method: Built refinement tools (by region, by example, by concept) for a pathology image retrieval system and tested with pathologists.
papers.result: With the tools, pathologists trusted the system more, found it more useful and felt more in control, with similar accuracy.
papers.tools: Deep image retrieval (SMILY), user study
papers.gap: Small user study, retrieval task only.
papers.relation: Our clinician must be able to amend or reject AI outputs. This shows control tools raise trust.
papers.limitations: Small sample. Future: clinical workflow testing.
papers.methodologyDetail: When a pathologist searches for past biopsy images similar to a new case, the AI's idea of 'similar' may not match what the doctor needs. The authors interviewed pathologists, then built tools that let them steer the search without changing the AI: crop a region of interest, mark good results to get more like them, or turn a clinical concept up or down. In two studies, pathologists using these tools found more useful images, trusted the system more, preferred it and kept the same diagnostic accuracy, and they used the tools to test how the AI behaves and to work out whether a mistake was the AI's or theirs. For our PhD it shows that giving clinicians simple controls over an imperfect AI improves trust in the right way, a design idea for the O4 clinician interface.
papers.studyDesign: Formative needs study followed by two within-subject user evaluations with pathologists (mixed methods).
papers.datasets: Prostate biopsy image patches with a deep-learning similar-image search system (SMILY); practising pathologists as participants in formative interviews and two evaluations.
papers.preprocessing: Patch embeddings from a deep neural network; region crops snapped to acceptable aspect ratios.
papers.modelDetails: SMILY (Similar Medical Images Like Yours) with three refinement tools: refine-by-region (crop the query), refine-by-example (pick good results to retrieve more like them) and refine-by-concept (slide a clinical concept such as fused glands up or down in embedding space) - without retraining the network.
papers.training: Not applicable for the study (pre-trained embedding network).
papers.evaluation: 7-point Likert ratings of diagnostic utility, mental support, NASA-TLX effort and frustration, trust (capability and benevolence), likelihood of future use and preference; diagnostic accuracy; think-aloud observations.
papers.baselines: Traditional similar-image search interface without refinement tools.
papers.results: Refinement tools increased the diagnostic utility of retrieved images and trust in the algorithm, were preferred over the traditional interface, and caused no loss in diagnostic accuracy; pathologists used the tools to probe and understand the algorithm and to tell ML errors from their own errors.
papers.statistics: Paired comparisons of Likert outcomes with significance tests.

papers.title: A Human-Centered Evaluation of a Deep Learning System Deployed in Clinics for the Detection of Diabetic Retinopathy
papers.authors: Beede E, Baylor E, Hersch F, Iurchenko A, Wilcox L, Ruamviboonsuk P, Vardoulakis LM
papers.aim: To see how an AI screening system actually worked in clinics in Thailand.
papers.method: Field observation and interviews in 11 clinics before and during deployment.
papers.result: Poor lighting, image quality and slow internet caused many images to be rejected and delays. Nurses and patients faced extra steps.
papers.tools: Deep learning DR model, qualitative field study
papers.gap: Fixing the socio-technical issues was not tested.
papers.relation: Very close to our low-resource context. Shows we must evaluate the full workflow in Sri Lankan hospitals, not only accuracy.
papers.limitations: Single country, qualitative. Future: design changes and follow-up.
papers.methodologyDetail: Google Health deployed its diabetic eye disease AI in eleven Thai clinics, where nurses take retinal photos and previously waited weeks for an ophthalmologist's reading. Researchers observed and interviewed nurses before and after deployment. Real conditions undermined the system: about one in five images (393 of 1,838) were rejected as too poor to grade, mostly because clinics could not darken the room; slow internet delayed results; nurses with long queues struggled with extra steps; and patients told to attend a distant hospital because of an ungradable image were often unhappy. For our PhD it is a key lesson for O4: evaluate the system in Sri Lankan workflows (image quality, connectivity, patient load), and treat a deferral or 'cannot assess' outcome as something that must lead to a practical next step.
papers.studyDesign: Human-centred observational field study of a deployed deep learning system (interviews and observation), alongside a prospective accuracy study.
papers.datasets: Eleven primary care clinics in Thailand using a deep learning diabetic retinopathy screening system; nurses and staff interviewed and observed before and after deployment; system logs of 1,838 images in the first six months.
papers.preprocessing: Fundus photos uploaded to the cloud for real-time grading; images below quality thresholds rejected as ungradable.
papers.modelDetails: Deep learning DR grading algorithm (Google Health) returning severity and referral recommendation, rejecting images it cannot grade reliably.
papers.training: Not applicable (pre-trained deployed system).
papers.evaluation: Qualitative themes on workflows, expectations and post-deployment experience; gradability rate from logs.
papers.baselines: Pre-deployment screening workflow (photos sent to ophthalmologists, weeks of delay).
papers.results: 393 of 1,838 images (21%) were rejected as ungradable, mostly because photos were taken in non-darkened rooms; slow and unreliable internet delayed uploads (some 60-90 s or more); high patient volume (e.g., 150 patients queued) made protocol steps hard; referral burden and patient travel concerns affected the experience.
papers.statistics: Descriptive counts and qualitative thematic analysis.

papers.title: Human-computer collaboration for skin cancer recognition
papers.authors: Tschandl P, Rinner C, Apalla Z, Argenziano G, Codella N, Halpern A, et al., Kittler H
papers.aim: To test different ways of giving AI support to doctors for skin lesion diagnosis.
papers.method: Large reader study comparing AI output formats (class probabilities, content-based retrieval etc.) and testing with deliberately faulty AI.
papers.result: Good AI support improved accuracy most for less experienced doctors. Faulty AI misled doctors of all experience levels.
papers.tools: CNN classifier, reader study
papers.gap: Online study, not real clinic.
papers.relation: Shows the format of support matters and wrong AI is risky, so escalation is needed. Useful design for our reader study.
papers.limitations: Dermatoscopy only. Future: real-world tests.
papers.methodologyDetail: 302 clinicians from 41 countries - dermatologists, residents and GPs - diagnosed skin lesion images first alone and then with one of several forms of help from a CNN: probabilities for each of seven diagnoses, a single 'probability of malignancy', or similar example images. Detailed per-class probabilities raised accuracy from 64% to 77%, better than either the AI or the clinicians alone, while the other formats did not help. Less experienced clinicians gained most; confident experts gained nothing. When the AI was deliberately wrong, clinicians at every level, including experts, were misled. For our PhD it shows that the form of AI output matters (graded class probabilities beat a single score), that novices benefit most - relevant to Sri Lankan non-specialists - and that wrong AI advice is dangerous for everyone, which supports withholding low-confidence outputs.
papers.studyDesign: Large international web-based reader study comparing forms of AI decision support across expertise levels, plus simulations of second-opinion and telemedicine workflows.
papers.datasets: Dermatoscopic images of 7 skin lesion classes (HAM10000/ISIC-type data); 302 raters from 41 countries: 169 (56.0%) board-certified dermatologists, 77 (25.5%) residents, 38 (12.6%) general practitioners; crowd rating frequencies from 511 earlier raters.
papers.preprocessing: Images grouped in batches; raters diagnosed first without and then with one type of decision support; timing normalised per user and modality.
papers.modelDetails: CNN skin lesion classifier; support shown as AI multiclass probabilities, AI probability of malignancy, AI content-based image retrieval (similar images), or crowd-based multiclass probabilities; class-activation maps analysed.
papers.training: CNN trained on public dermatoscopic datasets (details in Methods).
papers.evaluation: Rater accuracy with vs without support (paired t-test), change of diagnosis, time to decision, effect by experience and confidence, effect of deliberately wrong AI predictions.
papers.baselines: Raters alone; AI alone.
papers.results: AI multiclass probabilities raised accuracy from 63.6% to 77.0% (+13.3%, 95% CI 11.5-15.2; p=4.9e-35, n=302), more than AI or raters alone; malignancy probability and image retrieval gave no gain; benefit decreased with experience (r=-0.18); novices changed diagnoses more often (26.0% vs 14.7%); confident experts gained nothing (-0.7%); wrong AI predictions misled all expertise levels including experts.
papers.statistics: Paired t-tests, Pearson correlation, 95% CIs.
papers.availability: Data and code described in paper (ISIC/HAM10000 public images).

papers.title: Automation Bias in Mammography: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence BI-RADS Suggestions on Reader Performance
papers.authors: Dratsch T, Chen X, Rezazadeh Mehrizi M, Kloeckner R, Mahringer-Kunz A, Pusken M, Baessler B, Sauer S, Maintz D, Pinto dos Santos D
papers.aim: To measure how much wrong AI suggestions affect radiologists.
papers.method: Radiologists with different experience read mammograms with AI BI-RADS suggestions, some of them wrong on purpose.
papers.result: When the AI was wrong, accuracy of all groups dropped sharply, and the less experienced readers were affected the most.
papers.tools: Reader study, mammography
papers.gap: Simulated AI, no real model.
papers.relation: Strong reason for our conservative default: when uncertain, the system must defer and not push a wrong suggestion.
papers.limitations: Single centre, small set of cases. Future: ways to reduce bias.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-supported screen reading versus standard double reading in the Mammography Screening with Artificial Intelligence trial (MASAI)
papers.authors: Lang K, Josefsson V, Larsson AM, Larsson S, Hogberg C, Sartor H, Hofvind S, Andersson I, Rosso A
papers.aim: To check if AI triage in breast screening is safe and reduces radiologist workload.
papers.method: Randomised trial in Sweden. AI risk score decided single vs double reading, and flagged high-risk cases.
papers.result: Cancer detection was similar or higher than standard double reading, with a large cut in screen-reading workload (about 44%).
papers.tools: Transpara AI, randomised controlled trial
papers.gap: Interim analysis. Interval cancer results needed later.
papers.relation: Good example of AI deciding how much human review a case gets, and of measuring workload. Similar to our escalation idea.
papers.limitations: Single country, mammography only. Future: final endpoint results.
papers.methodologyDetail: MASAI is a large randomised trial in the Swedish breast screening programme. Over 80,000 women were randomly assigned either to usual double reading by two radiologists or to an AI-supported pathway in which the AI scored each examination from 1 to 10: lower-risk exams were read by one radiologist, the highest-risk exams by two, and radiologists could see the AI score and highlighted areas. In this safety analysis, the AI pathway detected at least as many cancers (244 vs 203) while reducing the radiologists' reading workload by 44%. For our PhD it is a model of how to evaluate AI-based triage that routes cases to one or two human readers by risk - closely related to our confidence-based deferral - and of reporting workload alongside detection.
papers.studyDesign: Randomised, controlled, population-based, non-inferiority, single-blinded screening accuracy trial (MASAI, NCT04838756) - prespecified clinical safety analysis.
papers.datasets: 80,033 women aged 40-80 years at four screening sites in Sweden (12 April 2021 - 28 July 2022), randomised 1:1 to AI-supported screening (n=40,003) or standard double reading (n=40,030); 39,996 and 40,024 analysed; median age 54.0 years; 127 (0.2%) opted out.
papers.preprocessing: Automatic randomisation by PACS after image acquisition; radiologists not masked to allocation.
papers.modelDetails: Transpara v1.7.0 AI giving an examination-level malignancy risk score (1-10): scores 1-9 routed to single reading, score 10 to double reading; risk scores shown for all exams and CAD marks for scores 8-10.
papers.training: Not applicable (commercial AI system).
papers.evaluation: Early screening performance: cancer detection rate, recall rate, false-positive rate, PPV of recall, cancer type (invasive vs in situ), screen-reading workload; primary endpoint (interval cancer rate) pending at 100,000 participants.
papers.baselines: Standard double reading by two radiologists without AI.
papers.results: AI arm: 244 screen-detected cancers, 861 recalls, 46,345 screen readings; control: 203 cancers; invasive share 75% (AI arm) vs 81% (control) with 25% vs 19% in situ; cancer detection similar or higher with AI and screen-reading workload reduced by 44.3%; judged clinically safe so the trial continued.
papers.statistics: Prespecified safety analysis with rate ratios and 95% CIs (Stata and Python 3.8.5).
papers.availability: Trial registered; data per trial governance.

papers.title: Automated quantitative tumour response assessment of MRI in neuro-oncology with artificial neural networks: a multicentre, retrospective study
papers.authors: Kickingereder P, Isensee F, Tursunova I, Petersen J, Neuberger U, et al., Maier-Hein KH
papers.aim: To automate brain tumour volume measurement and response assessment from MRI.
papers.method: Deep network trained on Heidelberg data, tested on a multicentre EORTC trial data set, compared with RANO assessment.
papers.result: Automated volumetric assessment was a more reliable measure of time to progression than standard RANO, and worked across many centres.
papers.tools: ANN (U-Net type), multi-sequence MRI
papers.gap: Retrospective, mostly glioblastoma.
papers.relation: Brain tumour MRI clinical validation example, and supports our follow-up agent using tumour volume.
papers.limitations: Western centres. Future: prospective use.
papers.methodologyDetail: Brain tumour response is usually judged with RANO, which relies on manual two-dimensional measurements that radiologists often disagree on. This Heidelberg team trained a neural network on MRI from 455 glioma patients to outline the enhancing tumour and the surrounding T2/FLAIR abnormality automatically, then used the volume changes over time to decide when the tumour progressed. Tested on 40 local patients followed over 239 scans and on a large European trial run at 38 hospitals, the automated method agreed with expert volumetric judgement in 87% of cases, versus only 51% agreement between local and central RANO readers, and its progression times predicted survival better. It ran in about 10 minutes per scan in a simulated clinical setting. For our PhD it is strong evidence that automated volumetry improves reproducibility in neuro-oncology and a model for evaluating our segmentation agent against clinical endpoints in O4.
papers.studyDesign: Multicentre retrospective development and validation study with longitudinal testing and a simulated clinical deployment.
papers.datasets: Training: 455 adults with glioblastoma or lower-grade glioma at Heidelberg University Hospital (one MRI each, July 2009 - March 2017). Testing: Heidelberg longitudinal set of 40 patients (239 MRI scans) and the multi-institutional EORTC-26101 phase 2/3 trial dataset acquired at 38 European institutions; Heidelberg simulation dataset for deployment.
papers.preprocessing: Automated pipeline: brain extraction, co-registration of T1, contrast T1, T2/FLAIR sequences, intensity normalisation; reference segmentations by radiologists.
papers.modelDetails: Artificial neural network (U-Net-based, nnU-Net precursor from the same group) segmenting contrast-enhancing tumour (CE) and non-enhancing T2/FLAIR abnormality (NE); volumetric time-to-progression rules derived from CE and NE volume changes.
papers.training: Supervised training on the Heidelberg training dataset with independent longitudinal testing.
papers.evaluation: Agreement of volumetric time to progression with radiologist ground truth versus agreement of local and central RANO; time to progression as surrogate for overall survival (Cox models with treatment covariate); processing time in simulated deployment.
papers.baselines: Manual 2D RANO assessment (local and central review).
papers.results: Reliability: 87% agreement (266/306) for ANN-based time to progression versus 51% (155/306) for local vs central RANO - a 36% margin (p<0.0001); ANN-based time to progression was a better surrogate for overall survival (HR 2.59, 95% CI 1.86-3.60) than central RANO (HR 2.07, 1.46-2.92); baseline CE volume (HR 1.02 per cm3) and early CE change were strong survival predictors; about 10 minutes computation per scan in simulated clinical use.
papers.statistics: Cox proportional hazards models, agreement percentages, 95% CIs.
papers.availability: Software framework integrated into an application-ready infrastructure (DKFZ MITK-based).

papers.title: Explainability for artificial intelligence in healthcare: a multidisciplinary perspective
papers.authors: Amann J, Blasimme A, Vayena E, Frey D, Madai VI
papers.venue: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making
papers.aim: To look at explainability from technical, legal, medical and patient views.
papers.method: Multidisciplinary analysis (perspective paper).
papers.result: Says explainability is needed for informed consent, trust and responsibility, not only a technical feature.
papers.tools: Perspective / ethics
papers.gap: No experiments.
papers.relation: Supports our 'transparency of basis' principle and how we explain escalation decisions to clinicians.
papers.limitations: Conceptual. Future: practical guidance.
papers.methodologyDetail: This paper asks why explainability matters for medical AI, looking at it from four angles. Technically, it discusses how explanations can be produced and how they help developers. Legally, explanations matter for informed consent, approval as a medical device and deciding who is liable. Medically, doctors need to understand AI advice to check it against their own judgement, and patients need it to share in decisions. The authors then test these points against the four principles of biomedical ethics and conclude that leaving out explainability puts patient autonomy and safety at risk. For our PhD it supports building explanations and deferral reasons into the clinician interface and is useful for the ethics discussion of O4.
papers.studyDesign: Multidisciplinary conceptual analysis with ethical assessment.
papers.datasets: Not applicable (conceptual); AI-based clinical decision support systems as the case in point.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable. Analytical framework: technological, legal, medical and patient perspectives, then ethics by Beauchamp and Childress principles (autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative argument across perspectives.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Explainability is needed for informed consent, medical-device certification and liability (legal); clinicians need it to check and integrate AI advice and patients to take part in shared decisions; omitting explainability threatens core ethical principles, so it should be a requirement rather than an option.
papers.statistics: Not applicable.
papers.availability: Open access (BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making 2020).

papers.title: Real-World Integration of a Sepsis Deep Learning Technology Into Routine Clinical Care: Implementation Study
papers.authors: Sendak MP, Ratliff W, Sarro D, Alderton E, Futoma J, Gao M, Nichols M, Revoir M, Yashar F, Miller C, Kester K, Sandhu S, Corey K, Brajer N, Tan C, Lin A, Brown T, Engelbosch S, Anstrom K, Elish MC, Heller K, Donohoe R, Theiling J, Poon E, Balu S, Bedoya A, O'Brien C
papers.aim: To describe how a sepsis deep learning tool (Sepsis Watch) was put into daily use at Duke.
papers.method: Implementation study: governance, workflow design, training of rapid response nurses, monitoring.
papers.result: Tool was integrated with a clear team, workflow and governance. Lessons on clinician roles and trust.
papers.tools: Deep learning on EHR data, clinical workflow
papers.gap: Outcome effect not fully reported in this paper.
papers.relation: Gives practical lessons on governance, roles and monitoring we need for the registry deployment.
papers.limitations: One US hospital. Future: outcome studies.

papers.title: Foundations for an Empirically Determined Scale of Trust in Automated Systems
papers.authors: Jian JY, Bisantz AM, Drury CG
papers.aim: To build a questionnaire that measures human trust in automation.
papers.method: Word elicitation and rating studies, cluster analysis to form scale items.
papers.result: 12-item trust scale, still widely used in human-AI studies.
papers.tools: Questionnaire development
papers.gap: Not made for AI or medicine.
papers.relation: Ready tool to measure clinician trust in O4 (together with SUS for usability and NASA-TLX for workload).
papers.limitations: Old, general automation. Future: AI-specific validation.
papers.methodologyDetail: Before this study, questionnaires on trust in automation were written from theory rather than from how people actually use the word 'trust'. The authors first asked people to list words related to trust and distrust, then had participants rate how strongly these words relate to trust between people, trust in machines and trust in general, and finally collected paired comparisons for cluster analysis. Trust and distrust turned out to be opposites on one scale, and the meaning of trust was similar whether it was about people or machines. Twelve clusters became the 12 items of a trust-in-automation scale that is still widely used. For our PhD this validated 12-item scale is a ready instrument for measuring clinicians' trust in the brain tumour system in O4.
papers.studyDesign: Three-phase empirical scale development study (word elicitation, questionnaire, paired comparison with cluster analysis).
papers.datasets: Phase 1: 7 graduate students in linguistics or English (native speakers) listed words related to trust and distrust; phases 2 and 3: further participant groups rated word relatedness for human-human trust, human-machine trust and general trust, and made paired comparisons.
papers.preprocessing: Compilation and reduction of elicited words; similarity matrices from paired comparisons.
papers.modelDetails: Not a model. Analysis: comparison of trust and distrust word sets across trust types; cluster analysis of word similarities yielding 12 factors; 12-item trust-in-automation scale.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Overlap of words across trust types; cluster structure; stability of similarity matrix with increasing participants.
papers.baselines: Earlier theory-based trust questionnaires (e.g., Lee and Moray; Muir and Moray).
papers.results: Trust and distrust behaved as opposite ends of one dimension rather than separate concepts; trust components were similar for human-human, human-machine and general trust; cluster analysis identified 12 factors used to build a 12-item scale of trust in automated systems (later widely known as the Jian trust scale).
papers.statistics: Cluster analysis and rating statistics.
papers.availability: Scale items published in the paper.

papers.title: Is the Most Accurate AI the Best Teammate? Optimizing AI for Teamwork
papers.authors: Bansal G, Nushi B, Kamar E, Horvitz E, Weld DS
papers.relation: Argues that team performance, not AI accuracy alone, is the right measure, which shapes how O4 judges decision-support benefit.

papers.title: Role of Human-AI Interaction in Selective Prediction
papers.authors: Bondi E, Koster R, Sheahan H, et al.
papers.relation: Tests experimentally how telling humans about the AI's deferral changes their performance, which bears directly on how escalations should be presented to clinicians.

papers.title: Effective Human-AI Teams via Learned Natural Language Rules and Onboarding
papers.authors: Mozannar H, Lee J, Wei D, Sattigeri P, Das S, Sontag D
papers.aim: To teach people when to rely on, ignore or collaborate with an AI by learning data-grounded rules described in natural language and teaching them in onboarding.
papers.method: IntegrAI: collect human decisions with AI advice, discover regions in an embedding space (CLIP or text embeddings) where human reliance should change, describe each region with an LLM via iterative contrastive prompting, and teach the rules in an onboarding stage with a Human-AI card; evaluated in randomized user studies.
papers.result: Onboarding with learned rules improved human-AI team accuracy by 5.2% over no onboarding on traffic-light detection (BDD); on MMLU question answering onboarding had no effect, and showing only AI-integration recommendations hurt performance.
papers.tools: CLIP and sentence embeddings, GPT-3.5-turbo for region descriptions, Prolific crowdsourcing.
papers.gap: Lay crowd workers, not clinicians; gains task-dependent.
papers.relation: Onboards users with rules describing when to rely on the AI, which offers a way to build appropriate clinician trust before the clinical evaluation.
papers.limitations: Non-medical tasks; short-term effects only.
papers.methodologyDetail: People working with AI often rely on it too much or too little. IntegrAI first records how people actually use an AI's advice, then searches an embedding space (CLIP for images) for pockets of cases where they should change behaviour - for example, 'ignore the AI on highways at night'. A language model writes a short description for each pocket, refining it with contrasting examples. Participants then go through an onboarding session that teaches these rules with examples and a 'Human-AI card' summarising what the AI is and how well it performs. On traffic-light detection, onboarded teams were 5.2% more accurate; on general knowledge questions there was no gain. For our PhD it suggests O4 should include an onboarding step that teaches clinicians when the system is and is not reliable, alongside per-case confidence.
papers.studyDesign: Algorithm development plus randomized online user studies (IRB exempt).
papers.datasets: BDD100K driving images (is there a traffic light? noisy images) and MMLU multiple-choice questions; participants recruited on Prolific (English-fluent, >98% approval, >60 submissions), paid $3 per 20 BDD examples (+$2 bonus) or per 15 MMLU questions.
papers.preprocessing: Inputs embedded with CLIP (images) or text embeddings (questions); prior human reliance data collected before region discovery.
papers.modelDetails: Region discovery: regions as centroids with scaled Euclidean neighbourhoods in embedding space where human prior behaviour should be corrected; region description: LLM generates text then refines with counterexamples (contrastive); onboarding teaches each rule with examples; Human-AI card summarises AI inputs, outputs, training data and performance.
papers.training: Greedy region discovery optimising expected improvement in team decisions.
papers.evaluation: Human-AI team accuracy across conditions (no onboarding, onboarding, recommendations only, onboarding + recommendations); separate evaluation of region discovery and description quality.
papers.baselines: No onboarding; AI-integration recommendations only; prior onboarding where participants write their own descriptions (only 50% accurate).
papers.results: BDD: +5.2% team accuracy with onboarding vs none (significant). MMLU: no effect from onboarding; recommendations-only had a negative effect.
papers.statistics: Between-subject comparisons with significance tests and confidence intervals.

papers.title: Bayesian modeling of human-AI complementarity
papers.authors: Steyvers M, Tejeda H, Kerrigan G, Smyth P
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.relation: Gives a formal model for when combining human and AI judgements beats either one alone, which can underpin the O4 analysis of diagnostic performance.

papers.title: Conformal prediction under ambiguous ground truth
papers.authors: Stutz D, Roy AG, Matejovicova T, Strachan P, Cemgil AT, Doucet A
papers.aim: To make conformal prediction guarantees valid when ground-truth labels are ambiguous because experts disagree.
papers.method: Aggregate expert annotations into a non-degenerate label distribution (plausibilities) and apply Monte Carlo conformal prediction that samples multiple pseudo-labels per calibration example; extended to multi-label classification and data-augmented calibration.
papers.result: In dermatology classification with strong expert disagreement, standard CP on voted labels calibrated for 72% coverage under-covered expert annotations by about 10% on average (aggregated coverage 0.62 vs voted 0.73); Monte Carlo CP closed the gap empirically and theoretically.
papers.tools: Conformal prediction (split CP, Monte Carlo CP), inverse rank normalisation for plausibilities, MobileNet V2, AutoAugment.
papers.gap: Needs multiple expert annotations per case; synthetic and dermatology data only.
papers.relation: Handles uncertainty calibration when clinicians disagree on the reference label, which is common when validating diagnoses against expert panels.
papers.limitations: Monte Carlo CP gives slightly larger sets; relies on quality of the aggregation model.
papers.methodologyDetail: Conformal prediction turns a model's scores into a set of possible answers guaranteed to contain the true label with a chosen probability (for example 90%). But 'true labels' in medicine are often a majority vote of experts who disagree. The authors show that when dermatologists disagreed, standard conformal prediction calibrated for 72% coverage actually covered expert opinion only about 62% of the time. Their fix converts each case's expert opinions into a probability distribution over labels and, during calibration, samples several possible labels per case (Monte Carlo CP), which restores the promised coverage. For our PhD, where neuroradiologists and pathologists may disagree on tumour type or grade, deferral thresholds should be calibrated against aggregated expert labels rather than a single consensus label.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological study with theory and case studies.
papers.datasets: Dermatology (skin condition) dataset with multiple dermatologist annotations per case (Roy et al. 2022; classifier with 72.6% top-3 accuracy); ImageNet first 5k test images with 25 AutoAugment augmentations each (MobileNet V2, 71.3% top-1 on originals, 60.2% on augmented); synthetic data.
papers.preprocessing: Expert opinions (partial rankings) converted to plausibility distributions via inverse rank normalisation.
papers.modelDetails: Monte Carlo CP: for each calibration example sample m pseudo-labels from aggregated distribution, compute conformity scores, then choose threshold for guarantee w.r.t. aggregated distribution (with ECDF and p-value combination variants).
papers.training: Not applicable (post-hoc calibration on held-out data).
papers.evaluation: Voted coverage, aggregated coverage, prediction set size, across many random calibration/test splits.
papers.baselines: Standard split CP calibrated on majority-voted labels.
papers.results: Standard CP: target 72%, aggregated coverage only about 62% (shortfall about 10%); Monte Carlo CP restored target coverage with modestly larger sets; similar gap and fix for augmented ImageNet images.
papers.statistics: Coverage guarantees proven; empirical averages over repeated trials.
papers.availability: Code from Google DeepMind (referenced in paper).

papers.title: Are we using appropriate segmentation metrics? Identifying correlates of human expert perception for CNN training beyond rolling the DICE coefficient
papers.authors: Kofler F, Ezhov I, Isensee F, et al.
papers.venue: Journal of Machine Learning for Biomedical Imaging (MELBA)
papers.aim: To find out how well standard segmentation metrics match expert radiologists' judgement of segmentation quality, and to design losses closer to that judgement.
papers.method: Psychophysical rating experiments: experts rated glioma MRI and ultrasound segmentations on a 6-star Likert scale; correlations with many metrics (Dice, Jaccard, Hausdorff, sensitivity, etc.); compound loss functions built with classical statistics and tested in CNN training.
papers.result: Standard metrics and losses correlated only moderately with expert ratings, worst for the clinically important enhancing tumour; experts consistently rated CNN segmentations better than the human reference labels; new compound losses did not reach the intended gains.
papers.tools: BraTS glioma MRI, 2D ultrasound grey/white matter data, CNNs (nnU-Net / U-Net variants), Pearson correlation analysis.
papers.gap: Rating experiments on limited case sets; loss design did not succeed.
papers.relation: Links glioma segmentation metrics to neuroradiologists' quality ratings, which supports clinician-validated evaluation of the outputs used for surgical planning.
papers.limitations: 15 glioma raters mostly male from six institutions; single rating session per expert.
papers.methodologyDetail: Segmentation models are usually judged by the Dice score, but is that what radiologists care about? Fifteen radiologists from six institutions rated glioma MRI segmentations - some drawn by humans, some by CNNs, shown without telling which - on a one-to-six star scale, and the same was done for brain ultrasound. Their ratings matched Dice and other common metrics only moderately, especially for the enhancing tumour, which matters most clinically. Surprisingly, they consistently preferred the CNN outlines to the official human reference labels. Attempts to train with losses closer to expert opinion did not clearly help. For our PhD it means O4 should include blinded clinician ratings of segmentation quality and not only Dice, and should question how reference labels are made.
papers.studyDesign: Psychophysical expert rating study plus CNN training experiments.
papers.datasets: Multimodal 3D glioma MRI (BraTS-style; segmentations of whole tumour, tumour core, enhancing tumour, necrosis, oedema) from reference and CNN outputs; 2D ultrasound grey/white matter segmentations. Glioma raters: 15 radiologists (2 female, 13 male) from 6 institutions, 10.0 +/- 5.1 years' experience, mean age 37.7 +/- 4.8; about 50 minutes per session.
papers.preprocessing: Stimuli shown on neutral grey background with colour-blind-friendly palette; toggleable semi-opaque labels.
papers.modelDetails: Not a new model; compound losses combining metrics weighted by their correlation with expert ratings for CNN training.
papers.training: CNN training with standard Dice-based and proposed compound losses (GPU, PyTorch).
papers.evaluation: Pearson correlation between metrics and expert star ratings by label; comparison of ratings for reference vs CNN segmentations.
papers.baselines: Dice and other standard metrics and losses.
papers.results: Moderate metric-rating correlations, weakest for enhancing tumour; CNN segmentations rated higher than reference labels across all experiments; compound losses gave no clear improvement.
papers.statistics: Pearson correlation matrices; rating distributions.
papers.availability: Code and rating tool referenced on GitHub (Kofler et al.).

papers.title: Metrics reloaded: recommendations for image analysis validation
papers.authors: Maier-Hein L, Reinke A, Godau P, et al.
papers.aim: To give researchers a structured, problem-aware way to choose validation metrics for biomedical image analysis.
papers.method: Multi-stage Delphi consensus by an international consortium of 73 experts (156 contributors overall, plus crowdsourced pitfalls) producing the 'problem fingerprint' concept and decision guidance for image classification, object detection, semantic and instance segmentation, implemented in an online tool.
papers.result: Metrics Reloaded framework and online tool recommending metric pools (e.g., Dice plus a boundary metric such as NSD for segmentation; calibration metrics when probabilities are used) with documented pitfalls, demonstrated on many biomedical use cases.
papers.tools: Delphi process, Metrics Reloaded online tool, problem fingerprint questionnaire.
papers.gap: Covers classification-type problems only (not regression or reconstruction); needs updates as methods change.
papers.relation: Gives guidance on choosing validation metrics for classification and segmentation, which helps design O4's diagnostic-performance evaluation.
papers.limitations: Consensus recommendations rather than empirical proof; complex for newcomers.
papers.methodologyDetail: Choosing the wrong metric can make a poor model look good. Metrics Reloaded was built by more than 70 international experts through several Delphi rounds, with input from 156 researchers and a public campaign collecting metric pitfalls. Users describe their task with a 'problem fingerprint' - what matters clinically, how big and how many the target structures are, how imbalanced the data are, and what the algorithm outputs - and the framework recommends a set of metrics and warns about traps (for example Dice behaving badly on tiny lesions or empty images). For our PhD it will guide the metrics in O3 and O4: Dice plus a boundary metric for segmentation, lesion-wise detection metrics, and AUROC plus calibration metrics for classification and deferral.
papers.studyDesign: International multi-stage Delphi consensus with crowdsourcing and use-case demonstrations.
papers.datasets: Expert consortium of 73 members (image analysis, ML, statistics, epidemiology, biology, medicine); 156 researchers contributed (84 acknowledged); survey with 186 participants, 82 giving free-text feedback; kick-off workshop December 2020.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Not a model. Framework: problem fingerprint (domain interest, target structure properties, dataset properties, algorithm output) mapped to recommended metric pools and pitfalls for four problem categories.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Delphi agreement on each recommendation; application to biomedical use cases.
papers.baselines: Common practice (ad-hoc metric choice, Dice-only reporting).
papers.results: Consensus framework and tool; recommendations include combining overlap and boundary metrics for segmentation, per-object metrics for detection, prevalence-aware and calibration metrics for classification, and explicit handling of empty references.
papers.statistics: Delphi consensus levels.
papers.availability: Online tool: https://metrics-reloaded.dkfz.de and open-source implementation (MONAI).

papers.title: AgentClinic: a multimodal benchmark for tool-using clinical AI agents
papers.authors: Schmidgall S, Ziaei R, Harris C, et al.
papers.relation: Evaluates multimodal, tool-using clinical agents in simulated interactive settings, which is relevant to benchmarking the multi-agent framework before clinicians are involved.

papers.title: Towards conversational diagnostic artificial intelligence
papers.authors: Tu T, Schaekermann M, Palepu A, et al.
papers.aim: To build and evaluate AMIE, an LLM-based system optimised for diagnostic dialogue (history-taking, diagnosis, management and empathy), and compare it with primary care physicians in a simulated clinical examination.
papers.method: AMIE was instruction fine-tuned from PaLM 2 on real medical QA, summarisation and dialogue data plus simulated dialogues produced by a self-play multi-agent environment (vignette generator, patient agent, doctor agent, moderator and critic, all played by AMIE). At inference it uses a three-step chain-of-reasoning. It was compared with 20 PCPs in a randomised, double-blind crossover remote text-based OSCE on 149 scenarios, rated by patient actors and 23 specialist physicians.
papers.result: AMIE had significantly higher top-k differential diagnosis accuracy than PCPs for all k (p < 0.05, bootstrap n = 10,000, FDR-corrected). AMIE was rated superior on 28 of 32 axes by specialists and 24 of 26 axes by patient actors, and non-inferior on the rest. PCPs gave fewer diagnoses (min 3, mean 5.39) than AMIE (10). Diagnostic accuracy plateaued within the first 10 turns for both. Self-play dialogues were preferred over baseline dialogues by auto-evaluation (self-play preferred 0.24-0.33, baseline 0.18-0.22, ties 0.46-0.58 across four PACES criteria). Exact top-k accuracy percentages are shown in figures only.
papers.tools: Base LLM PaLM 2 (instruction fine-tuned); Med-PaLM 2 as DDx auto-evaluator; PaLM-2 for passage filtering; internet search engine for vignette retrieval; synchronous text-chat interface; MedQA, MultiMedBench, MIMIC-III; GMCPQ, PACES and PCCBP rating instruments. Hardware not reported.
papers.gap: No real patients and no real clinical workflow; text-chat only; no uncertainty estimation or deferral mechanism; no imaging; no fairness and bias evaluation; pediatrics, psychiatry, intensive care and inpatient cases excluded; no low-resource language evaluation; closed model.
papers.relation: Shows a rigorous blinded evaluation of a diagnostic AI by specialist clinicians, a model for clinician-rated assessment of quality and safety.
papers.limitations: Unfamiliar synchronous text-chat for PCPs, not representative of usual practice or telemedicine; patient actors may describe symptoms more clearly than real patients; AMIE's longer, structured responses limit blinding and may inflate empathy ratings; rubric is a pilot, not definitive; one specialist per case; not powered for specialty or location comparisons; no multi-morbidity or longitudinal cases; excluded psychiatry, pediatrics, intensive care and inpatient care; fairness and bias not assessed; multilingual and low-resource language robustness not tested. Future work: real-world prospective studies, assistive (human-AI) settings, uncertainty estimation for deferral to clinicians, red teaming, fairness frameworks, up-to-date knowledge.
papers.methodologyDetail: AMIE starts from PaLM 2. The team built a training mixture of static data: MedQA (11,450 train questions plus 191 with expert reasoning), 64 expert long-form answers, 65 clinician summaries of MIMIC-III notes, and 98,919 real US clinic transcripts, cleaned of nurse turns and paraverbal tags and split 90/10 (89,027 train, 9,892 validation) by condition and visit reason. Because real dialogues are noisy and cover limited conditions, they added a self-play multi-agent environment. For each condition, 60 web passages (20 on demographics, 20 on symptoms, 20 on management) were retrieved, filtered by PaLM-2, and turned into patient vignettes by AMIE using a one-shot format. Then AMIE played three roles: a patient agent answering from the vignette, a doctor agent asking at most two questions per turn, and a moderator deciding when the conversation had ended. A fourth critic agent, which knew the true diagnosis, gave feedback on empathy, question count and diagnostic coverage; the doctor agent replayed the dialogue with this feedback, twice. Each iteration produced 11,686 dialogues from 5,230 conditions (4 per common condition from 613; 2 per less common condition from 4,617). These refined dialogues were added to the next fine-tuning round (outer loop). Training predicted the next turn, sampling about 3 target turns per role per dialogue. At inference AMIE used three calls: analyse the case (symptoms, differential, missing information, confidence and urgency), draft a reply with questions or escalation, and refine for factual accuracy and empathy. Validation was a randomised blinded crossover OSCE: 149 scenario packs, 20 patient actors, 20 PCPs, text chat up to 20 minutes, ranked DDx of 3-10 items, and ratings by 23 matched specialists and the actors. Statistics used 10,000-sample bootstrap and Wilcoxon tests with FDR correction. A PhD student can reuse the critic loop, the confidence step and the OSCE-style blinded crossover design, adding a calibrated deferral rule that AMIE lacks.
papers.studyDesign: Model development plus prospective randomised, double-blind, counterbalanced crossover simulation study (remote OSCE). Google Research and Google DeepMind with OSCE laboratories in Canada and India; scenario packs from Canada, India and the UK.
papers.datasets: Training: (1) MedQA (USMLE-style, 4-5 options): 11,450 training and 1,273 test questions, plus 191 training questions with expert step-by-step reasoning. (2) Long-form medical QA: expert responses to 64 questions from HealthSearchQA, LiveQA and MedicationQA (MultiMedBench). (3) Medical summarisation: 65 clinician-written summaries of MIMIC-III notes (MIMIC-III has about 2 million notes across 13 types; 5 notes per category selected, minimum total length 400 tokens, at least one nursing note per patient). (4) Real-world dialogue: 98,919 de-identified audio transcripts of in-person US clinic visits from over 1,000 clinicians over 10 years, 51 specialties and 168 conditions/visit reasons; mean 149.8 turns (P25 = 75.0, P75 = 196.0); only doctor-patient dialogues kept. (5) Simulated dialogues: 11,686 per fine-tuning iteration from 5,230 conditions, drawn from Health QA (613 common conditions), MalaCards (18,455 less common) and MedicineNet (4,617 less common); mean 21.28 turns (P25 = 19.0, P75 = 25.0). Evaluation: 149 OSCE scenario packs (India 75, Canada 60, UK 14) covering cardiovascular 29, respiratory 30, gastroenterology 31, neurology 30, urology/obstetrics/gynaecology 15, internal medicine 14; 149 simulated patients (Canada 67, India 82). Excluded: pediatrics, psychiatry, intensive care and inpatient management.
papers.preprocessing: Real-world dialogues: removed non doctor/patient roles (for example nurses) and paraverbal annotations such as [LAUGHING] and [INAUDIBLE]; stratified split by condition category and visit reason into 90% training (89,027 conversations) and 10% validation (9,892). Target turns: on average 3 turns per role sampled per dialogue, from turns of at least 30 characters. Vignettes: 60 passages retrieved per condition (20 each on demographics, symptoms, management), filtered by PaLM-2 with a Yes/No relevance prompt. Few-shot (1-5) exemplars added for all tasks except dialogue and long-form generation.
papers.modelDetails: Base: PaLM 2, instruction fine-tuned with task-specific instructions (doctor role, patient role, QA/reasoning, EHR summarisation). Self-play environment: (1) Vignette generator: web search for the condition, PaLM-2 passage filtering, AMIE generates 2 vignettes per prompt with a one-shot format example. (2) Simulated dialogue generator with three agents played by AMIE: patient agent (answers honestly from vignette), doctor agent (empathetic clinician, no more than two questions per turn), moderator (decides Yes/No whether the conversation has ended: diagnosis and plan given and no patient questions left, or a goodbye). Dialogue starts with 'Doctor: So, how can I help you today?'. (3) Self-play critic: a fourth AMIE agent that knows the ground-truth diagnosis gives in-context feedback on empathy and professionalism, at most one or two questions per response, not revealing it is AI, and asking enough to identify at least two likely differentials; the doctor agent redoes the dialogue from scratch with its previous history; repeated twice per fine-tuning iteration (inner loop). Outer loop: refined dialogues added to the next fine-tuning round. Inference chain-of-reasoning (three sequential calls): (1) analyse patient information - summarise positive and negative symptoms and history, produce current differential, note missing information, assess confidence in the differential and its urgency; (2) formulate response and action - answer, ask questions to fill gaps, recommend immediate action such as emergency visit if needed, present differential if confident; (3) refine response for factuality, no repetition, empathy and clear format. No explicit numeric confidence threshold or deferral rule is reported.
papers.training: Iterative instruction fine-tuning: first round on static datasets only; later rounds also on self-play simulated dialogues (11,686 per iteration). Dialogue training predicts the next turn given previous turns. Optimizer, learning rate, batch size, number of steps or iterations, hardware and training time are not reported.
papers.evaluation: Randomised, blinded crossover remote OSCE: each of 149 simulated patients had two text consultations, one with a PCP and one with AMIE, in random order, maximum 20 minutes, agents told not to reveal identity. 20 board-certified PCPs (10 India, 10 Canada; 3-25 years post-residency, median 7) and 20 patient actors (10 India, 10 Canada). After each consultation the agent gave a ranked DDx (3 to 10 conditions) and recommendations on escalation, investigations, treatment, management and follow-up. Patient actors rated GMCPQ, PACES (Managing Patient Concerns, Maintaining Patient Welfare) and PCCBP 'Fostering the Relationship' items. 23 specialist physicians (India 14, North America 6, UK 3; 1-36 years post-residency, median 5), matched by specialty and region, rated both agents per case in random blinded order on DDx accuracy, appropriateness and comprehensiveness, management items, PACES, PCCBP and confabulations. Top-k accuracy = percentage of cases where the ground-truth (or accepted) diagnosis is in the top k, a match being exact, very close or closely related as judged by the specialist. Auto-evaluation: Med-PaLM 2 Y/N matcher for DDx; AMIE self-CoT 5-shot rater for four PACES criteria, validated by rank-order agreement on 149 dialogue pairs and against a second specialist on 139 pairs. Ablations: DDx by specialty, by location (67 Canada, 82 India; 40 shared scenarios), AMIE DDx from PCP transcripts, accuracy vs number of turns, and self-play vs baseline on 1,142 simulated dialogues.
papers.baselines: 20 board-certified primary care physicians (PCPs) in the same text-chat setting. For auto-evaluation prompting: 0-shot, 5-shot and shuffled 5-shot self-CoT; random guessing according to specialist preference distribution; second specialist (inter-specialist agreement). For self-play: baseline simulated dialogues without critic revision.
papers.results: DDx (specialist-rated, 149 cases): AMIE higher top-k accuracy than PCPs for all k from 1 to 10, against both ground truth and accepted differential, p < 0.05 after FDR; exact percentages shown only in Figure 3. PCP DDx length min 3, mean 5.39. Auto-evaluated DDx: AMIE better for k > 2 (ground truth) and k > 4 (accepted differential). AMIE DDx from PCP transcripts vs own transcripts: no significant difference, both better than PCP DDx. By specialty: AMIE matched or exceeded PCPs in all six, largest gains in respiratory and cardiovascular; both weaker in obstetrics/gynaecology and internal medicine. By location: higher accuracy in Canada (significant at all k) than India (not significant); on 40 shared scenarios performance equivalent. Turns: top-3 accuracy plateaued within 10 turns. Conversation quality: patient actors rated AMIE better on 24 of 26 axes (no difference for Respecting Patient's Privacy, N = 108, and Acknowledging Mistakes, N = 41); specialists rated AMIE better on 28 of 32 axes (no difference for escalation recommendation, treatment inappropriate avoided, follow-up recommendation, confabulation absent; N = 149). Self-play vs baseline (auto-evaluation, four PACES criteria): self-play preferred 0.24 to 0.33, baseline preferred 0.18 to 0.22, tie 0.46 to 0.58. Auto-evaluator rank-order agreement was above chance and about equal to inter-specialist agreement (values shown only in figures).
papers.statistics: DDx accuracy: bootstrap tests with 10,000 samples and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction across all k. Patient actor and specialist ratings: Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with FDR correction; 'Cannot rate / Does not apply' cases excluded. Significance levels reported as p < 0.05, p < 0.01, p < 0.001. Inter-rater: rank-order agreement between auto-evaluation and specialists, and between two specialists on 139 pairs (values in figures). Confidence intervals not given in text.
papers.availability: Not available. Model, code and the licensed real-world dialogue dataset are not released; a model card is given in Table A.5. Public data used: MedQA, MultiMedBench, MIMIC-III (credentialed access).

papers.title: Towards accurate differential diagnosis with large language models
papers.authors: McDuff D, Schaekermann M, Tu T, et al.
papers.aim: To test whether an LLM optimised for diagnostic reasoning (AMIE) produces better differential diagnoses alone and as an aid to clinicians on difficult cases.
papers.method: 20 clinicians assessed 302 challenging NEJM clinicopathological case reports; each case read by two clinicians who first gave an unassisted differential, then were randomised to assistance from search engines and standard resources, or the same plus AMIE; outputs scored for top-n accuracy, quality, appropriateness and comprehensiveness.
papers.result: AMIE alone beat unassisted clinicians (top-10 accuracy 59.1% vs 33.6%, p=0.04). Clinicians assisted by AMIE reached 51.7% top-10 accuracy vs 36.1% unassisted (McNemar 45.7, p<0.01) and 44.4% with search only (McNemar 4.75, p=0.03), and produced more comprehensive differential lists.
papers.tools: AMIE (PaLM 2-based LLM fine-tuned for diagnostic dialogue and reasoning), search engines, standard medical resources, specialist raters.
papers.gap: Text case reports only (no images or real-time history-taking); case reports are unusually difficult and may not reflect routine practice.
papers.relation: Runs a reader study of clinicians with and without AI assistance on hard diagnoses, measuring how much assistance improves decisions, which matches O4's design.
papers.limitations: Published cases may overlap with LLM training data; clinicians not specialists for every case.
papers.methodologyDetail: AMIE is a large language model from Google tuned for diagnostic reasoning. Twenty clinicians worked through 302 difficult published case reports: they first wrote their own list of possible diagnoses, then revised it with help either from normal search tools and references or from those tools plus AMIE, assigned at random. AMIE on its own included the right diagnosis in its top ten 59% of the time against 34% for unaided clinicians, and clinicians using AMIE reached 52% compared with 44% for those using search alone, with more complete lists. For our PhD the study design - unaided answer first, then randomised assistance, measured against a reference diagnosis - is a template for O4, and it shows that AI assistance can raise clinicians' accuracy on hard cases.
papers.studyDesign: Randomised reader study with baseline unassisted assessment and two assisted arms.
papers.datasets: 302 real-world challenging case reports (New England Journal of Medicine clinicopathological conferences); 20 generalist clinicians; each case read by 2 clinicians.
papers.preprocessing: Case reports converted to text vignettes up to the point before final diagnosis.
papers.modelDetails: AMIE large language model optimised for clinical diagnostic reasoning, used through an interactive interface.
papers.training: Fine-tuning of the base LLM on medical QA, reasoning and dialogue data (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Top-1 and top-10 accuracy against final diagnosis; differential quality, appropriateness and comprehensiveness rated by specialists; McNemar tests.
papers.baselines: Unassisted clinicians; clinicians with search and standard resources.
papers.results: Standalone AMIE top-10 59.1% vs unassisted clinicians 33.6%; assisted with AMIE 51.7% vs 36.1% unassisted and 44.4% with search; more comprehensive lists with AMIE.
papers.statistics: McNemar tests, p-values.
papers.availability: Model not publicly released; study materials in supplementary information.

papers.title: To Trust or to Think: Cognitive Forcing Functions Can Reduce Overreliance on AI in AI-assisted Decision-making
papers.authors: Bucinca Z, Malaya MB, Gajos KZ
papers.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)
papers.aim: To test whether cognitive forcing functions reduce people's overreliance on incorrect AI suggestions compared with simple explainable AI.
papers.method: Randomized online experiment (199 Mechanical Turk participants) on a nutrition task; three cognitive forcing designs (on demand, update, wait) versus two simple explainable AI designs (explanation, explanation + confidence) and a no-AI baseline; Need for Cognition measured as moderator.
papers.result: Cognitive forcing functions significantly reduced overreliance on wrong AI suggestions compared with simple explainable AI, but participants rated them as less usable and liked them least - a trade-off between performance and preference; benefits were larger for people high in Need for Cognition.
papers.tools: Web experiment, simulated AI ingredient recogniser with explanations, Need for Cognition scale.
papers.gap: Lay participants and a non-medical task; short sessions.
papers.relation: Shows interface interventions that reduce over-reliance at some cost to workload and preference, a trade-off central to clinician trust and safety evaluation.
papers.limitations: Simulated AI with controlled errors; crowd workers; single task.
papers.methodologyDetail: People often accept an AI's suggestion even when it is wrong, and explanations alone do not fix this. Using dual-process theory, the authors tested 'cognitive forcing functions' that push people to think before agreeing: seeing the AI only on request, deciding first and then seeing the AI's answer, or waiting 30 seconds for the AI. In an online experiment with 199 participants choosing healthier ingredients from meal photos, these designs cut the number of times people followed wrong AI advice compared with plain explanations or confidence displays, but people found them more effortful and liked them less; those who enjoy thinking benefited most. For our PhD it gives concrete interface options for O4 to reduce automation bias in clinicians, and shows we must measure both accuracy and usability.
papers.studyDesign: Between-subjects randomized online experiment.
papers.datasets: 199 Amazon Mechanical Turk participants; meal images where participants replaced the highest-carbohydrate ingredient with a low-carb alternative of similar flavour; AI right on most trials and deliberately wrong on some.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Conditions: no AI; explanation (SXAI); uncertainty (explanation + AI confidence such as 87%); on demand (click to see AI); update (decide first, then see AI and revise); wait (30-second delay with 'AI is processing').
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Decision accuracy when AI was correct vs incorrect (overreliance), trust, perceived mental demand, preference and usability; moderation by Need for Cognition.
papers.baselines: No-AI condition and simple explainable AI conditions.
papers.results: Cognitive forcing conditions had higher accuracy on trials where the AI was wrong than simple XAI conditions; lowest subjective ratings for forcing designs; interaction with Need for Cognition.
papers.statistics: Mixed-effects / ANOVA-style comparisons with significance testing.

papers.title: Explanations Can Reduce Overreliance on AI Systems During Decision-Making
papers.authors: Vasconcelos H, Jorke M, Grunde-McLaughlin M, et al.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)
papers.relation: Models reliance as a cost-benefit choice and shows when explanations reduce over-reliance, which informs how to measure appropriate clinician reliance.

papers.title: Who Should I Trust: AI or Myself? Leveraging Human and AI Correctness Likelihood to Promote Appropriate Trust in AI-Assisted Decision-Making
papers.authors: Ma S, Lei Y, Wang X, et al.
papers.relation: Uses the likely correctness of both human and AI to calibrate trust, which matches the calibrated selective-autonomy approach and its trust outcomes.

papers.title: Appropriate Reliance on AI Advice: Conceptualization and the Effect of Explanations
papers.authors: Schemmer M, Kuehl N, Benz C, Bartos A, Satzger G
papers.relation: Defines measurable appropriate-reliance metrics that can be used to judge whether clinicians accept or override AI advice correctly.

papers.title: Towards a Science of Human-AI Decision Making: An Overview of Design Space in Empirical Human-Subject Studies
papers.authors: Lai V, Chen C, Smith-Renner A, Liao QV, Tan C
papers.relation: Surveys how human-subject studies of AI-assisted decisions are designed and measured, which guides the O4 study protocol.

papers.title: Uncertainty as a Form of Transparency: Measuring, Communicating, and Using Uncertainty
papers.authors: Bhatt U, Antoran J, Zhang Y, et al.
papers.venue: AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2021)
papers.relation: Covers how to measure uncertainty and show it to decision-makers, which is relevant to presenting escalation reasons to clinicians.

papers.title: Rethinking Human-AI Collaboration in Complex Medical Decision Making: A Case Study in Sepsis Diagnosis
papers.authors: Zhang S, Yu J, Xu X, et al.
papers.relation: Designs and evaluates with clinicians an AI that supports intermediate diagnostic steps rather than only giving a final answer, which informs the workload and usability evaluation.

papers.title: Ignore, Trust, or Negotiate: Understanding Clinician Acceptance of AI-Based Treatment Recommendations in Health Care
papers.authors: Sivaraman V, Bukowski LA, Levin J, Kahn JM, Perer A
papers.relation: Describes how clinicians accept or reject AI treatment recommendations, which bears on trust and safety outcomes for surgical-planning support.

papers.title: Designing AI for Trust and Collaboration in Time-Constrained Medical Decisions: A Sociotechnical Lens
papers.authors: Jacobs M, He J, Pradier MF, et al.
papers.aim: To understand what clinicians need from machine learning decision support tools for antidepressant treatment selection under real-world time and system constraints.
papers.method: Iterative co-design with primary care providers: Study 1 needs elicitation (semi-structured interviews and focus groups), design of a prototype tool with prognostic and treatment predictions, Study 2 prototype feedback sessions; qualitative thematic analysis.
papers.result: Decision support must fit the sociotechnical system - clinical processes, patient preferences, resource constraints and domain knowledge; tools should be multi-user (support patient-provider discussion) and give on-demand explanations focused on why predictions differ from the standard of care; common XAI trends may be inappropriate in short clinical visits.
papers.tools: Semi-structured interviews, focus groups, design prototypes, thematic analysis; Harvard IRB approval.
papers.gap: Primary care and depression only; qualitative with one academic centre.
papers.relation: Identifies clinician needs for trust and workflow fit under time pressure, which guides usability and workload evaluation.
papers.limitations: Small purposive sample; no outcome measurement.
papers.methodologyDetail: Rather than testing accuracy, this study asked primary care doctors how an AI tool for choosing antidepressants would actually fit their work. In a first round of interviews and small focus groups they described their needs; the team built a prototype showing patient prognosis and treatment predictions, then collected feedback in a second round. Clinicians wanted tools they can use together with the patient, short explanations only when they ask, and especially explanations when the AI disagrees with standard guidelines, while respecting limited visit time, costs and patient preferences. For our PhD it informs O4's interface: brief, on-demand explanations focused on why the system differs from the usual pathway, and outputs suitable for tumour-board and patient conversations.
papers.studyDesign: Qualitative human-centred design study in two rounds.
papers.datasets: Primary care providers (physicians, nurse practitioners, residents) who prescribe antidepressants at a large US academic medical centre, recruited by email with a $20 gift card; Study 2 included new and returning participants.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Prototype decision support tool combining patient-level prognostic predictions with treatment selection support and access to validation data.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative themes from interviews, focus groups (at most two participants) and prototype feedback.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Key themes: time pressure in visits; need to align with guidelines and explain discrepancies; involve patients in decisions; consider costs and insurance; trust built through validation evidence and familiarity.
papers.statistics: Not applicable (qualitative).

papers.title: "Brilliant AI Doctor" in Rural Clinics: Challenges in AI-Powered Clinical Decision Support System Deployment
papers.authors: Wang D, Wang L, Zhang Z, et al.
papers.aim: To understand clinicians' real post-adoption experience with an AI clinical decision support system in rural clinics of a developing country.
papers.method: Ethnographic field study: in-situ observations, semi-structured interviews and contextual inquiries with 22 clinicians in 6 rural clinics in China using the 'Brilliant Doctor' AI-CDSS; thematic analysis.
papers.result: Tensions found: misalignment with local context and workflow (short visits, high load), technical limitations and usability barriers (poor EHR interoperability, low confidence scores such as 30%), and lack of transparency and trust; yet all participants were positive about AI as 'a doctor's AI assistant'.
papers.tools: Observation, semi-structured interviews, contextual inquiry, qualitative coding.
papers.gap: Single commercial system in one country; no quantitative outcomes.
papers.relation: Field study of clinical decision support in low-resource rural clinics, directly relevant to usability, workload and trust in the Sri Lankan setting.
papers.limitations: Small qualitative sample; IRB and access via clinic presidents may bias participants.
papers.methodologyDetail: Most AI studies stop at accuracy. Here researchers went to six rural clinics in China where an AI decision support system called Brilliant Doctor was already installed, watched 22 clinicians at work and interviewed them. They found the system did not fit local reality: visits were very short, the AI needed lots of typing, did not connect well with other systems, sometimes offered diagnoses with low confidence like 30%, and gave little explanation, so clinicians often ignored it. Still, every clinician wanted AI to become a helpful assistant. For our PhD, as a deployment in a resource-limited setting similar to Sri Lanka, it shows that O4 must test workflow fit, input burden and how confidence is presented - a low score should trigger a clear referral or deferral, not confusion.
papers.studyDesign: Qualitative ethnographic field study in rural clinics.
papers.datasets: 22 clinicians (9 female) from 6 rural clinics in China using the Brilliant Doctor AI-CDSS embedded in the EHR; clinics recruited via presidents who also secured IRB approvals.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Brilliant Doctor AI-CDSS (neural network and knowledge-graph based diagnosis and treatment suggestions with confidence scores) integrated in the clinic EHR.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Themes from observations and interviews about use, workflow, usability, trust and attitudes.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Clinicians often ignored or closed the system because of time pressure, input burden and low confidence suggestions; distrust from opaque recommendations; strong hope for future collaborative AI assistants.
papers.statistics: Not applicable (qualitative).

papers.title: BreastScreening-AI: Evaluating medical intelligent agents for human-AI interactions
papers.authors: Calisto FM, Santiago C, Nunes N, Nascimento JC
papers.aim: To evaluate how clinicians accept, interact with and are affected by an AI assistant integrated into a multimodal breast imaging workflow.
papers.method: BreastScreening-AI framework with a DenseNet severity classifier (BI-RADS) shown as an assistant that clinicians can accept or reject; within-subject comparison of Clinician-Only and Clinician-AI scenarios on test patients of different severities; quantitative (errors, time) and qualitative (satisfaction, expectations) evaluation.
papers.result: With AI assistance, false positives fell by 27% and false negatives by 4%; time to diagnose decreased by about 3 minutes per patient; 91% of clinicians reported positive impact on expectations and satisfaction.
papers.tools: DenseNet classifier, multimodal breast imaging viewer (mammography, ultrasound, MRI), BI-RADS reporting, usability and satisfaction questionnaires.
papers.gap: Small set of test patients; breast imaging only; volunteer clinicians.
papers.relation: Evaluates an intelligent imaging agent with clinicians for performance, workload, usability and trust, close to the O4 set of outcomes.
papers.limitations: Order and learning effects possible; single AI model.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors built an AI assistant directly into the image viewer that radiologists use for breast cancer diagnosis across mammography, ultrasound and MRI. A DenseNet model proposed a BI-RADS severity, and the clinician could accept or reject it. Forty-five clinicians from nine institutions diagnosed test patients both without and with the assistant. With AI, false positives dropped by 27% and false negatives by 4%, each diagnosis took about 3 minutes less, and 91% of clinicians were satisfied. For our PhD it is a template for embedding agent outputs in the clinician's normal viewer, with an explicit accept/reject step, and for measuring errors, time and satisfaction in O4.
papers.studyDesign: Multi-institutional user study (within-subject, two scenarios) with mixed methods.
papers.datasets: 45 clinicians from nine institutions (volunteers) diagnosing test-set patients of varying severity (never seen by the model), after practice on three predefined patients.
papers.preprocessing: Multimodal breast images loaded into the BreastScreening framework; ground-truth BI-RADS severity.
papers.modelDetails: DenseNet-based classifier producing BI-RADS-indexed severity recommendations shown within the viewer; clinicians may accept or reject.
papers.training: Model trained on institutional breast imaging data (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: False positives, false negatives, time to diagnose, acceptance of AI suggestions, satisfaction and expectation questionnaires, qualitative feedback.
papers.baselines: Clinician-Only scenario without AI.
papers.results: False positives -27%, false negatives -4%, time -3 min per patient, 91% positive satisfaction.
papers.statistics: Descriptive and comparative statistics between scenarios.
papers.availability: Framework code referenced by authors (GitHub, MIMBCD-UI project).

papers.title: Experimental evidence of effective human-AI collaboration in medical decision-making
papers.authors: Reverberi C, Rigon T, Solari A, et al.
papers.aim: To study experimentally how clinicians integrate AI advice and whether human-AI teams outperform either alone in medical diagnosis.
papers.method: Multicentre 2x2 mixed-design experiment: 21 endoscopists (10 experts, 11 non-experts) optically diagnosed 504 real colonoscopy lesion videos without AI and then with AI (GI Genius CADx) advice; mixed-effects models of agreement, confidence and perceived AI reliability.
papers.result: Endoscopists were influenced by AI (OR 3.05) but sensibly: they followed it more when it was correct (OR 3.48) than incorrect (OR 1.85), weighting their own and the AI's reliability case by case (Bayesian-like), so the human-AI team outperformed both humans and AI alone.
papers.tools: GI Genius CADe/CADx device, video-based reading platform, mixed-effects logistic regression; power analysis; STROBE reporting.
papers.gap: Optical diagnosis of colorectal polyps only; offline video reading rather than live procedures.
papers.relation: Measures experimentally how clinicians weigh AI advice by their own and the AI's confidence, which informs the analysis of escalation and reliance.
papers.limitations: Fixed session order (no-AI then AI) may introduce learning effects; 21 readers.
papers.methodologyDetail: Twenty-one endoscopists from five countries looked at 504 short videos of polyps from real colonoscopies and judged whether each was an adenoma, first without AI and later with an AI system's suggestion.
